SLZ has a history of making a game, patching it up to a point and then moving on. Bonelab has slowly but surely fizzled out over the past two years of silence, and while the latest update brings some nice polish under the hood, it's going to be hard to overcome that.

While the modding community has done its best, it's ultimately not the VR Garry's Mod we had hoped, and may never be. Consider waiting for their next game, it will likely have more of a true campaign and make use of all the upgrades they've made to this tech demo.

This is a genuine achievement in physics simulation, but is running behind the current VR industry as an entertaining game in its own right. To be frank, this is one case where it should have released in early access to set the proper expectation.

If you're still in the market for a moddable physics murder simulator, Blade & Sorcery has hit its full 1.0 release and is continuing to receive smaller updates, with a proper SDK coming sooner than 2 years.

review_text:
Key thing to remember is "Free to Play" = "Pay to Win"

All the best ships and equipment are behind paywalls so you won't get any T6 ships without paying $$$ to open loot boxes or buying Zen credits.

That said, the game is ok but very dated. It certainly looks and feels like it was made in the early 2000's, gameplay is rather basic, NPC "AI" is primitive at best. The episode missions feature good stories, but some of the later missions just go on and on and on and get quite tiresome. Mission difficulty scales with player level which is good, until you hit the top levels (65) when the scaling seems to assume that you are using top tier ships and equipment (from loot boxes which cost $ to open). This means that they become very difficult if you aren't paying to win.

Some missions are bugged, usually involving scripted events not firing or unresponsive NPC's which can usually be got around by aborting the mission and retrying from the beginning. Very frustrating when you spend an hour getting to the final boss. Frequent issues with loadouts disappearing, traits resettings, bumping into invisible "forcefields", rubberbanding, and other lag based effects. Daily extended maintenance issues which seem to fail to address issues.

Away mission controls are horrendous out the box. I remapped the WASD keys to match every other game and using B to enter shooter mode makes it tolerable. Space combat I was imagining something like EVE Online, but instead its more like the old Star Trek Starfleet Command of the late 90's and hasn't been improved upon.

If you're really interested in Star Trek and want to explore the stories and lore then go ahead, if you're looking for a space based MMORPG or single player shooter experience then there are much better alternatives.

Oh, and there are no Steam achievements despite what the store page says.

review_text:
I've had to start and stop this game 3 times to finally finish.

The Good:
- Lovely music that is beautiful in its simplicity.  In fact, the music almost makes up for the other flaws.  Almost.
- Some of the story is emotionally impactful.
- I love the sci-fi part of the plot.  Technicians that grant a dying wish, via memory alteration?  VERY well done, and the execution is probably the slickest part of the game.


The Bad:
- The game will lag.  There are fixes to this, but they're imperfect.
- The humour is so terrible, it's the reason I've had to quit the game several times.
- The main characters are fine by themselves, but they have terrible chemistry together.
- The gameplay...exists.  
- There are plot twists in the game.  Some work, some don't.  The ones that work are brilliant and emotionally impacting.  The ones that don't will have you curse your screen.


Recommendation:  The production company put a lot of love into this game.  I don't want to bad-mouth their work and their effort, because I know a TONNE of people walked away from this game, sobbing.  I felt emotional during the game because I thought it was going a certain way, but a plot-twist damaged my perceptions going forward.  But the music is lovely. I cannot personally recommend it based on my own playthrough, unless you get it at a discount (which, once again, I hate to say, because I know that a tonne of work went into this).

Even still, because of the effort and love put in, I've already bought the sequel because there is enough promise here that I want to see if they improved on the formula.  BUT, that promise does not translate "To The Moon" as a good experience to me.

review_text:
Game lacks basic QoL the genre invented decades ago.  Namely:

Click to drag the map.  No, too easy.  Instead, you right click to steer the map (in the opposite direction of dragging) in a floaty manner.

Pausing while navigating menus.  You can pause the game at any time.  But you can't pause while mousing over tooltips, placing buildings, or allocating jobs.  This isn't a necessary feature in your average competitive RTS (starcraft for example), but in a complicated PvE game - especially with a doom timer (They Are Billions, Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress) - the ability to pause and issue commands while paused is necessity for the average gamer.  

After encoutnering the above, I checked to see if I was missing something.  I wasn't.  The above issues aren't isolated incidents. review_text:
Recommended: 55 points over 45.

To leave a fair review of this game and my verdict to recommend it is still a yes, I'll try to keep it simple enough. 
It's not exactly super-different from its -real- (Japanese) counterpart, but here's what I feel. 

The "greater" good: 
-It's mechanically superior to the original for a few hat-tips; for one, it's still cross-play across all its possible platforms, and setting up one's data to connect isn't exactly too difficult. 
-Making payments is easier here as well on each of the platforms (save I can't mention for a basic Windows Store type or Epic Games type, this is coming for the steam version). 
-This version was also the first to have introduced "Mission Pass" mode which gives players prizes for some effort that aren't exactly easy to find, and can add more to where that came from if boosted from Gold Pass. 
-Finally there's the fact that this version is bi-lingual for both JP & EN voices which means there's a few more options (but this has a drawback, will be explained soon.)
-This version has some things somewhat easier on a few cases and have less requirements in some access than the original version; there's currently no "expert" title requirements, so one doesn't have to feel left out if not exactly good enough. 

Naturally, this version however does have drawbacks compared to the real version so not everything is better...

The "worst" bad:
-If someone was a veteran JP version player, be prepared to have to start from ground-zero because your data does not carry over and is not shared. For some who didn't keep an eye on it, you have a lot of work to do... and that won't be fun if you spent a long time in on it. If you didn't start on since the regular 'O2 side, well that stuff will have to be done again, despite both versions of New Genesis (we call "NGS" around here for short) started at the same time but was also the first time when the "real" side isn't exactly easy to get back into anymore. 
-While overtime playershop prices have started getting a nasty inflation of prices vs nice items in the real (JP) version, expect those prices in this version to be multiplied much worse, if not exponentially increased. Good luck trying to get stuff from these "sellers". 
-(My own problem) On the JP side, people are alright with you letting loose to a bit as long as you don't go too far on your appeal, but this version is the exact polar opposite: a stiff-necked community. Accept "parties", "friend requests", or joining "alliances" (teams) carefully at your own risk. Hopefully your experience won't be like mine... 
-While peeps on the real version are somewhat slow on the uptake but eventually get a 40% chance to take down intense Mega-Bosses such as Dark Falz in his Aegis Armor with a very small chance of causing a Meltdown-Kill as well at least, don't expect this version to be able to win; be prepared for high chances of group-wipes, Rangers who don't use Weakener-Bullets on his weak spots to support, or quitters disappearing suddenly. 
-While said: the game is bi-lingual and the male voices are more overall better with few exceptions (for both NPCs and Protagonist boys), the Protagonist girls' voices are subpar to almost downright horrible compared to the real version, and at that note, not every voice was on this version that is in the original either (such as the one I'd like was "censored" as being left out, so I had to have a rough time adapting to a lesser one instead. Subject moot due to mayhap chance future content could possibly bring some in, until then this is a thing.)
-When they said things wouldn't be censored, it was not exactly true. 
-Some complications on other devices half bust the myth that this game is not exactly free, but this version for Steam at least actually is confirmed true. 

Aside of these, most of the game is no different from its real counterpart. My last verdict is 55 over 45 points: Yes. Give it a go, and enjoy the most of it.

I wouldn't necessarily all this a metroidvania.  It's more of a souls-like platformer.

It's very fun and exploration isn't clunky.  Some enemies are a little cheap and can stunlock you into oblivion.  After you beat the game once you can play a secondary mode as three of the bosses which is very fun.

There's virtually no ability gating.  Some treasures are locked behind abilities but the whole map is accessible without any extra abilities.

Overall I give this a 6.5/10.  Good platforming soulslike, bad metroidvania.

review_text:
Pros: 

Nice community of players but that's about it.

Cons:

The gameplay gets dull after a certain amount of hours

The "pay-to-win" of this is that you can buy items with real money then sell them for a very high price so you could buy some high level gear from the profits you make.

Rare items may take a while to drop, at which point it becomes like working a job where you don't get paid.

The battles are very repetitive and the open world is very boring to explore.

The gear gets released in seasonal intervals which take a while and most people end up spending real money to get it every season, so its a good strategy for the business but very predatory towards the consumer.

It seems any game published by Sega is heavily divided into micro-transactions(ex Total War series)

The "End Game" of this is "fashion" according to most players, and that consists of you either spending real cash or a very high amount of in game currency for an item that gets bound to a character and cannot be sold to others.

If you want to change or customize your character you'll need a "Salon Pass"

It feels more like a chatroom vs an actual game

Conclusion:
You can still enjoy this but very minimally, if you stay longer you'll end up wasting money on mediocre lootboxes. Unless you're broke then you'd probably going to be grinding for this like its a real job lol.  Also, if you're looking to play this because of PSU like I did, don't bother. The company is not what it used to be.

I can't honestly recommend this game to any deep fans of you know what, but I am sure it may appeal a younger generation.

And the graffiti designs are awesome.

review_text:
I have refunded this game. I simply do not like it.

In my opinion, this game is not worth the $25 price tag for what appears to be only six maps. While I used a controller, of course, I still found the controls very hard to use. I understand I may have only played for around 90 minutes, but mapping the A button to both jump and perform tricks is a poor design choice at least in my eyes. For example, when trying to repeatedly press A to quickly grab onto ledges and other obstacles during a heated game of tag, I would suddenly just do a backflip and ragdoll.

The developers also need to provide a more extensive tutorial. There were a ton of mechanics I was unaware of, despite seeing things like crawl spaces and hangable ledges, that were clearly suggested those actions were possible.

The game's pacing, while its probably intentional, feels slow for a parkour title. I want to always be sprinting, but the running speed felt more like a jog much of the time. The main reason I purchased this game was for the Tag game mode to play with friends, and the control scheme made it unbearable. Trying to hit LB or RB to tag someone while simultaneously holding down two other buttons was awful. Multiple times, I would collide with a friend and be on top of them for a solid five seconds without a tag registering, or I experienced tagging them from an unreasonably far distance.

Overall, the controls were not intuitive or easy to learn. I constantly found myself ragdolling or forgetting that I needed to hold LT to grab onto or vault over objects. Playing with myself and only two other friends made the matches feel quite slow and empty.

Runs excellently on Steam Deck too as an added bonus.

I hadn’t heard of the developer before I started Shadow Tactics - but now I'm looking forward to playing their other titles (Desperados III and Shadow Gambit) next.

review_text:
I returned the game, as it was not what I expected. First, let me say there is a suspicious amount of uncritical reviews, so be weary of that. Second, this game is not really a squad based tactics game, but a puzzle game with a medieval Japanese theme. Lastly, take my review with a grain of salt since I only played the first two missions.

The reason it is a puzzle game is because there seems to be one path plotted by the developers. The developers box you into figuring out how to kill these set guards before you move can move onto the next area, rinse repeat. I mean, if you like puzzle games, then it is great for you. However I expected a squad based tactics game. It really breaks the immersion once you realize there is a set sequence of specific actions to perform.

Next, it really is not a squad based game. Sure, you can command multiple characters, and set them to take specific actions at the same time. However, the limited nature of the levels means you are just figuring out what the game wants you to do. Moreover, you command one character at a time, and can only use the squad mechanic to take ONE action with each character. It does not feel innovative, and again, is just an easy puzzle game.

Next, the story did not hook me within the first two missions, but at least some of the characters were interesting. Some characters die on the alter of medieval Japanese tropes, but others, namely the old man, are really interesting. The story regrettably did not hook me at all, and maybe that would have changed, but the game does not really wow within the first hour and a half. It just seemed like, insert some stereotypical medieval plot. Maybe there is more too it, but I will never get the chance to know.

Lastly, for a unity engine game, the art design was quite nice. Maybe I would have wished for better use of shadows, but the colors all seem to pop well. The design also communicates things quickly to the player, without sacrificing immersion. The medieval Japanese theme is also executed really well. 

Ultimately, this game was just not fun. I had more fun writing this review than playing the game. Steam recommends it to me because I love tactical games, but this was not a tactical game. You spend the whole time figuring out which specific ability, in what spot, and at what time, the game wants you to use, which is a puzzle. I expect a real tactical game to allow me to approach a situation with multiple choices, with maybe some of those choices being less optimal. Moreover, I also expect to be able to make more complicated actions than  "use x ability at the same time,," also with multiple characters, to be able to call it a squad game. This game forces you to go down one path, especially on the harder difficulty, which is why it is a puzzle game and not a squad based tactics game.

If you like big medieval Japanese puzzles, go knock yourself out, if not, then I would pass.

After enjoying Act 1, I expected puzzling and item combining, together with some over the top humour. 

What I've got is a short visual novel, with very detailed scenes that have little to nothing that can be meaningfully interacted with, most puzzles amounting to talking the right amount of times to the right amount of people with very little item or environmental based puzzles. The "Trial" scene, in particular, an homage to the Ace Attorney series, did overstay its welcome significantly and should have been much shorter. 
Overall, it's hard to recommend this to anyone who's not a big fan of the original material; you're better off scratching your puzzle itch somewhere else.

The dialogues between Joey and Xefros though are quirky and funny!

review_text:
If you're a fan of the original Starship Troopers movie, then you'll likely enjoy this game. This is the kinda of game you'll play after a long day of work and you're hoping for some mindless fun. The different classes, weapons, bug types, and customization are all amazing. Everything in this game feels like it belongs to the universe. You really feel like you're part of the mobile infantry and doing your part. 

This game is far from perfect. You'll deal with a fair amount of bugs and glitches, some funny, others, nearly game breaking. Server lag spikes, which can make the game unplayable. And few modes. There is three modes, though, they're basically all the same, and with there only being a few maps, it quickly becomes repetitive. Not to mention, there is no gore in this game. If you seen the movies, you know they don't shy away from gore. While that of course, would defeat the ability to being revived, a mode that only offered one life and had fun kill animations would be nice. Also, the Morita rifle not having the underbarrel shotgun is a let down, but that's a personal preference. 

Overall, this game hugs its price point very snug, and is a decent amount of fun to play. If you like the movies, and the universe, and want another fun PVE bug killing experience, then this game has it.

review_text:
This game is basically the equivalent of Dark Falz in PSO.  I.e., it's a parasite that took over the host that was PSO2 and is now dangling its corpse around while waving whatever new abomination NGS is supposed to be.

It was a cool idea on paper - open world and all that.  But its execution is abysmal.  The content updates take too long. It mostly just shoves gacha/premium cosmetics down folks' throats.

But the worst part is that it's bundled with PSO2 proper, the game that took almost 8 years to finally come to the US... and NGS came out ~13 months later while they abandoned further updates for PSO2 outside of basic maintenance and event rotations.  Not to mention PSO2 was Microsoft Store-exclusive for a good period of time.  You can't just download PSO2 on its own, you HAVE to download New Genesis too like the cancerous tumor it is.

This obviously isn't the first time SEGA has made hilariously baffling decisions and crippled their game franchises for absolutely no discernable reason.  Just look at the fall of WH40K Dawn of War.  Or the fact that they never let Obsidian do another Alpha Protocol game.  Or the dozens of Sonic games that were the equivalent of them throwing feces around a room full of whacky theme posters to see what sticks.  

It's just sad that PSO2 had to be dragged down by a vastly inferior, horrendously uncooked sequel-ish game.  It's like if Overwatch wasn't totally assimilated into Overwatch 2, but instead its corpse was dangled around in a secondary game mode.  And Western players only got to enjoy an officially translated version of Overwatch for a year and one month before it got assimilated into Overwatch 2.  FFXIV didn't even bother to do their end of the collab with PSO2 and I see it was for good reason.

It's astounding how incompetent SEGA is.

review_text:
What can I say about Carbuncle Protocol?

It’s a game, one they want you to think is of ‘quadruple-A’ quality, so what does that mean, and does it hold up to that claim?

It’s got great sound design, nice graphics, it’ll set your CPU to broil for downloading/installing and shader cache collection on first boot, that guy from every fuckin’ transformers movie except the three most recent ones, and boring gameplay.

There isn’t a real way to summarize that last part effectively. You look at this game, in every review video, and think “wow, it looks so good, no way that is boring to play!”—but it is.
Exploration is composed of walking around and either stabbing in the back, getting jumped by those stupid fucking pod things that can only be avoided if you played the game and remember where they are so you can shoot them ahead of time, cutting the same serial cables on every box, crawling in vents, shimmying through gaps, and occasionally crouching. As a ‘spiritual successor’ to Dead Space, this feels alright, at first, but then you realize there’s no tension.
Despite the sound quality making you think there’s someone around the corner or behind you, 9/10 times you’re alone and don’t need to worry. Enemies are louder than women in spring, so you won’t doubt there’s someone behind you, maybe one will slip past, but you’ll turn the camera and see them just in time. But then there are these screams from the enemy that just grab you, make you turn around—you can ignore those. I’m confident 98/100 are just background sound clips on some kind of shuffle.

The graphics, where do I begin?
They’re ok.
That’s it.
Ol’ Transformer Actor himself is recognizable, but his head activates that part of my brain that makes me remember the uncanny valley. Everyone looks recognizable as humans, but there’s something off. It’s somewhere between Mass Effect Andromeda and Fable. With this absolutely stellar sound design, the visuals are so lackluster in comparison that you are forced to focus on it. You’re not buying this game because it looks good, and if you are, you’re going to be disappointed, especially when you get into—

Combat! Don’t bother shooting. Melee is how you will win, but it’s tedious. Dodge an attack by picking left or right, then tilt your controller in that direction, and start alternating until you’re ready to beat them in the face like they suck.
You will repeat this process from start of game to finish, with the only variety being windows of opportunity, how long you will beat them in the face, or special weaknesses…which are ignorable.
The security bot is the only time you’ll really need a gun. If you need help finding their weak spot schedule a visit with your local lobotomist expert. Enemies fight neatly one at a time which…they’re fucking feral, right? Why are they so Imperialist-era England about it? All they were missing was starting off the battle while standing in a line. You can sever limbs, or shoot them—but this is dead space, so shooting or dismembering the head is worthless, so why have a gun? What about the quick shot system? Honestly, that works well, and all it really does is serve as the gun in Bloodborne; you will use the quick-shot to stagger enemies so you can interrupt their attack and beat them in the face. If you’re not doing this, you’re doing it wrong. So even in combat there’s no tension, no reason for you to feel rushed or intimidated.
What about all those fucking death animations? What ABOUT them?
They shitty, and rarely happen. 90% of the time Transformerdude just falls over dead and I’m wondering when he’ll get up, because he doesn’t look dead when this happens, it looks like a lifealert moment. He’s fallen, and he won’t get up—-oh, wait, he’s dead. That’s awful! I should know when I’m dead immediately, so the moment I actually get a death animation how do you think I react?
I’m disappointed! They’re well made, brutal, but they feel soulless, and without the weight Dead Space 1&2 originally had. You don’t get excited when you see them, you rarely do anyways, so if it’s why you’re buying the game save your money and look up a YouTube video, trust me—please.

And that’s it! Explore through the game, find secret audio logs and shit. It’s not difficult, it’s tedious, and boring. The story never picks up, you’re constantly waiting for things to explode and get real…then it’s over, and they’re asking you to pay for the real ending because it’s hidden behind DLC. With games I’m normally hooked to see how things end, but with this game I’m not. It’s boring and tedious to the point where I don’t even care what the story is, or what will happen.

These quadruple-A games that I’ve seen and played are a sign, and that sign has the same writing on the gates of hell.

-2/5 – this game sucks.

review_text:
The first thing to note to anyone wishing to enjoy this game is to understand this is part one of two games. By purchasing this game, you are purchasing only half a product, in my personal opinion. This game should be treated wholeheartedly as an introduction to these characters and the build-up to the central narrative. I enjoyed this game, but I can only recommend it when it is on sale, arguably a deep sale.

 There is a good story, solid characters, and seriously great music here but it holds itself back in my opinion. The thing that holds this back to a 5/10 (while worth playing, don't get me wrong, it is a decent read) is first, as mentioned previously, this is half of a product-- and secondly....what the hell happened with the translation? It feels so utterly bare-bones. When characters aren't awkwardly cursing and emotionally confusing the tones of normal conversation, then the rest of the piece feels so stripped of the atmosphere, tone, and much-needed fill-in details that usually elevate the reading of visual novels. I wouldn't say it ruins the experience but it drops its score by several points for me compared to better visual novels of its kind. It's a shame and rather bizarre to see because there is a complex story being told here in the native language, but man, the English translation couldn't keep it together. 

5/10, I guess, deep sale, and I really hope more effort was put into the second half, "Edo Blossoms".

review_text:
It's a pretty fun little sniping game with large multi-approach areas, pretty scenery, and decent gun play/feel.

-It's a little short: only five missions/areas to play through
-Most of the upgrades feel utterly useless if you're playing it ULTRA SNEAKY (which, why WOULDN'T you? It's a game about SNIPING)
-The return fire if you DO get spotted is RIDICULOUS. E.G. Heavy soldiers firing an LMG from standing position nailing pin-point bursts from 300+ meters away INSTANTLY on getting spotted is just...laughable.
-The autosave system is GAAAAAARBAGE. FREQUENTLY putting the player in the MIDDLE of an area once more swarming with enemies AND re-enabling any and all de-activated enemy equipment regardless of how long ago it was de-activated

But, all in all, it IS fun and it IS probably worth a play if you like sniping games. Depending on your value scale, you might want to wait for a sale though. I sunk 21 hours into it and that was ULTRA sneaky-mans style (+ smoke breaks).

review_text:
The AI in this game is one of the worst, lazy written AI I've ever seen in a very long time.
The enemies figure out where you are, without any way to know it.
They are basically all strong in the force, since another explanation ain't there.
They know where you are, due to "any sound", even from your drone or just the fact that several enemies died due to remote controlled detonations or traps.

The game mechanics feel so artificial, you might want to barf.
It's 0 immersion.

Some detailed examples:

Create a sound with your drone while creating an EMP to disable devices.
The enemies hear that sound and know where YOU as in the drone operator, that's a hundreds of meters away, hidden in a bush, is located, so >you< are being shot at in response.
If you use the drone feature "lure", then they react as if >you< or rather the disturbance, is where the drone made that sound. Meaning very very bad coding. Like learned how to write code a few weeks/months ago bad.

Kill-count making your position known:
If you play the game on middle or hard, don't bather. The game experience is SO bad, because you can shoot several enemies from over 1 mile away, every single one alone, without whitness. The higher the difficulty, the less dead enemies it takes, for them to "just know" where you are, doesn't matter how they died or where, just the time in which they died.
So because you killed a certain amount, the enemies suddenly know, where you are.
On normal, the very same thing still persists, but the enemies "take longer" to magically know where you are, meaning you can move after like 10-20 kills or so.

What you end up with:
If you feel as if there might just as well be a console running on the side, showing you the stats and parameters for every method call being executed. It just feels so fake, so badly and lazy written, it's boring as hell.

I really...Don't like this game. It's not for me. It's far too long, reminds me too much of K2, and is reminiscent of a five year old telling a story where "This happened...oh, and then this happened! Oh,...but this happened too!!" 

I didn't need to know that much about baseball, they did my boy Saejima dirty, and now the game is crashing my computer over and over again in the finale. Hopefully I can even *finish* this game at all.

Update:
I was not able to finish the game. I'm one of the poor souls who's computer has decided that this is the port that makes my computer spontaneously restart. And I'm talking, like, every twenty minutes or so. I was saving over and over again just to try and get some movement in the game, and after the ninth or tenth time of crashing, I gave up and used a walkthrough to spoiler myself on the end of it. I've been playing through the series (mostly) in order, and it really sucks that I couldn't see this one through to the end, ESPECIALLY because of how much time it took to slog through what I *could* get through.

This game, ultimately, feels like too much is being thrown at you at once - five(!?) characters for NO reason other than to just convolute storylines further. I hate how they connected Shinada into this -- hell, I hate Shinada's character as a whole - and I know this might be a hot take, but by this point I really just wanted Akiyama to go *away.* (Spoiler alert: he doesn't.) 

The only part of this game I truly enjoyed was Haruka's chapters in the main story - and that's literally ONLY because I really like rhythm games, and that's the part of the game where I spent extra time because I actually enjoyed what I was doing. (There was also a substory or two that I found vaguely entertaining, but I had no real motivation to do the substories just because this bored the hell out of me so much. 33 hours and I still couldn't get through the finale chapters. Slog.)

Saejima's part was y4 rewritten, Kiryu was nothing more than a depressed taxi driver, and I just...God, for all of the time I spent in this game, it felt like nothing *happened.* I couldn't care any less about how it ended up. The thing I hate the most was the fact that I wasted so much time, and couldn't even finish the game.

Good on you if you like this one. Hell, let it be your favorite, if you want. But whoof, for me this one was probably the worst so far (other than Kiwami 2, which is apparently still a super hot take. That's cool, I guess, everyone can have their opinions.)

At least I have the context, even if it still feels like *nothing of value happened* in all the time I spent trying to slog through this one.

review_text:
Rogue-lite shooter in a dark medieval fantasy setting pitting witch hunters with a religious background against the evil Witch and her abominations. Movement options include sprint, crouch, (double) jump and dodge making the Preyer feel pretty flexible while navigating forests, islands and castles. Depending on what you want to do in a run you can spend anywhere between 10 and 30 minutes on a map before returning to the Sanctuary hub area.

There's a level system for your typical RPG stats (Ascension level) as well as a meta-level system (Gnosis level) that increases difficulty as well as gained currency. The latter also changes what events and enemies can be encountered and what secrets can be uncovered and is directly related to meta / story progression. Then there is a passive ability system, represented by equippable Rosary Beads you can find scattered around the maps, that can net you important bonuses depending on your leveled stats. New equipment is unlocked by leveling up Gnosis to make it available for research first and then spending time on a map and eliminating enemies. That's a lot of different progression systems you're playing around with at the same time but they all play into each other so well that they still make up a coherent progression journey.

Every weapon in your arseneal feels completely different from the others because of their unique abilities. It's easy to see how much care goes into creating new weapons and explicitly making them feel distinct from everything that's already there. And with three unlockable levels per weapon - and some levels not just increasing the previous level's ability but adding completely new ones - there's a lot of variety here.

It's still in Early Access so that price tag might seem unusually high but in my opinion the content quality, frequent patches and community updates justify it. The devs give detailed updates, blog posts and explanations for what they change and why they change it, which is pretty cool as one of the most important things about proper use of Early Access is looping in the community and reacting to their feedback. Looking forward to the release in 2026 (probably?) but Witchfire is already in a very playable and polished state right now so supporting the development early on and checking in along the journey has been (and hopefully will continue to be) a treat in itself.

review_text:
To start, This game is absolutely Beautiful in its own Macabre, H.R. Geiger-esque style. It nails atmosphere and tone amazingly.

HOWEVER

That is the most I can say about this game in a positive manner. The puzzles, While challenging, are annoying. not because of difficulty, but because of this games absolute disrespect for the player's time. Every action is time consuming, every animation un-skippable, every puzzle piece a hallway or five away from its counterpart that you must slowly walk down, while dodging slow, stupid enemies who also are the most miraculous shots you've ever seen in your entire life. I've been told that combat is mostly avoidable in this game, and yet there are entire Gauntlets where you are put in a hallway, a dead end at your back, with 3-5 enemies in front of you, and the worlds slowest six shooter in your hand, and no room to maneuver around or paths to sneak by. 

The game is slow, the combat is slow and not fun. the puzzles are slow, and the "Story" Can only be gleaned if you can manage to discern which pieces of meat that look the same as all the other pieces of meat surrounding it are important, and their significance without any sort of indication at all. 8/10 This game is pretty good. (9/10 for me personally)

The Story - itself is what i would say is the 'DMC3 effect' where in that it's entertaining as hell but has some surprising depth to it (and some dark messed up implications) that at some points gave me the feels.

Gameplay - will be quite difficult for new players as it was for me but once you narrow down the mechanics it feels really good with all the weapons, ranged weapons and magic at your disposal. The variety of builds you can conjure up is astounding. Not to mention the amazing enemy variety that the game presents that will keep things not only entertaining but challenging as well. Likewise, the bosses really test your skills (and knowledge of mechanics as well).

Visuals - are gorgeous and aesthetically pleasing.

Loses points - due to the certain items being a bit too strong in that magic builds in the (very) late game are a bit too strong (for me personally). Inventory item swapping and usage (which you'll be doing a lot) can be streamlined further to lessen the monotony of it a bit. Finally, there should've been a new game plus for the veteran difficulty which in my opinion could've added late game enemies to the earlier stages whilst keeping your inventory so you can use all that OP stuff as well as your skill throughout a new replay. Maybe throw in even harder new enemies because why not?

Conclusion,

Instead of wasting money on some in-game micro-transaction, buy other games and experience something new. Lost Ruins is one of those experiences, simple and entertaining with surprising depth to it. Has its flaws yes, but it is an overall satisfying product in the end.

review_text:
This is a colony building-roguelike-tower defense-god simulator mashup. A really interesting combination of genres.
The premise is that you start on a map, build out your colony and survive the onslaught of the "corruption". You then migrate to a new map and do the same all over again. 

The graphics have so much pixely goodness that you just cannot fault it. The music is fantastic and matches the game perfectly and the game loop is extremely addictive. 

Some (maybe) important things to take note of:

1) The game is brutal on the higher difficulty levels so take care if you venture there.

2) The game is not really "winnable". The whole premise of the game is to survive the onslaught of corruption and by doing better and pushing the corruption further, you only get more and more resistance from the enemy. This is one of the main problems I have with the game as it seems kind of unfair as the better you do, you get more and more punished for it. Having that said, "beating" a map by removing all corruption is possible but an extremely hard thing to do.

3) The game can feel that you are doing the same thing over and over again which in a sense is true. Even though each map is unique and poses different challenges, you build out your colony, survive and move on. Once you have a working recipe for survival you execute it and that's it. On higher difficulty levels, if you F up something, things start cascading usually and you get overrun.

4) There is no win condition. This is mostly a sandbox game even though it does not seem like one, and you make your own goals and wins as you please.

I rarely review games and it is even rarer that I put over 100 hours into a game but this little gem just keeps sucking me in. Would I recommend it? Absolutely!

Sigh. Also, the heroine is incredibly weak. She carries a sword around but never uses it, instead needing to be saved time and time again. She doesn't learn how to fight. She's content cooking and cleaning and running messages.

Once more I wish a "mixed" option existed for reviews, oh well.

The ambience of the game grabbed me immediately, good graphics, good performances, immersive audio.
The world building, the creatures, everything was gripping and tense, the combat was sluggish and death came quickly, reinforcing the oppressive environment and the dire situation our character found himself in.

That being said...

I will not complain about the ending and keep this review spoiler free.
After completing the game, I briefly started a new game to collect the hidden achievement, pondered for a moment: "Is that all?" and uninstalled the game.

In the game industry, if you do not release a game, you have nothing. There is no consolation prize for never-released games, I know this reality on a personal level.

It is pretty clear at this point that the game had to be aggressively cut down for release as evidenced by the lack of tier 6 locks (despite the visuals indicating there are 6 security levels) and the myriad of evidence from the art book, teasers, and mentions (on the steam store as of today) about non-linear, open world adventure, that the game was supposed to be "so much more" than what it is.

There is no real way of knowing how much was axed in the end, or even why.

As a result, I cannot recommend that you get this game, it might be worth playing if Giger & body horror is your jam, but otherwise? Wait for a sale.

review_text:
Incredibly player-hostile design, and not in a hard-but fair Hollow Knight way. The game features slow, clunky movement  affected by barely visible surface effects (like slimy, oily, or simply wet floors), and a useless dodge roll with a painfully long recovery that leaves you wide open. The combat is built for maximum frustration, with even the “fastest” weapons being painfully slow. Anything that deals any kind of damage takes a comically long time to deliver a blow, while enemies have no trouble spamming projectiles and lightning-quick attacks.
Aside from some charming and well-animated sprites, the visuals are murky and hard to discern, so you often aren't even sure what hurt you. The game doesn't give you any way to heal or replenish MP early on, leaving you to scavenge a menagerie of borderline useless items that heal you a couple of HP at a time.

And then there are abnormal status effects. Every, and I mean EVERY enemy gives you abnormal status with their attacks. Got hit by an insect - poison! Got hit by a goblin - bleed! Stepped into a barely visible puddle of water - wet (enjoy that 50% movement speed reduction for the next 5 seconds in a middle of a fight). All effects are unavoidable and instant, and all of them will absolutely kill you in seconds if you don't pause the game, open inventory, scroll to items tab, scroll down through a long list of confusing junk, and find the exact thing that heals this particular status effect. Close menu and get a new status effect right away.

Despite how frustratingly difficult and un-rewarding the “normal” mode is, the game doesn't even deem it pertinent to give you an ending, as, you see – you only get endings if you play on “veteran” or higher. 

On top of it all, the game is confusingly horny, to the point where I feel like it was originally meant to be an H-game that got neutered for wider release.

An amazing version of 1987's Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!... unfortunately. Critical mistake to try to design around an over-the-shoulder camera. One way or another, the gameplay has almost no legs.

It's impossible to make the combat work for a long stretch, necessitating fewer encounters paced out by more cutscenes, more crawling in vents, QTEs, and shimmying around. So much so that even as a 10-15 hour story, it feels padded.

The core gameplay doesn't lend itself to a $60 game with a $30 season pass. 
It's no longer relevant, but the other critical mistake was the Denuvo that wasn't removed for 16 months, which killed the game's performance.

Excellent accessibility, presentation, graphics, and animation.

review_text:
Scorn is an absolutely gorgeous art piece that, at its best, is moody, immersive, and completely a visual marvel. However, Scorn is also not just an art piece - it's a game; and the game part of Scorn brings it so very low that I'm not sure I can recommend the actual product.

Barring the lack of story and context - which is a bit of a shame but not a dealbreaker - the levels are pretty poorly paced, puzzle mechanics are "introduce ---> reuse until any semblance of uniqueness in its design is lost ---> repeat", and the combat is at once unsatisfying and unfair. The weapons themselves are actually fine and I think feel pretty good in isolation, but they're just not in a sandbox where they can shine.

Ultimately, you can buy the art book and witness the artistry of these guys at a much better pace - that is, at your *own* pace - with no distractingly convoluted level design, annoying enemy encounters, or nonsensical mechanics to draw you out of the experience. And I do think you should support these developers one way or another, because art like this is once in a generation and I would hate to not see more like it. I just think the medium of art is sometimes as important to consider as the art itself.

review_text:
One of the most fantastic but frustrating games I have ever played.

To start off, the game is fantastic in the sense that 2K & Irrational games have created a game that is truly unique and vastly different than any other game at the time.  Almost 10 years later, Bioshock has aged very well and can easily be played for many more years to come.  The weapons & combat system offer great variety and satisfaction.  Shooting an enemy with a pistol to taking photos of hideous splicers for damage buffs, each weapon offers something unique for every combat situation as well as enjoyability.  

Visually, Bioshock is beautiful; considering it's age, the graphic design really is ground breaking compared to many other games that were made of the same year.  There are many small details that Irrational games added to give a strong emotional feel towards Rapture - the environment and atmosphere in particular.  The water and fire effects are pleasing to look at.  I believe the graphics in Bioshock will withstand the test of time.

The story is very well done.  From beginning to end you will most definitely be engaged,  I don't want to put any spoilers on this review so I will keep this part short; the game's story is very good.

Now,  this is the kicker for this game - not the game in particular, but, STEAM's version of the game.  There are MAJOR MAJOR MAJOR bug issues with this game on STEAM.  First of all, you cannot play this game without a microphone plugged in; don't even bother starting it up because you're game is just going to crash before you even hit the main menu.  

The next part is where Bioshock on STEAM will make you drop to your knees and cry.  The game WILL CRASH ON YOU.  I have tried everything in my power to make this game fully operational but nothing worked.  I had to save this game EVERY 30 seconds to a minute.  Since Bioshock does NOT have autosave you have to do it yourself; guess what happens when you forget to save the game? That's correct! You lose all your progress! YAY!

I somehow managed to finish this game, considering how much I enjoyed it while it managed to run for 10-15 minutes at a time before I had to reboot it.  If you can withstand this kind of frustration and headache then you will love this game - otherwise, just buy an XBOX 360 and play this game on the console.

5/5 Gameplay, Graphics and Story

0/100 for STEAM's horrendous port version of this game.

The game is unfinished. You can see through walls, there's no real physics engine (the game is weirdly inconsistant with where you can do tricks and where you can't, and as I found out from Nova, a community manager, they get zero dollars and zero cents for the work they do. Furthermore, the Dev uses his friends as moderators (ofc giving them ZERO compensation for their efforts), and the moderation job is generally pretty shabby. This server is literally on the home-screen, so it is a part of the game, but the Dev still doesn't treat it as such. He's deserted the game after the initial launch, and as someone who bought and refunded the game, and then recently bought it again... there isn't that big of a difference from the EA to now, and while I could excuse the game's lack of polish then, I cannot do so with a clear conscience anymore, especially with the blatant exploitation demonstrated by this "single" dev (even though he uses his wife's music and gets help from others). The game has *no* recovery animation. Instead the character teleports to a standing position. The controls have *jump* and *tricks* on the same button, so if you hold the jump button for longer than half a second, the character does an *unskippable animation* that causes you to ragdoll (unless you're really high up), which kills your score and makes achievements tedious to get, not to mention the overall gameplay effect it has. The game has a "wall-eject", but it has zero transition frames or anything, and it only works like 30% of the time. 

The simple fact that the game trash talks it's contemporaries, uses it's community members to do unpaid labour (this has been going on for over a YEAR), while the Dev sells an overly expensive proof of concept... I find it hard to reccomend, and because the SteamDeck counts it's hours differently, I can't refund this scam game. 

TL;DR, it doesn't give anything back to the community managers (even though he's made thousands upon thousands of dollars from tricking people with promises of a good game. This evidenced by the game being on all major platforms, and even being on the PlayStation YouTube channel, yet he *still* refuses to give them anything), won't fix fundamental issues, ditches the game post-launch, and makes this out to be a small little project when this is his *full time job*. If you want to buy a buggy game that exploits it's customers, then be my guest.

review_text:
World of Goo is a game that has followed me through my entire life. I first played it on Wiiware and fell in love with it immediately. This is the debut game from publisher 2D Boy, (now known as the Tomorrow Corporation) and despite it's rough edges is a wonderful example of the creativity of the puzzle game genre. In this game, you are tasked with navigating a group of goo balls to a pipe, usually on the other side of the level. You can tether the goo balls to each other to create a tower to the pipe which allows the stray goo to exit. As the game goes on you'll meet new varieties of goo that create new and interesting puzzles. The game is a perfect length, at four chapters and an epilogue. It's story is short and straight to the point. I look back fondly on key parts of the story, especially chapter four. It goes in a direction visually and in it's puzzles that is wildly unique and unexpected. All throughout the game Kyle Gabler's compositions complement the interesting world and storytelling, though I wish there were a few more tracks. The OST is a good length, at 27 pieces, but several levels reuse the same tracks and it'd be fun if this didn't have to be the case. On top of this some of the tracks feel a little unpolished, but this can be overlooked considering the conditions the game was developed under. 2D Boy, especially at the game's release in 2008, was a very small indie team. I still think the music is beautiful, even nostalgia aside. I recommend tracks like "Are You Coming Home, Love MOM," "Ode To The Bridge Builder," "The Goo Filled Hills," and "Tumbler" to see the wide range of styles this game covers. The soundtrack is free on Steam and easily accessible on youtube, Kyle Gabler's blog, and other platforms :)
Overall, World of Goo is an excellent puzzle game, an excellent indie game, and well worth it's low price tag. Please give this game a chance if you somehow haven't in the last decade.

This game is so boring, story is so dead, cutscenes so arse that I dont even know what I'm fighting for. 

The whole ''oh Ive been defeated I need to start from square one'' is a fair enough way to progress a characters growth but comparing to jc3, the grappling hook and its boring balloons, detract and whatever the other one is (its that shit idk what it is) really feels like a downgrade to the simple boosters and retract tools to these new tools.

The characters are lack luster ''omg lets bring back sheldon but old omg he was so good in JC2'' yes sheldon is a solid character but now it just feels like seeing that one alcoholic annoying family member again. Who am I even fighting for? Wtf is this Army of Chaos? It literally seems like the new Saints Row cast. Yes, realistic quirky hipster group is realistic but cmon I dont want to seem like a baby sitter to these repetitive ''go to A - Destroy, B - Destroy, C- Dest... Etc Etc''. Now I type this, why isnt there any money system and I know JC3 had no money system but for JC4 a money system may have made a good structure for doing these repetitive missions.
Yes unlocking areas unlocks new guns and vehicles but with the mess of a map, grapple, ''feats'' and supply menu with its disgusting controls, I really want to spend as much time away from that menu.

review_text:
Callisto Protocol didn't deserve the fate it received and is still a phenomenal take on the dark grounded sci-fi horror many of us love. Sadly, due to this hypocrite mob of people, uncapable of just being adults and admitting the game isn't for them, we will not be getting more from this franchise. It's truly a shame given that there are almost zero attempts at this niche by any sort of  AAA-standard, and that is for reasons like this.

Let's start off with the graphics, the fidelity here is incredible in everything from the art and the models to the geometric detail, texturing and level design. It's oozing with atmosphere and is another take on that very industrial chunky type of future that many of us envision or have seen in similar takes with franchises like Alien, Deadspace, Event Horizon and so on.

The pure engineering here makes it stand out from any of your average template Unreal Engine games or blueprint cheap shot asset flips. The objective criticism valid here is the PC launch, it wasn't okay, but it is in a much better state today.

Animation and acting is on top, smooth, realistic, and they all look excellent on screen, nothing is budget or cheap here. The writing could at times have been better and less cheesy, especially from the main antagonist, but overall it's very well executed. They do the world building good, and it's the sort where one would just love to have gotten more from this world.

Regarding gameplay, it is also very chunky in a good way, you're not spinning your character around like it's souls or quake 3, and it all fits the tone and vision very well. People seemed to have a hard time with the melee system, fine you can subjectively not like it, but really it's a meaty and satisfying system that keeps the combat tense.

A lot of things are close to great in this game and I feel like if it had just gotten a few more  months in the grinder the last bugs would've been ironed out, and we'd also get a more complete set of bosses and combat arenas. 

I originally played it on the PS5 and had a great time even from the early day one version/patch platinizing the game, so the game itself is probably more polished than most of your games out there already. With that said, things I've encountered in rarity are save bugs. If you rely on the auto-save and quit, I have found myself being set back several minutes, which may be a lot more if the difficulty is high. It's a small thing, but it's still in the game and can be frustrating, I'm not sure what triggers it.

Another valid point is the reuse of a certain boss. It is quite obvious this wasn't meant to be and the boss itself is really cool and well done, but the repetitive nature of fighting it X amount of times does shine through as well as a quite simplistic dodge mechanic that could've used some spice, at least for boss battles. 

The same goes for certain combat encounters. Now I'll approach this from a less dicky buhu side and say that this game is meant to make you feel underpowered constantly, way more than Dead Space. It's not a power-fantasy, and that seems to really get to people for some reason. Again, just admit it's not for you instead of whining and complaining. With that said, certain combat setups and encounters does seem poorly tested when it bugs out with the dodging of the melee system and quirks like that.  Given another 6 months of balancing and bug testing and flushing out these combat spaces and chess pieces a bit more, and I think it could've been superb. 

One thing is that if you play on Hardcore and use the explosive tubes you barely get anything out of it when the enemies have evolved. Many times it fails to make any damage/impact and just bounces right off the enemies, and in certain situations the enemy intro animation will make them invincible and therefor you might completely  waste an explosive tube too early. This is very apparent and can happen in the chapter LOST. In those kinds of situations the game really does let the player down. I also think they could've rewarded exploration a bit more, resources are extremely rare which is fine but rarely are you rewarded for going into the extra rooms which is a shame.

Sound then..
Sound design is fantastic, everything from the chunky footsteps of Jacob to the ambient noises and environmental metal-stresses makes for a really enjoyable experience at Black Iron. It is to be said that I've had situations where certain sounds cut out or cut off, it's rare, but another thing that could've been polished away given just a little more time.

Another thing that holds the game back is the requirement to ship on last gen. You'll end up shimmying through tight sections a lot which starts to feel very artifical after a while. It's fine to have your average vent crawl and and trick here and there, but here it's so common and obviously used  for the onboarding and offboarding of resources. Not really the devs fault but it's another small thing that adds up.

So is Callisto Protocol perfect ? No it isn't, but I think the fans of these type of games really let this game down. It's a huge and impressive production that fell on the finish-line, but even with those quirks and given the patches for the PC it defiantly didn't deserve the shitstorm it got or the rating it has. This is as deserving of praise as the Dead Space remake, and I'm glad we got one entry and attempt at this rather than nothing. Defiantly the best looking game of 2022 and one of the best looking games of all time.

review_text:
TL;DR
- Does JC4 deserve all the hate comments you've read right here? Nope; game runs fine and the story's not better nor worse than the other JC episodes
- Is JC3 better than JC4? Yep. JC4 tried to change stuff but JC3 feels better overall.
- Is JC4 _fun to play_? Certainly!

The Good
- Everything that makes Just Cause fun is there : grappling action, lots of vehicles to drive, crazy chases with the local militia, blowing stuff up... you name it!
- Conquering an area doesn't require you to spend ages looking for the very last transformer to blow up anymore \o/
- The JC4 soundtrack is the best of the series

The Bad
- Extreme weather (of of JC4's major selling points) is limited to a few scripted areas
- Not as much variety in vehicles / vehicle colours as in JC3
- Vehicle collecting mechanism has become ridiculous : "find Waldo and cross the ring" vs. JC3's "bring it to the garage in one piece" which was tons of fun

The Ugly
- Incomprehensible heat level meter
- Enemies may pop up out of nowhere to keep the pressure on, to the point of nonsense

All in all, game's worth $15 imo. Go for it if you've finished and appreciated JC3. If not, play JC3 first  =D

Dead by Daylight is probably one of the most chaotic 4v1 horror games out there, emphasis on the "horror" getting jumped scared it the best part. Survivors must work together repairing generators while the Killer relentlessly chases them down like they owe him lunch money.

If you consider playing Survivor you can expect to panic, miss easy skill checks, or die in a sort span of a few seconds. Of course there's counter play to ever Killer that you'll eventually learn in due time but don't worry, I have nearly 600 hours in the game and I too still run into walls while being chased (It's gotta be the chase music, I swear it's too good.). On the other hand, if you consider playing Killer there's plenty of versatile builds and abilities each killer has that you can to aid you in your ruthless hunt against the Survivors. Both parties have cool and fun builds you can use to either try and befriend each other or make people disconnect because of your pure raw talent at the game.

With all being said the community can be back and forth at times, there's friendly people and there's toxic people. Although, that can be said about a lot of games. You'll have fun or you'll have the worst game of your life that makes you want to get off and uninstall but you'll always come back eventually it's a very addictive game and the Devs are trying to make it better for both parties to have fun. I wouldn't give it a perfect 10/10 but maybe a solid 8/10, I would shake my ass with a map and chase "Hex" names all day long if it means playing this game, it's truly a great experience with friends.

review_text: I was confused when I first put the disc in all those years ago and was told I had to download something called Steam from some company called Valve. I was familiar with Half Life and Portal, but not with the company that made them. So the one good thing I can say about this game is that it introduced me to Steam, which I suspect was the whole point. I feel like this game was always just a virus to infect as many computers with Steam as possible. This is a very flawed game that for some reason is considered immune to criticism by its many fans. Simplistic. Minimalist. Repetitive. No character progression or customization. You do not unlock new characters, weapons, attachments, abilities, or anything. Every level is exactly the same with a linear path to follow and no real incentive to explore. A few hours of mindless fun, followed by a pointless grind. The excuse has always been, "It's meant to be multiplayer. You're supposed to play it with friends." Do you like doing the same thing over and over again? Because I sure don't. Neither do my friends. This game is one of many that represents a dark turning point in the history of the video game industry when things like offline and single player started to go out of style, when you needed to create an account and install a special program just to play, when developers once again began to use repetition in place of actual content. If you had told me ten years ago that this type of game would become the norm, I would have laughed in your face. I thought it was just a minor cold. Surely we could just take some medicine, get some sleep, and it would all disappear like a bad dream. But now, there is a plague of these kinds of games that provide about 10 minutes of content and put it on a dizzying, endless loop. I think I'm going to be sick. Excuse me while I throw up, question my life choices, have an existential crisis, and find a good single player game to wash this horrible taste out of my mouth.

I have been looking forward to Scorn for six years. After reading some negative reviews, I thought those reviewers misunderstood the game. But after playing it, I can confirm that the visuals are a fantastical Giger-esk hellscape, the sound work helps communicate that wonderfully, but the puzzles aren't very developed, and the combat is cheap. The combat is perplexing because it helps establish the rot and decay of the world, but mechanically isn't designed very well. The best tactic is to employ cheap tricks against the AI, and that is as far as it goes.
1/5

This is an old otome game, I know about it but never play it since I don't really like history based game.  
I decide to buy it because discount and I have nothing to do, so I play all the routes.

First of all for new player, read the button config first (esp how to show up the menu screen during game).  I can't seem to make the display into Full Screen, it annoy me at first but I get used to it.  For visual novel, this game sure takes a lot of space, unlike others. Worst routes for me are Sanan (his mood swing) and Okita (I can't handle this brat, his unrequited love ending made my blood boil in anger, but I like his bad end and his CGs). 

Heisuke is the best boy, he's constantly caring for MC in almost every routes, my fave.

Kazama can be annoying in other routes but playing his, what he said about humans do make sense, personally I agree with him.    
 
Overall this game is worth playing (even though I still don't understand the war politics), the arts are nice, the trio friendships are enjoyable to watch.
  
Now, I'm off to play Edo Blossoms.

review_text:
Let me start this off by stating one key detail about this game: It is not, by any means, a metroidvania nor souls-like - although the tags and some online reviews may suggest it is. It's best described as a 2D survival sidescroller with RPG elements. I originally wrote a negative review, but the sole reason for that was because I judged it from a metroidvania point of view.

I really love the artwork, OST, sound-design, dialogue and characters (Sigh... yes, booba included). The gameplay mechanics, however, are quite clunky to say the least. Stationary attacks, no combos, lackluster movement and way too much menuing (ESPECIALLY if you're using magic). The shield literally breaks some of the bosses and so do the invisibility options. Playing without the shield, however, is near impossible when you're up against multiple enemies because the mechanics are too slow to allow you to have any sort of control.

The boss fights are nothing spectacular although still fun (except for Rosie, I hate Rosie and the fact that her entire phase 1 is irrelevant due to shields while phase 2 is bugged in the sense that her jump attack deals contact damage while she's still on the ground/preparing to jump). Generally speaking, the game is somewhat challenging on veteran difficulty - IF you're reckless, that is. The devs reward a methodical approach and if you use everything you have at your disposal, then you shouldn't have too hard of a time. Some of the items have really cool synergies, too.

review_text:
Bioshock is one of the most overrated games in the history of FPS. First, the only good thing of this game is level design: it is clear that the people from 2k put a lot of effort and detail in map design, this is evident in the Medical Pavillion map.

Now for all the flaws:
a) Vita-chambers: lots of players argue that it removes all tension and difficulty from the game. they are used for free and turn Bioshock from a complex-FPS-with-hard-enemies-wannabe into a kill-until-I-die-and-then-resurrect game.
b) Unoriginal weapons: let's see, pistol, shotgun, machine gun, grenade launcher, sniper (crossbow). Meh.
c) Enemy splicers do not use their plasmids: yup, I have 6 plasmids under my sleeve and the r-tards of my enemies who are sinking in ADAM overdose do not even use electric bolt.
d) Useless weapon powerups and false sense of "choice": so, you apparently get a dozen weapon powerups that put you in a difficult position to choose. Yeah, right. It makes a lot of sense to have high fire rate in a 4-shell shotgun (sarcasm), or an extended mag in a pistol in a game where I can use a machine gun.
e) Side characters I could not care less: so, through the game you pick recordings that supposedly tell you stuff about what happened in Rapture. Who cares? A woman complains she got spliced until becoming Quasimodo... why would I care? At least if it had a video, but nope. Audios are supposed to create a "story" (note the "") for side characters who have no relevance at all.
f) Useless plasmids: face it, from all the plasmids you can choose from, you will only use and need electrobolt (paralyze and kill Big Daddys), incendiary (not necessary anymore after you get the flamethrower), hypnotize big Daddy (to fight against the other big Daddys), decoy (to draw Big Daddys to groups of proximity mines) and that's it. The rest are completely useless and irrelevant. Which leads me to the next three points.
g) Lack of compromise in decissions: you can change your plasmids anytime you want in a gene station,. This allows you to equip yourself as you want before a fight, thus relieving you from facing the compromise of plasmids that are good against splicers but useless against powerful enemies.
h) Redundancy and false sense of choice: most powers granted by plasmids do not add anything new other than the "fun" of killing an enemy in a "fun" way (why use freeze, when you can use electrobolt? no good reason) and can be obtained through weapons (why upgrade freeze when you can use your nitrogen in the flame thrower?).
i) Useless ADAM: ADAM is supposed to be the ultimate reward. Thing is, several of the plasmids or powerups you buy with ADAM can be created by crafting things in the "U invent machine". As a result, you get to a the 60% of the game and wonder what to dowith ADAM as you got all you need.
j) Useless powerups: why use "hack expert" powerups to have reduced alarm tiles when hacking if you can use the "camouflage" powerup and become invisible to everyone by standing still while hacking? I escaped 80% of the alarms of a failed hacking by standing still, becoming invisible, and watching the bots flying while I took pictures of them (added bonus of increased damage to bots).
k) Lack of compromise 2: as 75% of plasmids and powerups are redundant, your quest for ADAM becomes a horse with 5 legs (who would want to buy one?), removing all tension from decisions. Rescuing little sisters should put you in a position to decide where you will be selfish and harvest ADAM to get "awesome?" powerups or save innocent children. FAIL.
l) Boring, cliched and I-couldn't-care-less endings: both endings were written by a 5 year old kid.
m) No gibbing: seriously? yout game required a top notch computer and I can blow a guy's arm off? A Big Daddy pushes a drill through the rib cage of a splicer and no hole in it? give me a break!!!!

I could keep going and going, but I think I made my point. I paid 4 euro for this load of rubbish, the only thing that justifies my "investment" was the splicing screaming "Ay.... me muerooo!" every time I used incendiary on it.

review_text:
This game defines "I enjoyed the journey, but hated the destination". Definitely play Y5. It's a good game, despite the ending pitfalls. Grab a bottle of Suntory Whiskey and give it a play. But I can't give this one a thumbs up with pitfalls outlined below. The story was phenomenal as always, but the ending was just... bad. Trying to piece everything together, even though it's blatantly spelled out for you multiple times over still leaves you with questioning as to "why even bother going through all this effort?" The final boss fights were just downright awful. Some were far too easy, some were far too hard.

Kiryu's final boss fight was for some unknown reason, the hardest in the whole franchise up until this point *and* who Kiryu was pitted against made next to no sense. The biggest thing for me is the difficulty curve. Saejima fights the aforementioned boss a few chapters earlier, and it was **trivial** to take them down. When Kiryu does it though? 10+ stage health bar, with a constant barrage of damage. Generally, I could figure out what to do against a given boss, I couldn't with them. It's pure misery. I don't know if it was because Kiryu was the first character you played, and for me, this ended up being over the course of 3-6 months, or what. It just sucked imo.

Even in the final chapter, there are some things that make me question RGGs understanding of good enemy design and the triangle. Generally they're really good at this, but the finall chapter made me go "wtf". "Quantity of enemies", "Strength of enemy", "Health of enemy", if you have a strong character, they can either be tanky or a lot of them, but not both. There are several instances where I can point to in the final chapter where they threw tens of enemies at you who were both tanky and strong. The portion I'm thinking of... They weren't even "bosses". Just annoying, regular high healthed enemies in mass quantity. They just dropped the ball on this one.

The economy in this game is pretty unbalanced too. Saejima is likely to end up being the wealthiest character due to the side quests. Akiyama, despite being a canonical millionaire carries around zero yen. Tatsuo being handed millions of yen at the end of his story also carries around zero... It's pretty easy to walk into the final boss fights being completely unprepared as there's zero health item pickups, zero weapon pickups, zero heat pickups... 

Side quests were also pretty unbalanced, It seems like Saejima had the most/longest, Kiryu's second, Haruka third, Tatsuo fourth, and Akiyama Fifth. Which again, really leads to some characters feeling super underleved while others have basically maxed their skills. I feel like the final boss fights without completing any side stories would just be awful.  

Lastly, major spoiler: ||I understand why Haruka threw her idol career away. It wasn't really ever her dream, she was just fulfilling Park-sans dream of performing at the dome. Her true dream was to be with and provide for her family, and I think it's wonderful that RGG went that direction with the story... **BUT**, running off stage, saying nothing to Horie-chan, or Yamaura-san? Even after him coming to the dome after being thrown off a roof with them being in the crowd? not having backstage or VIP seats or anything? It's honestly comical to look back at it. I checked the Wiki and the last time Horie/Yamaura was seen was in Y5. This basically means Dyna-chair is left to die. Horie and Yamaura are out of a job with pretty much their only hope being Osaka Talent to take them in and hope they can find a place for them. Again, after Horie was thrown off a roof????  They didn't do poor Horie-chan justice. Haruka didn't even go see him in the hospital. There was **one** side story about getting him a signed thing from Airi. I'll say it again, they didn't do Horie-chan justice.||

Anyways, I'll conclude with this: Justice for Horie-Chan.

review_text:
If you've been hungry for some half-decent VR co-op it's finally here.

This is definitely "Left 4 Dead in VR," but at the same time that might be too reductive. If you've played Saints and Sinners or any VR FPS you know head-shotting a zombie with your own arms is satisfying in a way the flat classics can't match, and unlike S&S which at most threw ~10 zombies at you here you'll be seeing actual [i]swarms[/i] of enemies. Frantically slamming in manual reloads when you're slowly being surrounded is an experience I can't say I've felt after hundreds of hours in L4D.

I played on the second difficulty with two friends and regular enemies began spawning with armor, forcing me to make my shots count instead of spraying center mass. We had to get organized calling out wave spawns and specials and rationing scavenged supplies; pick the right difficulty and you will be getting an active co-op experience, not a shooting gallery where your friends are only there for moral support.

Although there aren't many missions there is an extensive crafting and progression system. If you play for completionism's sake there might be a few months of content in there alone. Guns have unlockable achievement skins (i.e. flame decals on the deagle require a 100 accurate shot streak) and also attachments that significantly change their behavior: extended magazines, reflex sights, grip tape, and even special mods like batteries that add crit chance. I've barely scratched the surface but pimping your favorite gun or unlocking a new toy seems like the main reason to load back in.

A few more thoughts:
If you're having trouble with manual reloads go to game settings and change "grip type" to "manual" OR turn off hand swapping.

So far I'm not impressed with the specials, especially compared to L4D or Back 4 Blood. For the most part they're just slightly different bullet sponges. Classic enemies like the Witch would have been incredible in VR, or lickers from Resident Evil (even the normal snowies will climb on ceilings).

Performance is definitely playable 60+fps w/ Quest 2 on a rtx 2080 over airlink 5ghz. As part of the PC master race we're getting dramatically improved visuals compared to the Quest & PSVR players. I'm still hoping there are small performance improvements with patches though. 

We'll see if people are still playing it weeks from now but as it stands I think it's easily worth full price. This is the new benchmark for VR co-op.

review_text:
This game is not good.

Starting with the visuals, the game is built on CryEngine. A Game Engine known for some of the most advanced visuals in graphics, and so it is amazing how terrible the game looks. Weird screen space shadow artifacts, funky lighting from player and enemy flashlights, and distant assets looking like they come from the original Half Life.

The gameplay itself is tedious with moments of frustration. It's not difficult, it's just annoying. They give you a ton of aiming assist, even playing with a mouse and keyboard, and on the normal difficulty. Which is frustrating as you can't tell if you actually had good aim when you took down that target at 400m, or if the game just gave it to you. 

The enemies spotting you doesn't seem to have consistency, with an enemy further away spotting you faster than an enemy that is essentially standing on you. The enemies are also apparently telepathic, and can see when their friends get shot even behind them. The players guns feel weak, while the average soldier has the aim and precision of a veteran Navy Seal.

But worst of all they made a Sniping game that seems to just discourage sniping. The distances are too short to make it interesting and challenging, there is no skill involved, there is little benefit in spending time getting set up and taking down a big target. You're much better off going in with a silenced pistol and clearing dudes out as you creep along.

review_text:
It's a remarkable game with many flaws.

THE GOOD:
Lots of content: Story, interaction, characters, action.

There are 2 kinds of battles: Ground or Space
Space Missions: You control a ship, which you will have many through the game. Currently Tier 6 (T6) ships are the best ships and there are hundreds of them to choose from.
Ground Missions: You battle on the ground as yourself with either your fellow friends or Officers (NPCs)

The game is VERY complex. It took me quite a while to understand what effects what and how. After a month, I wasn't the first one to die and after 2 months, I can confidently hold my ground, or die trying.


The Bad: Story design can be frustrating. As you progress in the story missions, sometimes someone starts to talk to you, which covers almost the entire screen. And sometimes enemies start attacking you at the same time. So I either skip the dialogue missing the story content or just wait till they finish talking and miss the entire fight (My officers are great, they usually handle the fight on their own). 

Same, when you kill everyone on a level, a pop-up conversation forces you to leave the place, while the room is full of uncollected loot. VERY Frustrating. So now my priority is always to collect the loot while the enemy is shooting at me. 

This is an old game and it shows. Play it if you like complicated games, or just to shoot stuff (STO users call it pew pew... ) but only if you think you can handle some of the frustration of the bad game design and bugs.
