review_text:
At the time of writing this review, I have just 100% Just Cause 3. And intend the same for JC4. So, I’ll be revisiting this review as I complete the game. Now, please remember I’m coming into this game assuming its mechanics are similar to JC3.

First 5 hours:
My initial response reflects my previous review, negative… The game feels off, with mechanics that feel clunky. For example, movement. While I expected there to be some changes, I didn't expect to change most of my keybinds. On top of that, ground movement feels delayed. Rico, my sweet boy, tends to forget about running. I’ll try to walk forward, and my man here is lost to the wind. While I’ve gotten used to this, it lowkey pissed me off for the 1st hour. Another pet peeve of mine is the auto retractor. It bugged me early on, but I’ve gotten used to it. Another issue I’m having with JC4 is the UI. JC3 was clean, easy to understand, bright, and interesting. But they’ve ripped up the previous mechanics. On your map, it’s become a lot harder to see bases and places you’ve been. The map is also much darker, and while I don't mind me some dark mode. When I get flashbanged every time I exit the map, it sorta sucks. Traveling to the next tab, you’ll find what's replaced the gears tab. Your grappling hook upgrades. It's a less interesting, more boring waste of space. Moving on with our UI tour, the “supply drop” (replacing the previous rebel drop) isn't half bad. I don't entirely mind it, I just miss the ability to drop 1 car and 3 weapons. Now it's one at a time :/ But it's not too big a problem when Rico, God bless this man. He throws his gun, the second its empty… In JC3, when you ran out of ammo, he kept his gun, letting you get more ammo. But na, this man is praying on my downfall. Now thankfully I’m a pro gamer, and get a new gun. But I’ve found myself without guns a few times, and that's extremely annoying when the black hand is constantly on your ass. It’s very hard to tell how much heat you have and how close you are to losing it. On top of that, it doesn't help when it feels like you're heat 4, 24/7! I appreciate them showing some love for the vehicles, letting them get used by the AI. But god dam bro. Cut me some slack! Now venting aside, a few thing I am enjoying about this game is the map. It’s pretty beautiful, and knowing if you can see it, you can go there makes it a lot cooler. Another thing I like is that if you’ve purchased the “Toy Vehicle Pack“, when you hop in one, the black hand will also pull out their reserve of tiny vehicles. So, summary? Ya, I’d get this game. Just need some time to adjust. Hopefully, my next update is all positive! :)

18 hours in:
So, my next update is Positive! While it failed to meet the bar set by JC3, it’s only slightly under par, and is still a fun game. So to start of with, I’m really starting to miss those 3 gun slots. I liked carrying a rifle, sniper, and special weapon. But now I have to pick and choose, which is tough because there are so many options. You also can’t holster your weapon anymore, and Rico is officially always on edge now. I also feel like the old (JC3) map was more memorable, with landmarks I could recognize and say, “Oh hey, I know where I am.” But in JC4, the map is so large that every place I go feels new or like I've never been there before. It’s not too big a deal, but it can be overwhelming sometimes. As I mentioned in my last update, Everything feels just a little off. JC3 hit the vibe perfectly. gameplay, UI, and mechanics. And while JC4 is right there with it, it somehow misses the mark. Don't get me wrong, I love this game. But compared to JC3, when I’m playing, I get the feeling that “something's missing”. It's probably something to do with the new territory system. Now, while I quite enjoy it, I miss the gameplay mechanic where you could capture a base, destroy it, and see it marked as reclaimed on the map, with your previous destruction remaining. Adding to this, they removed the ability to freely claim regions and destroy bases. Long gone are the requirements to blow up a base. I understand that JC4’s gameplay isn’t meant to be like that, but at least repaint or remove targets once a region is claimed. Another pet peeve of mine, is that planes don't really shut down, which is pretty annoying… thus, if you land and park up, it just slowly keeps moving forward. On another note, the weather was kind of underwhelming… I liked the tornado mission, that was fun. But the main selling point of this game was so unimportant that I barely came across it during gameplay. But, on some high notes, I do enjoy the small frontline battle portrayed at the edges of your fronts. There's flak, tanks, and checkpoints set up. Writing of tanks, personally if any game has military vehicles, 9 times out of 10, it wins me over. And these new vehicles are very well thought out and designed. Each has some character or purpose behind it, and I really appreciate that. And while I’m still getting used to the fact that you can’t drop 4 items anymore, I do like the ability to set a loadout for each pilot. Very convenient! I also like the new parachute animation. It looks more realistic and physics-based. But even with this new animation, I thought my rocket-powered wingsuit wasn’t making a return, but my beloved Bavarium Wingsuit did come back! I also find Rico’s (somewhat) random voice lines (especially “Ride Of The Valkyries” one) very entertaining. Theres also a bunch of random events making the game more lively, along with plenty of well-animated cutscenes. So for now, I rest my case. I shall return once i’ve completed the main story :)

review_text:
On the surface, MXGP Pro seems like a solid step forward for milestone's series of dirtbike games. The fourth MXGP title boasts a much improved physics system, and track deformation graphical enhancements. First, lets dive into the all-new Pro physics.

In my mind, Milestone has always created the most enjoyable and challenging riding experience when it comes to physics, but it had some major issues that needed addressed. Many were, here with Pro physics. Gone are the days of casing a jump, or drifting through a corner at ludicris speeds. Pro physics require attention to detail at every level, from speed, cornering angle, power input, jump takeoffs and landings, braking, and put it all together in order to make successful laps. For me, this makes even Milestone's latest release, MESX, unplayable. That's impressive. 

Another welcome improvement is track deformation. Simply put, it's some of the best I've seen in a dirtbike game, and defintitely the best Milestione has produced. Hopefully it's here to stay.

The compound is back, and more beautiful than ever. Although, that does come with it's issues. While most of the game performs outstandingly well on my 6th gen i7 and Nvidia GTX1080 (1440p @ >100fps) the compound has some severe stuttering and frame rate drops. Fortunately, I don't spend much time there anyway, but if that's your thing, be aware of this issues. Within compound mode, you can compete in MX or SX races or time trials.

The menues and ui have not been improved whatsoever, and in fact, are worse off than in MESX. Some major issues still remain, for example, when selecting your number, you still cannot manually select it. You still have to scroll through 900 and some numbers, which is obviously frustrating (especially just after you buy the game and are excited to get racing). There also is a bug with the tv camera in replay. Some players have mentioned it's just after certain motos, however, whenever I have tried to use the replay, tv camera has not worked for me. Also, when backing out of replay, the screen and sound freeze for about 10-15 seconds before resuming. Asthetically, I personally find the ui a bit dated looking and unattractive. 

The sound is gernerally underwhelming, as per usual. The commentary is corny and adds to the dated and childish feel of the ui to start the events. The bikes don't sound bad, but I don't feel immersed in the race due to poor sound engineering and mixing. The general atmosphere is also not captured, and theres alot of issues with dynamic track events, such as running through water, but I'll get to that. Overall, the sound isn't bad, but I do notice it taking me out of the experience sometimes, which obviously isn't good. 

Multiplayer currently has two options: quick match and create a match. So far, I have not seen a way to browse games like you could in MESX. Another missing feature from MESX in multiplayer, is the ability to vote on weather conditions for the race after voting for the track. That was a great feature that should have been implemented into MXGP Pro. So far I've had a great experience racing in multiplayer, especially when locking the physics to pro. 

Career mode is back and only has a couple differences from previous versions. A new fame rating has been added, which affects which sponsors you may choose. Your main sponsor determines your livery. Again, there are no factory teams available. Fame also dictates what brand/level parts you may install on your bike. These act as secondary sponsors. Each sponsor will have a goal for you to perform at each event. The completion of these goals reward you with credits and fame. Credits may be spent on outfit parts. This is career mode. Yay.

I think there is alot of room to grow in career mode. It'd be great to see drivers have ratings on different riding skills, the way many  other sports games give ratings to players in different skill categories. It'd be great to start off as a low level in skills such as "balance", "cornering", "starts", "jumps (takeoff and landings)", "agressiveness (affects ability to stay on bike when making contact with another rider)", "toughness (affects ability to stay on bike when another rider makes contact with you)", "stamina (affects all abilities over duration)", "whoops", etc. This would add a great level of gameplay and replayability to the series and could even bleed over into sponsors looking for riders with certain skills above a certain level. It'd also be nice to see contracts added into career mode as well. (And factory teams)!!

Other single player modes include, Grand Prix single races, Championship, etc. The usual. 

So overall we have pretty much what we are used to with a couple of really great upgrades. But is this good enough? 

No.

You still can't change the camera view before the race starts and it still resets to the default third person camera. Why?

The upgraded physics are awesome, and were necessary. But they are a wasted effort when the tracks lack dynamic physical properties. Sure, they look great, with ruts, deformation, water when it rains, etc, but none of that translates to the bike, or even the rest of the environment. The bike reacts only to the surface type and inclination/elevation of the track, and very (very, very) few scripted ruts and puddles. You feel the surface you are supposed to be racing on very well, but not the track you ARE racing on. This is a huge and experience ruining problem. You skate over any and all ruts that aren't huge and explicitly placed in the track by the devs. Again, not dynamic. If you hit one of the puddles, you hear it....but if it's raining and the whole track is covered in water? You aren't really driving through water. Theres no sound of water. Theres no splash of water. Theres no resistance on your bike as if driving through a massive trench of water or any other affect on your bike for that matter, be it grip or what have you. There's also no splash animation for water, or any being thrown up by tires. In fact theres not really much dirt, dust, or any of that thrown up but tires whiles accellerating, skidding, landing, etc. Of course my next suggestion couldn't happen until all that stuff does, because it'd be totally unbelievable, but wouldn't it be cool to have some dirt, water, dust, etc on your camera, or goggles, while you're racing. I see AI ripping off tear offs during races and I think, "yeah right". 

Speaking of AI, it still sucks. 

Overall, the issues ruin the experience. If you want to check out the new physics, wait for a sale. 5/10

review_text:
You were dreaming. Your body lies in the dirt entwined with living tendrils that hold you tight and suck your life juices out of you. Then you wake up. It wasn't a dream!

Scorn throws you into an unknown, strange world. The game gives you the privilege of exploring and experiencing a world like no other. There are no explanations. There are no dialogues. No one will take you by the hand to show you around. And that's exactly what makes the game so unique.

There are many games that take the player into strange worlds. But unlike Scorn, after a while players realize where they are, what is required of them and what they have to do. Scorn throws you into a world so strange and alien that you won't know where you are, what's required of you, or how to escape this nightmare. All you know is that you have to leave the area you are in. This world is hostile. This world is dangerous and you want to live. So you have to get out of here.

Every level is different, looks different, and challenges you with new tasks. The game never gets boring and keeps surprising you with completely unexpected events until the very end. This is euphoric. Again and again, you stare at your monitor in fascination while you think to yourself, 'This can't be true!'. It's absolutely intoxicating.

Beside occasional combat with amazing creatures, Scorn's gameplay is mainly puzzles. Sometimes you have to solve puzzles directly on a wall or in a mechanism, but often the whole map is a puzzle on which you have to activate machines, move levers and find upgrades to open doors or move gates. 

All puzzles are challenging, but at the same time cleverly designed so that you can always solve them. Since all maps are large labyrinths, you often run back and forth trying to solve everything, and occasionally you might feel lost. I was a little frustrated, once in level 4 because I wasn't able to find the last of three mechanisms. But then eventually I found the last one. 

Scorn is an achievement friendly game. Except for the first two achievements, you will collect all of them automatically. As for the first two, you can only collect one of them during a single game. Therefore, after finishing the game once, you just need to replay the first 15 minutes to collect the missing achievement.

Scorn has received overall positive reviews, but some players are annoyed by the fact that the game costs 40 $/Euros but only offers 7 hours play time. I doubt you can complete the game in 7 hours without instructions. It took me 11 hours without guide. Nevertheless, I can understand the criticism. At the same time, Scorn is a very special game, and I can imagine how much work it took the developers to create it. Wait for a sale. Personally, I think $20 is a reasonable price.

If there were Oscars for games, Scorn would collect many of them. In my opinion this game is a masterpiece. It’s a work of art. Scorn is like visiting a gallery of absurdities, where you can't help but be amazed. It's scary and brutal, and there's a lot of blood in this game. Scorn is simultaneously cruel and incredibly fascinating. I only played the game at night with headphones because I wanted to enjoy every moment, and I succeeded. I love Scorn. It's a great game! I strongly doubt I will play anything better this year.

[h1]Pros[/h1] 
- breathtaking world
- brilliant atmosphere
- beautiful graphics
- fantastic soundtrack
- fantastic sound effects
- very innovative 
- unique (there is nothing like it)
- smart
- exciting fights
- mysterious
- surprising

[h1]Neutral[/h1] 
- very brutal

[h1]Cons[/h1] 
- if the map is the puzzle it can get a little frustrating

review_text:
I love this game like an abusive spouse. 

It's is borderline busted. Your hand will get caught in geometry and it feels impossible to escape it. The holstering system is janky at best. About 70% of the time, when you reload your weapons before emptying your clip, your mags will fall straight to the ground even though you release the mag directly inside of your belt. 

The campaign is frustrating, sloppy and short, consisting of long stretches of the funkiest, most infuriating platforming sections you've ever seen, depending on unreliable mechanics like vaulting to climb on top of objects and ledges, and crouching to avoid a moving train that will probably hit you regardless of how low you get. 

Honestly guys... why so much platforming? You guys really thought the platforming in this wonky psychics sim was so fun it needed to be the highlight of this game? 

Still one of the best VR games on the market. That should tell you everything about what this market is like.

There isn't another game that has a better body implementation in VR, (Other than Boneworks.) Gun play shines as some of the most fun I've had in VR. Exploration is great, love the music, the world, and the meta storytelling. Lots of interesting secrets to find. Mod support is great, although there is still no in-game mod browser. 

TL:DR Buy Bonelab for free mods like Fusion, custom maps, guns and skins. Buy Boneworks if you want a fun, well thought out single player campaign. There's no good reason why this game costs more than Boneworks, a superior package in pretty much every way.

review_text:
There will be some spoilers in this review. Read at your own risk.

Lucius is a murder centric puzzle game where you play as the titular Lucius Wagner, a child of Lucifer. The premise of the game is rather interesting. Lucifer visits Lucius in a dream and bestows him the unholy mission of garnering the souls of people around Dante Manor. This is done through rather unintuitive and lacking puzzles. 

The story takes place in the painfully large Dante Manor. From nearly the very beginning of the game, most of all of the manor is open to you. With the mechanics that exist in the game, this is NOT a good thing. It does not reward exploration (save for the aptly named "Explorer" achievement). Furthermore, the puzzle solutions are extremely unintuitive and, quite frankly, boring. At several points, there shows potential for many possible ways to kill the chapter's target, but as the game requires deaths to be the ones laid out for you, it does not help at all (for example, one kill requires you to set someone on fire, but simply setting them on fire does not work. You have to douse him in gasoline and then setting him on fire will allow the kill.). More than that, the way some of these events transpire, it will severely test your suspension of disbelief (if you were to light a ciagrette at a stove, would YOU stick your face into the stove fire?) and the game simply can't be taken seriously. 

Even worse still, this game at one (potentially two) point(s) tries to hopscotch between puzzle and action game. The controls and camera for this game are already pretty clunky as is and making it into a third person action game with a terrible camera does not help the game's case in the slightest. Lucius also suffers from having quite a few bugs (several things can go wrong during some chapters and will force you to restart the chapter) and collision issues (getting caught on nothing comes to mind).

Other bugs that come to mind are broken achievements. Some achievements do not work at times and can cause potential frustration.

All in all, this game is NOT worth your time or money. I got it on sale for 75% off ($4.99 instead of $19.99) and I still feel like I got ripped off.

I had high hopes for this game, since I really enjoyed SGW 3, despite its quirks. But I was let down oh so hard.

The mechanics feel rough like they weren't properly tested at all, the AI is not good, either they are completely unaware of you, or you get detected and literally everyone on the map knows where you are, up to your precise location. Once detected, everyone will start shooting at you with deadly accuracy, and the alarm keeps blaring in the background, also you will stay detected indefinitely, even if you hide. 

The weapons are fine, but none really stand out apart from the 50.cal that can dismember enemies. The maps feel like they weren't thought over twice since some passages are unusable and the terrain is incredibly rough. I got stuck on the dumbest things including but not limited to twigs, little rocks, bumps on the ground, etc. 

One moment I was having great fun and the other I was frustrated out of my mind, because of ALL the bugs. The autosave feature is clever but poorly executed, as it saves very infrequently, to the point where you have to play entire sections again, just because it didn't save.

If this game is going to be playable, it's going to need a HUGE overhaul, every feature needs to be re-evaluated to work more smoothly. Also, the animations are super laggy, even on a reasonable pc. So I hope they fix their game, but in the meantime, only get this dirt cheap, because it simply isn't worth the money in its current state.

review_text:
Decades pass. Young people get duller, their Jokers get uglier, and their Batmans get smugger.

This game has similar problems to Prototype (2009). They give you an expansive-but-samey open world, with an overabundance of overpowered weapons, tools and abilities - and then the level designers have to restrict all that freedom to be able to tell any story - by corralling you into industrial facilities with only one route through them.

Early on, the fights with gangs of thugs felt surprisingly true to the 1960s TV series Batman, but for there to be any challenge they had to add thugs with guns, to turn each room into a puzzle. The whole gangs aspect of Batman is aging badly - groups of identi-kit bodybuilders, standing in alleyways all day, even though there isn't anyone else around for them to rob. During the first several hours I ran in and mashed buttons rather than using the awkward controls to do anything else. The situational tactics stuff had a very slow learning curve, perhaps it gets more interesting but I doubted it would ever compare to Crusader: No Regret or a hundred others. Whatever the situation, Batman has too many options to choose from.

The storyworld/setting is so contrived that whatever the writers did with it was going to be boring, the plot unfolds in a linear fashion, using rubbish plot devices to set you up for the next twist. In the first few hours, Batman gets knocked out and tied up three times: by Dr Strange, then the Penguin, then the Joker. Like it's the only way the writers knew to advance from one chapter to the next. The individual cutscenes and lines of dialogue aren't any better - thugs give away clues whilst talking to each other every 5 minutes, Catwoman and Harley Quinn both make the same risque quips, and Batman betrays slight hints of inner fury... by saying... less... words.

I wish DC Comics and Hollywood and the people who make big-budget games would stop churning out paler and less demanding versions of Frank Miller Batman from 30 years ago, and that they would put some production cash into some of the niche Batmans. We don't again need to see what a kids' pantomime would look like if they spent millions of dollars on it.

review_text:
Having nearly 150 hours into this thing, I have some thoughts that I think are worth sharing.

Pros
- The general flow of a run is absolutely fantastic. You can get pretty crazy with some combos and abilities that you earn, especially by the third leg of an attempt. 
- Core hockey is generally great, and the foundation is here for something special should they choose to keep improving on things
- The different teams are all fairly unique and fun, with the exception of the meatball team in the first leg (I can't remember the last time I DIDN'T mercy them). And the Greasy Lettuce could use some buffs, but are closer to the latter half of the special teams than the meatballs.
- The great abilities are truly wonderful to play with. My personal favorite has to be the Dash, since it opens up all sorts of wild possibilities when combined with other powers. 
- The various superstars that you unlock are the best part of the entire game in my opinion. That kazoo, though. Too tasty!
- The overall visual style is consistent, fun, and effective. I like the direction they chose, and look forward to more wacky creations from them in the future
- The UI is clean, clear, and does its job. The main menus are snappy and responsive. One of the cleaner early access games I have played in terms of how sharp it is.
- Have never run into any game breaking bugs, with just some minor annoyances here and there like weird audio problems that they are aware of.
- For the most part (more on this in the Cons), the difficulty curve is satisfying and generally satisfying. Winning a run against those Golfers is delicious beyond words.

Cons
- Holy hell the passing in this game is so bad sometimes. It doesn't need a complete overhaul, but it's close. I would say 40% of my passes go not only to the wrong person, but to the WORST POSSIBLE person on my team. It is the single biggest drawback for me at the moment and needs addressed in a huge way.
- The goalies are better with the latest patch, but still need some tweaking. I can score almost 100% of the time by just rushing past them with Dash, and that shouldn't happen.
- The Princesses are absurd. As a person who has pulled off a mercy on the Golfers, I can safely say the Princesses are straight up broken. They have the fart (incredibly powerful, albeit funny, ability), sticks to throw at you, insane speed, accuracy, and buckwild checking power. If they were a freakin boss they would be too good in my opinion. Of all content in the game that needs a nerf, they win that award by about 1,000% for me
- Some abilities just straight up suck in my opinion. The whirlwind is bad, and the dragon shout is a neat idea but is just a Disco Ball with a different name and longer cooldown. 
- Goalies make the dumbest passing choices, and sometimes they don't even respond correctly. If I am pressing up/right towards my only guy on screen...why is my goalie passing down/right to the point that the puck is mere inches away from going into the goal? 
- We need a better way to switch players. Let me assign hotkeys to everyone on my team, or stop thinking I want to choose the slowest player that is furthest from the puck instead of the fastest player that is closest to the puck. Please for the love of god lol
- There needs to be a teammate AI basic script we can choose. I want my players to become aggressive or focus on checking or racing after the puck instead of going into canned movement animations when they are on "offense" or "defense." 
- The point above is painfully apparent when facing the Prince. The only reason he is even a threat is because your team doesn't even try to check him, and it's a dumb way to increase the difficulty. They need to let your team check on their own and just cut his wind up speed in half. It would feel less cheap while retaining the flavor of what they intended him to be in the first place

Overall the game is absolutely fantastic, and for being in early access I don't think any of the Cons are unreasonable to be present in the product. Making games is hard, and they are clearly taking their time to make this one correctly. Even if all my gripes go unanswered because they consider other feedback more valuable, I will keep playing it for as long as they keep releasing new content for it. 

Loving this. Keep it up, Excellent Rectangle!

review_text:
I find it difficult to call this a horror game even if on paper it hits all the right notes. Yes it is about a young antichrist killing all the occupants of the household in a gorey fashion but I only ever found myself exasperated by the game mechanics or laughing at the stilted voice acting and the underwhelmingly cliched story. 

Personally I think it would have been just fine if it was only the story that underwhelmed me. The real attraction of this type of game is the gameplay. An Omen-Hitman style crossover sounds really cool and one day I hope we get to see that game fully realised but as it stands what we have is a nonsensical linear puzzle game that isn’t particularly impressive. 

It’s also buggy as hell. 

You’re assigned a target each chapter, with a cutscene playing when you interact with them. Not only was it not always clear who you’d be killing at the beginning of each level, sometimes the wrong cutscene would trigger a few chapters early for a character. Leaving the player to run around trying to figure out how to kill them until they accidentally bump into their true target. For example: [spoiler]Agnes’s cutscene triggered before Jed’s.[/spoiler]

I’d clip into walls frequently and found that the ending of the game was broken. I looked up a tutorial to see if I was doing something wrong but no, I’d done everything I was supposed to and yet [spoiler]my father was still beating me to death with a fire extinguisher[/spoiler]. Thankfully, the game also managed to bug it’s way into ending with my sweet little antichrist clipping into the door and into the final cutscene. So, there’s that. 

In my experience Lucius is more fun to watch someone else play than to actually play yourself and so with that in mind, I cannot recommend it. 

TLDR: I got this game on sale and still feel like I paid too much for it. It’s very reminiscent of an old B-Horror movie, cheesy and a little dated.

review_text:
What a bunch of wasted potential.
I started Callisto Protocol with a clear head and no real expectations, being both a fan of survival horrors and sci-fi genre in general. I have finished the base game [spoiler](and if I buy a DLC, call 112 because I got a stroke)[/spoiler] but from half of it I felt forced to do so and I can not recommend the game.
I have played a game on hardcore difficulty and from what I have noticed it has a lot of good ideas but everything seems to be... half baked.

1. Melee aspect of the game is interesting at the start unless you understand that almost every single fight is "dodge 2 or 3 times, couple of light attacks, repeat till enemy is dead", the dreaded mutation is actually making the fight only slower because nothing changes except for enemies health. Are you afraid to be ganked by a group of enemies? Well, no need to worry because they always form a queue waiting for a beat-up, just like in old Assassin's Creed and even if the other enemy decides to focus on you, the one you are fighting right now will back out and wait in line.

2. Projectile weapons suck because outside of special "QTE" like moment during the fight they do unsatisfactory amount of damage and you need to save ammo for the "bosses", which 3/4 times is the same enemy with the same attack pattern that will absolutely shred you in melee combat.

3. Do you remember the amazing idea of limb cutting in Dead Space? This one has it too but it does absolutely nothing except changing the attack pattern to one dodge only when the enemy has one limb! Amazing, isn't it?

4. The plot is a standard set of genre cliches which is not bad in itself, but yet again, it's half baked. Most of the story is rushed with nothing explained particularly well, and the Callisto apparently has an atmosphere, snowfall, bearable temperatures (protagonist survives more than 10-15 seconds without a mask which would be death sentence in hard vacuum), EARTH LIKE GRAVITY while in real life it has roughly 12% of it. But hey, it got explained in one 2 sentence video log - you might not even find it if you are not careful - with a magical word "TERRAFORMED". And no, if you expect the rest of the story to make more sense, you are very naive.

5. Level design is for worms, I mean 90% of a level is a linear tunnel and rarely present junctions usually allow you additional 2-5 minutes of exploration.

6. Jacob, the protagonist, has basically no personality whatsoever, which is amazing because Dead Space 1 Isaac Clarke was mute, yet he was more likeable than this guy. Half of the game I couldn't even remember his name and I am pretty certain I will forget it by tomorrow. At least he dies in cool, Mortal Kombat like fashion.

7. Bugs, bugs, bugs. My favourite one is the art of chair- and bedomancy, you can use the gravity gun to push enemies on top of furniture, if the game detects they are in spot they are not supposed to be, they will instantly die. Saved me a lot of ammo! Also, some enemies without eyes can't see you, others have sonar vision. There is no consequence in the enemy design at all.

8. Game economy. Out of 5 guns available in base game, you are handed only 2, the rest of it you can print in crafting station, which is nice but I couldn't afford it even once, split between GRP, melee upgrades and a constant supply of ammo for bosses (maybe I went into wrong "build" but the game never warned me I am making a mistake, it actually encouraged use of melee for the most of playthrough.

5. This one is subjective but I, not even once, felt dread or fright, even a little chill playing it. I still remember the chills of exploring Dead Space Ishimura or Alien Isolation's Space Station, I still remember the clip I emptied because one of supposed victims raised a hand to me pleading for help in the first game, and the alt+F4 combined with a real life scream in one moment of the second game... This one? I felt hopeful for the first half, irritated for the second.

6. Biophages are "we have necromorphs at home". Nothing else to say.

7. The good stuff: graphics (if you care) is mostly consistent and playing it on ultra was eye candy. It contained Licorice and anise, but still.

So, [b]to sum up that wall of text[/b], I am truly disappointed, it was supposed to be a new Dead Space, and all I have is hollow, ill-judged game, where every piece of puzzle of making a nice experience is theoretically here, but if you look closely, every piece of it is cut improperly.

Shame...

review_text:
Must-play for SAO enjoyers. It's gorgeous, fun, authentic and the music feels straight out of a 2000s eastern MMO game (good). The character interactions are endearing and often funny, cute, wise or emotional. The way characters smile after delivering a line of dialogue is adorable, and the lipsync tech they used is very enjoyable to look at.

The combat is satisfying for several reasons, but I think the one I'd like to bring up is the iconic red slices that appear as your blade slashes an enemy, accurately displaying where your attack landed. Combine that with weak points on monsters and it makes for a combat system that feels very deliberate and cool.

Every character feels unique to play as because of their different abilities. Not just attacks, but movement as well. There is some skill overlap of course, so as you play the game and increase your familiarity with the mechanics, you'll get better with every character. So don't hesitate to try them all. Loot is fun to collect and I love that there's alternate outfits and accessories to find in each level.

Overall the game has a very pleasant atmosphere that sucks you in and makes you want to keep existing in its world. A rare sight indeed these days. Of course, you should watch at least a couple seasons of SAO before playing this, as it is a game for the fans.

Speaking of, this game is so good it got me to watch Ordinal Scale and start Alicization as well. I basically wake up every day and put on my metaphorical NerveGear to watch SAO, before fulldiving into this game and experiencing more SAO. Then I go to bed and dream about SAO. This game really makes you FEEL like Kazuto Kirigaya.

review_text:
I loved SGW3, I know it was buggy, but I can live with getting stuck in a rock once in a while or on an elevator in the missile silo in exchange for the amazing open world go-anywhere-you-please-ability. If I wanted to get in my truck and spend 10 minutes driving to the top of a mountain across the valley from the target in order to take a long shot, I could. With this game the "open world-ness" is just an illusion, you are just funneled through the playing field with fences, mine fields, un-climbable rocks and cliffs on either side everywhere you go. If you do happen to find a spot to try to slip away, it immediately gives you a warning message that you have left the area and you have like two seconds to return or you just die.... The AI sucks, half the time the baddies just stand there and let you shoot them all, other times, you will be completely alone, nobody in sight, but then a camera spots you and thirty dudes are instantly on top of you. The other snipers rarely ever fire at you, they spot you from thirty miles away, but then just lay there... violently shaking for some reason.  In the whole game, 99% of the shots were at 200 yards or less. Most of the time the Desert Eagle pistol was the most effective way to clear a scene... The 12 gauges are useless unless you are three feet apart. Again, I loved SGW3, the only thing about this that was better was the ability to blow baddies arms, legs and heads off. I turned the "bullet cam" off right away because even though the footage was cool, it was like you were holding your breath the whole time and when you return to the scope view, you're out of breath and the baddies have all ran away.  I hated it compared to SGW3. 
Dear CI, please make more maps for SGW3, fix the getting-stuck-in-the-terrain bug and add the dismemberment stuff. 
 Thank you.

review_text:
God sim meets Tower defence strategy game. Peaceful townbuilding by day, relentless warfare by night.

I've been following and playing this game for a few years now and have only enjoyed it more as the long awaited achievements were added, as well as new buildings and occupations. Even though my 8 year old laptop chugs along a bit now and can't run it as fast as it used to, we still manage. To date this is one of the few games where I can consistently sit down to play and sink 3+ hours in no problem (and as a mum of a 1 year old currently I do not often get that privilege these days.)

The learning curve is indeed, steep- but you are rewarded for your efforts and boons to your world are carried over time and time again, the more hours you play, the more you learn, the more upgrades you will be gifted from the heavens.

I would love to see even more achievements added someday, I think I'll eventually get through all of these and worry that the traditional "end goal" of surviving a year in every region will never come to fruition. But I can try. Oh how I can try.

review_text:
I've been enjoying it so far, but there are a few things that sort of break the flow of the game itself which I find to be a slight pain to overlook.

The biggest issue is the forced alone story missions. The game encourages you to play with others, but [u] very [/u] often forces your party to split up and handle their own missions, which is really bloody annoying and killing the game for my friends. Do one mission together, 2 more alone; over and over.

Second is how long it takes to unlock any of the characters, which my bothered my friends as we all are forced to play the starting class for 6 hours before getting to touch any other character, and even then, you still don't get to pick.

Third is the bugs. I've had 3 different crashes at seemingly random times for no apparently reason, and also had multiple missions just, decide not to load when they're finished, forcing me to repeat them. You can even use abilities when stuck on the black loading screen, which is odd.

Fifth is the enemy variance. The bosses are pretty interesting, but the enemies are boring as hell, the forced "Kill X with Y element" quests are a pain in the ass, especially if you already setup autogrinding to eat garbage items, as the ones they give you for the quest are destroyed immediately.

Sixth is how spread out the main town feels, the bounty vendors are placed waaaay outside of the town for no reason other than artificially inflating the size of the town to make it seem interesting, and all it does is add 20 extra seconds each way every time you want to do the quests.

Seventh is that you often find notification blips in your menus that can't be cleared and have bugged out, and won't be removed until you reboot the game, namely the cosmetics tab.
Having the Inventory also require you to hover the EXP books every single time to remove the blip is also a stupid decision design-wise.

Eighth is the sheer forgetability of the characters, story, and any of the world building. Everyone is just mashing and holding X to get through dozens of cutscenes and dialogue between every mission, and often during the mission.

Ninth is the fact that there is no option to stop other people from forcibly progressing the area. Needing to make verbal callouts "Are you done here?" while we make sure eveyrone is done exploring, or have claimed their level completion crates, and that other people can literally just stop you from exploring, gathering, or hell, even claiming your level rewards, is just absurd.

[strike]Tenth is that there is no way to track if you have the nodes and crates from the map you're on, you can only see what you can get before you enter a level, then you're blind. No completion options during the mission, no map outside of the minimap, just, run the same level half a dozen times and hope you got them all. [/strike] Developer made me aware of the map.

The gameplay itself is fun, as well as the synergies and levelling perks; but there is a lot wrong with this game that i simply can't recommend it yet until they iron out some of the annoyances that take away from the game. I'll still play a bit more of it, but I'm not sure how much yet.

review_text:
The moral of this game is microtransactions.

You can do everything to level 65 however the game ends at 50 for free characters. After 50, you need to pay around $15 for the next level ship and various other things if you failed to 'spec' your character correctly. In addition, there are about 20-30 ship variations which means to unlock them all on a single character would be very expensive.

End game content is plenty but the role system is broken. Everything revolves around DPS with tanking and support defunct. Especially when some factions seem to just bypass shields entirely.

All in all, it's a broken non-social MMORPG. It'd be better as a solo player game.

review_text:
I enjoyed this game! It has a lot of style and charm and the developers clearly put a lot of passion into it.

The art direction and style of the game is amazing. I love the Y2K aesthetic and everything in the game was just great to look at. The animation is really good too. The different skating and dancing animations are really well done and everything has a good weight and punches out at you.

The core gameplay of skating around and tagging things was fun, and it was always rewarding to get a new tag. I was a little disappointed, however, because I thought there was going to be more mechanical depth to the skating. It's very easy to just keep your combo going forever and I felt like I hit the skill ceiling halfway through the game. None of the challenges of having to beat the other crews or replicating tricks they did were difficult. It's still super fun to just vibe and skate around tagging things though, I just thought it was going to be a little deeper.

Combat was also very shallow and I wish it wasn't in the game, because all it did was make me want to be done with it as quickly as possible so I could get back to skating. The final boss was actually very fun though, because it didn't really use combat and instead made good use of the skating mechanics.

This is just personal preference, but the music was pretty hit or miss for me. A lot of the tracks were just very repetitive and just wasn't really my style.

The story is totally nonsensical and crazy. Not necessarily a bad thing, you just have to roll with the sillyness and you'll at least somewhat enjoy it haha.

Very fun game that's oozing with style. I recommend it!

review_text:
Classic case of a game that hasn't aged well. At all.

Perhaps I'm not the core demographic for physic puzzle games, but I distinctly remember finding games like Angry Birds or Cut the Rope more fun than this title.

The music is fine, graphics cartoonishly pleasing, and gameplay concept simple and effective. However, my main gripes come from the culmination of lackluster features that nearly all titles have nowadays, including recent puzzle games.

- Lack of music/volume/sfx menu 
- Inconsistency of move undo-ing for levels (It's there sometimes, not others, and often doesn't work the way it should)
- Screen is WAY too zoomed in, with no settings to change the window resolution
- The water physics are simply .... indescribable (It's near impossible to tell what's caused by your cursor or the objects themselves)
- Selecting goo balls that constantly move around make it easy for you to grab one you didn't intend, or worse, one that kept your structure up 
- Can't retry a level even if you complete the level unintentionally (OCD Achievement Hunters beware)
- Goo structures fall over each other in layers (Doens't make any sense to me why a structure is able to hang from itself)

[b] (Even though things like sound and screen resolution can be easily fixed with some file and mixer changes, it simply didn't improve the more apparent frustrations I had in the gameplay. So moreso, just a little insult to injury.)[/b]

Call me petty or downright stupid, but playing the same level over and over left me more frustrated than amused due to points such as these. [u]I'll appreciate the pioneering this game had done around a decade ago, but that doesn't mean it's the pinnacle iteration of puzzle games. I'd say it's best to leave the past behind on this one.[/u]

review_text:
Not normally a person that would take the time to write out a review. I work a blue collar job and typically work a seasonal part time/ odd-jobs on the side. This game had a compelling story and combat that was fun. I looked forward to playing it. Very seldom has any game stood out and made me want to make time to play it. Personal context aside; I truly enjoyed this game. It reminded me of crawling through infected zones in the last of us. The cut-scenes play out a lot like the ones in Uncharted. I really liked the main character Jacob he was wonderfully voiced and gave off intellectual trucker vibes. I found the characters and the dialogue to be excellent. Everything flows for the most part smoothly nothing left a bad taste in my mouth or left me confused. Honestly they did a better job than many TV shows. I really enjoyed the sound design; the ambient noise of infected prisoners climbing through vents or in proximity of the player kept me on my toes regardless of if I was in a confrontation or not. The level background music/noise of low bass tones, basement-esc noises, sped up piano and violin tones kept me sharp. Environmental ambiance stacked with the background noise really kept me immersed. I enjoyed the combat a lot though that's probably where the game can feel limited as well. Early - Mid game felt very melee focused. I'm the type to save as much ammo and prioritize inventory space for valuables to max out my gear asap. I felt like I didn't have nearly enough inventory space until about mid game when you get Armour; It increases your inventory space. I stuck with the hand cannon and riot shotgun[first weapons you receive] because when I purchased/unlocked the other weapons in the game it felt like I had no inventory space because each ammo type takes up its own slot. The game seems to prioritize ammo over high dollar components so once you unlock a new weapon, its ammo type starts randomly spawning around the map, it seems to drown out sell-ables. I might not be accurate but that's would it seemed like. I ended up going back to a pre-gun purchase save, and just maxed out my melee weapon and the first 2 guns. Regardless of that I don't feel like that dampened my fun just a minor play-through adjustment. It seems like its better to invest in your arsenal on newgame+ when Callisto credits mean less. Overall I truly enjoyed the story and had a lot of fun playing through the game. 

Negative:
The worst experience I had was when I thought I had lost my main save and 6 hours worth of progress. Ultimately it seemed to be a bug that other users had, had. It still scared me regardless. I wasn't able to load any saves they seemed gone. I played the last checkpoint it had left me from 6 hours ago until I hit a new checkpoint, and once got through it. I checked my loadable saves and everything missing had re-appeared. I reloaded to my true progress. 

The worst frustration I had was at the end of the game. There's a minor boss fight in a server room that one taps you once half its health is depleted. before that point you can tank 2 hits on normal difficulty. ultimately I just got good, won the fight and moved on. I just found this frustrating because this game doesn't present the consistent challenge in the way that you would expect to die consistently like in other titles. The final boss was slightly similar once your health bar gets low there's an enemy that crawls into the arena. If it gets close enough it will trigger a death cut-scene just by being in close proximity to you, not damaging you; that felt  more like fighting the game mechanics thing than a skill issue. GTTOD has a decent foundation. The guns and shooting are responsive and satisfying. The visual design of the game is unique but sadly not for everybody. The soundtrack fits well in here as well. It runs quite well too.

No matter how high I jump or dash, I still get hit. It's quite a challenge to "charge up" the door to progress to the next level.

Then I tinkered around with the Settings and managed to make it look "playable" to my eyes. I'd definitely encourage others to tweek the Graphics settings a bit if the default settings aren't pleasing. However, even after setting everything to what felt somewhat comfortable, it's still taxing on my eyes to find my bearings and shoot at enemies. The colours are just way too saturated.

* Parkour. I like the idea of being able to wall run during the combat but not every single time before I make it to the first level. The parkour (especially pressing "Shift" to jump high) is not always consistent and if you fall down, you have to start again. Not really fun.

review_text:
I really, really want to love this game.  The mechanics and design are wonderful, the Japanese voice acting is great, the Edo period is always a fun one to run around in, and it feels like Commandos: Sengoku Jidai Edition.

The problem is that the camera is often the worst and most persistent enemy in the game, camera controls are bound exclusively to the mouse (because there are too many keybinds for everything else to bind the camera to something responsive like WASD), and the biggest issue?  Lack of a pause function.

There is a "shadow mode" function that lets you issue an order to multiple units to execute them all simultaneously but in practice I found it to be virtually useless because it doesn't pause or even slow down time, and it was very rare that I had multiple units that would complete their task (typically killing or otherwise incapacitating a guard) at the same time because different units move at different speeds and have different animations (Yuki takes much longer to kill someone than does Mugen, for example, and Aiko moves much faster than Hanzo.)

There's also the potential problem that this is basically Save Scum: The Game.  The devs have explicitly said that save scumming is part of the intended design... yet have also said that they didn't put a pause function into the game because it wouldn't fit the deisgn... presumably because it would break the flow or feeling of the game?  So pausing the game to issue a single command to your dudes breaks the flow of the game, while quickloading literally every 5-10 seconds doesn't?  I mean... if they say so, I guess.

There's also the issue of the game having guards and NPCs with Skyrim levels of stupidity and obliviousness, and NPCs rigorously do the same thing in an infinite, unchanging loop.  They do not react to the world around them in an even remotely believable way - a rock randomly falls on someone and after an exclamation of "I noticed that!" and about 30 seconds of "search mode" behavior, they return to what they were doing before... even if the rock just fell on someone that, as far as the mission narrative is concerned, is an important person and not some bottom-level mook.

The game HAS to be this way because the developers apparently refused to try putting in a pause function or anything like it that would allow for more tactical complexity and more detailed AI behavior.  Because it might take you thirty tries to execute a plan (because you have to issue the commands in real time and wrangle with the camera the whole way through), everything needs to be in a constant state of stasis - guards patrol the exact same paths (which are typically just a simple loop, nothing complex, and never a series of different loops or paths), civilians pick up the same pile of wood and bring it to the same location at which point it vanishes and they go retrieve another identical pile of wood, an important NPC you need to steal documents from always goes and prays at the same shrine by himself for the same amount of time at the exact same time interval even as you're gradually picking off his guards and dumping their corpses in the bushes one by one every time he leaves the immediate area.

I really do want to love this game.  It's clear a lot of work went into it and the production values are absolutely fantastic.  But it's hamstrung by the developers making a staggeringly stupid decision to not allow any sort of slow-mo or pause function into the game.  By refusing to go down that path, they're forced to dumb down the rest of the game to compensate and as a result the entire thing is badly limited.  I cannot recommend this game because of that.

review_text:
As an avid fan of Act Raiser from my childhood days of yore on the SNES, this game is it's true spiritual successor and does what the devs could only dream to have done. It has many similarities to popular titles such as Dwarf Fortress, but does not suffer many of the same flaws. In DF, for example, you have highly specialized dwarves that feel terrible to individually lose if you want to play the game with combat on. Exploit the game with danger rooms and trap corridors, or don't bother dealing with combat. Corrupted biomes? Flat out forget it lest you deal with flying buffalo fur terrifying your dwarves into starvation.

Rise to Ruins gets the combat angle right. The game on Nightmare difficulty is highly punishing, and dooming words is a regular occurence (60 some hours of play in, and I still haven't got through my first winter.) However, successfully navigating it feels extremely good and the challenge is not as static as the tower defense angle shown in the trailer. Carving out map control is essential for being able to manage the tougher seasons like Winter, but the game doesn't let you do it for free. Settling up mazes is a novelty -- you'll have things flying over your walls, elementals blasting down your front door, and blood moons raining fire and mayhem into your town proper.

The end result is a fantastic world simulator with very unique maps, some which seem nice to embark on initially and others where it feels like you need to succeed on an easy map and feed the harder map to even stand a chance. God powers and cullis gates at first feel overpowered, but as you make it later in the game you realize it's all extremely well balanced and everything comes with a cost.. Balancing all the different environmental needs and roguelite elements of the city management along with the intensity of the encroaching corruption is extremely difficult to manage but very rewarding to conquer. Not once have I felt like any of my failed settlements were a result of anything other than me needing to play better.

Simply put, if you want Dwarf Fortress smashed together with Act Raiser and the potential for a very challenging world building simulator, this game's for you. The Dev is a one man team who clearly cares immensely about the game and has a solid head on his shoulders for gameplay, aesthetic, and balance. Don't pass this one up if you're a fan of the genre.

I was extremely close to leaving a positive review but there is just too many things that make the game sub-par. The graphics are the only thing the game has going for it. The story and weapons are passable but the combat is easily the worst part about the game and ruins a lot of the horror and immersion that should be the most important thing for a game like this.

There is no general dodge button, you can only dodge a single enemy that you are engaged with, and there is no indicator of off-screen attacks. Why are these monsters waiting in turns to attack you? The whole thing is just a mess.

review_text:
I bought The Callisto Protocol on 85% sale for 8,84€, and here are my "no spoiler" thoughts on it after 3 hours...

Firstly... Callisto Protocol is a game that tries REALLY hard to mimic Dead Space in many ways, to a point where you might actually Google whether or not it is the same developer.

Most bad reviews you read, will call it "B-tier Dead Space", or criticize it because it's "not as good as Dead Space", and see the differences as a negative, rather than trying to rate it for what it actually tries to be. The main two differences between this game and Dead Space, is that combat is entirely different, and this game feels A LOT more linear.

And because of those two differences, people will see them as negatives because the only thing they can think is "is it Dead Space?"... Which is too bad, since Callisto Protocol is a pretty solid game that holds its own.

[b]THE GAME IS LINEAR[/b]

This is a big difference between Callisto Protocol and Dead Space, since Callisto Protocol is VERY linear, and has you basically go from A to B without much deviation. Same goes from exploring, which there is very little off besides a few "secrets", that you can find easily by simply checking out the area.

However... Callisto Protocol being linear isn't a bad thing, since it is obvious that the game tries to come off as a bit more of a "cinematic experience", than Dead Space did. Basically it half'n-half feels like playing a movie.

[b]"COMBAT IS BAD"[/b]

If you are looking for a challenging "survival horror game", then you might need to amp up the difficulty a bit in this game, since enemies basically just attack you one at a time, even when there are multiple around you. And this is obviously done to make the melee combat feel a bit more forgiving and satisfying. And combat DOES feel satisfying, but some might find it too easy.

While you DO have guns in Callisto Protocol, the combat is mainly focused around melee combat, with you dodging or blocking enemy attacks. This is very different from Dead Space, where combat is more centered around shooting.

The melee combat feels VERY satisfying in this game, but some might find it a bit too repetitive, since dodging and blocking is "half-automatic", where basically you just need to hold down a button, and not "tapping it at the right moment". 

So all in all, combat isn't bad. In fact, it's VERY satisfying. If anyone says it is bad, it's because they can't refrain from comparing it to Dead Space combat.

I personally enjoy the combat because I see it for what it is, and not what it's not.

[b]IS IT WORTH BUYING?[/b]

On the 8,84€ sale I got it on, it was an amazing buy. However the 58,99€ price tag it normally has, might be a bit steep.

The game IS good, but apparently people claim it takes 7 hours to beat, and because of how linear it is, it doesn't have much replay value. So I recommend getting it on sale. :) Not necessarily as cheap as me, but at least 25% off is a good price.

It's OK for the hour it takes, but I'm glad it didn't go on much longer than that.

Nice for an afternoon if you like the genre, maybe especially fun as a "co-op" playthrough with an SO or a kid, but really not much to write home about.

The visuals are amazing, as many have pointed out, but beyond that, this game also includes excellent level design, smooth playability, and a story that uses your ignorance of what's happening around you to not only ramp up the tension and suspense, but to also allow your own imagination to fill in the gaps in a very personal way.  While the lack of hand-holding does make it more challenging to understand what you need to do sometimes, it's not unlike older puzzle games like Myst.  Eventually you'll figure it out and it feels rewarding when you do, not frustrating.  

The length of the game (8-10 hours) feels about right, and the quality in the visual and sound design makes every second feel like a AAA experience.  I struggled to come up with any really significant shortfalls.  Perhaps an explanation of some of core mechanics, like healing, at the very beginning would've been helpful, but not absolutely necessary, and I will note that there aren't really any difficulty settings, so you get what you get.  Despite paltry opportunities to reload and recharge my health, I still made it through eventually, and I don't consider myself an expert gamer.  

From an accessibility standpoint, I think this game will be fine as long as you have access to an acceptable control device.  I played with keyboard and mouse, but I'm sure the experience with controller would've been excellent as well.  Precision controls and timing didn't seem to be required in any sections.  There's no dialogue, and other than hearing enemies coming (which you'll usually see anyway), sound is not required for deaf players.

Overall, it's a gross, slimy, confusing experience, and I really really enjoyed every second of it.  I highly recommend this, if you can stomach it.

overall presentation is still rough around the edges, and sometimes AI companions are annoyingly glitchy in their path finding, and I needed to go back and help them navigate around obstacles such as dead bug bodies to continue following me to next objective.

even though this game is currently definitely not perfect, it's got SO much potential if Offworld keep fine tuning and responding to constructive feedback from fans, and fans keep supporting this game. 

You can tell the small team of Offworld developers are passionate about the Starship Troopers IP and this game is a nice and faithful adaptation of the IP (especially the original 1997 live adaptation).

Do your part and support this game!

review_text:
I had low expectations for this game going into it, but it has still managed to disappoint and frustrate me before I had even made it past the tutorial mission.
I'm left handed and as such need my movement input swapping over to the right thumbstick, however something so basic as this I'm not able to do. There is a "left handed" option in the settings but this does absolutely nothing as far as I can tell. I can usually get around older games that don't have this (Pavlov for example) by going into the steamvr bindings and swapping the thumbsticks around. However this game seems to have the thumbsticks locked to the same binding so they can't be edited. This is the main reason that I find this game unacceptable, especially since it's predecessor Arizona Sunshine had this ability built in.
The advanced reload A.K.A manual reload of the weapons seems like an afterthought as it doesn't play well with the Oculus Touch controllers. Either I have to send my reload hand way past my gun hand or my controllers just bump into each other and only insert the mag half way into the gun which immediately drops the mag when I let go instead of finishing the reload for me. How can something so basic as this to a shooting game be missed?
Also the game seems to pick and choose which settings it wants to be set permanently. By this I mean I can change the settings to how I like them (mostly) but then reboot the game to find some of those settings have returned to their default setting.
The graphics are ok, but only a touch better than Arizona Sunshine which considering how old that game is now I honestly expected a little better.
I could have looked past all of this if it hadn't been for the lack of right thumbstick movement. With so many basic features absent from this game I really don't find it worth my time. Refunded.

review_text:
Edit 12/26/23

When I first downloaded the game and saw it was ~2gb I was genuinely surprised. How did they manage to fit so much content into such a small package? (btw JSRF compressed is about the same amount, maybe a little more)

....

Then I played the game. There is no content. This game was obviously made for the switch first and everyone else second. It sucks that consoles are what holds games back from their true potential nowadays. And after sitting on the game for a while, modding it (which did improve my perception of the gameplay) and beating it, I have come to the conclusion that I am still right.

I remember when some of the first trailers about this game were coming out back in 21 and they were looking for a voice actress to act as an analogue for DJ Prof. K... They used her for 1 trailer and did nothing else. I really expected a sort of narrator or something similar which would have added some excitement to the story but nope. Yes I am aware that JSR had minimal voice acting but I strongly feel that since this game heavily relies on its story element, it needed that extra assist in the voice department. The same 3 sounds for each character just doesn't cut it. Assets are constantly reused and the game is boring by the third level.

This game is a sad, sad reincarnation of a fantastic series that thankfully is being revived by SEGA. If there's one thing this game did right, it's make SEGA realize the massive mistake they made abandoning Jet Set Radio. 

One thing I did like about the game is the pattern-specific graffiti, that was a cool idea. One thing I absolutely hate in this game is the police system, its not exciting to be chased by the cops, its a major annoyance. (Luckily mods fixed that)

I like Team Reptile, and I think they absolutely nailed the cel-shaded art style. However, a game of this genre shouldn't feel as flat as an arcadey fighting game like LLB does, and so in this aspect, they failed. 

If I had to give a rating for this game out of 10, I'd give it a 5. So buy it half off and have fun.

Or just download an emulator and play Jet Set Radio Future and have some real fun!

review_text:
Let me start by saying that, from the beginning, I have been deliberately ignoring the criticism towards this game. I wanted to like it very badly. And don't get me wrong: the art and atmosphere of the game are amazing and worth experiencing (although not for the full price). But there are too many things that do not work. The combat is terrible; clunky and, most of the times, unavoidable (stealth is barely non-existent: you cannot crouch and the game is very linear, corridor-like). The checkpoint system could be improved (even if previous patches already worked on the issue). On top of that, the game has (a few, but important) bugs, like elevators that drop you to "the void" and make you start from the last checkpoint. All in all, I feel sad, because the world is amazing but the gaming experience unpleasant. Therefore, I cannot endorse this game. Many people might enjoy it due to its theme and environment, but I don't think this experience is for everyone.

EDIT: I have fully completed the game. If you really love horror, you get a big discount and you don't mind dealing with the aforementioned issues, I would recommend it. After getting used to it, I'd say I enjoyed finishing it. Still, not for everyone.

It's incredibly easy to lose your time playing this game, and it's a game that, once you stop, you want to pick back up ASAP. 

Although it is not officially licensed by the NHL, downloading all the updated rosters and facepacks takes little more than 5 minutes, and is well worth the download. It makes the game much more enjoyable as you get to have players on your team that actually exist in the NHL.

Being able to decide what your entire staff will consist of, from scouts to coaches to freaking physio guys makes the game incredibly indepth. The addition of being able to adjust specific coaching styles to specific players, as well as being able to adjust how each and every line performs night after night is incredibly indepth and rewarding as you lead your team towards stanley cup glory! (or whatever other trophy the team you chose is qualified to win, because you can basically manage every professional hockey team on the planet.)

This is essentially a much more indepth, almost overwhelming version of EA's NHL GM Modes. Once you get past the learning curve, you'll see no reason to give EA $70 every year for essentially an updated roster pack. While EA's NHL games are losing features, this game is gaining more and more features every 2 weeks or so. Give your money to this team instead of EA, because they're converting your $17 into a much better game at a much lower cost than any of the recent NHL games. 

This game will likely cost you all of your free time, and may even dip into your... non-free time. 10/10

review_text:
You and everyone you love in this game will die.

Oh, and all your animals too. If you can cope with that, then the game is fun. As somebody who struggles with depression, the game is kind of a downer. But I'd be lying if I said I didn't enjoy it. I just had to take breaks, as the funerals started piling up and all the cute guys I was interested in earlier start to walk around looking like they're one breath away from the grave. Sure, I know that's Life, but I play games to get away from Life. 

On the plus side, I was pleased to see that this colonial village was pretty open-minded for the time period and had no problem with me courting another man. In fact, the first marriage announcement I received was for a same-sex couple. I thought, "Oh, my God! (Yay, verily?) There's another gay couple in town! I should go meet them with a casserole."

It turned out, we weren't all that rare. Pretty much EVERY marriage announcement after that was for same-sex couples. I'd stumbled into the colonial equivalent of Fire Island. (Old man reference. Look it up, whippersnappers.) The next issue was, how are all these gay male and female couples supposed to have children without committing adultery? The game doesn't have poly relationships (sadly), nor does it have an orphanage. I gather if you have diseases turned on, you can wipe out half the adult population with smallpox and give yourself a pool of orphans to choose from. I... did not choose this option. 

Fear not! Our little LGBTQ+ colony also had mpreg! I got knocked up twice and wandered around town holding my belly, passing several other men who were likewise with child. In fact, even among the few straight couples in town, it wasn't unheard of for the man to be the one who got pregnant. Ah, the wonders of 17th Century medicine!

I swear, I did not select the "Children of Dorothy" checkbox under options. Fortunately, the game does have other options a player might find useful, from whether or not food rots to whether or not people get sick. You can even turn off aging, though I'm not sure if that prevents others in the village from aging. 

At any rate, I'm enjoying it and still haven't given up after 47 hours. My biggest issue (apart from the "everyone is dying" thing) is how fast things rot in my inventory. I wanted to have it on, since it would be ridiculous to have fruit remain fresh for months, but on average everything rots after just a few days. This makes it impossible to keep basic supplies on hand, so when someone asks you to bake them a pumpkin pie, you'll have everything you need except sugar, and all your pumpkins are guaranteed to turn to mush before you can find someone who has sugar in stock. But as I said, I can always turn that off, I suppose.

It's a cool concept well done but the player base is there. 9/10 you'll wait several minutes for a match with 1 real person plus bots, but you never get a run of matches. Whoever is actually playing this is only staying around for 1 match apparently, because it's several minutes more for another match. And the matches are only about 2 minutes long, so you are spending way more time waiting than playing.

I hate to say it, but this needed to be FTP, because it will die with no players.

There are things they could have done to mitigate this. Let me play through the solo challenges whilst I'm waiting, instead of making me leave the queue to do this. Make a live lobby where I can just drive around and practice. Put me into a match with all bots if the waiting time is more than 30 seconds.

Ultimately, I don't understand who this is marketed to. Somebody with an attention span of less than 2 minutes, because that is how long the matches are, but who also has patience to wait around doing nothing for several minutes in between. Who is that person? And this is why I'm giving it a thumbs down. I would have liked to be positive to encourage more players but it's just fundamentally pointless.

The game would have been 1000% better if it was just offline against the bots for fun instead of a FTP-like experience with but an upfront cost. As such this does not belong in my library.

I guess you can say the game have an Isekai story, but sadly it is so simplistic and it have an OBVIOUS AS FUCK villain that you won't bother with the details. Well, to be fair it has a plot twist that could have been interesting…but let be honest, we are here for the action and the cute girls.
 
So it is metroidvania with a classic save system! Normal to God save! YES! I like those so much! No bullshit autosaves and collecting your exp again trying to not die again.
 
The start feels a little hard at first, but believe me when I say this: you will end up changing different play styles to suit your needs non-stop because it is so much fun! My earlier build was using a fast axe and a shield which with each block I healed myself, then I switched to magical swords and healing spells with armor/weapons filling my mana pool over and over again,oh and a demon bear doll that when it gets hit I get mana back.
 
Getting back on track, another thing I liked a lot was the nice art of the characters when you had a chance to talk to them. I have big praise for some specific monster girls. My favorite from all of them is Jun. Ironically her reveal was also the biggest plot twist as well.
 
A big negative I had (aside from the forgettable story) was the map. It is detailed enough to show you where you are going, painfully bland when you want to reach specific items. Also you can fail a mission if you are not careful, a very important one.
 
If you are a metroidvania fan who also wants an extra challenge managing your loot and gear, and cute anime girls, "Lost Ruins" is the perfect choice.

8/10

review_text:
10 out of 10? Not even close.
If circumstances were different, I would give this game a neutral rating. 

The best parts of this game are straight copies from either JSR or JSRF. It wouldn't be a bad thing if there were improvements over older games or some new ideas, but there isn't anything worthwhile. 
Ok, maybe a trick system is an improvement. And also the addition of skates, BMXs, and the ability to run. The combat is new, but it's awful.

BRC copies style, mechanics, and levels from the JSR and JSRF, but somehow makes them worse. Levels are now bigger, but they're also bland and empty. A lot of space is being wasted, and there isn't a good flow to them. 
The main goal is to tag graffiti, but there is a lot of filler in between. You need to go from point A to point B to meet a guy, who will tell you to meet another guy. Rinse and repeat. 

The tagging system is similar to JSR with a small minigame. However, in JSR, there wasn't any animation when you tag small graffiti, but there is in BRC, which ruins the flow and momentum.

BRC came out 20 years after the JSRF, but I would argue that JSRF looks better visually. They copied the cell shaded of JSRF, but everything looks empty and dead. There are hardly any pedestrians or NPCs walking around the streets, while JSRF featured large crowds of people on the original Xbox. JSRF also had better VFX, for example, when you use boost.
The controls are better than JSR but pretty much the same as JSRF. Maybe a touch less floaty.

Music is subjective, and some of the tracks in BRC are good and fit the overall vibe. However, there's a weird choice to have the same tracks play over and over again while you're in the same area. After a while, it became grating and I had to turn off the music. 

I don't put JSR or JSRF on a pedestal. I know those games were flawed even at release. JSR controls were super janky and floaty; there was a bunch of filler and badly designed levels, like the sewers. JSRF dropped all the challenging aspects of the game. Despite all of that, those games were cool and unique. BRC is not cool or unique; it's a copy of the older games. That would be fine because there hasn't been a sequel to JSRF, and there are no other games like it, but I feel like we deserved better.

Here, you have to obtain the metaknowledge of exactly what to do in the game to have a chance your second time through, which could mean like 15-20 hours wasted, and then the exact same amount of hours spent retracing your exact steps up to a point.

Although there were a lot of things that were left to be desired. Combat could have been more complex as the gameplay gets repetitive and does not have enough depth.  I like the idea of melee, but instead of just holding the stick one direction maybe they should have added more aspect like having the enemies swing from different angles and you had to match up the dodge direction.  They also could have done more with timing of dodging and blocking for more perks and advantages.  Combat gets a little cheap as it is obviously designed for more one on one battles but later on fighting multiple enemies at once, particularly ones with ranged attacks can be frustrating. Game also could have used more puzzles in order to break up the gameplay.  From a "Survival Horror" standpoint I didn't really feel like I was struggling for resources to survive which could have also added to the tension, it mainly is just action with horror elements.  One that note, the horror tends to be just going for the shock and gore factor, seeming like it is just trying to be as disgusting as possible instead of actually building up suspense and horror.

Overall, average game that is ok if you are a fan of Survival Horror action games, but coming from Dead Space left a lot to be desired. 6/10.
