review_text:
[h1]Bizarre and Brutal, it's an impossible sell for everyone but its unique charm absolutely has appeal[/h1]

First I'll state by saying that you do not have to have played the first game to understand anything here, it's something of a reboot/remake that focuses on only one of the routes from the original game which is fine with some elements of being an actual sequel. 
Point is, it's completely fine to start with this one.

Onto the main stuff, this game's one of the more notable ones I've played, incorporating time-management and survival gameplay to make an experience that made me never want to waste a second or slip up and waste precious resources.

[h1]It may sound basic but it's when things go wrong that Pathologic shines[/h1]

Without going into spoilers, depending on certain factors like the day, decisions made, people neglected, etc.
The townsfolk get put in danger, all those people you get introduced to can and probably will die without intervention.
The hard part is managing your resources, like weapons, food, medicine and most assuredly... Time!

With each passing day, times grows shorter and shorter, at first you may not notice it but as the days go on, you'll find that the game ain't lying. Your hunger depletes more rapidly, you find longer events may not be worth the time investment, and each day brings new problems that helped me understand the general gameplay systems by force.

Things only get worse as you'll need resources to make it through the day, and as the days go on, things get worse.
Stockpiling is a massive boon but can be hard in practice, looting houses is a mixed bag of results for a variety of reasons but bartering can get you far.
Trading for items and figuring out what people want can be the difference between life and death, make use of it.

[h1]Life is unfair, and that's (mostly) alright[/h1]

Despite the survival gameplay being harsh and time being hard to manage (you can't be everywhere and do everything), things can be relatively managable, but sometimes the game will decide to mess with you.
Sometimes people are put in danger or straight up killed based on chance, while there's stuff you can do to mitigate that, odds are you'll run out of luck eventually and have to live with it [spoiler]or savescum but please don't[/spoiler].
 
While certain interactions will change, you're never really outright punished for a characters death, life goes on and you will make it to the end so long as you persevere, but there is one lasting consequence you might end up cursing, and that's your own death.
Outside of day 1, the town remembers how many times you've died, regardless of reloading, and will punish you as it sees fit.
From lowered max health to worse loot, it can only make your life harder, but it's NOT the end of things.
The punishments start out tame and like I said, the town remembers, while it's mostly the punishments that will remind you of your death, there are other reminders that are decently interesting to encounter.

[h1]Speaking of the town[/h1]

An incredibly odd mix of rustic environments colliding with almost cult-esque themes.
Most of the houses look normal, if a bit copy/paste, but then you'll spot structures that defy the laws of gravity, massive towers meant to house the work population and the scenic steppe belonging to the local tribe with it's "odd" people that isn't even taking into account their culture and exploitation.

This is the thing that ultimately got my attention, and while you'll see a lot of what it has to offer pretty quickly, there's still info waiting to be uncovered which makes it interesting.

[h1]But there are some downright bad comments to make[/h1]

Combat is quite frankly just bad, it's incredibly easy to stunlock most enemies to the point where I would say my preferred weapon was my bare fists, but realistically it was my legs as running away is mad easy. Considering how combat is frowned upon by the local population and knives/guns can drain my health from full to nothing in a second, I'd much rather just leave it alone whenever possible.

While I think the death system is very cool, there's little reason not to reload before you think something goes wrong as, when you die, it just boots you back to your previous save anyway, so you might just be in a very similar spot that lead to your death without any escape other loading even further back.

While I did want to keep the town population alive, I'd be lying if I said I cared for even half this cast, as most times I try and interact with them they just don't have any dialogue, usually needing an event to trigger conversation, this makes wandering around the town feel downright pointless at times, especially as certain places become empty as people start dying.

Thirst feels kind of pointless, it's rather easy to maintain and to my understanding, never decreases past a certain threshold, making it the only meter you don't actually have to manage for survival outside of stockpiling your sprint duration.

[h1]If you're interested, go into it with the expectation that this is something different and will use its difficulty to try and sell a setting instead of appealing to a larger demographic[/h1]

It's hard, but fair, and personally I thought the experience was well worth it.
It might be boring, stressful or annoying at times but it works FAR more often than it doesn't.
If you're looking for something different, would highly recommend.

You run around shooting things that used to be people but are so messed up that they aren't really anymore. While you yourself have to use the same "plasmids" they do in order to survive against these monsters, you need to be just as strong if not more so! With these new powers you can shoot lightning out of your hands and other fun things. The concept of big daddy and little sister encounters I think are pretty cool. review_text:
Scorn is probably going to be a pretty hard game to recommend for most people, because the thing it struggles the most with is actually being, yenno, a [i]videogame[/i]. It kind of meanders between being an environmental puzzle game, and a survival horror - but with such scant gameplay, it's often even labelled a walking simulator. Although at least in those moments of downtime, the horror dressing still poses a persistent sense of tension and threat.

But with Scorn, if you get it then you GET it. It's primarily going to appeal to the kinds of people who have taken one look at its presentation - the promotional art, screenshots, videos, and so on - and decided that they [i]need[/i] to experience this, no matter what form it takes. Unlike the gameplay, which can leave much to be desired, it completely delivers elsewhere in its style and atmosphere. Scorn is absolutely a triumph of artistic direction and execution.

A fairly short experience, my playtime here covered two somewhat leisurely playthroughs. If you're into more artsy gameplay experiences, and are keen on the idea of some kind of gruesomely interactive artpiece experience (in the style of greats like H.R. Giger or Zdzisław Beksiński), then Scorn is going to be right up your alley. But whilst the puzzles can get you thinking, and the combat encounters can keep you on your toes, those who require a more robust and well-rounded gameplay experience will probably want to give this a miss.

★★★★✰

I have never felt contempt for a game since F3AR. If The Callisto Protocol was intended to be a spiritual successor to Dead Space, it failed in every way.

The gameplay boils down to: Jacob has to open a door, so you press E to open it... and it plays an animation of Jacob preparing to pry the door open, prompting you to press E again to have Jacob open the door. Or Jacob opens a door by playing an unskippable animation of Jacob opening a power box and cutting a cable. These things can happen in sequence. Sometimes in that order exactly. Back to back even.

Oh and sometimes you get to fight enemies. Very poorly.
The combat is: hold left or right, hold right or left, attack enemy. Rinse and repeat. Such interesting and engaging gameplay.
Then they introduce tentacles and enemy mutation, and it FUCKING sucks. NOTHING QUITE LIKE EVERY SINGLE ENEMY DOING IT IMMEDIATELY AFTER INTRODUCING IT.

Then the game deleted my save 6 hours in. Forcing me to go through it all over again.

I cannot in good conscience recommend this game for anything less than the price of free. If anything they should pay you to play the game. Though even THAT is a stretch.

Edit 8/24/24:
It deleted my save again. Fuck this game.

review_text:
A modern masterpiece, one that is sadly overlooked. My usual format for Pathologic 2 doesn't quite work here, because it's a game unlike anything I've ever played before, apart from my brief go at the original Pathologic of course.

Pathologic 2 is essentially a remake of 1. But even then calling it a simple remake is doing a disservice to both games, as it earns the 2 in its title due to some clever narrative motifs. It's a do-over, a take two of the first game on many interesting levels, thus you won't need to play Pathologic 1 to enjoy 2.

On the surface, Pathologic 2 is a survival game with elements of horror built on top of immersive sim design; it's a game that makes you uneasy, dreading the challenges you're about to face, fearing for the fates of the characters you love and constantly pressuring you to look after yourself as you survive a truly terrible plague. How you go about surviving the harsh town on the Gorkhon or whether you should use your medical skills to find a cure for such a terrible foe that beset the people is entirely up to you, freedom of choice but almost every choice you make has great consequences.

Everything is a resource; your health, your needs, your reputation, your crafting items, your weapons, your common folk and even your time is all a resource, a currency even. You're always having to trade something off to do something else, you will never be able to do everything so you need to manage everything wisely, plan well ahead of time and choose who should live even if it means someone else has to die. 

The story, world building, characters, etc are all absolutely phenomenal - the writing alone in the story was more than enough to keep me hooked on what's going on and that writing is so good, so well thought out, so meaningful that almost everything everyone says has some hidden meaning. Small inconsequential details almost always culminate into some major revelation, giving you an insight in what characters think even if they don't say it out loud - the game kept me constantly reading between the lines and even then it still managed to surprise me where every big story moment hit as hard as it should have.

The game's systems allows for some great emergent storytelling with the characters who can die, some huge arcs can be completely missed if you neglect others, and seemingly normal conversations can hit so much harder when the plague takes those who you live the most, allowing for some really emotional and impactful moments that other games simply don't have. The game's treatment of important characters dying in the most uneventful way possible, treating them as just another statistic of dead townsfolk, just twists the knife in your heart ever deeper.

Sure there are some issues; performance leaves a lot to be desired, some animations are straight up not very good to say the least and it is technically an unfinished game. But elements other people see as flaws such as the janky combat, the punishing difficulty and such are totally intentional - because you are Artemy Burakh; a healer, not a fighter. Your job to keep the sick treated, to find out how to beat the plague and to save as many lives as possible. The game even makes a remark multiple times to not get into fights and to take good care of yourself as much as possible, combat should only be an absolute last resort option to keep yourself alive or if you manage to get the jump on your enemies via stealth or stocked up on powerful firearms to get much needed supplies. But even then you will spend resources, you will have to repair those weapons, bandage up your wounds, etc, and all of that can cost precious other resources, reputation and, most importantly, time.

Is it an unfair game? Yes, absolutely. But don't let that dissuade you from playing Pathologic 2, because that struggle is built into the core systems and even the storytelling, and most importantly the presentation of that storytelling. It takes some incredibly clever, weird and meta turns in how it presents its narrative and "the point" of what Pathologic 2 is trying to convey to the audience - which is you, the player. And like I said, the story alone is absolutely worth the trials and tribulations ahead because the pay offs of those arduous build-ups is always worth it, every single time.

Honestly, I can gush all day about this amazing game, if you have a friend who talks your ear off about Pathologic 2, then just know there's a VERY good reason why they do, because I honestly can't recommend it enough. It really is that incredible, so much so it's easily in my top 10 games of all time, I'm already excited to do a replay to see how differently things can play out if I approach everything in different ways. 

Even at full price I strongly recommend you play Pathologic 2, there's a ton of game to sink your teeth into with about 25-35 hours for a first playthrough and it is filled to the brim with incentives to replay. And if you find it too tough then don't despair, because the game allows you to tweak as many elements as you could possibly with some of the best difficulty customisation I've ever seen in a game, you can't get rid of that challenge entirely but it is approachable to many people. And can also be made so much more dread-inducing to veterans of the game, if you're a glutton for punishment.

review_text:
This would actually be a solid 5/10 or maybe even 6/10 game if the execution was decent, but the game is overall of poor quality.
I will not include the story in my rating as I think it's irrelevant and almost non-existent in this title.

there's a couple of things that I like in this game, and it's the pretty decent equipment variety and side objectives/challenges, especially bounties, some of which have unique scenarios that keep things fresh. but that's all that's going for the game.

My biggest problem with this game is how clunky everything you do feels. Jumping, climbing, placing gadgets, throwing knives, ADS-ing etc. all feels off, and all of it has that very awkward split second where you feel like you can move on but the animation is not done yet. I think the biggest offender here are the throwing knives, which take 7 business days to allow another input in.
Another huge problem the game has is the AI and its hivemind like behaviour, where ALL of the enemies in the area suddenly know my location. What's weird is there are aspects that indicate some work has been done to make a proper AI for a stealth game, like a delayed alert state spread or enemies investigating bodies alone before alerting others, but it feels like the system was rushed and/or cut short.
The balance of weapons and mods is also atrocious, there's no reason not to slap a suppressor and a special mag on your heavy sniper rifle. Mobility is a cool stat, but it's not enough to deter people from using heavy SRs.

Overall, the game has a lot of problems that cripple it on every step of the way, souring the whole experience which could've been a not so bad casual shooter to boot up from time to time.
I'm guessing the game was on a strict schedule or just rushed in general because it feels like it desperately needs another month or two of development at the very least.

review_text:
Fun game, with some of the best player housing I've ever seen in an MMO. It's worth checking out for C-Spaces alone (you get one immediately and for free), and the constant weekly stream of little things to do is also pretty fun. 

NGS isn't perfect, no, but coming from another MMO where everyone waits six months between paltry content updates and the developers are cheered on for it (and also your house explodes if you ever leave), this is a nice change of pace! Especially since there's no subscription fee...

Complaints about the gacha aspects are understandable, but you can often buy those same items on the player shop from other players. Yes, they're expensive, but at least it's possible. You can't say the same for most other MMOs with cash shops. There hasn't been a point yet where I've felt like I HAVE to buy something. Even Premium Set just feels more like a bonus than a requirement, as you often get short-term passes to unlock the player shop, extra storage, that sort of thing.

NSG definitely isn't for everything, and there are gaps in the content that I'd like to see filled. Some randomized dungeons similar to the missions in Base PSO2 would be really fun, and I kind of agree with the people who say that not everything should drop the same items everywhere. You should have reasons to grind different content! Still, having options is nice, so there's good and bad with that idea. The gear stuff and augments can also feel pretty overwhelming at first, but it's really not that bad.

If you're looking for an MMO or even something to just kind of hang out in, play with outfits, and build stuff in C-Spaces, I think you should give it a try!

Company: "Meh, close enough, I'm tired of working on this"

In general this game is average. The use of CryEngine and trying to make this game to be a Triple-A game is just that; a try. I don't make video games and can imagine the creative process and development take time and at the end of the day you need to make money as a company... BUT this game cut a bunch of corners to make it out the door and the experience is far from great. It's like they wanted to make FarCry for sniping but basically just sh*t the bed. Needs more quality assurance.

First, the Pros:
- The sniping feels good, you get a silenced rifle from the start and don't have to worry that you need to upgrade to it like in various other games. You need to adjust for wind and distance, hold your breath, and the gratuitous kill cam will be your reward for patience.
- Main missions along with challenges, rivals and bounties help add play time for the completion-ists out there.
- Fast travel in the map is useful but limited

Cons:
- Good lord are there many bugs I've experienced: NPCs floating mid air, falling between two things and can't get out, placing C4 and then can't get your weapons back cause system thinks you're still placing C4, you complete an objective in a mission and then that objective is still on the screen and marked for you to complete, ... the list goes on
- The save system: plain sucks. This is basically checkpoints, find the right one and you can save. This isn't some old limited system that requires a memory card. The user should either be allowed to save anywhere or be able to load from some list of recent (checkpoint) saves. This bit me quite hard a few times as I was trying to finish a mission a certain way (like using only a knife or not setting off alarms). I messed something up and reloaded last checkpoint and found myself halfway across the map once and the other finding out that my mistake was retained and I basically would have to redo the mission.
- For some reason your secondary weapon and sidearm are not silenced from the get go. 
- Upgrade system is available but the upgrades don't seem linear. The upgrades are decent.
- The scripted events are pretty painful; to trigger them you have to take a very specific path like enter through a specific door or else the guards don't move. There are multiple ways to achieve goals so that is great but when the guards are standing somewhere and you want them to move you have to go around the other side of the building climbing here and there so that you trigger the scripted event and can get to the objective.

review_text:
Torn on the negative, but even through all the moments where I was stuck in wonder and awe at the visuals and setting, the gameplay itself is atrocious at best and made me not want to finish it several times at worst. 

In the era of Twitch streamers, Let's Players, Vtubers, whatever you want to use to consume your media via watching someone else play through a game, it's the mark of an actually good game where you'll want to play it yourself despite the option to watch someone else play it (or even after doing so) - SCORN is not that. In fact, the only benefit you'd get out of not watching someone else play it, is that you can take your time exploring the environment yourself. And at the end of the experience, I spent maybe 10-20 extra minutes that a content creator wouldn't have admiring the scenery. For 40$. 

In exchange I got to deal with the extremely frustrating combat, where you get absolutely swarmed by enemies in tight hallways with a melee weapon that swings twice with an absurdly long recharge, with only one of the four enemy types in the game being killable in those two swings. Ammo is scarce, even if you can identify the weird looking ammo stations in the winding areas you'll be constantly walking through as most of it kind of blends together. Movement during combat is lackluster, as you move slow, even when sprinting. Reloading or changing your weapon slows you down even further. Catching on the terrain constantly in these tight hallways was an additional nuisance. Enemies have near pinpoint accuracy with their ranged attacks or in the case of the big chargers, charge you relentlessly (and stunlock you when you get hit). Several times I died because I was simply cornered and couldn't get around what was attacking me. Each time I died I considered uninstalling and not finishing the game.

There was a lot of complaints about puzzles, but as I have a slightly above room temperature IQ I didn't find them too bad. Lots of trial and error got me through them relatively quickly. And again. Four hours for the total experience.

If ammo had been more plentiful, or combat was more responsive, if killing the myriad repeat enemies was satisfying in any way shape or form, then I could easily recommend SCORN. It's an experience that left me with questions and an appreciation for the artistry of the setting. Hell, if the game had been a walking simulator, I still think it would have been worth buying, simply because of how unique it is. But unfortunately, the gameplay left it feeling like there was a lot of wasted potential and as a result I cannot recommend SCORN.

review_text:
Super game! The writing from the Homestuck folk is always so full of character, cheek, and intelligence (many of the devs here are writers first, gam devs second); the art is basically always gorgeous and rich; and there are a few moments that I think will stick with me for a long time.

Actually, let me mention one (maybe my favourite). Spoilers incoming!

So there's a long trial scene that serves as the centrepiece, I suppose, of the game. It's pretty hard to "win" it, and this is partly imo a fault of the devs' ability to see things through a new player's eyes - but also this isn't really a serious weakness, because here, as elsewhere, the fail-states are also really good. One in particular is I think one of my favourite moments from *any* game. Right, so in this trial, if you follow the evidence in one direction, you get plausible guilt for someone who you honestly think might've done the crime in question (Lynera). In fact she didn't do it, though! You're told this by your guide (Tyzias) after the fact. Your character, Joey, is understandably mad as hell at Tyzias for not stepping in before the verdict came in that unjustly damned Lynera. Tyzias's whole schtick is that she's fighting for reform of the legal system in Alternia (which is grossly, cartoonishly unjust) - but she's okay with injustice getting done anyway!?

Tyzias explains herself to you: She shares your ideals of people not getting done in for crimes they didn't do, but it's not possible to reform the extant legal system that radically that quickly. Justice is still entertainment and still has to maintain social order. Reforming it has to be done gradually or not at all.

This is obviously an allegory for the sort of incrementalist political strategy we get in real life too; and here, too, it is tempting, and often seems like the only possible outcome. But here, too, it has the immediate consequence of people having their lives ruined for no good reason. Hiveswap enacts this tension really marvellously. 

And this is the outcome if you *fail* the game! Now that's a mark of seriously good game-making.

I don't want to sound as if I have no problems with the game. It needs polish at various points; how to do a thing is often unintuitive (though is the ameliorated somewhat by the help button that always has what you need); and there's a general sense of pedestrianness in the game that I can't articulate, but which I think is to do with how little the overall quest, or the frame of the game, changes over its course. You're still basically the same person at the end as you were at the beginning, and this seems a little complacent, as if you (or your character, or "us") doesn't need to develop as a person, or as if she/we have nothing left to learn. But against this, it should be remembered here that this is only Act 2 of a much larger story. Maybe I'm being unfair to expect so much of this.

So anyway - great game: great writing, lovely art, lots of jokes and some great philosophy... check it out!

This game is like if Fyodor Dostoevsky, Anton Chekhov, and Franz Kafka came together, got drunk, learned Unity engine and decided to make a game together. It's uniquely surreal and literary but never in a heavy-handed or pretentious way. Every piece feels like its cut exactly as it should be and fitted together to form a cohesive and meaningful whole. This game might not be for everyone-- it's a game that certainly demands a lot from the player, it will have sections of grueling, unbelievable cruelty and difficulty-- but if you should choose to stick with it, it will reward you with something truly unique and special. I don't think I've played a game that I've thought about so much and so long after finishing it.

10/10 - one of the best games I've ever played

review_text:
Let me say that while I don't feel as if I'd recommend this game, I'm not claiming it was a wholly unenjoyable experience. It just might not be what a lot of people are looking for, and the number of positive reviews are a bit misleading.

Positive:
-Some well-crafted storytelling, I'll admit.
-Good worldbuilding, some clever ideas.
-Positive representation of autistic characters, not a lot of misinformation that stood out to me that might have ruined that.

Negative:
-Short.
-While the story is inventive, it is also linear, and I hesitate to call To the Moon an "interactive storybook" at all, but that's the best description I can think of because it kind of falls short of being a game.
-Moving around is a chore. The characters are often slow, and you inexplicably bump into things on the map sometimes that are arbitrarily solid. (You can walk through cars, but not over flowers? Really?)
-Puzzles are simple and boring. Does not feel like much at stake. They don't really add much to the story by being there other than giving the player something active to do.
-Gameplay mostly consists of walking around and clicking things until you click on something "important." Click on enough important things and you can unlock the simple tile puzzle and move on to the next memory. There's nothing really fun about it.
-On that note it would have made sense for the game to be more passive. The components that were there seemingly just to make it "like a game" felt out of place.
-IF YOU USE THE INTENDED CONTROLS (the mouse) YOU'RE GONNA HAVE A BAD TIME. You click somewhere for the characters to go somewhere, but they often don't quite reach entirely, maybe because of an obstacle, and so it feels like the characters are never going where you want them to go. Getting to objects is exhausting. When I discovered you could use the traditional arrow keys to move and the space to interact it was a life saver.
-Too much dialogue, I hate to say. Wayyy too much bickering between the protagonists bogs down the whole game. Way too much melodramatic prosey monologuing at times, too, taking away from the impact of actually beautiful and important dialogue. Just too much. It's clumsy. You spend much of the game inundated in wooords.
-What's worse is the characterization is weak at best. Most of the characters don't have much in the way of personality, which you kind of expect from this kind of game especially if it's supposed to be carried by character interactions.
-A lot of it... was not funny. When it was trying to be funny. A lot of inward groans to be had at the unnecessary snark. (There were funny parts to be had, definitely. Most of the annoying stuff was in the dialogue between Watts and Rosalene, who as I already said, spend way too much time bickering.)
-This is a bit of a personal nitpick, but I wish, if they were going to make a game about asperger's, that they might just name it outright. I don't understand why everyone was so cagey and vague about River's "condition," it struck me as unnecessary.

Verdict: If you are going to get it, get it on sale. Then stick it out past Act 2, because that's where the story starts picking up and you don't have to put up with the puzzles and junk. Don't approach it expecting much in the way of a game, or much in the way of replay value. It's a decent story, not decent enough for me to wholly recommend the experience, but not bad enough for me to say there was nothing worthwhile about it, either.

review_text:
Review of Batman: Arkham City  
Rating: 0 out of 5

This game is a poorly executed mess that leaves nothing but frustration.

1. Hitboxes:
The hitboxes of the main character are clearly larger than the character model. This is evident when dodging knife attacks or punches from enemies. Even when they visibly miss and hit the air, damage is still applied to the player. This is unacceptable and ruins the combat experience.  

2. Finisher Animations:
The finishing move animations are deliberately slow, allowing enemies to close the distance and attack during the sequence. This feels intentional and makes combat frustrating, especially since these slow animations make it impossible to react in time.  

3. Combos and Controls: 
Some combos work only intermittently, and the game often fails to register key inputs properly. The control system feels clunky and unresponsive, significantly affecting the flow of gameplay.  

4. Harley Quinn's Revenge DLC:
The DLC is riddled with poorly implemented scripts. Enemies deal excessive damage to your armor, far more than in the main game. Sniper and gun-wielding enemies seem overpowered, with much higher health compared to their counterparts in the base game. Even weaker characters like Robin struggle to take down enemies who, logically, should fall after just a few hits.  

5. Electro-Baton NPCs:
The design of enemies with electric batons is nonsensical. Even when you strike them in a way that should disarm them, they somehow manage to deal damage instead. The idea of needing to flank these enemies for a takedown is absurd and unnecessary.  

6. Weapon Retention: 
Enemies holding guns or batons never drop their weapons, no matter how hard you hit them. This completely breaks immersion, as weapons should logically be dropped after a significant hit or during a takedown animation.  

7. General Gameplay:
The overall controls are poorly optimized. Combat and movement feel unpolished, leading to a frustrating and unsatisfying experience.  

Conclusion:
Batman: Arkham City is a disaster in terms of gameplay mechanics and design choices. From broken hitboxes to nonsensical combat mechanics, this game fails on every level. It’s hard to believe this was the product of a professional development team. Avoid this game at all costs.

review_text:
Holy. f*cking. sh*t.

Just played the new update, and that is my conclusion after 4 hours with it.

Let me explain. I've been playing GTTOD since back in the day, when the levels were procedurally generated, the graphics were nice but flat, there was no ammo, and holy hell was the grenade launcher op.

It was a decent time killer back then, with really fun mechanics, but not alot more. I really liked the movement (Although i would have played a f*cking hello kitty game if it had wall riding at that point. Jesus was i down bad) but didn't think much more of it. A fun time waster, with fun gunplay.

After not playing the game for a while, i came back just in time for the (appropriately named) Excessively late update.

It was... not what i hoped for.

Don't get me wrong, the game got way better in many ways. Graphically, the game felt like it finally got out of puberty, and was starting to figure out a direction. The guns were more refined, more satisfying, and felt way better to use overall. The enemies were becoming diverse, not just, y'know, a dude and a drone. I had to actually pay attention to who i was fighting, but the enemies were visually distinguishable, so there was no difficulty there. And the music, oh lord, whoever produced it is a genius.

But, as much as all i've said above is great and all, one thing took a noticeable hit. The movement.

It felt incredibly clunky. Instead of feeling like an agile hyper-soldier, outmaneuvering my enemies, i felt like a brick in a space suit. To be more specific, the wall running was sh*t. 

You could be going straight for a wall, after gathering a f*ck-ton of speed, and just straight up face plant into it. And you could say "Well maybe they made it more difficult to be more skill expressive". And i could accept that, if it wasn't for the fact that it felt like i had no control over it. Sometimes i would get sucked to walls that were behind my back, sometimes i'd be hitting the walls at the perfect angle, and my dude would just go "Nah lmao" and fall like a bag of bricks into the f*cking abyss.

Point being, i hated the movement, so i dropped the game.

Now, you can take all i wrote above, and wipe your f*cking ass with it, because the dev decided to seclude himself to the tibetan mountains for 16 months and came back with the best update i've ever seen in my life.

Here i was thinking the guns were good in the last update. Nah. The sound design of each and every gun (i've tested so far) is godlike. The impact of every shot feels incredibly satisfying. The level design is on a whole 'nother level. The enemies, more striking. And while not everyone would agree, i prefer the new music over the old one.

But the movement. The f*cking movement.

Smooth. Fast. Incredibly f*cking addicting. I might as well be playing "the floor is lava"  with how much time i spend not flying through the air. It is, without a doubt, the best movement in any game i played. And f*ck me, i have around 600 hours in titanfall 2.

I could go on for days about it. And hell, that's not even where this update ends, not even close. But i don't wanna write a whole ass paper boosting low_hanging_fruits(the main dev)'s ego, so you'll just have to discover all of it by playing the game yourself. All jokes aside, this update is absolutely incredible, and i cannot recommend enough that you should get the game and try it out for yourself. 

As a last note, i do have to say i'd highly appreciate a waypoint/minimap system, since my ape brain always forgets where all the bunkers are when i have 3 keys.

review_text:
Only played for about 9 hours, but I know for a fact that this is something I'm gonna spend a large amount of time in.
Not only is the story and general atmosphere incredibly interesting, having to survive in the world of Pathologic is incredibly engaging and extremely fun. The close-range combat is not my favorite part, but successfully getting a hit in on an enemy and taking their stuff means that I'm willing to take it for how it is.
On another note, the trading system is incredibly simple, but I've never seen any other game do it quite like this. Store-owners are the only NPCs that take money, and they're locked inside their establishment, while regular people roam the streets. Vendors are pretty scarce on the map, and you have an extremely limited amount of time to do things during the day, so you don't wanna make huge detours unless it's necessary. Regular civilians will trade in items, and every one of them has their own preferences, so while in my current playthrough I have a bit of money, I'm barely managing to get by on the slim amounts of food and healing items I can obtain.
What little jank there is I am able to look over due to the immense amount of enjoyment I've already gotten out of it.
The atmosphere and story go hand-in-hand, and both are unlike any other game I've played before. I tried the first game, and found it to be far too difficult and complicated for me to actually get into. This, however, I am more than able to get into. The music is tinny and weird, the way characters act and talk is bizarre, and I've realized that I become extremely nervous and greedy when playing it. 
A good example of this is that I was originally hoarding money for a particularly expensive item, but recently I decided not to buy it. So if I'm not in need of the money for the expensive item, why am I still insistent on hoarding it? I need food and various other things to keep me alive, but I'm still looking to make a profit when it's not that important. I should just buy food and supplies, but I'm not. 
On another note, due to an early rep-hit, I'm now constantly looking over my shoulder and worried about someone chasing me even though my reputation is positive everywhere. The enemies that only appear at night are not helping my paranoia.
It's so good at what it does that it makes me fall back on self-destructive and neurotic tendencies in-game. Hopefully the devs keep making stuff, 'cause they're extremely talented and I want to see more of whatever ideas they come up with. 10/10.

review_text:
From Legacy to Letdown – New Genesis Fails to Uphold the Phantasy Star Name

As someone who’s spent countless hours in Phantasy Star Online (Dreamcast, GameCube) and Phantasy Star Universe, it’s painful to say that New Genesis feels like a massive step backwards — not just from PSO2, but from the series as a whole. This was meant to be a bold new chapter, but what we got was a shallow reimagining that lost much of what made the originals special.

Let’s start with the world. While NGS boasts a large, open-world format, it feels hollow and lifeless. Exploration quickly becomes tedious due to a lack of meaningful content. Gone are the distinct, varied environments of PSO1 or the social hubs and stylish cities of PSU — replaced with bland landscapes and a repetitive cycle of gathering materials and doing the same few tasks.

Combat is faster and flashier, but ironically, it’s also less rewarding. PSO1’s deliberate pacing and meaningful enemy encounters have been traded for mobs that feel like filler. There’s little sense of progression — most classes feel the same by mid-game, and the “build depth” of previous titles is largely absent.

One of the most glaring issues is lack of content and identity. At launch and even well beyond, NGS feels like an early-access shell. The story is wafer-thin, the characters are forgettable, and core features like compelling loot, challenging dungeons, and team-oriented gameplay (a staple of the series) are either undercooked or missing entirely.

The social aspects are a shadow of what they once were. PSO1 and PSU had vibrant lobbies, strong community interaction, and reasons to play with friends. In NGS, despite being an MMO, it often feels like a solo experience with people just running past each other in the open world.

And perhaps most disappointing is the sense that New Genesis tries to be like other MMOs — but loses the unique sci-fi charm, music, atmosphere, and quirky depth that gave the older games their soul. The sleek UIs, gritty space-fantasy tone, and mysterious worldbuilding of the early titles have been traded for generic anime tropes and gacha-driven progression.

Final Thoughts:
Phantasy Star Online: New Genesis is a textbook case of how not to modernize a beloved franchise. Flashier doesn’t mean better, and open-world doesn’t mean deeper. For longtime fans, it’s a heartbreaking regression — a game that feels disconnected from the magic of its predecessors. PSO1 and PSU still stand tall in comparison, despite their age. Sadly, NGS feels like a beautiful but empty shell.

It appears that this is an unfortunate ongoing trend within the gaming industry.

I really wanted to like this game.

[h1]PROS[/h1]
+ GREAT concept (akin to the Omen)
+ Well-crafted map layout

[h1]CONS[/h1]
- This game WILL crash on you. 
- Limited storyline that starts strong and then disappears
- Poor voice acting and sound design
- Linear, point-and-click puzzle game masquerading as a 3rd-person adventure game
- No variability in mission-completion pathways (there is only one way to complete each mission)
- Unstable and buggy AI interaction that breaks immersion completely
- Limited mission-guidance results in aimless walking around and clicking on everything around until the path becomes obvious
- Limited to no player agency -- point and click your way to the next goofy cut-scene.

I cannot recommend this game. Once the novelty wears off, this game quickly becomes [u]not fun[/u].  I played through the first six missions and decided that my time was worth more to me than to spend any more of it on a game which I kept hoping would be better.

review_text:
Can't recommend it yet. Let's run through it. 

The game is fun, but a bit obnoxiously harsh on occasion that really just takes the piss out of you and those pisstakers are where I'll be focusing.

Clunky, I believe you need 1.5x-2x the BASE stamina you get now if you want to be the dashing dastard witch hunter the game wants you to be. Still don't know how regaining focus works, don't care until I come across something I need focus for. 

AI is a little bad, especially for the Swordsman enemy. For being a decently HPed lunge enemy they sure like to run around and not do a whole lot until they do a lunge around a corner and clip you. 
Most automatic guns feel absolutely awful. No wonder humanity is losing the witch war we are using paintball guns. 


Another thing is that when you first get a weapon, the flavor text lies to you. It tells you what it WILL do, not what it does after you spend about 40 minutes with it to level it and actually get the weapon mechanics. There are some basic errors here that severely hinder this game. I do not recommend this game as it stands, and I am even further negative than I was to begin with.

Largest issue, in my opinion, is the Calamity system. It just sucks, its bad, its dumb. Kicks you when you are down as taking damage directly correlates to you having less HP/healing. Oh, you triggered the ice mine a guy you took down 10 seconds ago? Hope you were finished up because the Calamity is coming and your run is done either way. Rewards are pitiful for interrupting the event for it being normally end running. The ritual site seems to spawn as far away from you as possible, and from at least my experience, in the most heavily populated area on the map. Right now, about 10 hours in, I have not found a way to reduce the calamity counter. I do believe clearing mob areas (the ones that result in a witchfire shard) should reduce the counter, and if not that clearing more dangerous areas/rituals should reduce it instead. 
EDIT: I still maintain what I said about the calamity, however at higher levels the calamity is more absolutely obnoxious than anything else. It destroys the flow of the game and can be triggered in areas, like boss arenas, where you cannot counter it. I assume that will be changed as it SUCKS but for now it makes the game strictly worse.

Spells really dont feel good either. I am not a fan of any damage spell so far, I find the CC much more valuable but that is neither here nor there. Also along that line, give me a more visible sign that spells are off cooldown. They current UI is far too minimal for those. Tie them to the crosshair or something.

Edit: This game hates you and wants you to know it. There are several mechanics for objectives further in that will require a replay or two. Flying Ship calamity, right? Hide from it's broadside, right, maybe dash from building to building so you avoid its shots? No. In fact, it shoots homing balls of darkness that are so accurate at patrolling they can hunt you down through the bowels of a castle. After countering it, it is an absolute push over but still doesn't really make sense. Stick your face out during its barrage pass to hit a weakspot or turn around the...shoot the cannonballs? What? If you have anything but a rifle, you just lose as the damage drop off will ensure you can't actually hit the weakpoint of the ship well. The counter for the ship is moronic and boils down to 'shoot the shinies' instead of actually dealing with the giant piss big ship. Should have made it a floating priest or something instead those balls of shadow would make a lot more sense than from a SHIP. Endless arena that actively damages you? No idea wtf to do, no direction. Had to rely on a guide. You just die the first time which yeah its a roguelike but with enough skill and PROPER direction you should be able to burn through objectives after understanding the mechanics on a fundamental level.

Another thing is that when you first get a weapon, the flavor text lies to you. It tells you what it WILL do, not what it does. You must spend about 40 minutes with it to level it to get the actual mechanic and so far, the upgrades kinda suck. There are standouts but for the most part I am disappointed to uncover their upgrades. There are some basic errors here that severely hinder this game. I do not recommend this game as it stands, and I am even further negative than I was to begin with.

EDIT after webgrave update. Reset my character to experience the full game. Man, it does not feel great. I don't think I've experienced a game before where I've looked at my guns and went 'damn I wish I had one I liked'. Movement still feels shit, this game has far too complex of systems for its own good. Gnosis is still a crutch the dev team relies on to not balance the game properly.

What I love about manager games is to take a small team and build it up to greatness. Sadly, that's not possible in EHM - if you don't own your arena (small teams won't) you can't expand it and you can't build one and thus you can't build up an income. Some teams will even start with 0 ticket price, so you'll never get money from home games (which means you'll never have any money - you won't go bancrupt, just no possibility to invest or pay salaries).

There are also bugs and a distinct lack of customization - hopping between different info screens because if you combine them you get 2/3rds of the info you want. Graphics and sound is poor, not that it matters to a manager game but it feels really outdated.

I wish this had been in early access still, because then there would have been a decent chance of some of those issues being fixed. Right now I fear that the game was released and abandoned.

review_text:
To me, it feels way more luck based than skill based, bottom line. Not a good recipe for a puzzle game.

Simple game with great visuals, a fun soundtrack, and a solid premise. However, I do not recommend this game because of the physics. It is a physics puzzle game, but with zero control over what the free gooballs do and with unpredictable goo placement, it is needlessly difficult to build a cohesive tower without it toppling over. The puzzle should be in deciphering how to build a structure to get to the end pipe, not endlessly working the goos over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over because you can't get them to drop where you need them. Example: the Tower of Goo level should be a fun introduction on how to build tall towers; the solution is extremely obvious. Instead, you need to spend all your time retrying because the goos all run up one side of the tower and pull it down, or you can't get the goo to span the right previously placed gooballs. If I know where to put it to add integrity, and I simply can't because the game won't let me, I'm not solving a puzzle I'm rolling the dice. Even following a freaking youtube tutorial where someone beat the level, I couldn't replicate the solution. Does that sound like a puzzle to anyone else?

I'm no stranger to difficult games, but at least with many of those you know what you're doing wrong. This isn't intellectually stimulating or challenging, it's just tedious.

I really have tried to like this game - it has so much style, great influences and the soundtrack is fantastic, but ultimately I do not have fun playing it.

I'm a huge Jet Set Radio fan, so this was on my radar for a long time. It doesn't take much to see the influence and all of the ways the studio have tried to recreate that magic. It has all of the things it should have, and especially the art team have gone nuts on this game.

But I just do not find the gameplay fun. It is quickly repetitive, mechanics that aren't enjoyable on pretty lacking level design. The objectives are rarely fun, the direction confusing and it just becomes... quite frustrating to play.

Nothing is more frustrating than the police system, which seemingly only exists to make the game less fun. Do you want to be grappled and slowed constantly? How about a mandatory combat segment with some of the most laughable combat mechanics? I do not understand why it was added other than to emulate the (pretty great) police system in JSR.

Jet Set Radio was a lot of style, but at its core it was an enjoyable game. I do not think Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is, as much as it pains me to admit.

I recently played the game "Imscared" and I have to say, it was a unique and unsettling experience. The game is described as a "metaphysical horror game," and it definitely lived up to that description.

The game starts off innocently enough, with the player exploring a seemingly abandoned house. However, as you progress through the game, things start to get more and more surreal and disturbing. The atmosphere of the game is incredibly effective at creating a sense of unease and fear.

One of the things that really sets "Imscared" apart from other horror games is its use of meta elements. The game actively breaks the fourth wall and plays with the player's expectations and perceptions in clever ways. It's hard to go into too much detail without spoiling the game, but suffice it to say that "Imscared" takes some unexpected turns that left me feeling deeply disturbed and uncomfortable.

Overall, "Imscared" is a unique and highly effective horror game that I would recommend to fans of the genre. Just be prepared for a truly unsettling experience.

review_text:
At this time I do not recommend this game, and it's for a good reason, trust me. The biggest being there's a lot of gameplay and mechanic issues that haven't been addressed or fixed since release, and no info on when they will be fixed.

Also keep in mind I didn't play the story mode yet, only arena mode so far. I play with the Valve Index.

Before I even review the game, I'd like to say I believe this could have been a really cool DLC of Boneworks. I believe this didn't need to be it's own game and could have just made an update to Boneworks. This game is literally an improved version of Boneworks, nothing really life changing. VERY little is really new about the game. Sure, there's some new gimmics, but it's the same game.

First off, I've played 179 hours of Boneworks as of typing this review. I'd play it mainly for the arena mode. I'd put on my favorite music, and just vibe. Sure, there'd be some slowdown, there are days I wish they'd fix some things, but it works.

As for this game, they broke a lot of what I enjoyed about Boneworks. The gun play is broken, guns don't like to stay in one place and move on their own, and the horrendous addition of forced virtual stock. Yes, there's a virtual stock, no you can't turn it off. Some times it works great, reloading the shotgun SOME TIMES feels good. Other times I look down and the weapon I'm holding is completely upside down. Tracking seems to break more often in this game than any other, I genuinely thought it was my headset, but I tried this game on another headset and had the same issues.

Things I actually liked so far:
- Arena mode is looking good, but you run out of ammo VERY quickly. There's only a VERY small amount of new weapons in the game, so not much changed since Boneworks. I very much look forward to custom arena areas.
- FPS remains pretty steady, not as much lag as the first game.

Biggest issues:
- Guns don't work like they should: As mentioned above, guns would randomly shake and pop out of your hands, turn upside down, or you just can't grip them. As someone with nearly 200 hours in Boneworks, I know how the game works and it's genuinely annoying.
- Forced virtual weapon stock: For those who don't know what it is, it's game mechanic that mimics the way you would put the stock of a gun to your shoulder. 99% of ALL games allow you to toggle this on and off, but this game has no option to turn it off, so guns with stocks will feel VERY different than they should.
- I don't care what anyone in the forums say, starting your VR game with the player literally hanging themselves is NOT a selling point and isn't going to help with sales. I have no earthly idea why this is a forced LITERALLY the FIRST thing you do in the game. My advice is to just have a platform in front of the player, they step on it and they are transported to that exact same scene but their arms and legs are bound to something while it's set on fire. GOING THROUGH THE ACTUAL PROCESS OF HANGING YOURSELF ISN'T NEEDED OR ASKED FOR IN VR.

Until they update all the issues others and myself have outlined about the game, I cannot recommend this yet. Stick with Boneworks. For now, I'll leave this review as it is.

🦇 Batman: Arkham City Review 🦇

🕹 Length:
• 12–20 hours (main story + major side quests)
• 40+ hours for completionists
• +3–5 hours with DLC (Harley Quinn’s Revenge + Challenge Packs + Skins)

💰Price vs. Content: Excellent — a massive base game plus DLC that meaningfully expands replayability
 ⚙ Optimization: Strong overall, but still needs tweaks to unlock FPS (capped at 60 by default)
🎮 Difficulty: Fair on Normal; Hard, New Game+, and DLC challenges add serious difficulty

🎮 Gameplay

Batman: Arkham City takes everything Asylum started and evolves it into a sprawling, atmospheric open world filled with iconic villains, meaningful side activities, and some of the best combat/stealth gameplay ever designed.

The FreeFlow combat system is deeper, faster, and more tactical, with new enemy archetypes and expanded gadget integration. Predator (stealth) encounters are more open and creative, letting you plan takedowns in bigger, vertical environments.

Traversal is one of the game’s highlights: gliding across Arkham City with dive-bombs, grapples, and momentum chaining feels incredible — quick, stylish, and empowering.

Side missions enrich the world, each villain getting their own storyline (Mr. Freeze, Deadshot, Zsasz, Hush, and many more), while Riddler puzzles return with greater creativity and scale.

Challenge Mode is expanded with new maps, modifiers, and playable characters, making it a major part of the experience, especially for players who want mastery.

🧩 DLC Content Breakdown

🎭 Harley Quinn’s Revenge (Story DLC)

A short but story-heavy epilogue taking place after the main game.
• Play as both Batman and Robin
• New environments and enemy setups
• Darker tone with Harley leading her own gang
• Adds closure to certain story beats

Length: ~1.5–2 hours — short, but polished and atmospheric

🎮 Challenge Maps DLC

Includes multiple packs:
• Nightwing Bundle Pack
• Robin Bundle Pack
• Challenge Map Pack

Adds:
✔ New characters (Robin & Nightwing)
✔ Dozens of Combat and Predator challenges
✔ Extra achievements and progression paths
✔ Extremely replayable content for mastery-focused players

🦇 Skin Packs

Multiple Batman suits, including:
• Batman Beyond
• The Dark Knight Returns
• Year One
• Animated Series
• Sinestro Corps Batman

Purely cosmetic but beloved — adds flavor for replays and Showcase runs.

✅ The Good:
✔ Enormous open world full of atmosphere and secrets
✔ Best combat/stealth hybrid gameplay of its generation
✔ Superb story with memorable villains
✔ Challenge Mode + DLC adds dozens of extra hours
✔ Traversal is fluid, fast, and fun
✔ Harley Quinn’s Revenge gives meaningful post-game story content
✔ Character DLC (Robin & Nightwing) expands gameplay variety

❌ The Bad:
✖ FPS is locked at 60 unless manually edited — disappointing for modern systems
✖ Harley Quinn’s Revenge is short for a story DLC
✖ Some challenge maps can feel repetitive if you're not into mastery play
✖ Side missions can be easy to miss if you don't explore thoroughly

💻 Technical Aspects

🎨 Graphics: Stylish, atmospheric, and surprisingly detailed for its age
🎶 Sound: Legendary voice acting (Conroy, Hamill, North) and a powerful orchestral score
🐞 Bugs: Mostly minor; some movement stutter until the FPS cap is manually removed

⭐ Final Verdict

Batman: Arkham City remains one of the greatest superhero games ever created. Its combination of world-building, combat depth, emotional storytelling, and replay value is unmatched. With DLC included — especially the challenge packs and Harley Quinn’s Revenge — it becomes an even more complete experience for fans of Batman and action games.

👉 Rating (Complete Edition): 10/10

I'd love to give this a positive review but uhm... I come back after like 2 years, all all 'sweet it's out of EA let's see if my investment paid off; get some of that end game content, atmosphere, and polish' and the thing they added... was... trash...??? ...???????? Literally it's just now you have to burn trash like who was thinking 'yes, good, this is the thing; the thing this god simulation needed - janitors.'

It also doesn't make any sense from a logical standpoint, even whilst suspending disbelief. Why do rocks turn into trash if they're on the ground too long? "That rock's been sitting there for nearly a day now. It's starting to smell."

This was a really big failure of imagination. You could probably make it less ridiculous by saying 'oh you know, the corruption, you know the corruption you're constantly fighting? It gets into the land and ruins anything not nailed down; the decay is a constant of life here and it has to be contained or destroyed." and then a few sprite changes, a couple wispy black shaders, renaming burners to 'corruption destroyers' or w/e and you have yourself a cool system where you're defending your villagers from another vector of awful corrupt death instead of just picking up their garbage, and you still make resource management meaningful. Instead, we have trashcans, middle-ages style.

review_text:
TL;DR/ Conclusion: The game is fun, charming, isn't expensive and is from a developer who cares and strives. Even if you get 10 hours out of it, it isn't a bad deal. Some might get 50 hours out of it in the current state. Please take my criticism below with a grain of salt and remember that the game is still in early access.

After 5 hours of game time, and about 3-4 runs, I beat the campaign on normal. It does seem a bit short and I'd love to see a bit more content added to the game.

When that is said, I think it's an incredibly satisfying game to play. First time starting the game, it felt so nice to skate around and pass the puck, to the degree I wished it was just a normal hockey game with more emphasis on the mechanics that already felt great to its core. There are a lot of rogue-lites out there lately, and I play a lot of them, that's why I wish it was not following the same formula.

But before you know it, You get that sense of satisfaction that those games give you. The feeling of OP abilities, upgrading our character, buying new superheroes in the store and all that good stuff. It's just a cozy game, not a try-hard/ super tactical game. Most of the fun comes from just trying out different things, enjoying the hillarious art style and either doing permant upgrades or upgrades within each run.

I'll play this game more before the full release, just to chill. It isn't really the game I want to play with a great challenge. That's why I'll wait with hard mode.

Nitpicking/ tips for the developers:

- The difficulty level of a run goes from extremely easy to pretty hard fast. Mostly because one playthrough is so short. I'd love to feel more invested in each run and to see the gradual development of my crew as well as the enemies. Right now, it can feel like all of a sudden I got completely OP or that the enemy got completely OP.

- Tuning down the power of each roguelite element. Some of the abilities we can use are quite OP and become the thing we lean on to win. Maybe I'm wrong about the enemies since I got better at understanding them and therefore beat the game, but it feels a bit like their unique powers are too overwhelming. This is just my opinion: maybe they should have higher base stats but lower boosts to their powers. The little prince can have less accuracy or shot power, the freeze that one team has can have reduced duration. Or else I at least feel that I am playing against only that power and not a complete team. It could be that this is solved in hard mode if the powers are still the same but base stats are increased. Can someone confirm?

- Currently, the 3 players who aren't your main character or superhero (they're called benchwarmers, right?) aren't good enough for me to want to give them the puck. The game revolves too much around the two stars of the team. It's not very out of balance and yes, they do bodycheck and score from time to time. I just miss the feeling of a fully coherent balanced team in a way. To be fair though, this will get better once my main character is fully upgraded so that upgrades during each run can be distibuted more to benchwarmers. I don't really want a team full of unique powers either since it will be a lot to try to remember while the game is already fast paced. Just a bit higher base stats would solve this for me.

- I want more customizeability for my team. I'd like to first of all be able to choose how my main character looks, choose team logo and colors. I also want to be able to buy players like benchwarmers, either permanently or maybe better just within each run. But since there's no currency within the runs, this might be a bad idea. You probably already have the best choice the way it is now.

- When I went into settings to rebind my gamepad controls, the first screen shows me keyboard. I started pressing the D-pad where I thought I had to go but it got stuck somewhere and I couldn't press anything. I had to restart the game. It feels a bit clunky to do the right thing. It did work the second time, but still, it was a long way up to "gamepad" at the top. No big deal, very much nitpicking.

- Each act is a long flat field. I'd love to see it as a mountain instead with each parts of the mountain changing based on the enemy. It would feel so epic. The terrain would be more interesting to look at and I'd get the feeling of climbing a ladder. Flat is just a bit boring. Also just nitpicking.

- Please be aware that I might not be right about anything I write here as feedback. It's more of a philosophical view that I wish I could play a long playthrough (let's say a season of 20 matches + cup matches or something) where the development and progression feels slower, yet more balanced. To reduce the chances of getting shocked because you got OP all of a sudden or getting absolutely crushed after an easy win before. It would also help me feel more invested in the game. In a longer season, it could be nice to have powers for the manager, or a unique button for a power done by an insider in the stands or on the bench. With this idea, I would still like that you keep the increase in difficulty from the enemies. It wouldn't make sense to be too weak early and too strong late compared to the opponents. As I'm writing this, I am not sure it would work at all because games that scale with you aren't really fun either. Rogue-lites aren't supposed to last long each run either. The way you give the player a chance to become OP is what makes a good rogue-lite. I just kinda miss a longer gameplay loop to feel more invested, that's all.

Once again, as I'm writing I'm coming up with a better approach to my idea here. Just please give us season mode without barely any upgrades or rogue-lite elements. Just give us the chance to buy new players, go up in tiers after winning the league, add more generic (less interesting) teams to fill up spots. Less focus on powers and humor, but more about the conquering of a league table and forming your entire team. Many sports games have different modes such as: manager mode, season mode, quick match. You have the perfect thing as a foundation which is the awesome rogue-lite game mode with really great mechanics. I want to complete every single mode you add. Variation is healthy and would make the game feel feature-rich.

review_text:
Guns and movement feel pretty good, but enemies and level design are basically awful and make the game unplayable. 

Just on a basic fundamental level the enemies are badly modeled, designed, and implemented. For starters enemies have hitboxes that range from 2-3 times their actual model, which becomes very bizarre to aim at AIR 5 meters away from something and still hit targets. Normally hitboxes are larger than models to account for jank movement, but this is just out of line. Besides hitboxes being totally out of wack with their models, the actual models themselves are just some bright glowing lines. This would be very cool, if enemies didn't bunch together and create an incomprehensible mass of glowing zigzags. Differentiating enemies even when they are separate is rather annoying, but in a group I don't even know what the hell I'm firing at most of the time. Not that it really matters though, none of the enemies really add anything to the gameplay. Melee enemies might as well not exist since you will be in the air for 99% of the time, and the ranged enemies lack the depth that strafe shooters like Serious Sam has. The absolute worst enemy design though is this mech(I think its a mech?) that fires from what I understand to be as homing 0 counterplay missiles. The only "counter" to them I found was breaking LOS and then waiting for shields to recharge before getting back in LOS so I can shoot them down. Assuming of course - I can even see the glowing outline of the mech in a sea of other glowing lines.

The level design is just strange, its sometimes vertical - but without fast ways to go up and enemies have no way to follow you quickly if you drop down anyways. review_text:
Lucius is a very interesting game about a 10 year old going on a rampage in his family home. Granted, to actually go on said rampage, you'll need to follow a steam guide (I recommend this one right here: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=182953522) as there is only one way of killing each target and if you struggle with common sense like I did, you'll need it. Trust me, since the game doesn't really give any hints as to who or how your going to pull off each murder.

The game has you scheme to kill each of the human subjects (mother, maid you name it), spread over 18 chapters, as you progress unlocking Lucius' powers: Telekinesis, mind control, combustion and memory erase given to him by the devil. As well as doing side tasks like cleaning lucius' room, taking out the rubbish, grabbing a buttler a bottle of 1930s champagne and collecting dirty washing for you to sort into seprate baskets, you'll also be collecting Items and weapons that will come in handy for future chapters. 

(If you're an achievement hunter, there are a few housekeeping ones that need you to repeat an action/task multiple times to unlock like: opening cupboards, smashing/dropping items, turning on and off TVs and using Lucius' abilities as you unlock them)

After a while, it does get repetitive, so I would come back to it on and off if you get bored easily. 

Graphically it was OK. I was playing this on a Steam Deck at medium settings, so I know the game is capable of more on better hardware. 

My only main issue with Lucius was the control scheme. On Steam Deck, the game wasn't responding properly with the set buttons, so I had to find a useable layout on Steam Input and then edit it to what I liked as I started the game. It might be helpful if you plan to play on a controller or steam deck. Search for "Playable control scheme for steam deck - Lucius" on the steam input page (It's not perfect but it gets the job done) 

Overall, since I got this game on sale, I would say it was worth it. Mainly because of all the different ways Lucius kills each victim, and although the game's narrative feels uncoincidental to justify each killing, if you haven't played narrative based games in awhile (like me) it's a good game to get started with.

Kyoto Winds is 1 out of 2 parts; it's more of a buildup and getting to know the characters and the payoff really occurs in the latter half Edo Blossoms. This being said, I really like this game!! The couple nitpicks I have are simply this: you'll be skipping a lot of dialogue if you want to go through every route, and Kyoto Winds does, at times, feel like a long exposition dump to get to the good stuff in Edo Blossom. Where as the latter game feels like a period romance, this one feels like political drama. It's not enough to not want to play it, but I do think first time players should know this before picking up the series.

There were a number of technical issues with the third and final puzzle of this game which soured my enjoyment of this game. For the octopus platforming puzzle, most of its difficulty stems not from figuring out which platforms to jump to based upon where they'll move, but rather, jumping a certain distance and hoping that a.) you don't collide with the lights, b.) you don't clip through the platform you're jumping to, and c.) that the platform moves quickly enough to follow you if you happened to be jumping to the same platform. This didn't appear to be intentional game design, and even if it was it wasn't fun or engaging for either me or my friend to get stuck on this specific section.

The selection of the servers also generally didn't reflect where my friend and I were located, which resulted in latency issues that made finishing the rest of the time-sensitive section not worth the additional hours we'd have to put in.

review_text:
This is a game that focuses on looking good, which it does sometimes.  It does not, however, capture you in any meaningful way.  Thankfully I bought this on sale, but it would still not be a good buy for me even if it were $5.99. 

Why do I feel this way?  

Simple:  

You don't know who you are, have zero time to figure that out and develop a reason to play, and you have to run around with 1 combat style.  Sure, it is a fight for your life....but even combat doesn't engage you, and it takes way too many hits to drop these enemies.

But of course, the evil Warden has plans for your meaningless life, and whenever someone says your life is meaningless, they have their own plan on how to make it meaningful.  And how that unfolds is like games from the 90's.  It is a poor idea with worse execution.  You listen to random recordings laying around that fill you in on the story, yet the little bits they give you aren't enough to make you want to find another.  

Speaking of holo-cartridges, you can hold as many of those as you want, but you are limited in inventory.  You will find your standard health bits, ammo, and other "loot" you can sell.  It's good to see I can get credits to buy things in a derelict prison...cause inmates need to buy guns at the 3d printing gun stations...and nothing is cooler than the "hand cannon".  Yawn. 

The perspective is really weird for the camera, you can't change it either.  Your character looks awkward most of the time, and sneaking through all the vents in this prison is just to waste my time.  

Your time is wasted, literally.  Slow, tedious, and boring gameplay...like fuse finding and partially working security mechs to sneak around make it feel like the devs had nothing in mind to begin with.  They had to slow you down to make the game last longer.  

Performance on a RTX 4070 is fine, this is not a game that needs more than 60fps either.  It does look really cool sometimes...othertimes the fog effects remind me of 80's horror movies.  It is incredible that they used so much fog.  Someone in a planning meeting mush have had a 10 minute speech on "atmosphere" and the use of fog.  They missed the memo that atmosphere in games means something different than actual atmosphere in real life...but gots to have that scary fog to build intensity...gots to.
  
The jump scares are lame, and almost always the same.  You new friend that helps you navigate the prison has "special" privileges BRUV (but not enough for him to not ask you for help).  After you try to help, he can just go where he wants, but not you.

You have to sloppily tear your way through a crap hole, cutting access shards out of dead employees. 10 hours prior was a functioning facility. Now its a spark shooting hellhole that has some doors locked (privileges), way too many escape vents, and doors that you are somehow strong enough to use your weak, fleshy hands to pull open...but only partway (because it is a prison after all, can't completely open those spring loaded doors).

Truth is that I bought this game because I love ray tracing...I should have listened to the other reviewers who I had a feeling were telling the truth.  This is boring garbage that is getting uninstalled.

EDIT 2/4/24

I found that this is now on sale for even less than I pad for it.  That made me feel even more unhappy with it.  I am now playing it all the way through out of spite, and I will update this if I change my mind (doubtful).  Dead Space is the better game, though I have not played the remake, it was a classic back in what I consider the best age of gaming 2007 through 2016.

review_text:
A dud on the Deck.

I've played nearly all Lego games, starting with the first Lego Star Wars back when there was no dialogue. I recently got Lego Jurassic Park and thought I'd try it out.

I usually like to 100% Lego games, as that's kind of the point . . . It's a collect-a-thon, and in the past, I didn't mind retreading each level for a second or third time to pick up a mini-kit I missed. 

But I gave up on this game. There were several times where I had no clue what to do to get a mini kit or a gold brick. One time was when I had to shoot the T-Rex in the mouth during the a chase. Another time was playing as the Mosasaur, and I couldn't figure out how to get the last gold brick. I tried everything, including eating the sharks in the tank. With other collectables, a little 1/3 or 2/3 would pop up, telling you that you are doing the right thing. But not with the sharks. You have to eat six of them. I guess I ate 4 and gave up because there was no indicator that I was supposed to each the sharks. 

So, no. I shouldn't have to look up a Youtube video on how to get a minikit or a gold brick. 

This is exacerbated by poor design. The movement is the most clunky I've ever felt in a Lego game. In one section, the arena, you need to shoot some targets. Except that to get close enough  for your aiming reticle to stick to the target, when you shoot, the bullet hits the railing. There is ONE very tiny, specific spot where you can shoot the target without it hitting the railing. It is SO FRUSTRATING.

Another example is a little wooden tunnel you need to go into as a Compy to get a Red brick. First of all, all the Compy tunnels are Green, and usually on walls, except for in one part of the open world, it is brown and made to look like logs (I guess?). No worries, I can see where the red brick is. But there is no indication where you need to go to enter the tunnel. I walked around for several minutes, randomly trying different "holes" before I accidently bumbled into it. 

This is a shoddy game, with shoddy gameplay.

review_text:
Honestly not worth the 40$ at the moment. Feels like a downgrade to Boneworks in a lot of ways, with the story being much shorter, mechanics being changed in unfavorable ways, and patches that hardly even fix any of the real issues that plague the game.

Hell, the main thing they flaunted about it being "Sandbox" and sort've build your own world Isn't even complete!

That's right, the base game's modding SDK isn't even finished and yet they flay it around like it's a huge feature of the game because there's not much else content besides it even though you can barely even make working guns without ripping the game's own code. 

It's just so disappointing in so many ways compared to the original. Especially since it's meant to be for the Oculus quest.

Just to name a few issues: 
 *The Arena mode can barely have any enemies on screen because of them needing to keep in line with the Quest Version (or they're very reluctant to add more). 
 *Fog being EVERYWHERE and pretty noticeable so they can hide the LOD. 
 *You unlock the game's one gimmick more than halfway through the story, AND not to forget how the Story (which you HAVE to play to unlock said gimmick) doesn't even show you or give you any pointers on where to go or how to even start it or even what any of it means or if you're even doing it right.
 *Some of the levels just feel so terrible to play, especially the Parkour ones (Looking at you Tower Climb)
 *Can't forget to mention all the issues I personally have with with absurd load times (Yes, this game is on my SSD with currently 100 gb free and yet I still get load screens that are 5-20 minutes long. No, I do not have that many mods installed. I've tried several fixes including reinstalling it, yet I still get stupidly long loading times for even the smaller maps. Might as well call the dude that fixed GTA's loading times to get on this shit cause I think he needs to figure this game's issues out too.)

I wanted to put so many hours in this, but it's just gonna have to hold off indefinitely until they start releasing patches that at least fixes a few of the issues I have, at the very least being the load times and literally unfinished mod tools.
