review_text:
Oof, this is rough.

The game has really pretty pixel art, visually Lost Ruins is great, but on the gameplay side it's just not fun.
Your attacks are slow and even the largest weapons barely have enough reach to hit an enemy before they are able to get our their *much* faster attacks.

Also almost every enemy in this game will apply some sort of debuff onto you, like bleed or poison damage, which can last up to 30 seconds for certain enemies, dealing 1 damage per second, when that's more than your total HP.
But hey, there's a ton of consumables that let you heal a tiny bit and remove such status effects.
That however means you constantly have to go in and out of your inventory, looking for the right consumable to get rid of effects every time you get hit by an enemy.
And again, enemies get much quicker attack animations than you, so the chance of getting hit isn't exactly low.

And what do you get for defeating enemies?
Well since there's no XP system or anything like that, if you're lucky they may drop another consumable...
Sometimes, but only rarely will enemies drop some coins you can use to buy equipment at vendors.
But prices are super high and the amount of gold dropped by enemies is tiny.
Like a piece of equipment may cost you like 150G, but every 5 or so enemies you may get 5 gold to drop.

To keep it short, gameplay isn't fun at all.

Sadly, the story and characters are just as bad.
It's already weird enough to see all these girls running around in japanese schoolgirl outfits in a dark fantasy setting, but the story revolving around summoning girls from another world for some sacrifice is just extremely threadbare.
The main character, merely named "Heroine" is as milquetoast as they get.
She never has a single interesting thing to say in dialogue nor does she react to things like characters getting straight up killed in front of her.
There's a small handful of other characters here, mainly they're the bosses, but their writing is just as terrible.

It's such a shame, since the they really seemed to have put a lot of work in the pixel art for Lost Ruins, but everything beside the visuals, this is terrible.

Wouldn't recommend this at all sadly.

review_text:
As quite a lot of people have mentioned, Bioshock has not aged well. The games does work on Windows 7 64 bit (the os I ran it on) but I had to do a bit of tweaking to get it stable, for instance, I had to run it in Dx9 mode. With Vsync on the game suffers from frequent slowdowns and stutter (with i5 3570k and hd7950) and if you have the mouse sensitivity on low, the in game menus are near impossible to navigate. Turning off Vsync will alleviate these problems but you will get a lot of screen tearing.

The game itself is an interesting idea but suffers from a poor user interface, the environments all look pretty much the same and the objectives are mostly 'kill something and collect items from corpse'. This involves lots of random searching for enemies in the hope they might hold the item you need. You can also 'hack' certain things in the game (security systems, vending machines etc) but the hacking game is so annoying that I didnt bother for the entire game, I just used the auto hacking tool.

Overall, the game was fairly enjoyable in spite of all the flaws, this was helped by the interesting story and freaky characters. If you can put up with all the flaws I am sure you will get some enjoyment out of this but as a full price release I cannot recommend it.

review_text:
I have a fair bit of experience in boomer shooters, especially the wave of modern ones, as well as a couple years in EFT and I've played Remnant for a little while. 

This game actually has delivered on all of the various tags so far; I'm not that familiar with Dark Souls specifically, but the rpg system has felt robust enough to make me want to start a bunch of characters, and still smooth enough that I didn't feel the need to pull up a wiki just to play the game. 

The stamina and health mechanics do a good job of making you commit to actions; I've seen some criticisms of enemy placement and stamina limitations, and I can't really agree. These games sometimes have the problem of over-mobility; it's fun to move fast, but past a certain threshold you become functionally untargetable, and so games like Doom Eternal have to turn up the enemy projectile speed and aggression to demand that you use the movement that way. That's fine if the entire game is built around that style of combat, but this game is an RPG, and so the choice to allow you to be quick without necessarily being generally fast, was a good one. Enemies have clear and distinct animations and timings, and while they can be unforgiving, that's only in the sense that you have to be patient and deliberate; if you're constantly dodging or sprinting, the enemy timings will eventually catch up with you.

I think this sort of design is something that games like Borderlands have always struggled with; balancing shooter mechanics in an RPG framework seems difficult, and this game (at least so far) has married the two nicely. I also like that you get sign posting, and a general progression, but the game is cryptic with a lot of information, so I did have a satisfying feeling of slowly discovering more and more complex layers to the game. The only concern I have is replayability; I don't know if the content currently in the game can support multiple long term (dozens to hundreds of hours) characters, like Dark Souls or Fallout, but so far it has stayed fresh and interesting. I'm curious what late game challenge looks like in this game, because I can see space for it to have depth, but traditionally that's one of the places where RPG shooters struggle, so we'll see. Heavily recommend.

This is a metroidvania with souls like mechanics and quirky anime girls you may or may not care about. There are outfits and items you collect that benefit you (such as  a swimsuit so you can cast shock while standing in water without dying and oven mitts that protect you from fire). You start off with low hp (20 total). You recover your hp by using items that work like estus flasks, so you can die while healing. There are status debuffs, such as bleeds, that can instantly kill you.
The level of difficulty and the time spent playing this game is mainly reliant on which difficulty you are playing (there are a bunch of them). IF you are playing on the default difficulty, be prepared to basically die all the time. 
the game is not "short". It's the same length as your typical metroidvania, and said length is based off game mode/skill/ familiarity.

Having never played this before, I just downed the first boss and made it to the second boss in just under 2.5 hours. Most of this time was spent dying constantly.

Fun game. A bit quirky with it's themes, but fun none the less.

review_text:
This game will almost assuredly be a good game in about a year if the devs keep it up.  

However, my advice is let this one bake in the oven until then.  Even on sale, $18 is a big ask for a game that occasionally fundamentally is broken.  If that sounds harsh, just a reminder that this game is a single elimination (i.e. one loss and you restart) rogue-lite hockey game that has absolutely no rules whatsoever implemented currently other than one corrupt ref in one specific boss fight that will almost consistently call one of your (valid) goals off because the gimmick is that they are corrupt.

Every other match is a glorified tennis match due to no offsides or icing, and the best strategy is often to get the puck to one of your fastest mates and have them burn down the timer once you get a lead.  Alternatively, you can just position your best shooter offscreen by the enemies goal, and as soon as you get puck possession simply whip it up the ice towards your winger waiting for a free shot.  The CPU does this as well, and if you try to play normal regulation hockey you'll often get countered by the CPU exploiting the lack of rules.

Being hockey, losses can be subject to a random bounce.  This is why most regulation hockey has series, or best of 5/7/etc.  In Tape to Tape, that one lucky bounce can end your hours-long run.  

There's a lot to like about this, but it's gotta bake and work out the issues.

review_text:
My take after beating the main story.

Great 20-30$ game - Release day content and general game quality does not justify the price tag.

GBFR for more dollars. The combat is somewhere between better and worse - the character and play style variations are much better in SAOFD than ReLink imo so a lot more replay there. The live service concept is an odd choice given I don't imagine this game will hold very much attention similar to the way GBFR fell into oblivion due to being unplayable once queue times took a dive as fewer and fewer played.

The Bad:
-Insanely limited enemy pool makes for very boring and repetitive missions.
-Dragging story that bars the actual multiplayer content - even skipping every cut scene the story mode drags on for hours and is just repeatedly fighting groups of the same 7-10 enemies from game start to game finish with the bosses being the only real unique experience of any mission.
-Very poor targeting system
-Horrible FoV / Camera
-Ranged enemy design and positioning often more annoying than anything engaging.
-Clunky animations - one of the final bosses spent most of the fight clipping in an out visually like an old oversize texture in a Valve game from 2004.
-Load screens - not duration here but sheer quantity. Even running an m.2 just the sheer number of times the game needs to load when transitioning from mission to cut scene or menu to mission or menu to cutscene to mission back to cut - it's absurd you spend more time waiting for the game to be playable than you do playing in some missions.
-Level design not being linear in some missions and constant back tracking really add to the tedious feeling of killing the same repetitive enemies over and over
-Escort missions zzzzzzz

The Good:
-A lot of different characters with very unique combat styles/roles.
-Bosses are fun
-Cosmetic loot rewards are a refreshing take in world where all cosmetics are monetized in most games.
-20 Person Multiplayer is a pretty awesome experience in a game of this style.
-It's an SAO game that's actually fun to play once you've unlocked and cleared everything.
-Loot!
-Numerous options for building a character.
-Perfect dodges feel good and reward you.
-Play with your friends!
-Dope cosmetics
-Maybe the endgame will be better and I'll change this whole review!

TLDR: Balanced, but grindy rougelike FPS with amazing leveldesign and atmopshere. It's good!

[b]Leveldesign![/b] I used to work as a leveldesigner. It takes a lot to get me giddy about leveldesign. Witchfire is amaaaazing in that respect. Easily the best part of the game.  [b]Sounddesign[/b] Great. Nothing that stood out.. but that's a hallmark of great sounddesign. They nailed it! It's atmospheric, subtle, dark.. perfect.

But i'd rather have more story and a bit less grind. But then again.. the game is what it is and to complain about a banana not tasting like pineapple is silly when you bought yourself a banana.

review_text:
This game is boring as hell. You're basically going to sit watching villagers chop wood for hours and not be able to do anything else because you are unable to expand. 

The reason being is that your population will basically never grow. Villagers won't reproduce unless they're assigned to doing nothing. Plus, after you do make a baby, it takes about three game days for it to grow up and enter the labor force, which turns out is quite a long time. 

Every building requires a dedicated workforce. You start with 40 villagers, so fine. You will have enough free villagers to assign them to work in your first buildings—say, a lumber mill. But the more you build—which you will want to do because you're going to want a population that is well fed and watered and well armed—the more you get spread thin. So then if you lose a villager to fighting zombies, you may well have lost the only person that smelts ore for all you know or who makes arrows for the ballistae.

You also don't really get nomads adding to your population from the outside. As game events go, notifications of nomads in the area are few and far between. Plus, after day four or so, it's unlikely they'll even be able to make it to your base because there will be so many graveyards and monster spawns on the map that they'll probably be killed en route with nothing you can do about it.

Plus, there's a fairly ungenerous building cap that requires you to continually expand your city center before you can add more buildings. Meaning more waiting and boredom while you watch your dwindling number of villagers chop wood. Your villagers are also very dumb. They will go all the way across town to chop wood instead of chopping the wood you've assigned right next to them/the building you told them to build. Also, don't try and build more than one structure at a time because they are so addlebrained that they will start one structure, get halfway through completing it, then go to the next one and start it until it's halfway done, then go back to the first one. So, more waiting.


So bored. Do not recommend.

review_text:
I'll start with addressing the fact that this game is not as good as Just Cause 3. I can't fully put into words how, but a lot of what it does just doesn't feel as fun as the chaos that was Just Cause 3. 4 attempted to be more grounded, I would say. At least in terms of story. Your introduction to 3 was standing on top of a plane with a rocket launcher with infinite ammo, blowing up everything in sight. It was insane, over the top, and everything that Just Cause needed to be. Just Cause 4 starts with climbing a big tower.
There are a lot of other ways that Just Cause 4 fails where 3 succeeded, some things just didn't flow as well, didn't feel as fun. 3's story was never going to win any awards, it wasn't exactly War and Peace, but it got the job done, and it wasn't bad. It felt unintrusive, you could enjoy it if you wanted to, but if you didn't care, no problem. 4's felt like it had poorer writing, the characters were forgettable, kind of annoying in some cases, and the story just didn't feel as interesting while also being a lot more in your face.
Despite all this though and many other things, I'm still recommending this game. Why? Because even if it isn't 3, it's still fun. It's a game that you can enjoy, even if it's far from perfect. There are a lot of changes to the game that I didn't care for compared to three, but also a lot of new things they introduced that I really like. The new grappling system is a lot of fun to play around with, already having ten hooks giving you a lot of potential to mess with things. The new weapons are fun, with their secondary fires being interesting and able to change the game flow. I still miss the eDEN Spark, but there's also a lighting gun in this game, too. They added a lot of new vehicles, and a radio in cars, which is fun, and it's great to have tanks with actual treads this time. While the map may not be as pretty or interesting as Medici, I did appreciate how it had different biomes and looked different in other areas, and the graphics are really good, too. While I prefer the old liberation and mission system, I did find it interesting how taking over a base would also involve some kind of task to complete. They could get repetitive and some of them just kind of sucked, but it was still interesting, and some tasks were actually fun. With a redesign, I think it could work. The rebel drops in this game also felt a lot more precise and useful, which is saying something because they were already very useful in 3.
I think how this could all be summed up as while 4 changed a lot of things for the worse compared to 3, it also introduced a lot of new things that I had a lot of fun with, and I still find myself sometimes coming back to this game to mess around with them. If there ever is a Just Cause 5, I'd hope the developers can learn from both their mistakes and wins in this game and design something that had the foundation of something like 3, with all the fun innovations 4 had. That's what sequels are meant to be, if you asked me. Building on each other.

Absolute garbage. I've been trying to play this game for three days, and due to the utter incompetence of the developers, I can't even get to the actual game. Why? Because, after downloading the "game" (or so I thought), the game launcher needs to download some kind of patch, which fails every time after anywhere between 2-20 minutes, and then has to start all over again. What is this, 1992? We've had downloaders that can survive connection failures for a pretty long time now. In 2022, there is simply no excuse for this kind of issue. The game lives on platforms (Steam, Epic) that have built-in downloaders that update every other game without problems like this--why on earth would you build a proprietary downloader that can't recover and resume a failed download? There is no option to download the patch file directly from a server, and the game's support website offers up a whole host of suggestions for this failure, which all distill down to "it's not our fault because... your internet is crap, your neighbors are hogging your ISP's bandwidth, you live in some part of the world where there's no reliable internet, or 'stuff happens'." Forum users suggest various solutions that consist of steps like "download it on a device that was blessed by genies in the tribes of Peru, manually transcribe the file using a hex debugger onto an airgapped flash drive, climb Everest to place it under the light of a full moon, then do a rain dance, climb back down the mountain, delete your entire hard drive, unplug your computer, plug it back in, reinstall Windows 3.1, copy the files to a new directory, making sure to leave a single file from the original installation directory, install Windows Vista update 8.6.7.5309 (not any other one, it won't work), offer a sacrifice to Tim Berners-Lee, then launch the game and pray that it works or you'll have to start all over again.

If on the astronomical chance you're still reading and thinking to yourself, "My God, this person is insane," all I can say is that hopefully this ridiculous diatribe illustrates the scope of my frustration at this debacle and it spares you the time and headache you would have spent trying to install this travesty. You're welcome.

***Edit***
After letting it run overnight a couple of times, much to my shock, this morning I found the game sitting on a faction selection screen. "Unbelievable," I thought, "I must have finally appeased the Q continuum! For joy, I can finally fantasy role play my beloved Star Trek!" Then I remembered that I have a job and couldn't spend all day frolicking at the Dabo wheel, so I put my PC into sleep mode. Hours later, having dreamt all day of fraternizing with my new crewmates, I awakened my machine, only to find that the launcher screen was back, now rendering in its entirety at roughly 300x300.

Can you guess what happened next? No, seriously, guess. I'll wait. Really, I mean it. Go on, guess. Did you say "It started patching again?" THAT'S RIGHT!! Oh, what a wonderful guesser you are! Patching again. AGAIN. As if it never happened. As if this morning was all just a lucid dream. Oh, how I had hoped I could come back and take back all my unkind words. But no, it is not to be, because I am back at square one, unable to play at all due to the cruel, cruel failure of the amateur programmers entrusted with such an unfathomable goal as making a game that can actually be played. These honorless fools may only atone now by ritual Hegh'bat, as tradition demands.

review_text:
I love the dark humour of the developers when they conceptualised this farming game set in the 1700s. The characters are simply adorable visually but what is remarkable is the different conversations that you can have with the NPCs. I didn't expect my pregnant spouse to complain about his favourite food or my children to bemoan the constant presence of me because they have plenty of chores (those brats). 
You need to talk to the NPCs and they give you delightful nuggets that would help you. eg. Watering twice a day in spring will make your plants grow faster.

The main quest is rather straightforward: survive...survive and survive. No, I'm kidding. (I think) You have to complete several quests to help the spirits stuck in the limbo. After that, it's really up to you. There isn't side quests to keep you going back to the game.
Visually, it is really a pretty game, matched with a delightful soundtrack. I really enjoyed autumn. The warm, golden hues along with its sombre music create a very pleasant experience.

OK, Let's talk about some mechanics.
The game is tough and the developers know it. You have options of turning off hunger and illness which is very useful at the start. If I want to be truly nit picky, there is no constant market to buy things that you pick, which makes it difficult to start a sustainable income. You actually need to know who has the deepest pockets (ahem, the mayor) Don't worry, the locals will eventually have more gold to buy your products if you sell things to them constantly.
Hunger is a major issue at the start since it is expensive to buy food. The easiest recipe, bread, requires egg and flour. That means you need to have the resources to build a coop to have chicken and you'll also need to grow wheat to have flour : not too doable until at least 2 weeks into the game.
Next, the fruit trees.
I think they must be considered a luxury item for year 2 and later since it takes 15 days for them to grow and bear fruits. Given that the season is only 21 days long, by the time the fruit trees are grown, you'll be in a new season. That means if you missed planting these trees by the first week, don't expect to have any fruits.
Next, events.
I love the unique conversations of NPCs during the lead up to the event. However, I think Autumn as a season is poorly designed for events, which is a waste. There are two major events which is Halloween and Harvest festival in a 21-day season. There was little hints about preparing for Halloween and I was caught by surprise. I was quite frustrated that I could only give the kids stones for trick and treat because I didn't know that you need to prepare caramel apples (1 caramel + 1 apple) As mentioned earlier, the fruit trees take 15 days to mature. That means that you can't have apples even if you planted them at the start of the season since Halloween is on day 12. Besides, caramel can only be bought from ships that visit during the weekend and you can buy only 1 each time. See the problem? You probably need to prepare from spring just to have enough apples for 7 kids. Anyway, it feels a little like the events is set up to fail even though it can be so cute to see the kids running around in their costumes. Now, you have to prepare for the harvest event in a week while prepping for winter..... YIKES.
Finally, FOOOD.
I used a guide for this after I realised the complexity of having sustainable food. Most of the recipes require produce from multiple seasons which mean that you need to stockpile while turning off the item decay option. I think I settled for buttered cod for the all cod seasons. I think that there should be more recipes that uses only produce within the same season so that cooking can be explored.

In all, it is a game worth playing for hours. There are some rough edges that can be smoothed and the developers have made it easier for us to survive by allowing us to turn off troublesome options like hunger, illness and decay.

review_text:
This game is not a classic life simulator and any comparisons with the well-known game "Stardew Valley" can be safely flushed down the toilet.
Echoes of the Plum Grove - EotPG for short - impresses with its "Paper Mario"-like graphics and the setting in old England.

In the menu you can set things up so that the difficulty level can be adjusted from ridiculously easy to monstrously devilish. Depending on how you prefer it. The advantage of this: Even in a running game, you can change these settings at any time.

For my part, I turned off hunger for the first month to familiarize myself with the game. However, in the 47 hours - aka 2 years - I only had one severe and one mild wave of illness. From other comments, I was probably luckier.

Thanks to the fishing rod (and the forums), I hardly had any money problems and the farm was basically only used for the pillar.
You don't get any real depth to other characters here. They are randomly generated. You shouldn't look for reality in general either (men can get pregnant, men & women can marry each other (I don't have anything against it, but it doesn't fit the setting - but it makes the game a lot easier)
I had to look for a lot of things on the internet because there was little to no information about it. I only knew some things thanks to previous knowledge of other games.
So I wouldn't recommend the game for beginners.
I definitely got my money's worth with 47 hours and I enjoyed it. In year 2 I concentrated more on the pillars, so that in spring 3 (that damn pineapple that was missing) I "finished" the game. But the game definitely has a high "replayability" value

review_text:
First impressions of this game are that it's kinda janky, very basic textures and environment design that appear quite dated in 2025.

Deeper impressions are that this game is actually a great deal of fun. It seems pretty clear this is a AA budget game with devs who are pushing every penny to try and make a horde combat experience that can beat the best AAAs in it's core gameplay design.

Thousands of bugs with a nice amount of variants (Inferno bugs, Grenadier bugs, Gunner bugs, Tanky bugs, little minion bugs etc) that can ambush you at any point. Really flexible base building and good objective based modes that mean you have to leave the safety of your base with little skirmish teams to get resources to build the base more. This experience is actually really close to how you would imagine the movies to feel.

The moment I fell in love with this game truly felt like a movie. It was me and some random medic were on our way to nuke a hive that the rest of the team were ignoring. We didn't have mics on to talk to each other (if it was real you'd probably not want to talk around these bugs anyway). We just understood it was a necessary mission even if we would not make it back to base. We managed to nuke the hive but got ambushed on the way out. We found ourselves backed into a little crevice that was too small for the hundreds of bugs chasing us to get into but we were desparately running out of ammo and nobody was coming. So we were stuck waiting for death or an opening to escape with only a bullet or 2 left in our pistols. What an experience! It actually felt like one of those movie scenes where you hope the main characters get out but there's an ominous sense of doom.

So really, give the game time to grow on you. Take time to experience these fantastic moments. You will get past the rough edges of a AA budget and find a gaming experience that is really intense and actually immersive into the Starship Troopers universe.

review_text:
One of my favourite games of all time. If I'm not feeling any other game, I usually just start this up and the next thing I know, hours have passed. It's literally endless enjoyment if you're into hockey and simulation and enjoy watching numbers go up and down (preferably up).

I originally used to play a very large amount of the NHL series on my PS4, and while it was fun to occasionally hop in and actually play the game, I found myself just simming through the franchise mode, season after season to watch my players and team progress. Once I found EHM, I almost entirely stopped playing NHL on my PS4. I realize not everyone will be like this, but if you are a fan more so of the sim aspect of other hockey games, this game will be perfect for you.

EHM is very deep in comparison to the NHL games on console. You can hire and fire all staff (scouts, medical, etc.), scout deep into any league you include (more on this later), set specific practice routines with the coaches you hire for specific players or your team as a whole, set specific tactics for each line, set tactics down to the specific player ie. if they carry the puck, if they have shoot/pass tendency, et cetera, and a very fleshed out drafting system and player development system which can seem entirely predictable until your #1 pick goes full Nail Yakupov. And there is much, much more.

The beauty of this game, to me, is that it's very customizable. You can add leagues, teams, players, mostly anything you want to do if you wish to invest the time in it. The steam workshop has plenty of add-ons, including rosters, facepacks, team logos, some of which I would argue are almost mandatory. Some might call this a knock on the game but it is not licensed, so while you don't get all of the logos and player's faces by default, it's easily added later. I personally roll with all of the facepacks and logos, as I feel it adds to the experience of the game and there's no negative. This part is entirely up to you, you could roll with default everything including roster, if you wanted to. There's generally current rosters in the workshop as well.

There are a couple negative factors to this game but they are rather minor. I had some crashing issues with a specific roster I had downloaded which likely stemmed more from the roster and less from the game. If I were to check the stats of some staff, the game would freeze. Not entirely too awful as long as you have an autosave, but annoying nonetheless. I've never had this problem with TBL roster, which could almost be considered the "official" roster update. Beyond that, the game -can- run slow if you turn on too many options or don't change the detail level. For example, if you use the largest database, and have more then one league on full detail, it will take quite a while to sim a day. In my experience, if you change the detail levels and use only one league, it sims quite quickly. Not a huge deal. Beyond that, I guess the only other thing I can think of is the learning curve. At first it's very steep, and you might find yourself a little overloaded, but if you persevere it's very rewarding and deep.

All in all, I'd highly recommend this game if you're passionate about hockey, or even if you just enjoy sports sims. As the game says, "there's a lot to like here".

review_text:
This has quickly become one of my favorite farming games. I love how unique it is, from being set in the 1700's, so the emphasis on generational gameplay, to the amount of chaos you have to deal with on a regular basis. There are a lot of challenges built into the game, but the settings allow a lot of flexibility to turn off harder settings. I've been playing with everything on except the fishing mini-games, since I don't like mini-games in general and the one in this game is rather terrible. 

THINGS I LIKE:
- The challenge. It's a difficult game with all the settings turned on. If you're not going to adjust the settings, you have to be willing to put up with some frustration and grinding, particularly early on. But this also makes it more rewarding when you get to a place when you're comfortable in the game and don't need to grind as much. 
- The  seasons. Seasons are only 21 days, which means you move through your character's life at a fairly reasonable pace so you can get to the next generation by the time you're bored with the current one. Also means that winter, which is generally the most boring season in farm sims, is less of a drag. I also love how much the weather varies. Winter isn't just all the same amount of snow; it fluctuates day to day. Days are shorter in winter, longer in summer, just like IRL. 
- The art style and world. Everything is very pretty. The map is relatively large. It does get less exciting the more you wander around looking for the same resources day after day, but it's still very nice looking. I love the character art. It was a little hard to adjust to the 2.5D because I've never played a game like that, but once I was used to it I really like it. 
- For being set in 1700, the game is fairly inclusive. Anyone can marry anyone, and anyone can get pregnant. There's also adoption options. 
- The festivals and events are all very cute. There's lot necessarily a ton to do at every since one, BUT I love that people actually move around and do stuff. In a lot of games, the characters just stand there doing nothing as you move around, but in EotPG, they participate in the activities and chat with each other. 
- When you move onto the next generation, their skills reset but you still maintain your inventory and all the recipes and stuff you've learned. I like that you have something you can still focus on for your next generation by building their skills back up, without making you feel like you've lost ALL your progress. 
- There is no shipping bin/box. At first this annoyed me, but I actually ended up liking that you have to go interact with the town to sell stuff. It adds to the challenge. And almost every villager is capable of buying from you (although their money amounts vary each day).
- While the game lacks conveniences like a shipping bin, it has a few other nice quality of life details. The inventory you get is large right from the beginning, and you have immediate access to fast-travel around town. 
- The magical elements. It's not enough to overshadow everything else, it's just a fun touch. 
- It's fun to get to know the villagers. They're simple but quirky. Are they super deep? No. But do I care? Also no. In a game where people drop like flies, I don't really need to be emotionally devastated every time someone is unalived. But it's fun to see how they pair up over the generations, who kicks the bucket early, and who takes over what profession. I've also had my current character go on a bit of a murder spree to cull some of the villagers and encourage new blood to come in. Sorry not sorry.

- Resources like trees and rocks do not regenerate on your farm. While it's nice in a lot of ways to not have to stay on top of keeping your farm clean, there aren't enough other ways to gather wood and stone. You can shake trees in town for wood but it's very grindy, and you can only get a few rocks per day in the mines. Occasionally you can lucky out and get these resources from villagers, but it's rare. 
- The mining is tedious. It takes more time to walk down the shaft to the mining spots than it does to actually mine. Once there, there are only two spots to mine from (and later a third) and you don't get very much from them each day. I get that it's probably meant to be more realistic to have to walk down deeper, but I could live without actually having to witness it. Same with the journey down to Limbo. It's unnecessarily long. You can use various things to make your character walk faster, but these are still a chore.

I've had to look up what a lot of the artisan machines need for you to put in them, since they don't tell you in game. I also had to look up how long each life stages last. There's a progress bar for the pages on adults, but that's the only stage you get it for. And it still doesn't tell you how long the progress bar goes for. 
- There are a few other things I dislike, but I think I'm going to raise them as suggestions before I complain about them in a review.

[NOT RECOMMENDED IF YOU DON'T HAVE PATIENCE]

I have mixed feelings about this game. Having a hard time not rating Yakuza 5 negative because it's a ''meh'' game at most.

Yet another filler game after Yakuza 4.

You get to play as Kazuma Kiryu, Haruka Sawamura, Shun Akiyama, Taiga Saejima and Tatsuo Shinada. Apart from Kiryu and Haruka I really have little to no interest in rest of the side characters. I felt so frustrated playing other characters' stories because it pulls the player from the main storyline. Now of course one could argue that side characters are a part of the main storyline, but they could very well be excluded from the main storyline and the game still would achieve telling its main storyline successfully.

To me, plot seems weak and story telling is done poorly on Yakuza 5. Saejima's city exploration and errands works, Shinada's city exploration and errand works could very well be excluded from the game because the game is unneccessarily stretched at least +20-30 hours in length. Is that a bad thing? Yes, if the content is recycled boring errand work in each character's episode.

These aside, the character dialogues are unnecessarily too long (10-15 mins in-game talks) and repetitive and then comes the 15 minutes (average) cutscenes after each part/chapter completion. Good luck not losing your mind. You can't even save your game before you are free in the free roam. 

My favorite are Yakuza 0, Yakuza Kiwami and Yakuza Kiwami 2. After these games, Yakuza 3-4-5 seem very poorly done. These are filler games at best. I was seeking for an amazing story but I am just disappointed.

For anyone looking to enjoy Yakuza series, I'd recommend playing Yakuza 0, Kiwami and Kiwami 2. Those are the golden games of the series.

review_text:
I wont give a super in depth review on much of the actual game mechanics, but I can give you a bit of my emotional journey starting with this:
If you do not already have experience in games like this, do not play on the hard difficulty. (unless you may be a secret video games masochist?)

Coming into this, I had never played a game like this before, but I did a quick google on difficulty and found the "true ending" is locked behind the hard difficulty, so I started a run on just that. I didn't expect it to be too bad, but damage thresholds are one hell of a thing. So many one shot kills... I think I died a little under 10 times during the tutorial section of the game.

I got hard stuck about 2 and a half hours into the game on the giant slime boss (just long enough for sunk cost fallacy to not restart the game on an easier difficulty), and tried (unsuccessfully) editing my save file to the regular difficulty for about 20 minutes. Because of this, I had to just keep trying, and I tried and tried to "Get good." Eventually, there was a moment of clarity, my skills did not get better (at least not at the time, by the end of the game I used literally the starting sword with generic damage buffs in one final blaze of glory), but I did remember the very first thing this game tells you when you press start. 

"This is a survival game." As it turns out, trying to get good was the problem. The entire first two phases of the boss are just a puzzle with an incredibly simple solution. Hint: Consider the implications of your item descriptions, and don't shy away from using magic, even if it's impossible to regenerate early game outside of consumables.

After solving the "puzzle" the first and second phase was me pressing a single button about 6 times. And from what I can tell? That was the correct way to beat the boss. Like, they said "This is a survival game," I solved the puzzle on surviving the boss. That's what combat in this game is like. The tools they give you can trivialize large portions of the game when used cleverly, as the developers intended.

I'm going on a tangent now, but like really, the hard mode was so hard what the fuck man. I died 126 times to beat the game. I probably enjoyed the game more because I played it on what was basically a fucking challenge run (hardest difficulty and no opening chests for an optional quest that only affects the games ending, despite chests containing all the good early game items, as well as some of the best items in the game), but if I was even a little bit less motivated I'd have quit the game 5 times over.

Despite the fact that the difficulty often felt like "hard but fuck you" instead of "hard but fair" whenever I didn't understand what the game wanted (make clever builds with in game tools to abuse enemy weaknesses and play it safe), I can't help but give this a positive review. It was damn fun, but devs what the hell man. I think some of my hairs went grey when I played this game.

review_text:
[h1]If this game goes 100% off on sale it's already too expensive.[/h1]

Pathologic 2 had the potential to be an outstanding hidden gem but in the end, it suffers from the same bloody fate as many other brilliant games out there: [b]f*cking terrible devs doing an utterly bad job in order to delive a pinch more of challenge so they're able to brag about their game being difficult (even if the cost is ruining it entirely), forgetting to test their own game and squash bugs instead of adding more useless dialog throughout the empty town you find yourself in.[/b]

Pathologic itself is complex, unforgiving if playing as intended, mind twisting, narrative-driven feturing an ocean of text and strange language, and 100% psychological horror. You will get lost many times, lose opportunities many times, but after all you realize that's the catch.
And that's fine. It is supposed to be difficult. The set up prepares you for a miserable experience since the very beginning, and it warns a dozen times you are to get the grip of things instead of being led by the hand.

HOWEVER, as no game is perfect, you find out soon that Pathologic 2 has some game-killing, deadly serious defective systems:

1. Basic needs. While the whole world feels unnatural but somehow very realistic at the same time (put aside the lack of character model diversity), basic needs are very very very very poorly handled, tearing down immersion. Artemy needs to eat barrells of food per day and drink gallons of water if he is to not die while sleeping - which can absolutely happen - and the food is UNGODLY expensive. I mean, yeah, the town is facing a huge shortage of many products but that's not possibly an excuse. You struggle to make 1k coins, then you find out a fish that heals a laughable amount of hunger [b]and recovers no health at all[/b] costs you nearly 700 coins.
As one would expect, jumping and running consumes stamina by a lot, bringing even more variables to mess with need meters. Turns up to be awful as hell when we barely have enough daytime to explore and uncover the world around us, summed with the f*cked up mindless economy system they implemented here.

2. [b]Death. Dying DOES NOT take away even 1% of your exhaustion (not to be confused with stamina), leading to scenarios where you can be HARD LOCKED WITHIN A DEATH LOOP if you have no healing items in your inventory. I guess it is just too hard for russians to use their brains and acknowledge the fact that when you move a respawning character back to the last saving point while giving a random death penalty but no chance to heal, no chance to search for items or sleep (you can't sleep in any bed/bedroll/couch you find) WITH NO PREVIOUS WARNING ABOUT IT, you frustrate them. Would be better to make it permadeath and clarify the real importance of dealing with exhaustion above all.
I've been gaming since '97 and I can't really remember a game that failed so miserably in the SIMPLEST MISSION that is respawning a character.[/b]

3. Performance issues. Notorious and gross. Devs say recommended settings are a 16GB RAM rig with NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970 plus an intermediate 3GHz processor but mind you: even far more powerful PC owners reported stutterings and issues that shouldn't happen. Yes it is a beautiful and demanding game indeed, but f*cking ugly optimized.
If you face crashes, textures not rendering correctly and less than 50fps with even minimum requirements, check out forums on how to fix those by changing params directly inside Pathologic 2 files.

4. Bugs. You won't immerse yourself in a town where you fight a spreading plague; you will be fighting [b]all unsolved bugs devs were too lazy to NOT MESS WITH during this REMAKE.[/b] I mean yeah, let's make a remake, but let's not touch any glitch, bug or whatever.
I promptly lost interest in Pathologic 2 due to 2 unnaceptable bugs for a game like this where loading a previous game does not erase your death (yeah I know it is laughable but, remember: russian devs. They have no clue): first was a guy teleporting right behind my back and stabbing me to death in a single hit while I had half HP left as soon as I opened a random door. Second was a guy crossing a prop barrier a.k.a invisible wall when I was chasing him.

Devs made the impossible true: failing miserably at a game that is 95% talking to people, trading, walking, collecting herbs and fast travelling. If I bought my 7yo son an Unity license he would come up with a better game, like everyone else around here could.

If you still want to play this overpriced garbage, then read about how every core mechanic works and avoid playing vanilla Imago difficulty. There's a mod that do what devs apparently couldn't (aside from being humans with more than 10 IQ), fixing game balance by a bit.

review_text:
World of Goo Review

Ahh, this is probably the first video game I have ever played. EVER. I still remember the times where my cousin and I would play this game on his iPad (1st Gen), having so much fun. Remembering this, I gave World of Goo a shot, and boy howdy did I instantly fall in love with this game.

World of Goo is a physics game on building Goo structures to reach a certain goal. Usually, this is a pipe that you need to build to, but on the last levels of each world (there are 6, including the Epilogue and the World of Goo Headquarters), there is a different objective to advance the story line. The levels aren't overly difficult, they're just difficult enough to intrigue you, but not to rage-quit the game. I really enjoyed this game.

On every level (except the first), the Sign Painter (A.K.A. The Sign Writer, SignPaintr4evr, [spoiler]The Telescope Operator[/spoiler]) writes messages on signs. They can either give tips, advance the story line or simply be humorous. If I were being honest, I would not have been able to complete the game if it wasn't for this mysterious, funny and slightly creepy (he can see you even though his messages come in the form of SIGNS. Give me a break) man/woman that is the Sign Painter.

Every once in a while, you can encounter different types of Goo. Some worlds are completely based on that specific goo. One example is the Green (Ivy) Goo. These types of Goo have 3 attachment 'arms' and can detach from the Goo structure if you so wish to. In the words of the Sign Painter: '[i]Maybe they have commitment anxiety, I'm not sure, but it looks like they can be easily detached from each other.[/i]'

The story line completely revolves around one company: The World of Goo Company. This is the company responsible for controlling (not making) and modifying different types of Goo. Once you complete a certain amount of levels, you unlock a special world: The World of Goo Headquarters. This is where all your goo get placed when they go into the pipes. Once again, in the words of the Sign Painter: '[i]As you complete levels, the Goo Balls you collect are sent here. How nice to see them again! Though they seem to have lost their essence[/i].' The World of Goo Corporation refine the Goo into a special type of Goo before sending it into the world. The special Goo Balls (which I will call WOG Goo) are kind of a mix between the normal Goo and the Green Goo; they can detach from the structure, like the Green Goo, but they have similar colouring and the same amount of attachment arms as the normal Goo. In this world, you have only one goal: build UP (or do nothing). [spoiler]And you can totally obliterate the Headquarters near the end of the game.[/spoiler]

The story line is great. The animation and sprites are even more so, and the puzzles in the game are really clever and fun. 2D Boy did a great job with their games (they also made Little Inferno, the game which had the trailer that is scary, Human Resource Machine and 7 Billion Humans). I thoroughly enjoyed this game. If you want a puzzling but intriguing and fun gaming experience, why not play World of Goo?

As someone who put over 10,000 hours in the Japanese version and currently have XX hours in the NA version, I've got a few things to say.

NEW PLAYERS READ THIS
These are the things you should know right away if you plan to play as a free player with as little trouble as possible
Do NOT feed your mag until you've done your research on how they work
Points in the skill tree cannot be reset without a free reset pass, which is usually handed out often enough as the game updates. But due to the NA version mostly having combat content that JP already has, it's not as often for now. If you have a reset pass feel free to mess around with the class tree to get a feel for things, but if not then you should do your research before putting your points in things you regret. Most of how well your class does depends on how you use these points.
You get 3 characters for free, server-wide. You can put those three characters in one ship, or on different ships.
More characters are your way of making in-game currency, which is how you upgrade your gear and get cosmetics
Don't worry about making your character look perfect on the first try. You can change most things at any time (accessories, eye pattern, tattoos, etc). The things you can't change whenever are things related to the size of the character, shape of their faces, things related to that. But you don't have to worry about that either, because every so often you can obtain a free pass to change your characters looks without paying, and they come often enough. The only thing you can't change at all after making your character is your gender and race.
If you want to avoid paying a cent but want to play every class type, make a character per atk type (Striking, Ranged, Technique)
You can use as many skill discs as you want, there is no limit
Every weapon and unit you pick up is trash, sell it in an NPC shop. Upgrade your gear if it's better. You do not need to hoard them until you start getting 10* drops or better, which in that case you put them in your storage until you learn how to use the recycle shop.
You make money by doing Daily Orders every day, which is located on the left side of the quest gate from an NPC behind a counter. You make the most money by the time you can run things in the Super Hard difficulty. All characters can run them, making them the best way to make money.
Start by talking to Officer Cofy and doing all her client orders, then from there start messing around and have fun!

Now, here are my personal opinions about this game.
I like to describe this game as something like Monster Hunter with Devil May Cry combat. As a free to play MMO, people will approach this with caution. But I'll let you know, this game is very free to play, you can play as well as you desire without paying a single cent. The pay for stuff is mostly for cosmetics and conveniences, to make you in-game money faster through real life money means. But if you know your way around the game, you never have to do this.
Starting out, the game is great! People don't really like to call this an MMO since most quests are only done with up to 12 players in a quest, but who cares. The combat is really fun, the random stuff that occur while going through maps is an experience. Then when emergency quests happen and multiparty bosses appear, those are really fun too! Upgrading gear can be kind of confusing, but isn't hard to do once you talk to others or do your research. It used to be a very frustrating RNG process but not so much anymore.
The only downside is that when you reach endgame, there's sometimes not much to do other than wait for emergency quests to happen and go through your daily CD's (which usually doesn't take too long). Also emergency quests that do not have an objective can be pretty stale, since it's mostly just running around in the circle on a map and one shotting any boss that spawns. A problem can be that bosses aren't all that fun to fight with too many players, since they flinch until dead. But this is mostly fixed later on when harder difficulties are unlocked. Either way though, games combat is too fun to easily put down.
The game is a beautiful anime game, and customizing your character is really great! If you want to make your perfect waifu or mimic a favorite character from a series, it's likely you'll be able to do so in this game. Also, being able to make mech's as well will make the mecha lads pretty happy!
There's talk of censorship but I don't see it. I still have my sexy bikini's, I still can make a character with the fattest and finest tits and ass. When there's cosmetics that pretty much reveals almost all of your characters body, I don't see where the problem is.

review_text:
The combat loop is a lot of fun, which is good because there's not much else to it. The game (at launch) consists of 5 levels, one of which is mostly a boss fight. Graphics are great with SteamVR/Index and I find myself playing a game or two a day to work towards the unlockables. 

There is a weapon skin system where different skins unlock at different kill/headshot tiers. e.g. 1000 kills with a weapon for the solid white skin, or 200 headshots for a camo skin. The gun modifications you get from playing make a huge difference, but they are mostly just increases to a guns "stats" such as damage, recoil, or ammo count.

The matchmaking is pretty poor, and just loading into maps can sometimes be a challenge. It's not uncommon for you to lose a player or two when the map finally starts. This leads to an awkward wait while the matchmaking times out and you are given an AI instead. The AI is perfectly fine for the easy difficulty, but will quickly die on anything higher.

If you enjoyed Alyx and want more VR gunplay then I definitely recommend this game. If you want anything else, like a story, or a good solo experience then you should look somewhere else.

I know I joined the party late for an Early Access game (I got it after the Webgrave update), but this is great.
Lots of different guns, a level up-mechanic for both your character and the guns, nice gear with exchangeable boni (provided you got the stat to equip them first) - an acceptable difficulty curve and combat overall, even for someone like me who's past their "prime" in gaming (reaction time, target quisition and tracking were a lot better 15 years ago) I will list the things that I personnaly liked most:
- a very wide array of firearms (>20 at the time of writing, havenÄt used all of them), ranging from revolvers to submachine guns, to snipers, even a stake thrower like in good old PAINKILLER - it's all there and nearly a guarantee that everyone finds weapons to suit their style
-a good armament of magic spells (which can also be leveled up, alsoe around 20 or so at the time of review), damage spells, stun, crowd control, everything covered to fit your taste
- a reasearch mechanic (great so far - i hope they maybe add some parts to it to make it viable for even mroe replayability, or maybe it's already there, haven't reached high enough level of unlocks to see the final stage and it's in active development enyway)
-the ability to give yourself different buffs to make some runs more doable (was very improtant for me and helpful to flatten the challenge curve many times -which sometimes spikes up noticeable between different levels and gnosis stages (raises enemy hp and xp gains, you pick when to apply it, but can never go back to lower rating) 
- good level design so far with , 5 levels as i write this, with more in development and some planned additions to existing ones, levels are small to medium size so far - you are able to move from one end to teh other in accepable time and also many little collectibles (which is a good thing, since even when you need to backtrack you might find stuff that you missed the first time)
- good graphics (to clarify for readers: I don't really care about this myself, but they might not be as super  high-res realisticly overwhelming like some new RPGS or other shooters, but hell, this is a FPS with mystical creatures withces and zombies, and everythign looks nice, the essence is in the action and overall it looks pretty good, the screenshots don't lie, it's solid and good looking) - performance is great with my rig, 32gb ram, rtx 3080 and a Ryzen 9 5900x.
- every run is moreless unique, in a sense, the map stays the same, but enemy locations, challenges, traps and other stuff switches around places - there are some constants like enemy types in general, but it makes for good replayability/farming
I could maybe think of other points (ad maybe format this better), but this shuld suffice for now. 
All in all I can say, although I rarely buy new games and am very careful of Early Access Titles, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game in it's current state, it's already a solid experience and hopefully will only get better. If you can, grab it at a sale, and even for "full price" now in Early Access it's worth it in my opnion and very likely will be worth your while, if you found any of the listed attrivutes intriguing.

tl;dr: It's a very good game in my opinion, good gameplay, nice graphics, might be too easy for a DOOM-veteran with good reaction time, but challenging enough for someone who knows their way around shooters (with more stuff to come to tweak it according to your skill level, according to the roadmap which I look forward to).

review_text:
Even after almost 2 years, I still think back to this game. I honestly consider it one of my all time favorite games. Scorn has such a weirdly beautiful world that part of your brain is telling you to look away from, but you just can't. Discovering how to progress can sometimes be a challenge, but moving around the environment and seeing all the little details while trying to do so really helps show the morbid beauty of the game. 

While I think that the look and feel of the world is intoxicating and can go on and on about it, i don't think the game is completely infallible. At some point there will be combat and it feels out of place, and a little wonky. Don't let that discourage you. It may be a little tedious, but almost every combat encounter can be completely avoided by just sitting and waiting away from an enemy, and waiting for them to crawl into a hole or around a corner where they cant see you. I think that this approach to combat will help immerse you into the world and also helps in the long run by letting you conserve as much ammo as possible for the unavoidable combat encounters. 

Scorn is a genuinely interesting game that has a few hiccups when it comes to combat. With that being said it is absolutely well worth your time and will definitely be a game that sticks with you, just like it did for me.

review_text:
This game is a masterpiece.

After waiting for it since its very first teaser and initially playing it on Switch, I finally bought it again on Steam. Team Reptile managed to capture and enhance both the gameplay and aesthetic of Jet Set Radio Future. Just like with Lethal League, they added a strong dose of personality and elevated the formula even further.

I’ve seen some comments saying the game feels repetitive. With three years of hindsight and a more objective perspective, it's true that a certain sense of repetition can emerge, especially from performing similar actions in each new area. That said, the platforming segments in Red’s dreams are very engaging. I would have loved to see that level of challenge in the regular platforming zones or boss fights. The game is much more vertical than its predecessors, though it’s not exactly a hardcore platformer.

Once you understand that it's the corners and the signs that grant multipliers, and you’re playing through the game for the third or fourth time, the difficulty drops significantly — which makes sense, since you’ve mastered it by then. Still, it would be interesting to see the difficulty curve rethought for a potential sequel, to keep things engaging for more experienced players.

All that may sound negative, but if you’re playing the game for the first time, the gameplay is so satisfying that you likely won’t even notice this potential repetitiveness. The colors, environments, characters, story, and especially the music immerse you in a rich and highly creative universe.

The game's overall atmosphere alone is enough to make you love its content and what it has to offer. Mods further enhance the experience by adding new content, unique experiences, and great fixes. Sort the mods by popularity on Thunderbolt, and you’ll find some really cool stuff to check out after just a few hours of play.

I sincerely recommend playing this game. I waited for it as a spiritual successor to Jet Set Radio Future, and I was absolutely not disappointed. It’s a game I love, and one I regularly come back to — especially to play online with friends. Go for it!!!

review_text:
I was looking forward to this after being kinda concerned it would never be, and based on my enjoyment of the first part, this one did not disappoint. Classic point and click adventure with the worst possible part being a puzzle or two that can be a bit difficult to figure out exactly what the game wants you to do. I had heard of some possible buggy parts, but did not encounter any on my playthrough so I can't say for certain what the deal is behind those.

Definitely a high point is the richness of the setting while simultaneously not requiring you to know the super dense lore from Homestuck to get into. The bite sized approach is as appreciated this time as it was last time. Characters are generally quirky, fun, well designed, and generally memorable. That even random background characters have unique designs is an especially nice touch.

On the downside, I do feel that [spoiler]the trial sequence dragged on quite a bit and could be frequently unintuitive to solve all for an overly long Phoenix Wright parody. I feel that section was disproportionately lengthy compared to the other sections and not quite as entertaining due to the gameplay deviation, though admittedly, I've always found trial sequences in video games rather tedious.[/spoiler] It did create a feeling that the other sections might be underdeveloped or rushed in comparison, though I did still enjoy them.

Also, the choice in music track for one particular section [spoiler]the gold/olive car[/spoiler] had a classic 8 bit sound that got kinda annoying to hear on loop given how long I spent in that particular area.

I do hope Hiveswap is able to fully complete it's story and while I understand that game development is a complicated matter, it would be nice to not have to wait several more years for parts 3 and 4 given how relatively short these are.

Edit: Given the length of time that's passed, it would be nice if nothing else if there was some kind of update or disclaimer so people know what they're getting into. It's been years and while Hiveswap isn't cancelled per se, I would definitely caution getting invested without more substantial and official proof of continued development. Personally, random youtube videos and rumors on social media don't cut it for me. If development is continuing, something more official posted here on Steam would be a big reassurance.

review_text:
It's not a bad game, but it could be a much better game.

At it's heart, it's a little town sim, which is cute enough on its own, but to make things a bit more interesting your town gets regularly attacked by monsters. These monsters follow "tower defense" logic where they don't attack walls and take the shortest route to anything else they can break, so your mission is to build a maze of some complexity, plop down some towers, and behind said maze nurture a society that can upgrade and maintain it.

This is a pretty great concept, but for some reason they thought you'd be up for playing the exact same game like 20-something times. Once you've gotten a self-sustaining society behind the maze, and figured out which towers are pointless(bow, phantom dart and any of the bullet ones, really. Why would I ever build a tower that couldn't shoot over walls?), you've won. So really the only challenge is whether you correctly guess the shortest route and defend that within the first few days, and then you've pretty much won.

Hell, half the citizens' basic needs, like social interaction, you don't even notice because just by existing they satisfy those. Things are automated enough that your only real active control of the world is where to put down buildings, but the AI automation isn't interesting enough to cough up any scenarios as a result(your villagers, for instance, have no personalities, specializations, etc. and only two monsters have abilities beyond "walk towards thing, hit thing.").

It feels like an early access game that slipped through and got released early, because there's just a lack of content and depth.

Not to mention pretty goddamn lackluster tutorializing, it took me until my second year(in-game, not real-time) to figure out that what looked like a bit of UI fancy bordering under the available spells was actually a menu allowing access to more spells.

You can complete challenges to unlock stuff, but they're literally all just "have a +% to do thing in game." None of them change up the gameplay experience or open new options.

There are also some weird AI issues, like how you can organize all village constructor tasks in priorities... except for clearing terrain, which they'll always obsessively do first.

Even just some minor things, like being able to waypoint locations or patrol routes for your rangers and defensive golems would have added a bit of stuff to do. Why does the Medic even exist? I don't think I ever had a villager get injured outside of random weather events, but then they just self-bandaged or went to chill at home for a few seconds and were right as rain. You can't manually order villagers to slaughter livestock, so it's up to the vagaries of the AI whether an animal pen generates any food or not. You can't focus on acquiring iron or gold for gear/trading, respectively, since they're all just random drops from mining generic rock. Storage is completely boned, all storage is available in the same amounts, which means that for relatively rare things, like tools and weapons, you'll never need specialized storage because your stock buildings have enough spare storage for all of it. While for super-common things like rocks, wood and food, you'll always be starved for storage and the buildable storage buildings are almost a waste of your time because they don't give *enough* extra space.

Water seems like an afterthought of a feature, terrain-wise, since it's all hip-deep and wadable, being just a movement speed modifier, and you can effortlessly pave it over. So you can't, for instance, spice things up with stuff like a moat.

I can't really recommend this game, because it could be so much better, and it feels like the dev(s) just didn't want to bother going that last stretch.

After that, the game's bland mechanics and incessant crashing just were so much more apparent, and further distanced me from the game. The crashing was beyond annoying, because the game would only crash after a long period of textual exposition that would not allow a save, and require sometimes multiple reloads to get through just the "cutscene" in order to get far enough to save again. The resolution was so low that when it crashed, getting the game to fully close was difficult because Task Manager was impossible to call up due to the fact that there was nowhere on the taskbar to right click, and alt+tab wouldn't fully work to call up other applications because they were too large for the screen. Eventually I had to run it in windowed mode, and scale down my desktop resolution to 800x600 just so I could properly deal with a crash. So in the end, no, I don't recommend this game. The story was good, but not good enough to not walk away frustrated and disappointed.

review_text:
Have you ever consumed a piece of media that was just okay? You watched it, your opinion wasn't one direction or another? Realistically, that is my experience with Callisto Protocol. 

The game is fine. The story is generic, the setting is generic, the combat is repetitive; however, it still holds a charm that many games miss. I will not advocate you to buy this full price. This is not a game worth more than maybe ten dollars at best, but if the setting/plot interests you, I'm sure you'll get value from it.

Many of the original complaints for this game regarding performance and lack of "dead space-y" vibes have been addressed with content patches and actual development time. For people craving the DS experience, there is dismemberment mode now, and that more or less, makes enemies lose limbs whenever you shoot them or hit them hard. It's satisfying and certainly more interesting than the combat of the main game which most revolves around you holding directional keys to avoid attacks then counter. 

This isn't a huge thumbs up review, this is however, a review that is middle ground. It is not absolute dogshit like some may make you think. The game functions, there were no crashes, there were no huge audio/visual/control bugs. 

If you want space horror and are okay with a bit of slop, you'll get a nice 6-8 hour playthrough from this.

review_text:
Incorporates 3rd-party DRM: SecuROM™  So, for that, you may want to skip it entirely.

Largely fixing the control problems of Arkham Asylum on PC, Arkham City takes you and throws you into a large environment that allows you to explore and fight in many different interesting and entertaining ways.

Control problems out of the way, you are largely free to play the game without concern for what is happening next, you can just go with the flow and not worry about a lack of gadgets.  Of course, Arkham Asylum's silly idea of RPG elements are still around, and shouldn't be, but the developer needed to shoehorn in a reason to collect things - other than just it being an entertaining set of puzzles.

Unfortunately it does have a problem with game design, Batman does not fight armies of men in hand to hand combat...  He fights small groups from time to time, but it is quite rare to see Batman taking on 50 men.  Yet in this game, it happens on several occasions, as though the developers wanted you to feel super badass for doing this amazing thing that Batman would think is incredibly stupid and a waste of his time.  Batman does not take down armies, he would use a clever gadget to take down most of them, and then mop up the rest.

The game is fun, the story is a bit contrived, but that is kind of standard for Batman stories.

I could easily recommend this game to players who enjoyed Arkham Asylum and were looking for more.

review_text:
(Hey! This review will receive an update when the game does! My opinions will change along with the state of the game!)

Honestly, I hate I am leaving a negative review for this game. Bonelab isn't atrocious, in fact it has a ton of potential. An openly moddable VR game a la gmod? Sounds  great, right? Well, at the moment of writing this, it's a bit more convoluted than that. 

First, the campaign. In short, it is horribly executed. It doesn't even feel like a campaign with how random it is. However, I can't really get into the criticism without getting into the meat and potatoes of the campaign. So, if you care about spoilers then skip ahead.[spoiler] Anyway, the game doesn't stay consistent within the first two levels of the campaign. First you start of with the hanging scene, which I will say really sets the tone and motivation for our story despite how brutal and sensitive a subject matter it is. Then it transitions into structures similar to Boneworks, its predecessor, which is cool to see the continuity. We approach the titular Bone Lab in the definitely-safe-to-use elevator, surrounded with... gamemodes? Huh? Ok, uh, we then progress by... hopping... through... different gamemodes? Wha- *ahem*. My dear reader, there is the continuity break, the first one at least. There's more? Oh yeah, later in the game you hop around different unrelated (and bland) levels collecting avatars with different stats so you can continue with the continuous part of the game. Why am I so frustrated about this? [/spoiler] Because Boneworks had a WAY better campaign that Bonelab, and Boneworks had that continuity to fuel that feeling of progression. Boneworks had visible landmarks getting closer by the level, keeping the rush of accomplishment lively. Bonelab has a body collectathon. Yikes. A majority of the store page goes over the content included with the game, the minority of it goes over-

Oh yea, the mods.

Um, how do I put this uh...

The SDK is still in development. 

It's last update was aboooout...

Six mo-

...

six months... ago...

...

WHAT?! IT'S BEEN THAT LONG!?

Oh boy, this is my absolute FAVORITE part of this game. The modding system is incomplete in a sandbox game about modding. How was this flubbed? HOW?! What if gmod added really basic features into the game you just couldn't mod in without a hackey workaround? What happened in the officially supported modding scene over the past six months? Nothing extraordinarily ground breaking. I think a group of modders was half way through porting Boneworks in the game, which just proves how desperate people are to play a different campaign. By the way, the mod makers for this game are awesome people for even putting up with these honestly silly limitations. Speaking of limitations, you can't search for specific mods. Nor can you link a mod.io account for the game. Y'know, this feels more like a Bethesda moment right here. Ship a incomplete mess and leave it to the community. What's even funnier is that most of these problems can be resolved by an external mod extender.

MelonLoader is a god send. What happened over the past six months with MelonLoader? Oh, just fully functional multiplayer and mod sync with mod.io, nothing too extreme for a single player game. A problem with MelonLoader is that it is PC exclusive at the moment (LemonLoader is the WIP quest port for MelonLoader that has issues with certain mods), leaving a massive chunk of the player-base on quest stranded.

The lack of SDK updates isn't the worst part. It's the lack of transparency. There has been no sign of life from the devs over the past six months. No official communication. If there was even a speck of reassurance that something was in the works, I would have been way less harsh on the game. Unfortunately, that isn't the state the game is in. I love the potential this game has, I love what this game CAN be. I hate what the game is, I hate what the game was left TO be. The modders can't just do all the heavy work SLZ, they need official support.

Well, here's to six months, and here's to possibly six more.

review_text:
I wish I could recommend this game. I really do, I was so excited when I first saw it and I waited so long for it to come out... but it just... fails as a game.  As other reviews have pointed out, the game description is 50% lies. 

First the good,
The game LOOKS great. Well it looks gruesome and awful, but it's very well detailed.  For most of the game I felt I was seeing all unique assets and structures.  The sound is great. Very visceral.

But now the bad.
The combat. The early gameplay trailers made it seem like combat was always a choice. You COULD fight monsters to make your path safer to navigate, but also fighting them was risky and used up some of your already scarce resources. It seemed like sneaking was much more viable. This is not the case in the final game. You either kill the monsters attacking you, or run, trying to dodge their attacks. There is no sneaking. The closest you come is staying out of aggro range until the monster moves out of your way. 

The puzzles. A lot of the puzzles... well they're not the worst but like 90% of the puzzles amount to 'hunt around this environment to find the lever we hid'. Sometimes with the modifier of having to pull the levers in the correct order. They're not good or bad, they're just serviceable.  And for this game to call itself a 'puzzle' game, that is a big failure.

The story. I like implied storytelling. I like having to infer from the world around me. I do not like the story in this game. You have to give me SOMETHING. There is literally no given player character motivation. There is player motivation in the form of "this is a video game, keep moving forward". That doesn't count. Throughout the entire run of the game I was wondering why I was in this place and what I was trying to achieve.  The (spoiler) fact you actually control 2 different characters over the course of the game doesn't help either (it's a very early swap, so barely a spoiler).

The ending. I'm not going to spoil the ending, but I will share my thoughts on it. The ending sucks. It sucks because of the just mentioned story issues. If the game had ended right before solving the final door puzzle (or the final door puzzle could have been solved differently), I would have felt much better about the game. The game honestly could have ended like 5 minutes sooner and have been better for it, because it would have actually given me what the motivation was, even if it was retroactive. But no, the game ended the way it did and destroyed that theory.

However, there's not much creativity involved as you have set ways in which to get about your evil ways so the replay value is really low. The controls are clunky which often leads to frustrated mashing of buttons and a complete loss of  immersion. Oh, and it doesn't matter if you've already figured out what to do, the game just won't let you do it until you've gone through the entire house looking for Lucius' thought processes so that HE figures out what has to be done. 
Oh and the achievements are ridiculous. I finished the game and then spent 12 more hours on it until I could take no more and still am as far from the damned "I Love Lucius" achievement as ever.

I can only recommend this game; especially if you are a fan of the movie(s).

I'm giving this a positive review, but with the conditions that you get it on sale and that you either haven't played Samorost 3, or you're willing to cut this one some slack for being older. The pros and cons of this game are similar to most other Amanita Design releases: surreal art, intuitive story and trial-and-error puzzling, amazing music and a few moments of baffled frustration. If you're not sure about it, try Samorost 1 since it's free.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
+Cute, surreal artwork and sound.
+Music is great (available for nearly-free on bandcamp).
+Easy to pick up where you left off.

[h1]YMMV[/h1]
~Full screen controls are a bit wonky.
~A couple puzzles aren't fully-intuitive.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
-Only about an hour of playtime.
-A few screens have some pixel hunting. I didn't need to look up any guides, but in every situation where I was stuck, there was something I didn't know I could click on. Be patient.
