review_text:
I bought the game after seing a story explained video and was really interested by the Universe that has a very unique spirit and uncommun artistic vibe. I was so happy to find an estheatic close to the movie "the war of the worlds" and Gigger's Art. 

Such a deception...

Frankly the gameplay with the gun is so broken I would have simply removed it from the game since it does not bring anything. This is the first time I'm playing a game with a gun hitting closer than my arm reach. This is crazy considering that fixing this element should take roughly 5 minute of coding and would make the game so much more enjoyable. Also, the gamedesign elements are not very optimized all the time which also break the fluidity of the "journey". 

Some puzzles are interesting though, but since the game is not presented as a puzzle game and they are sparsely distributes across the levels, we don't really understand why they are there? Honestly, at some stage, I just thought that their civilization has fallen apart because they implemented such weird mechanism just to open a door... Such a non-optimization may have only result in their loss. 

There are a few problems with the game even when considering the "Universe" as the main  "concept" of the game. Typically, you can't have such a poor sound design if the goal is to catch the players into your atmosphere. I understand that we are living on a silly and dying world, but even in such a case, musics and soundtracks can be used. You can introduce travelling point of view or cinematic to highlight the landscape or peculiar elements of the decor. Finally, you can put discret texts hidden in the levels (such as drawings on the wall) that would help the players to "get" the story you want to tell. 

Simply hiding your video game concept behind a creepy cruel and dirty world esthetic is not sufficient to claim 50$. I got it with a 75% discount and this was already too expensive for me and asked a refund.

As an example "Agony", that is far to be perfect, was definitely more successful in that sense.

review_text: This is an outstanding gaming experience, but a gentle one . Many people do not realise there is such a thing as a quiet action-adventure, a slow and gradual way of carefully planning and executing your moves. we have been so  immersed in games of high speed, explosive action in movies and games that we  neglect the stories of complex suspense  where the action slowly builds up, carefully stepping toward a goal. It's not quite a chess game, but it is a game of strategy. There is still sword-swinging, shuriken-throwing, gunpowder-exploding action, but it's done in a gentle phase at a time. This seems to fit the world of medieval Japan. The Japanese culture includes the furious, brutal warfare. But it also includes the graceful and beautiful arts like writing poetry and building Zen gardens. A mighty samurai warrior still has a quiet side.  ---- All of the elements of a Japanese action game are here: ninja, samurai, and martial arts. But you do it in a stealth setting. Even if you've never tied a stealth game before, I recommend you try it. I had never played one like this, and was pleasantly surprised.

review_text:
The intro to Just Cause 3: Shooting rockets while standing on an airplane flying over a war zone
The intro to Just Cause 4: "Follow the pipes Rico"

I haven't experienced the same crashing or technical issues others have, my gameplay has been rather smooth and unproblematic. Instead, I'm focusing my review on one thing: the fun factor, something JC4 distinctly lacks. The Just Cause franchise has evolved into a very clear gamplay loop: blow something up, go to the next thing to blow up, repeat. Just Cause 4 massively neglects the first half of that gameplay loop, there's far less to blow up in this game. On a technicality there's the same amount, but in reality there's no reason to do anything, so you won't do it. Why blow up a massive propane tank if you don't need to? You won't, you'd rather use that rocket on a helicopter. 

Just Cause 4 is an excellent game, but it feels gray compared to the colorful and explosive world of Just Cause 3. The movement is the same, so the core gameplay loop is undeniably worse in exchange for better graphics and more advanced systems. The comparison can be summarized in one sentence.

[u]Just Cause 4 is more impressive, but Just Cause 3 is more fun[/u]

How do I know the game will even run on my PC when the portion I can access basically amounts to a glorified demo? It's disappointing, because I really dig the aesthetic, and would really love to get into the badass, cheezy vibe that the game presents. *sigh~guess I'll have to wait for Cyberpunk to get my 80's fix...

review_text:
The .hack series has been one of my favorite series since childhood. Although the anime and movies aren't the greatest there has always been something about the games that have kept me coming back. The original .hack IMOQ series unfortunately doesn't stand the test of time so I understand why G.U. was remade first but I still wish they would port that series to Steam just to have the joy of grinding through it again.

As for Last Recode I think they did a great job making this game true to the original while also providing easier ways for new players to enter the series via things like cheat mode to have a decent amount of money and items to start your playthrough. Although Mass Effect is the first series that comes to mind for most people when you think about a playable save being ported game to game I always think of .hack first and it was just such a fun and innovative concept when playing through the series back in the day that continues with Last Recode.

If there is one recommendation I could make for people buying the game is to not use cheat mode unless you feel like you aren't good at these type of games. It is VERY easy to over level everything in this game and you can often clear content 4+ levels higher than your actual level to expedite the process. Between "The World" that you spend your time in, CrimsonVS, the party system, or just the fun and enjoyable story I think this will continue to remain one of my favorite games of all time and I would highly recommend this game to anyone!

review_text:
Dead by Daylight is not an easy or beginner-friendly game by any means. The biggest flaw? It desperately needs an updated tutorial and practice mode. New players have no way to rehearse basic skills like flashlight saves, flash bangs, loops, or facing specific killers. In custom matches, you can only fight bot survivors as killer—never the other way around.

I’ve introduced this game to several friends; 90% quit within their first week. The learning curve is brutal and full of odd mechanics (like having to line up exactly 90° for a fast vault). After nearly a decade, the same issues remain—tunneling and slugging still dominate matches, making the solo experience miserable. Solo queue players are punished by design, since survivors can’t communicate beyond basic gestures (“come here” or “follow me”).

The developers seem to prioritize new content over stability, balance, or beginner accessibility. The business cycle feels predictable: announce a new killer, generate hype, attract new buyers, they realize how unforgiving the game is—and then they leave.

A notable example I would like to point out is Dead by Daylight hasn’t been forced to evolve for nearly 10 years due to lack of major sustainable competition. Until Behaviour Interactive adds quality-of-life features that support new and solo players, I can’t recommend this game to anyone starting fresh.

Verdict: Great concept, deeply flawed execution. 6/10 for veterans, 2/10 for newcomers 

 [Overall]: Not recommended

I really wanted to like this game but I just wouldn't recommend it at the moment. Too unfinished and the difficulty is completely wack.

Enemy bullets are so fast they are impossible to dodge, they might as well be hitscan. Enemies will also just teleport to wherever you are, which is awful because the reason I ran was because my shields were melted by who knows what, and then literally every enemy on the map just teleports in front of me and annihilates my being from existence in the span of a microsecond. Very cool! Probably the biggest middle finger a video game has given me in recent memory. When that wasn't my cause of death it was instead doing just fine before suddenly getting two or three shotted by who knows- probably the same dude who was melting my shields in the other runs. Death is made even worse by the fact that starting a new run feels like several minutes as you need to run through the hub and do a parkour course each time. Go ahead and speedrun through it as fast as possible but that's still at least a solid minute for each of the dozen or so runs I attempted, would be nice to have a skip for those of us who get impatient after the third unfair death in a row. I know its probably there to get you immersed in the atmosphere but it doesn't do that for me.

There is nothing wrong with having high difficulty (I love the dark souls series) but I prefer a game where I feel like I'm at fault for my death instead of just getting nuked by nonsense. Go ahead and tell me to "get gud" but I've never had this issue with any other fast paced FPS game: I was pretty good at Titanfall 2 back when I used to play it and I can handle DooM slaughtermaps just fine.

I looked into older builds of this game and they were so drastically different from the current version they might as well have been different games, so maybe I'll check back in on this a year or two from now and it'll be a different experience that I will enjoy, because I really do like the concept and want to give it a second shot later.

review_text:
I like Lucius. A great deal, actually. For most of its run it's a fun, campy little niche puzzle-solver. Though it often lacks proper direction and explanation and has a plot that starts out thin and ends even thinner, you've got to appreciate the courage and originality it takes to put players in the role of someone unambiguously evil. You are the antichrist, and from the tutorial onward your tasked with murdering innocent people without being discovered. That's a hell of a a brave choice if you ask me. Unfortunately, its shortcomings as an indie title are clear throughout, culminating in one of the worst, confusing, even unplayable final levels to ever plead with its audience to forgive the lack of time it had to be actually completed, and for this alone it loses my recommendation

Without getting into any spoilers, before the final stage you're given the choice of two icons to pick between, and having attempted both it's still unclear what their exact meaning and purpose is. The final level will play out in one of two ways, but in each lead you to an inevitable "okaaaaaay... now what?" and it really brings the whole experience to a screeching halt. The entire atmosphere of impending doom and inescapable destruction all around you in your final battle is lost entirely as you wander between the same three rooms, pressing every button you can think of in every spot, desperately searching for a way to progress to the next sequence. It's then that you remember that the main menu is in Times New Roman 12pt font and understand why. 

In all honesty Lucius has a charm about it that just falls short of outweighing its flaws.

Honestly, after hearing so much bad things about this game I didn't expect much. Autumn sale came a long and the price dropped to just 9 euros so it was a bargain to say the least. And after playing it through to the end, frankly - I don't really get all the bad reviews out there. Sure, it may not win any awards (outside of maybe graphics, which are incredible), it's a tad repetitive and the story is a bit predictable and inconsistent, but it's far from a bad game. I have been playing this game since day 1 on global, these hours do not reflect my time on my xbox which in total ive spent over 8,000 hrs on this cursed game. I went out and bought a new Xbox Series S just for this game since my potato laptop could no longer run NGS when it switched over from base. 

The Pros: Great character customization, the combat is fun, housing system has a ton of options, the collabs are pretty cool, and I must say the new cell shading option is neat. 

The Cons: This game has no vision, no future to look forward to. Developers have already said things take FOREVER to create and they have no plans on adding new classes, new areas/planets, or new PA's (skills)! This means we are stuck stagnant for the next couple of years if not longer with noting new other than fighting re-skinned enemies in the same 4 generic, lifeless areas (forest, sand, snow, fire). We have gone back to the beginner area 3 times now to level up! Its just a maddening cycle. NGS has killed PSO. Sad. I had to quit the game several months ago, I would fall asleep in combat zones. People fight you over how to play because their way is the only way. NGS does not care about type 1 (male) characters, there has not been a new hairstyle in the AC scratch in I swear a damn year but type 2 (female) gets 3-4 new hairstyles every scratch. So unless you want to play as a waifu you are pretty much screwed. I could go on forever, how the player market is forever cursed due to SEGA not stopping PC cheaters tanking the market, how F2P players get one "3 day pass" to sell stuff on the market once a month. Not enough ways to earn money, and the other ways are so so boring you just skip it. They tried new modes like canon ball rumble but the levels are just grid training levels so it just looks so boring. The FOMO (fear of missing out) is strong in this game. They hook you in with daily login bonuses, and even exclusive items making you feel like you HAVE to play every damn day. The game pass or whatever it's called here is so lame, filled with pointless stuff, only a few new accessories that are still meh, and they recolor the same damn outfits over and over again and put them in the pass. Good luck trying to find a room of players to grind in a combat zone because everyone has to hoard into one room, all of em just sitting around the lobby doing pervy things all day! 

Conclusion: NGS has turned into a Sims/Minecraft game, if you do not mind waiting years for meaningful updates and want to play as a waifu then this might be the game for you. Its like IMVU but with some very light combat mixed in. If you are a new player you will get some fun out of the game at first, the more time you sink in the more you realize how empty this game is. I will forever miss base PSO2! The memories, the zany levels, the cool af characters, all washed away by the stain of NGS!

review_text:
A reasonably 'okay' sequel to Asylum, Arkham City will satisfy any gamer eagerly looking to jump back into the Batman universe. Where the game falls short, it falls short hard. And where the game excels, it does so only teasingly. 

To be quick, the game throws in bosses so meaninglessly that you're often wondering if they're just doing it to increase the amount of hours it will take to beat the title. Sure, there are some cool fights. Batman's fight scene against Ra's al Ghul is probably one of the coolest single-player boss fights I've ever played. It's not predictable enough to be repetitive, and it's not unpredictable enough to be confusing. It's a visually gorgeous experience and shows just how well Rocksteady knows the engine they're working with. But this one fight is the only unique fight in the game, and is not the norm you'd want or expect from what is considered the best Batman video game series made.

The gameplay is what you'd expect if you played Asylum. It's the fluidity of the punch/kick combos when facing off against mobs of henchmen that has always made Rocksteady's franchise a lot of fun. But in City, Rocksteady has milked that way too much. Overcoming the odds of taking down five henchmen at once was cool. Doing it to a courtyard of thirty just becomes monotonous. And no, that doesn't happen just once in this game. It happens frequently.

I think it's the plot which is the most dissatisfying. There is no sense of attachment to Batman whatsoever. He is emotionally stoic and his dialogue is weak. He's desperate to be friends with all the villains and Rocksteady has tried hard to make it seem like the villains are just frail people who, with enough small talk, will eventually go out to coffee every morning with Batman. It's a weird dynamic and it's just simply not enjoyable. Joker, the primary plot-driving menace, is not enough of a focal point to carry you through the mounds of dullness the other villains throw at Batman.

Eh, I could say much more, but I don't want to take the time here. If you're interested in playing as Batman again in the world Rocksteady created, you'll find more of the same as what you saw in Asylum. There's a ton of nostalgic elements in this one, and while some of it is fun to play through, much of it is boring.

review_text:
Hi Witchfire team,

I'm updating my review after spending more time with the Webgrave update, and I wanted to share some thoughts with you. I can tell how much care you've put into this game, and I'm writing this because I genuinely believe Witchfire has the potential to be something special.

Let me start with what I appreciate: the souls-like progression system you're going for makes sense, and I love those games too. The challenge and methodical advancement can be really satisfying when done right. But I think there's a key element missing from how it currently works in Witchfire.

In games like Elden Ring, part of what makes leveling up feel rewarding is that moment when you go back to an area that gave you trouble and just steamroll through it. It's that "wow, look how much stronger I've gotten" feeling that makes all the grinding worthwhile. Right now, your witch defense scaling system prevents that from ever happening. Every time I get stronger, the game immediately adjusts to match me, so I never actually feel more powerful, just differently challenged.

I understand the lore reason - the witch "reorganises her defenses" - but it ends up feeling like the game is working against my progress rather than celebrating it. Especially when the witch supposedly has limited / "very low" influence on the starting island to begin with, the constant scaling feels a bit inconsistent.

The new stats system from the update looks really awesome, but in practice, it still feels like I'm on a treadmill. Leveling costs more and more witchfire while enemies get proportionally tougher, so I'm putting in more effort just to maintain the status quo.

Here's where this really hit me: I decided to try playing a Slayer because the description sounded perfect for my playstyle - "Aggressive Spellcaster" who uses witchcraft in close combat. I was excited to lean into the magic side of the game and really embrace that fantasy.

But then I realised that despite being described as someone who finds "twisted delight in wielding witchcraft", practically nothing has changed. I can barely use spells because witchfire doesn't regenerate naturally. I have to constantly hunt down enemies just to scrape together enough mana to cast anything. I don't even start with a Light spell! I feel like a Gemini witch from The Vampire Diaries - always having to siphon power instead of just using my own. Fun in theory, not so much in practice.

This feels especially odd when you look at the game's own world. The witch uses magic freely, there are clearly powerful magical staffs like Saint Albert's Scepter, and these Preyers are supposedly trained in witchcraft. So why can't a character who's specialised in magic actually use it? How do they even create or power up their magic weapons if they can't use magic themselves without stealing it?

When I compare this to games like Destiny 2 or Remnant 2 that you've presumably drawn inspiration from, those games trust players to use their abilities regularly through natural cooldowns and regeneration. It feels like Witchfire might be a bit too cautious about letting us witchcraft-happy preyers actually feel magical.

What's frustrating about all this is that I can see all the pieces are there for something amazing. The shooting mechanics feel great, the atmosphere is genuinely incredible, and the technical polish is impressive for a team your size. I even noticed you added the DLAA support I had asked for in my Steam review months ago, which shows you're really listening to feedback.

But some of the design choices seem to work against the game's own strengths. Expeditions in the same start areas still feel like survival endurance tests even after I've grown stronger. Having skins is cool in terms of modding, but when the scale of your body changes so much that you can't perform  simple tasks any more or line up shots because the shoulder stock is now massive, that just becomes frustrating.

Boneworks had elements of tech demo under a nice campaign that kept you engaged with interesting encounters and puzzles that made use of VR. Bonelab is all tech demo with random levels strung together with a fade to black. I'm happy for quest players to finally be able to play something like this, but if you're on  pc, this is not worth your money. The only thing i really like are the functional vehicles and reskinned soldiered

review_text:
The idea is good but the execution is not to my taste. I hope that the dev will improve it such that I can recommend it.
The UI is pretty clunky, finding roles on the left pane was a pain almost every time, selecting a house to build was similarly painful. There are some useful stats but there is a lot of missing polish there. 
The game mechanics were pretty fun but left something to be desired in many places. The corruption encroaches rapidly at times and the methods I found to deal with it were not fun and not interesting. Mostly involving summoned walls and outposts.
The game is supposed to be challenging and unforgiving and I suspect that it's inspired by the idea of *fun* in Dwarf Fortress. Rise to Ruins is not fun, in the DF sense, at all. The reason DF is fun when you loose, often without any fault of your own, is that each loss tells a story which can be quite complex and nuanced.
Losing in Rise to Ruins was not fun at all as it just felt like I didn't manage the town well enough and no interesting story was being told. The game also doesn't tell you how to lose. You are probably supposed to just leave the region and reset the whole world if you lose but the game doesn't tell you this and just says that you are loosing all your progress by resetting the world.
The game is unforgiving in the worst of ways. I made the mistake of not preventing some corruption from entering a relatively thin strip of rock and the next thing I know, a very hard to reach part of a mountain had been corrupted. It would have been no effort at all to prevent this from happening but after it happened, It was going to take many hours to clean the corruption out of there. So I had a very successful town with a strong defense system practically ruined by not knowing the precise mechanics of the game, I didn't realize corruption went through rocks. Unforgiving punishments can be good game design but harsh punishments for rules that aren't explained nor obvious is not. 

I also think the game needs to be proofread. There are many strange sounding sentences like "Such a real shame." when someone dies.

I realize that It's just made by one guy but that doesn't make the game better or worse, it just explains why it is how it is.

The UX for example needs some adjustments to better indicate your objectives during a mission and something better to indicate to you when they change and where you need to go. Perhaps individual squad objectives that help complete the main objective and visual squad bonuses would improve sticking together in your squad of 4. 

Performance is another point, the carnage system is brilliant on paper and visually its really cool but it became difficult to keep up a stable framerate at 60fps, 1080p with upscaling and framegeneration turned on. This is most apparent when you have 16 people mowing down hordes of bugs in different directions during a defense event or everyone starts to spread out too far on the map.

Th wingsuit was the best thing brought to this series and thankfully this game kept it from JC3 however they took its take off capability away. 


This game also took away the idea of destroying everything in an area to liberate it, something i thought was a signature of the IP. The battlefronts and squads idea to take over areas just plain sucked.

I loved the challenges as quite a few had puzzle like elements like "how can i do this challenge?"

Who's stupid idea was it with gun system... i dont want to throw away guns or have to keep changing guns every five minutes. If somethings not broke why change and "fix" it. The amount of times i ended up with no gun at all because i wasnt paying attention...absolutely rubbish.

Also there was just far too many enemies appearing in places they shouldn't be able to get to me, far too many grenade spamming enemies, far too many super accurate enemies, and the amount of bullet sponge enemies were just awful and finally god how i hate the drones far more than enemy helicopters.

The Story didnt appeal to me the way JC3 did because the cause was more personal and this time it wasnt. The only parts i was full of adrenaline and was enjoying was the lightning storm quest, the sandstorm and the tornado quest.

The ability to reuse any of the disaster weapons just didnt make sense to me at all...as a "good" guy why would you put the people of Solis through that again?

The upgrades you can buy for your grapple from the 3 people...never used any of them the entire game they just served no purpose for me.

Why wasnt there an ability to help the frontlines by taking out a few of black hand operatives and explosives and advancing the frontline rebels that way to change it up as non mission thing?

Graphically the game looked brilliant except for clouds and the tornados for some reason even on top settings  and i dont have a potato.

Overall there was some new things i actually liked like the stunts and speed and wingsuit challenges. However far too much of the JC IP felt ripped out of the heart of it and i think id rather return to something like JC3. 

I cannot recommend this game as much as i can recommend Just Cause 3

3.5 out of 5 stars

review_text:
If you go into this game understanding it's more of an artistic experience than, like, overwatch, you'll probably really enjoy yourself. The visuals and music alone are captivating, like blending in and out of a nightmare. The awe and wonder I felt thinking "what kind of strange stuff is going to happen next" was what pulled me forwards in this game. Honestly, I wish they either went full puzzle or did a walking simulator, because yeah the combat isn't great. But it doesn't relinquish from the experience after finishing. 

DON'T PLAY THIS GAME IF YOU PLAY GAMES FOR COMBAT. If Scorn went full on Myst with its puzzles I think it would be absolutely perfect. The visuals and world don't have to be explained to you with a neat packaged narrative with every lore book handed to you to be incredible - it's way way way better that they keep it to your imagination. It's like abstract art, which I personally enjoy.  Again, I'd recommend this game to anyone that wants to come away thinking and imagining this strange place afterwards, probably to artists of all types as well. I'd buy this again just for the atmosphere alone. I think the devs should have just taken the combat away, not all games need it, and it seems the people that like combat > anything else don't care for it anyways lol. 

(being purposefully vague here to avoid spoilers) The ending isn't what I expected, but I get what they were going for and I can't be too mad. I'd prefer we both went into the light, together, from all we've been through.

Regardless of some of the faults it has, I'll be thinking about Scorn for months after finishing it. It's haunting and grotesque, beautiful and disgusting, and the strange eroticism adds to the uncomfortable atmosphere. I don't ever really leave reviews,  but I felt I had to to defend it a little. As I type this I just want to ask so many questions, and if you find speculation and art and discussion more fun than a neat tidy ending and THE FAST PACED THRILLING COMBAT EXPERIENCE *explosion noises*, you will enjoy Scorn!! Get it on sale if you're unsure.

review_text:
The game tells of a town on the edge of the steppe where a sickness takes hold and reason falters. Its people cling to rites and old faiths, they barter and gossip. The plague moves, and it moves fast. There is no hero’s work to be done here - only the long endurance of some puppet who knows, or should know at least, that survival is hard and the road is long. Time passes more quickly with each remaining day.

You play a surgeon returned from exile, a man bound by debt and bound by blood. Your hands can heal but never enough. Every decision costs something dear. To help one soul is to abandon another. Food runs out. Sleep is rare and shallow. Even the smallest kindness bears a shadow. Overall, the game’s stat systems (thirst, hunger, stamina...) are cruel but fair, as nature is 'fair'.

They do not mock you.
They only ask that you understand.

The writing is plain and deliberate, carrying a sort of mythic sorrow. Existential grief, you could call it. There are no revelations, only recognitions. Many a conversation reveals and thus, reopens wounds. Yet there is life in the town, in its superstition and in its hunger, and in the faces of those who still expect mercy. You come to know them, and when they die you carry their absence like a stone in your pocket. And as it gets heavier, you take every chance you can get to forget about your own burden, your own heavy heart, still beating in spite of everything.

What the game achieves is not pleasure but gravity. It reminds you that survival is a moral act, that knowledge cannot save anyone, and that faith is a thing both poisoned and necessary.

When it ends, there is no triumph, only the stillness of a place that outlasts its inhabitants. You put it down changed, and not entirely for the better.

review_text:
Yakuza 5 takes on an ambitious scope, introducing four new cities and featuring five active main characters, each entwined in their own compelling subplot, all of which are individually impressive. However, the game grapples with the challenge of uniting these diverse elements, resulting in difficulty tying everything together. The main story, marked by a few notable highs, often falls short. A pivotal moment occurs when a main protagonist questions the purpose of their journey, encapsulating the sentiment that permeates Yakuza 5's main narrative. While the character subplots are exceptional in their own right, the cumulative effect feels a bit overwhelming.

Despite these challenges, Yakuza 5 boasts the most extensive collection of mini-games in the entire series. The combat system, unfortunately, remains largely unchanged from Yakuza 4. However, within Yakuza 5, one can discern the early DNA of Yakuza 0, with this game laying the foundation for the exceptional aspects later refined in Yakuza 0. Despite its shortcomings, Yakuza 5 retains the quintessential Yakuza charm, offering hilarious subplots, intense action, and a unique style synonymous with the series. On these merits alone, I recommend Yakuza 5 to devoted series fans looking to complete the entire saga. However, for others, it may be prudent to consider skipping this one.

review_text:
I ramble so my subjects may jump all over the place. I tried this game a year ago. It felt awful then for multiple reasons. Now. It feels better... but still not good.

Boneworks was better in almost every way. Guns felt better, movement felt better, physics felt better, and it didn't make me motion sick. There were not an extreme number of instances where you could fall easily in Boneworks. Here in Bonelab falling seems to be a necessity and almost encouraged to get motion sickness with how many places i can fall extreme distances or the player character gets moved out of the player's control, like entering a minigame area. The "improved physics" feels like all they did was buff the player strength. That's it. It CAN feel more responsive, but almost everything now feels weightless. Sure its fun to grab objects and kinda chuck em around, but honestly feels less interactive to me. Two handing my pistol felt wrong because it'd cause it to weirdly wave around upon grabbing so aiming was off till it corrected out of my control. And then one handing a pistol well apparently our arms are made of noodles because I found it hilariously floppy when trying to aim one handed. Guns like pistols feel like toys now with the little movement they have when racking them. I'm not saying it needs to be the dramatic kick back when racking it like Boneworks, but it was satisfying to do that. review_text:
This was one of two or three games I actually expected to be good this year. Felt like Boneworks DLC. I held off on writing a review but since finishing it on my second session I have not once felt the "urge" to come back to it.

Shorter, more linear and less interesting campaign. Zero innovation besides the 'avatar switching' with 3 of the 6 avatars being completely redundant ("Strong", Light and Short). It's not a bad game, but I don't know if it's worth recommending if you've played Boneworks. When I saw the medieval setting teased in the intro I just wanted to go and play whatever game THAT was, not what I ended up slogging through for ~6 hours. You end up returning to that area later on but it's a LOT smaller and all the enemies just use their fists even though there are guns and melee weapons lying around everywhere (also enemies cannot use melee weapons in this game, and there is only one enemy type that can use guns; the same copy+pasted hologram enemy from Boneworks).

No new guns except a pump action and semi-auto shotugn, which modders added into Boneworks yonks ago (in fact the devs said they would add shotguns into Boneworks but obviously that never happened). Unless you want to count reskins of course. Good to see the same M4, MP5K etc copy+pasted into this game. On one hand, I want devs to keep content from previous games if the sequel is in the same engine, however I expect to see something NEW when playing a game sold as brand new rather than just picking up the same weapons to kill the same enemies in the same environments.

There are no new enemies except a short, fragile 'turret' type thing which  does a lot of damage but goes down in a couple shots. Only shows up in the last 2(?) levels. They also remodeled/reskinned a couple enemies from the first game. The blue zombie type enemies are not present in the campaign but are in the other modes, so there is very little variety when playing.

You've probably already read stuff about the Moonbase and 'Pillar' levels, though these criticisms pale in comparison to the other issues I feel the game has.

This game's only saving grace is ironically what probably made it such an underwhelming experience; massive marketing (externally and in-game, integrated into the canon story of the game lol) focused on modding and player made content - would've been no problem in my opinion if the initial offering wasn't so sparse and shallow. Hopefully players can add campaigns and new game modes to extend the longevity of the game as it currently does nothing better than its competitors; 

Blade and Sorcery wins melee and stealth, 
Hellsplit and Grimlord win 'dark'/difficult combat, 
H3VR and Contractors win firearms,
Hard bullet wins 'brutal' sandbox gameplay...

...not to mention the janky impact physics and amateur sounds that abound this game. Main draw of this game is structured levels so without that sort of content there is no real draw as long as there are other games with 'endless' modes that feel better to play.

But the worst of all is that the music in this game is somehow worse than Boneworks. Boneworks has one of the best OSTs in gaming, undoubtedly the best of any VR game. The main theme is subtly included in a few tracks here but otherwise the entire soundtrack in Bonelab is forgettable, and for some reason they decided to include strange, almost slurred vocals in one of the songs. Maybe my problem is that I am not a hipster but this was a total L and took me out of the game (the 'game' being walking around the HUB and being forced to try random minigames before being able to continue playing the walking simulator-esque campaign.

Finally, the game is unbelievably easy, almost as easy as Boneworks. The most trouble one would have in this game is climbing, as the legs sometimes go all wack and twist 90 degrees to the side or get stuck in ladder rungs. Maybe it was a few one-offs for me, so in general the climbing and movement was very similar to Boneworks so the muscle memory carried over. Most enemies die in one or two headshots and the enemies are typically few and far between, and you have a Borderlands-style 'last chance' if you die where you can revive yourself by getting a kill. I also detest the ammo system in this game just as I did in Boneworks; you have a total pool of ammo that carries over between levels, and you don't lose ammo in magazines if you throw them away so there is little care for ammo management. This means you use very little ammo in combat and will always be able to top up your mag without worrying about 'wasting' ammo. The weird thing about this is that the system had a use in Boneworks as ammo was a currency used to buy things (like weapons or developer tools) from vending machines, which are completely absent in this game. I wish they went with a different system, perhaps like having an ammo limit or needing to put ammo physically on your body a la H3VR/etc.

Anyway, rant over. While this review was mostly negative, the game is good, but not the revolutionary experience they advertised it as. The whole ending felt very on-the-nose, and there is even a Discord link to a modding server at the end for those looking to get into modding. There is a bit of polish compared to the prequel and they added one or two cool new things but this just seems like a modding platform - a double edged sword that I love and hate. Modded games last longer and the experience of tailoring your mod list is great, but there is a niggling feeling at the back of my head suggesting that developers use this as an excuse to underdevelop their game as players will just fix it later (Bethesda moment). Not sure if SLZ are like that, so far it seems not, but my main takeaway from this game was that it's an okay if underwhelming experience with massive potential for future improvement. Maybe in a year we will see videos titled "Bonelab is GREAT if you don't play the campaign..." or "This mod makes Bonelab worth playing again" or "This epic mod FIXES Bonelab".

tl:dr $50 for a $20 DLC, watch this space

review_text:
So I'm about 4 hours in, haven't watch a YouTube video or read any guides. Just decided to jump right in.

After reading the reviews I thought I was going to be in for a frustrating, difficult, fun experience. 

I'm on the second map and I haven't died once. I've killed 3 bosses without dying and barely taking any damage. The game is super fun, but I have no clue where all these comments about a difficult and frustrating experience are coming from. If you don't play the game like it's call of duty and use a fraction of brain power before engaging enemies, you'll be fine.

The game gives you every warning possible when you're about to take damage and the enemies light up and make obvious movements when they are about to strike you. The game even has a text narration feature that is supposed to simulate your thoughts, and these thoughts tell you when enemies are looking for you and when you're approaching a dangerous area. There are also audio cues to let you know you've entered a dangerous area. I mean seriously, what more can the developers do to warn the player?

Stamina is also not an issue. Again, if you're not running into the center of a horde of enemies like an idiot you will barely need to dodge at all. Aiming is incredibly easy. I get head shots 70 percent of the time. 

There have also been complaints that the guns lack range. Yeah so..... equip a sniper rifle? I'm clearing entire areas of the map from a distance before they even get close to me. Seriously I'm dumbfounded at some of these complaints.

You may think the game is too easy after reading this review, and maybe it is, but the gunplay and spellcasting is incredibly satisfying. It's a game where you can sit down for 30 minutes shoot some enemies, get some loot, level up, and put it down until the next time you're ready to play. It's a great game with unlimited potential. The reviews kept me from buying it for weeks. Don't be like me. Ignore the reviews saying it's too hard.

review_text:
I 100% recommend this game. I almost didn't play it because players seem so split on whether or not it's good. But I saw it on sale for $10, so I finally decided to dive in (3 years later, sadly).

As most have stated, this game isn't for everyone. I hate saying that, because most people see it and think "risk" (like I did) and either put off playing it or never play it at all. But the truth is, it's worth the risk, because if the game resonates with you, it hits hard.

Throughout the entire game, I wanted to see more, know more about this world I was in. This game is special in that it doesn't tell you anything, which means you have to use environmental clues, as well as your imagination. What is my purpose here? What happened to this place? Where am I? Unlike most games that leave you to imagine nothing because it's all explained to you, this game leaves room for plenty of imagination, and I love that about it.

But when I say this game doesn't tell you anything, I mean it. It doesn't even tell you the controls when playing. No map, no objective markers, nothing. I actually quite like this, as it makes me feel more attached and immersed in this world. I really only got stuck twice in this game for a brief period of time. But I wasn't frustrated about it, because I felt this really is part of the game design. This world is supposed to confuse me, disorient me.

The visuals are also superb, as many have already stated. You can tell if the art style is for you pretty easily based on the screenshots and videos. It really gives off Alien: Isolation vibes, and I love that about it. It's a unique style I don't really see in any games, and it made me feel like I am part of this world rather than just a player in it. It all just feels like it could exist, somewhere out in the void. Simply, it feels authentic.

Most reviews I read did not actually enjoy the gameplay. I personally did, in my mind, the puzzles made sense, and while the combat was slow and limited, I actually enjoyed it. Combat is easily avoided if you don't want it (minus a few sections). I don't think it was the best gunplay out there. But it really wasn't as bad as I thought it would be either, based on others' reviews.

I could go on and on, really. But I'll just end this review by saying: The game may not be for everybody, but everybody should try it regardless. Because if it is for you, you'll be more than pleased with what is on offer here. Just like I was.

review_text:
Having played many MMOs since when Ultima Online was the latest and greatest MMORPG, it was very interesting to play a game that centered around a "simulated MMORPG".  This game gets the simulated MMORPG aspect down very well in my opinion, with incredible detail-orientation to the Operating System, Online Jack, and related forums to make you feel like it's a fully contained "real" world that takes place 15 years in the future (which is now two years ago roughly in actual time, haha...it's interesting how much they got right).  

Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the story, which is REALLY unfortunate given this game's reputation.  The protagonist that you play is extremely tough to like until Volume 3 perhaps, which is primarily why I don't care for the game's story.  The one positive thing I can say about the story is that it is very approachable and not drawn out.  Except for Volume 4 (which is really Volume 3.5), each volume is roughly 20 - 25 hours in length.  Volume 4 is only 4 hours in length at most...thus the Volume 3.5 designation.

The gameplay is a little off-balance.  I didn't have to use any magic spells until Volume 2, and then it was sparingly, as one example.  Magic almost feels like an afterthought.  I don't get why they included the bike.  Sure there was some activities there, but it was not a fully fleshed out idea in my opinion.  

I can't say that I recommend, regardless of it's "modern classic" status according to some.

review_text:
Save Your Money! Not Worth $40!

I'll start with the complements to get them out of the way. HR Griger inspiration is phenomenally executed. The ambience and world-building is top notch. 

But that's all the complements this game is worth.

Kickstarter and trailers promised a horror game. Early trailers showed the use of guns with a hint that, just because there are guns, doesn't make it an action game.

However, the enemies in this game move quick, sometimes quicker than you. They have long-ranged projectiles and very good aim. You cannot out run their attacks if you were already close - you will get hit. Your best bet is to cheese the enemies by running in circles around the level, if any loops are available, or get behind something. You will have a close-range "weapon" that has 2 hits before a lengthy cooldown. You cannot help but GET CLOSE to kill these enemies. And there will be more than you ought to deal with for a game that wants to deny its title of being a "non-action" game.

Yeah there's not a lot of action alright - not a lot I can fucking DO about some of these enemies except get killed and hope that RNG is better next time. Most of the time I had to run away and wait for enemies to just leave as they crawl back into the environment. Later, I get better weapons but health and ammo is slim. The issues with slower movement and enemies having long-range projectiles still existed but was better. 

Then, you meet a bigger, faster, tougher enemy that requires use of your "magnum" gun. You HAVE to kill it. Good luck figuring out when to save your bullets. You're going to die.

Speaking of "figuring out when" to conserve resources and dying, later in the end-game, there is a game mechanic that requires you to take damage over time to solve a puzzle.

Let me say that again: THERE IS A GAME MECHANIC THAT REQUIRES YOU TO LOSE HEALTH OVER TIME TO SOLVE PUZZLES.

Tie that into the conservation design of this game and you have a recipe for screwing over your players and calling it "good game design". I almost forgot. You take health damage during cutscenes animations too. I hope you weren't finally making progress at 1 HP.

I love horror games. I love crappy horror games too. But this game lacks charm that those indie horror games have. 

I did NOT have fun playing this game. Scorn is not horrifying either. It's just gross and violent. I can get most of the same feeling I had playing scorn in a Mortal Kombat finisher. 

Scorn is also filled with cryptic and boring puzzles. People have compared it to Myst which I can say is very accurate except you die a lot and unfairly as I've already expressed in detail. 

There's no strategy to this game. The "game design" formula is as follows:
1. conserve ammo
2. kill the big guys
3. find keys
4. keep walking
5. (late game) have plenty of health because you WILL lose it during puzzles

I cannot in good consciousness suggest anyone spend their own money on this game. Not at $40. If it wasn't for the triple-A graphics I'd throw this in the "indie game" bin for anywhere $10-$20 which is worth the entertainment value Scorn provides.

The ending is a let down too. And there's no replayability either. I solved my puzzles. I spent hours patiently finding my way through hoping to find something about this game that I liked. I served my nickel and did my time.

In short, I'd call this game a huge dissapointment for horror fans like me who waited years since it was first announced on kickstarter. I wish I could get a refund.

review_text:
Tape to Tape is a very unique game concept. As a sports fan I thought the concept of a Hockey Roguelite was worth going in blindly even though I am not a huge fan of Roguelites.

On the surface Tape to Tape is a fun little arcade hockey game that is a heavily arcade-fantasy style sports game. My personal opinion its leans too much arcade as there are literally no rules. No, icing, no off-sides, no penalties.

[b]NO OFF-SIDES.[/b] This is the biggest rule that really affects game play and strategy. After a few games you will quickly realize that off-sides in Hockey is a huge rule that adds strategy and makes the game more exciting because without it you can easily cherry pick and freely skate around the ice with the puck where ever you choose.

This one thing really soured me on the gameplay. Each match devolves into the same thing, w/o off-sides the core Hockey mechanics quickly became quit stale.

There are other minor rule issues that I can look past as an arcade hockey game but off-sides, nope.

The game features crazy reality breaking abilities like AOE farts that knock down players, throwing your stick at players to knock them down. Slapshots to the head that knock down players, freezing players in a block of ice for long periods of time.

Earlier where I said the game leans too far into the fantasy aspect, this is where it got crazy for me and not in a good way. I likes some of the stuff like throwing your stick. Once I got to the AOE fart abilities or the Ice Block or the Teleporting stuff I began to think how stupid and how unrelated this game was to actual hockey.

Its frustrating, I want to like this game but 3 hours of playing I came to the conclusion that the only thing I like about this game is that its Hockey related.

I got annoyed early on at the music and celebration animations. I came to hate the humor and art style and the "quirky" aspects of the game. 

The core gameplay is quite bare-bones once sink your teeth into it. No stick/poke check. No deke. Checking is very poorly animated and controlled, movement feels pretty bad. You can't control the goalie while in goal. You can't manually select a player while on the ice, you can just cycle through them or hope you select the guy closest to the puck. You can't dive or kneel to block, there is no block button. There is essentially only one kind of shot, no wrist-shots. Most goals will look the same, crash the net one timers.

I think the concept has some potential but the execution isn't there. I honestly think you may like this game more if you don't give a shit about hockey but if you LOVE hockey you will see all the flaws that pile up and make this game NOT hockey at all.

This game is Early Access, maybe they can improve over time but I would avoid for now.

review_text:
AVOID THIS GAME LIKE THE PLAGUE if you're not someone going for a nostalgia trip of a god awful piece of shovelware that you were young enough to enjoy.

I've bought this game for 75% off and still feel i got ripped off harder than someone buying Fallout 76 full price.

This game is so terrible in every single aspect that it's in a "shelf" named S h * t in my library. 

The good: none whatsoever. 

The bad: 
- The story, even 1 hour in is so awful, with so many plot holes and complete idiot plot that it makes Sword Art Online look like a masterpiece.
- The world is completely disconnected to what a MMORPG should look and feel like to the point where you think the makers have never played one even though it came out during the golden age of MMORPG.
- The dialogue and script is straight up sewer buckets. The characters talk like 10 year olds who role play, the timing between lines in the english dub is mind numbingly bad. The lines themselves have errors and are at best high school dissertation paper level of depth.
- The gameplay is almost non-existant, hidden between tons of cringy cutscenes and text reading (such as emails and forum posts (yes it's as bad as it sounds)), yet they still managed to f*** the combat up and make it the most boring trash I've ever seen from a JRPG and also the most boring part of this game. 
- The controls are cancerous even with a controller. It's so badly done it feels incredibly unresponsive during combat (looking at you skill button), and moving to the sides also brings the camera angle with it, with no setting to turn that off (shoutouts to the Mario cam in Mario 64) You can't even jump or dodge or anything fun.
- The maps/areas/dungeons are just massive empty spaces with the same 8 types of enemies throughout the whole world. The map layout is the laziest garbage you find in mobile games with just super long corridors with strings of rooms in a straight line with no puzzle or even jumping or anything that could be fun.
- The game has a big history of crashing, which I didn't get (yet) because it seems I haven't reached the chapter where it allegedly starts doing so, but I still got massive frame drops for no reason whatsoever as I have a high end PC. 
- The characters and cinematography are all out from the imagination of a 10 year old who thinks doing a motion blur close up of a new character should be enough to convince players that they're badass. The characters do some of the dumbest looking movements for no reason whatsoever to "look cool" yet they only look extremely foolish. No character in this game seems to have anywhere close to an average IQ.

There is no semblance of realism or of any in-universe consistency. 

This is the first game where I will say that the best thing about it is its voice acting (if we ignore the original JP VAs because they're always higher quality than english), not because they were good, they almost never are for anime-related stuff, but because the rest is just that much worse.

Some people might say that this game is old so I shouldn't be so harsh, well there are tons of EVEN OLDER games that did literally everything better than this piece of garbage. 

I cannot understand how anyone would enjoy this game without being single digit age, or so blinded by their nostalgia that they're able to not be affected by the thousands of completely stupid plot holes and story defects and by the complete trash gameplay and world.

If you think you want to play this game even after all of that, then please watch a let's play of the first couple hours of gameplay AND make sure you try the game before your 2 weeks from purchase of refund trial time are up. If you still think you'll enjoy the game, then I wish you the best of fun!

This game is now in my top 1 of worst game I've ever bought for over $10 on Steam. 

Even if you could get it for free I would still recommend never adding it to your library.

1/10

Loads of fun!

Initially the car control may feel a little weird compared to its most obvious comparison (now not here on steam anymore), but thinking about that, it might partly just be due to Rocket League being based in small arenas, in this game you are often having to guide the ball over much longer distances, and be accurate at a longer range (while thinking ahead about potential obstacles like edges or bunkers). So controlling it accurately over these longer distances might be a little harder than what you might be used to in RL, at least initially.

Also keep in mind that most people having played Rocket League that their first few hours (at least) were chaotic and full of blunders. Don't blame this game if you feel the same here, give it a chance.

I highly recommend new players to play 15 mins or so of solo time trials, or at least far enough to unlock Shockwave (first active power core) and Big Ball (makes it easier, passive power core), before you go online, these will make your first matches so much easier. I was 2nd in my 2nd online match (lost due to my internet dropping momentarily at the end of the last match, DNFing me where I was leading after the first 2 matches) and 1st in my 3rd, but it seemed many players were brand new to controlling the ball, and I wouldn't want them to drop the game due to not practicing for 15 minutes in time trials.

Also all my gameplay so far has been on Steam Deck, and I can 100% say this game runs perfectly on there, and I hope it becomes officially verified soon, as it's completely deserving of it!

I just finished The Callisto Protocol over the course of 4–5 days – and I really enjoyed it.
The graphics, sound design, and atmosphere are fabulous. While the core story isn’t exactly groundbreaking, the details and worldbuilding offer a refreshing, alternative flavor.

The melee system feels a bit unfamiliar at first, but once it clicks, it's really satisfying. What makes it special is that it’s not 100% perfectly “readable” – and that’s a strength. It’s slightly unpredictable, almost raw and tactile in a way that makes every encounter feel intense. It’s this gritty, imperfect combat design that others might dismiss as clunky, but which I found genuinely compelling.

Level design is pleasantly varied throughout. I was surprised by how little the infamous vents and ladders actually bothered me – they’re used reasonably and don't disrupt the flow. Honestly, I don’t understand the heavy criticism on that front.

Small Note: this was the first game to crash my 7-year-old PC. But with some tweaking, I got it running smoothly – and it was absolutely worth the effort.

For a game with such greedy developers and a cash shop that must surely make them bank (enough so that one must wonder why there's not a STO 2 with next gen graphics), you've got to expect more, right? Poor sods.  

Anyway, the game has a very ugly and confusing user interface, movement is scuffed and feels sluggish and the same can be said for the space ship flight movement/combat. 

There are way too many buttons/abilities all clustered together and the game doesn't explain anything. Fair enough, I did start as a Jem'Hadar (the only species I actually was interested in besides Cardassian which wasn't an option) and it did say that was for experienced player but still. That's a you problem. Don't be so lazy and actually put in a tutorial. Maybe I don't want to play as a boring Human, elf or wrinkly forehead guy and want to play as the badass, scaly dude. 

Also can I just say that the Jem'Hadar in this look pathetic? Where's the jet black uniforms and badassery you see in DS9? The ability to play as one of these guys doesn't really fulfil the fantasy and it's a bit hard to take yourself seriously and feel badass when you're running around looking like you've just shit your pants.

The questing was pretty boring really apart from the first 5-10 minutes. Lots of [i] missions [/i] were just cluttered with 30+ enemies and the combat isn't much fun truthfully, especially the space flight. All the enemies outside of the first 5-10 minutes were insectoid - oh god, how original! As if there's not enough games with bugs in them.  

Seeing characters like Odo and other from DS9, etc, is pretty cool. 

The graphics are KOTOR level of fine I guess. I'm not fussy over graphics much. 

So I only actually played a few hours maybe but that was enough time to assess the basics like combat and space flight, etc, and I didn't feel like continuing. 

Now I'm not at all obsessed with Star Trek (only ever watched TOS, DS9 and some of the motion pictures in their entirety and couldn't stomach the rest) so that also plays a part in my decision. 

I would say 100% if you're simply looking for an MMO to play, just look again. WoW, ESO, SWTOR or hell, even Age of Conan (it's slightly more tolerable). Maybe Fallout 76 or Black Desert Online. review_text:
[h1]Excessive Listening Port Activity[/h1]

Open your resource monitor while playing. This is still an issue. It even uses your file/printer ports to monitor your activity. Advise you to play offline. It is perfectly doable.

As to the game itself: This would be a favorite of mine, if there were no listening port instances, or just 1-2 even, no insane male pregnancy, and a lower rate of homosexual marriages. 

I love the art-style. It looks like playing with paper dolls. 
I love starting with nothing and building something.
I love that you have given the proper incentive to keep playing and building your life.
I love the variety of crops and recipes; cooking as well as crafting.
I love that the various NPCs have their own personality, for the most part.
I love that the NPCs are out and about, except I do not love it when they are not at their business during their business hours, and there is no counter to interact with.
I love the seasons, even though 4 weeks would have made more sense for me. Three is just too short.
I love the animals.
I love the variety of decorations. Would love to see more.
I wish I could make a marriage contract with someone, without having to court them. That would be more realistic. Once I have my upgraded house (Saltbox House) and have over 1000 gold, and especially after I have my smelter and have caused a barn to be built for me, I should be able to attract a mate without all the social nonsense.

Yes, I'm autistic and proud of it.

I am irritated by some aspects of the game:
1. The richest man in town is never inoculated against the small pox. Neither is the black smith Rowland - EVER. Those two, plus the tailor and his wife ALWAYS die of the small pox. This game needs an algorithm that assigns inoculation based off of education and economic status. Thus, the mayor should be the first to be inoculated, and his entire family. The tailor should be the second, plus HIS entire family.  - This may have been corrected.

2. Having to walk across the entire island when the ghost shows up, and then get back home. Seriously????? Then, I am EXHAUSTED and have to sleep half the next day, but still tend my farm!! I always have a huge quantity of crops, because I learned in my first two start-up attempts that I will not have enough spring crops, if I do not get on it from the get-go. So, I have a huge field filled with crops and a small orchard already started, by day 3. (Thank you for these lovely mechanisms in the game!!!)

3. Male pregnancy. Monty Python did a skit on this in The Life of Brian, which we all found hugely hilarious, because we didn't imagine any male person being far enough divorced from reality as to want to become pregnant, or think they should be able to. Males have a mechanism for contributing their genes. It does not involve a womb. Personally, I do not think that the switch to either turn-off all visible pregnancies or turn-off all but family pregnancies is adequate. Make a mechanism to turn-off male pregnancies, and one where homosexual couples adopt children. After all, they would have actually been banned or beaten to death in reality. This game is set in 1701.

4. Excessive homosexual marriages, and NPCs that swing every which way plus loose. I think that few people care if there are homosexual marriages. However, in our modern world, it has gotten stupid. Games and movies act like 70-80% of human beings are homosexual or bi-sexual. Balance the numbers better. This is a huge complaint with The Sims 4, too. Have homosexual couples, please! I would not want a world where there are no homosexual couples. That would also not properly represent reality.

5. If you turn on all game mechanisms, this game is just stupid. I'm not sure why my gal made it into year 2 without hitting middle-age. I had her on slow ageing, as I did my guy, but he was middle-aged by the second year, so I turned off the ageing. No small pox hit in his game, although diseases are always on for me. So, he cannot adopt a child. I used a tool 7 times in the beginning, then should pay around 40 gold to fix it. Plus the taxes just become steadily more insane. Unrealistic. I would say okay if they SLOWLY rose every SEASON.

6. Adoption. It should be doable to arrange to adopt an orphan from the Old World. This game really was not thought through very well. We cannot have irrigation, because they didn't back then, but men are doing each other up the aß, and getting pregnant from it, we have to court people, and we cannot just adopt an orphan. 

7. No irrigation system.

8. You never have enough time. 

9. If you cannot fulfill a quest, people apparently dislike you now??? Or is it because I am too busy to take 3 hours out of the middle of the day to stand around doing nothing at a wedding and 4 hours for a funeral (you have to get to the graveyard and back)? I did not have this with my gal, or it was not noticeable. 

In spite of the historical notes, I am not asking the game to contain slavery to make it realistic. We're white-washing history as it is with shows pretending that blacks were noble people (which will bite us in the aß, when people cannot understand that they were NOT - not outside of Africa, certainly), but I think that racial and sexual equality are good things, along with the ability to have and create some homosexual couples. My gal can court various males in the game. Good on ya! The devs could even build a switch to allow or disallow homosexual relationships, or just work the weighting of it. That would be a logical thing to do. Make it like a 30% chance. What I've seen through several starts of the game is more like 75% of marriages in this game are homosexual.

Now, I know that people will get on here screaming homophobe, because they are ignorant, spoiled brats, who think that they can shame everyone into being silent, if people do not agree with them. I am very much in favor of consenting adults choosing whomever and how ever many partners they desire, as long as all participants are consenting adults. I just feel that we need to represent EVERYONE, and not just the ultra-woke community, who, since they think male-pregnancy should be a thing, are living divorced from reality, or have failed basic biology. They just do not want to hear any argument that involves the term "reality". Most misery in this world is born out of a mismatch between your expectations and reality. I'm advocating a realistic, representative balance in the entertainment industry, rather than representing it to children that all of humanity are bi-sexual or homosexual. It still does not match reality.

review_text:
Great classic online game with a lot of content but has minor issues.
Rather than say what is great about it, i'll say what isn't as I'm pretty sure plenty of reviews note the good things already.
So I will focus on what might make/break it for some people in rather situational & specific ways.

1. Limited compatibility with lower end pcs due to inability to configure many vital things and no "potato mode"
(While this might seem petty, the base game is crazy old and should run fine on a lower end modern pc but doesn't so it is in fact terribly optimized)

2. A bit convoluted and isn't completely true to the jp version, many things were reworked in negative ways.

3. Dated combat mechanics, it was shortly after we learned we wouldn't get a global version of PSO2 games like tera online released in example which had much higher tier combat quality. The former being 2012 and the latter being 2014, it's safe to say we should be in another league in 2024. Especially considering how hard they try to monetize the title.
(More-so if we consider NGS is like a pseudo pso3 which we might not get for another 10-20 years if ever! The mistake here is a simple underlying factor of not splitting base pso2 from ngs)

4. Steam/epic dependency, this hurts lower end pcs even more and over-complicates getting the game working well. Steam has an astronomical amount of issues and hardly any redeeming factor beyond marketability.

5. Some minor p2w, not purely to the definition of p2w as everything is reasonably achievable by playing. Cashers will undoubtedly have an advantage but it actually doesn't matter much because their gameplay isn't yours. 

If you can look past all of these minor issues and like what you've seen--
You'll have a great time on PSO2, notably I would add if you use an HDD it will cause many issues.

It has become a platitude that this is gaming at its most heartfelt and arty. If that's true, I worry about the medium of gaming.

I don't really mind that there is no game, per se, in here. I was genuinely excited to read something extraordinary & moving, and maybe my expectations were too high. So as I slowly clicked through this atrociously badly written click-fest, wincing at the poor characters and 'hilarious' old hoary references to things such as plants vs. zombies, I was more upset by the quality of the writing than the fact that there is no gameplay as such, apart from a few (maybe 10) simple logic puzzles and a lot of clicking and backtracking around illogical spaces.

Imagine 'Eternal Sunhine Of The Spotless Mind' if it was a daytime TV movie of the week, without the originality, and written by a snidy teenager thinking they're Joss Wheedon, but sadly falling short.

In short, the paucity of gameplay only highlights how meagre this is as art. I forgive a lot of games for having poor writing and characters, but there is nothing more to this. It's effectively a visual novel with decent pixel art (although the illogicality of all the buildings frustrated me as well), but as a novel, it would be strictly at an early teen level (some adult themes, handled clumsily)

If I had come across this with no preconceptions, maybe I would have admired its ambition. After hearing that this would show me that games can art, this was bitterly disappointing. Maybe this negative review will help others to avoid going in with such stratospheric hopes...

review_text:
I have not yet played the DLC. This review is solely for the core game.

As a game, this is quite fun. I very much enjoyed the banter between the doctors, as there is some seriously hilarious and well-written stuff there. To the Moon has a nice artistic style, and every character's body language is conveyed surprisingly well throughout. As a game plot, the story is satisfactory as long as you do not delve too far into it. You get what you see on the cover.

If you want a relaxing, relatively short game (about 4 hours) with great music and some fantastic dialogue, this is not a bad choice at all. I suggest purchasing it while it's on sale; don't pay the full price if anything I'm about to say resonates with you.

--== Why the Thumbs Down? ==--

I cannot in good conscience recommend this game. Its story is really not as fantastic as the community score would lead you to believe; it often feels contrived and forced, with heavy doses of cliche' and trope-ism. There are a couple things I will gently refer to as plot holes, as well. I wouldn't have been able to sit through this story as a book, a TV show, or a movie. I shed no tears, and felt no major attachment to anyone other than the doctors. I mean, seriously, the plot is predicated on mental instability and outright insanity at times. Was I meant to feel pity or empathy for that? No thanks.

Oddly enough, there's a noticeable difference in the quality of writing from the beginning to the end. A definite, gradual improvement.

I don't see where the hype is coming from. I accurately predicted the game from the beginning, though I didn't expect any plot holes at all, and only a few small details succeeded in surprising me. A number of interesting ideas are presented here, and some deep, insightful arguments are made... but it's all quite a bit too forced to be a -good story- instead of just the author's idea of what would catch the most attention.

I cannot give it the big blue thumbs up for those reasons.

The only downside is that it’s relatively challenging – without assists, combat can be unforgiving, but that difficulty makes survival in Black Iron Prison all the more intense and rewarding.

Overall, a highly underrated title that truly deserves a second look – especially for fans of sci-fi horror games in general.

The only good thing is slower introduction to [strike]all[/strike] most of the bugs. You are better off to play the basic bulding tutorial (that takes like 2 minutes) and have actual fun in PvE game.

I want to have company with my friends and play with friends. I wanna contribute to the war and earn the rewards.[/strike]

No, I don't mind the paid DLCs, even tho I expected the "first wave" being that, not orange hazard suit literally called "1st wave" but whatever, silly me. The original BioShock is one of the greatest games ever made, a true work of art that remains just as powerful today as it was at release. Rapture is not just a setting, it is one of the most charismatic and iconic cities in gaming history, a decayed utopia dripping with atmosphere and personality. It is practically insurmountable, even all these years later.

Gameplay mixes tense survival shooting with plasmid powers, giving you freedom to approach encounters creatively. It is not just about fighting, it is about experimenting, adapting, and surviving in a city that wants you dead at every turn. The balance of atmosphere, story, and mechanics is near perfect.

BioShock is not only a game, it is a landmark. A timeless piece of art that changed the medium forever.

Score: 10/10 - Atmospheric, innovative, and unforgettable.

review_text:
Lucius could have been a great game. It could have been gruesome horror  fun but man... It's an absolute mess of a game.

- Story is as cookie cutter as they come. They pretty much picked up everything from the "Omen" series there's nothing new or interesting done here.
- Linear to a fault
- Controls that feel stiff and unresponsive
- I was constantly struggling to grasp what I'm supposed to do almost at all times.
- The powers are as cliche as they come: Mind control, Telekinesis, Pyrokinesis and there is a WHOLE SLOT in your powers list dedicated to what ultimately adds up to a simple Use button. Yes you have to choose USE first and then you can use stuff or open doors. When is this game from? 1986?!
- Gameplay Does NOTHING to differ itself from better, more revolutionary games in the genre (e.g. Messiah). To be frank, it's quite a miracle the game runs at all.
- It's janky and ugly but plus side is that the manor itself is a cool place to hang out in for a while
- Boring in every conceivable way
- Not even in the "so bad it's funny" gamut of titles out there (e.g. Goat Simulator). It's just a plain bad game that feels super dated and the gameplay is boring and too linear to have any real fun with.

Props to the music composer though some nice tunes in the menus and during gameplay. Voice acting is also kind of OK for a "B-horror" (or more like D-horror) game like this.

Anyway, you can safely pass on this title without feeling like you've missed anything remotely worthy of your time. The only thing this game does right is portray the potential for a kind of game in this style which would actually work and play decently.

review_text:
Cutesy Colonialism-era Paper Mario-like aesthetics, otherwise it's Stardew Valley for realists: Food spoils.  Tools break.  People die of old age and disease.  Even your main character, whose gameplay continues through their children after death, Kynseed style.  Well, it's not realistic in all ways.  Witch magic works, and not a single clergyman around to burn them at the stake, because this setting satisfies all the political expectations of our time.  And yet, you can opt to bump off your fellow colonists if they rub you the wrong way, so despite the cozy, politically correct trappings of this colonial-era farming/life sim game, there's an edge to it.

The developers walk a fine line, but I dig what they're trying to do here.  I like Animal Crossing, but it kind of peters out into an endless furniture-collection and portrait collection game where you go nowhere.  I like the average Farming Sim RPG genre (Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons/Stardew Valley and its ilk) but there's often a static world, none of the familiar faces ever change, even if you can upgrade your homestead and the town.  So I was excited that Echoes of the Plum Grove was taking things a little further, and it delivers increased consequence.

That said, I would prefer they had gone further yet.  Intrigues among the NPCs don't go anywhere near what a player is capable of.  At most, some NPCs will be chronically grumpy or occasionally sad, they'll spread disease around, and they'll marry your crushes or pop their clogs when you don't want them to.  But that's about it, and you can expect whoever fills their shoes to be a fairly indistinct replacement to whomever was lost.  Given the setting, perhaps a proper Werewolf/Mafia-style game was in the cards at some point in development, but I haven't seen it yet.  I would have liked to be a sleuth but, instead, I'm just a settler trying to secure the bloodline before the reaper catches me.

Still, heartily recommended.  It's not a very expensive game, chances are it'll be good for at least 20 hours in its present state, and who knows what future updates will bring?
