This is the beginning of the better Yakuza Games in terms of game quality if you're counting by release date.

Karaoke, every minigame, things you'd expect from around this time (Yakuza 0's release date) is here, if not just still a little bit janky.

Gameplay wise, its still as frustrating as Yakuza 4's combat, but less so just a tiny bit. Enemies block less but have unavoidable damaging moves you can do nothing but try and dodge against a invisible wall to get around. 

This game is one of the longer games out of the entire series next to 6 (third longest) and 0 (longest).

I think the missions with Taiga were annoying, especially up in the mountains and into the snowy city, I just powered through that entire section without doing any side content because of how annoying that whole city was with combat, you had to stick strictly to the sidewalks, no way to avoid enemies in your path other than just fighting, most of them had weapons that always stunned you.

Same with the 4th character that was playable, (not Haruka), his city was also annoying and his side content involved him getting better at baseball I guess. Didn't really know why he was even included besides having a Daigo subplot and boss fight.

Haruka's section was probably the best because its the first time we're allowed to control her or do anything with a female protagonist in the entire series. It did only consist of things like Dance battles and idol things, but I still believe that side of the game was probably more of a highlight than Akiyama's own story.

Weirdly Kiryu's side (while having the best combat) was lackluster, and consisted of a power scaling fight structure, where the devs would put him in a scenario where he would have to fight an escalating number of enemies each new game release. This time made it extremely ridiculous and hilarious, but also removes a lot of the tension because there's not much to lose for him until Yakuza 6 at this point.

Overall I think this game is one of the beginning of the good Yakuza games, in terms of release date. Everything after and up to Yakuza: Like a Dragon is some of the best content gaming has seen in years.

review_text:
I was very disappointed with To The Moon. I spent around 3 and a half hours with this game, and only very rarely did I feel like the time was well-spent. The gameplay is virtually non-existent, player tasks boil down to point-and-click navigation through uninspiring environments to pick collect items placed sometimes in significant objects or conversations, and sometimes in random places that it's assumed you'll stumble over by chance. This is broken up by minigames, one repeating at the end of each sequence without becoming challenging at any point and the other one or two only appearing once each.

Basic gameplay is not necessarily a dealbreaker if the narrative and writing are good enough to provide an enriching experience. The reason I had picked up To The Moon in the first place was that I had heard tales of a compelling and emotionally resonant story, but I'm sorry to say the one I found was neither. The gist is you follow two main characters, whose job it is to reconstruct fake memories to bring comfort to terminally ill patients, as they meddle in the mind of an elderly man whose only regret is that he never went to the moon. It's an interesting premise which could raise interesting and profound questions. Is glossing over your real memories with ones that you think will make you happy wise? Are our choices and regrets something to be washed away, or an integral part of who we are?

In fairness, the final third of To The Moon does make a respectable attempt at raising these questions, but the characters through which it does so are neither interesting nor particularly likeable. The resonance of these themes and the story that is constructed from them rests entirely on how much the player has staked emotionally, and by the end I found that I didn't care what the outcome was. That combined with the fact that I found actually [i]playing[/i] the game fairly boring, meant that I really got very little enjoyment from the experience and would have preferred To The Moon to be lost in space, much like the last three hours of my life are.

review_text:
Definitely one where I wish there was a "eh?" instead of yes or no.

The good

The atmospheric everything is extremely well done.  There was clearly a huge attention to the appearance of... again, everything, and it all flows together in a great visual storytelling flow that leaves the player questioning the entire time what is going on.  The puzzles are satisfying and flow into one another, I only found myself getting lost for very brief moments, and only wound up looking up one thing online, because it turned out the solution was violence.

The mediocre

The combat system feels 'bolted on' and clunky, while this does increase the fear intensity, it often does so in a "why is this damn weapon change animation taking so long" way instead of a "oh shit the enemy is scary" way.  It does work, and there's a (good for genre) constant pressure of "do I really need to spend this ammo?"  but I think the game could have been just as good with no combat at all.

The bad

$40 full price for a 6 hour game is a little steep, but thankfully it's often on sale (as of writing, only $22) so that's not as huge a deal.  I'm more frustrated with the gaps in the storytelling that feel less like "we intentionally made it unknowable and scary" and more like "We just made it big and scary without caring about what it was".  There was a big reveal near the end I missed completely until reading stuff online that definitely could have been made clearer, and which I thought added a lot to the narrative once it was pointed out.  Throwing in a boss fight as well to a game with a clunky combat system (and no ability to reload for part of it, so if you don't immediately guess the correct way to win that part you're kinda screwed) just felt really out of pace for me with the rest of the game.

Overall, if you're a fan of atmospheric horror, like myst style puzzles, and fine with the prize, definitely a game to buy.  All in all though?  I was a little disappointed.

review_text:
My favourite Otome game, bar none.  This game has beautiful art, an excellent soundtrack, and complex stories that are rich with true-to-history detail.  This is a game best enjoyed by those who enjoy a more true-to-life historical romance; be prepared for a "slow burn" type of approach with most of the romanceable guys.

**Very Important**:  This is only the FIRST HALF of the full story for each guy.  This means more reading and fewer modern "romance" elements, at least in Kyoto Winds, the localized version of Hakuoki Shinkai: Kaze no Shou (the game was released in 2 parts in Japan as well).  Barring the supernatural elements, this game stays relatively faithful to the feel and standards of the historical setting, which is 1864 Japan (i.e., Victorian times, from an English-world perspective).  The second half of the game, with the final route endings, is Hakuoki Edo Blossoms (out Spring 2018).

If you read the reviews, you will see that what most people dislike is that the game ends halfway through the main story lines.  This was unavaoidable because this game has twice as many routes (romance interests) as the original and adds content even for the original characters.  If it is important to you to have complete routes from the get-go, I recommend playing the mobile version of the game (Android and iOS) or the PS3 version (still my favourite version, as it has so much fun extra content).  You will only get 6 routes instead of 12 though!

PROS:  One of the best otome games out there *if* you like historical drama and don't mind a slow burn romance style.  Good music, lovely art, characters you think about even after you're done playing.  Lots of choice!

CONS:  As in Japan, this game is only the first half of each story.  The common route makes up a big percentage of this game; while there are lots of choices and characters, you will find yourself with lots of rereading / skipping to do.  Also, I did not find the game as well-translated as it could have been.  I miss the translation values of the original game.

review_text:
As of the Webgrave update, I can no longer recommend this game. The stat system was significantly nerfed such that, at my same level of 455 prior to the update, I now have 45% less health, 60% less stamina and earn 2.5x less witchfire. You also carry two less healing elixirs for a total of three instead of the previous five. Moreover, each elixir heals you for significantly less while enemies still hit you for the same amount of damage. You can remedy part of this with their new rosary system in which you equip rosary beads, however the stat based ones are weak, you can only equip a few at a time, and they are scattered throughout each map or perhaps earned in other ways.

I feel it is important to continue the discussion around difficulty in gaming and the accessibility challenges it presents. I'm no stranger to difficult games - I've completed Dark Souls, Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne, Sekiro, and Elden Ring to name a few. But I feel these games established a standard of difficulty that can exclude certain players. Witchfire is a difficult and demanding game. But I had found a way round this by leveling up my character, pushing him higher and higher so I could enjoy the game. Even my playstyle changed - I was a long ranged, passive player at early levels, using sniper rifles and freeze spells to slow my enemies. I evolved to blasting my way into enemy camps and taking the challenge head on. But I could do so with the strength I had earned from the levels I earned. 

To make matters worse, the Gnosis difficulty curve system the game incorporates is essential to fully level up to even make it to the end of the game. If I'm struggling at Gnosis level 3 in the current form after the update, then in conjunction with your stat changes I no longer stand a chance on completing the game.

One of the most iconic, if not the most iconic, FPS games is Doom and, too this day, continues to have difficulty levels allowing everyone to access it at a pace that is comfortable to them. The developers of Witchfire have said that they changed their stat system because higher level players were essentially "playing with cheats." I find this statement bizarre. If I'm having fun, what does it matter? The prior stat system allowed everyone to play as they wanted - you could level up as much or as little as you wanted. There was even a video posted by the developers of a very talented player who completed an incredible challenge. Players will always find ways to challenge themselves within the limitations of the game.

I'm more sad and disappointed I have to let this game go. I was following it for years prior to its release. I bought it day one on Epic and bought it again when it came to Steam. I was having so much fun. It breaks my heart to change to a negative review. But this is a warning to casual and even mid-core players who may not enjoy the steep difficulty adjustments with minimal payoff from the new stat system.

Original Review:
I was walking around Irongate Castle in awe of the visuals, the small details, and the atmosphere. The music, audio, sound design - it's all on point. The roguelite aspect and the gameplay loop is absolutely perfect - the player isn't Doomguy with infinite stamina or access to countless healing items, but with limitations to his character which are entirely fitting in this grimdark world. That said, player movement is smooth, responsive, and in close partnership with each weapon - it is a delight to play. Everything is stitched together in such an outstanding way and is always authentic to the world around it.

The developers are also 100% engaged to feedback and have such an honest way about communicating that it is such a breath of fresh air. That said, they are also committed to their vision of this game and they've maintained such an excellent balance with player feedback.

This game is a labour of love. And it shows. I wish them nothing but the best venturing forward from Epic EA to Steam EA.

review_text:
This genuinely might be one of the worst "popular" games that I have ever played. I'm not even playing into the DBD hate hype train. I am absolutely shocked that it is not dead yet - Perhaps because there aren't other asymmetrical games like it, and the licenses keep player count high. 

This does not feel like a live service game. Year after year we have asked for specific things, and BHVR responds with "yeah that's cool, also look at this new license! But no, you're right, Game Health is important... so in honour of that, let's worsen the cosmetics UI for no reason". Also, there is a long-standing bug list for a bunch of killers that the devs haven't even sniffed, and I don't think they're ever going to get fixed. 

Speaking of killers, the balance team at BHVR definitely like to troll. The Krasue release was absolutely awful - and this was only exacerbated by the recoil from the terrible Walking Dead livestream situation prior. I literally stopped playing for weeks until she got nerfed. 

How many times have game-breaking things like this happened which make the game unplayable for an extended period of time? BHVR somehow manage to maintain a completely ignorant approach to all the things that they do. Like dude, if this was any other game, you would legit think the company hates their fans or are intentionally trolling, but when it comes to this game, you just say "Good Ol BHVR!". This company's name and reputation has become synonymous with "dogshit" for crying out loud. I will say that is not true in regards to the support team at least. The support team actually try to stay on top of tickets, unless they get inundated like all of the employees at BHVR do, which is why there are so many quick fixes. 

The game itself is so monotonous and boring, and the seasonal events and 2v8 do little to actually make the base game anymore entertaining. Imagine your soloQ team is trolling, so you have to sit on gens the whole game... 5 games in a row. Not fun, right? That's often the reality. And dude, fucking Among Us makes doing survivor tasks more enjoyable than a 10 year old, live-service horror game. Where is the courage to go out of their comfort zone and bring engaging gen completion ideas to the PTB. BHVR are terrified to take risks. This is another reason why DBD does not feel like a live service game. Rather, it feels like they are just keeping the servers running. 

If it wasn't for comp or JRM-style trolling, people with over 2000 hours would've left for another game like a mass exodus (and BHVR only recently started doing things like "supporting" creators or DBDLeague. For so long, there was such little community involvement in ANYTHING. I have rarely seen other western companies do the same with their popular games). 

I came back to Dead By Daylight from a month of not playing (during which I played CS2, Runescape, Metro 2033 series and Minecraft) to this game and was absolutely shocked at how truly unenjoyable everything was. Like I said, if it wasn't for comp or JRM-ing killers, the only way DBD would keep its numbers up would be with a constant influx of new players, as older players would be getting tf out ASAP. I have not played a game less rewarding to invest time into. 

Queue up in SoloQ against a good killer? That's always game over, because BHVR's "mmr-based" matchmaking will consistently give you bad survivors who should not be put in your lobby, so it's not even a fun challenge. Queue up in SoloQ against a bad killer? That's always ggez, because you stomp this poor baby killer who doesn't even know what a CJ tech is, again because the matchmaking is not coded with any common sense in regards to mmr, but done in a way to reduce queue times. 

Also they 100% lie slightly about the ping in public games. Whatever your ping is, add 30 onto it. 

I actually was working towards becoming a major content creator for DBD, but HensDaMonsta can take the spotlight, because whilst this game still has potential, the way BHVR manages it does not, and so I have lost faith in Dead By Daylight. What a letdown.

review_text:
When PSO2 first came to the west it was something special, something new, people had been waiting on the game to come to the west for 8 years and the wait was worth it. The game had come out with Episodes 1-3 with Episodes 4-6 being released later. The game even whilst being released in a technically incomplete state in the west was still filled with hundred of hours worth of content with the quality of said content ranging from standard MMO to just straight up mind boggling and there was always something to work towards. PSO2 wasn't perfect by any means, but is wasnt bad either and had  extremely strong foundations and additions that would make it very easy for SEGA to keep adding or improving upon for whatever would come next for Phantasy Star as a series or so you would think.

PSO2 NGS would get announced. SEGA showcases a complete refresh/new game using a whole new game engine, revamped Character customization, and the game is no longer separated by multiples maps with instances within them, NGS instead has and open world. NGS releases and its just okay, the first couple hours felt amazing, but the more you played the more empty the game felt and it just didn't feel as good as PSO2, sure the combat was more fluid, but its felt like it was missing something. it is now 2025 and while the game hasn't been abandoned i might as well be. Content roll out for NGS was always slow and too be honest i don't see a problem with it being slow, it's the contents of the updates that have absolutely killed this game for me and many others. For some reason SEGA has decided to take a page out of bungie's book and they consistently choose to release mediocre content updates and under deliver constantly. The game will not have a meaningful update for MONTHS and then when they do update it, they either release a small mediocre content drop that only lasts hours, give us another recycled seasonal event for the trillionth time or release another pay-to-win/ cosmetic gacha. The game as it is is a shadow of its former self and now shares more in common with Barbie Fashion Designer than the game it used to be. 

Until SEGA decides to open their eyes and actually take the development of this game seriously then i can't see myself recommending this game to ANYONE long-term or short-term unless they like throwing them selves into the empty hobby of whaling out on every gacha for "fun".

review_text:
[b]A cult classic adventure game you must try before Samorost 3[/b]

Samorost 2 is a sequel to the original free-to-play Samorost, an online Flash cult classic game created by Jakub Dvorsky long time ago. This sequel has been developed by Amanita Design (Jakub Dvorsky's indie game studio), same company responsible for other well-known titles such as Machinarium or CHUCHEL. Samorost 2 is a great point-and-click adventure game where once again, you play as the same small gnome character from the first game, on a quest to save your stolen dog. Along the way you’ll encounter some very bizarre and stranger creatures. 

Short and simple, this is a game you can complete in a single afternoon. As in the previous game, the player moves from one enchanting level to another after solving inventive puzzles or overcoming obstacles. Most puzzles are just pixel hunts, because essentially all you need to do is hit the few hotspots in the right order. Sadly, the lack of a proper hint system makes some ilolligical parts quite hard but in the other hand some of them are pretty obvious as well.

The world you explore is so enchanting, with the same art direction as the original with touches of Asian influence. The game's backgrounds often combine organic with inorganic elements and  each scene in the game contains movement, and the creatures, gadgets, plants and insects are beautifully animated. There is hardly any text or dialog in the game and little voice-acting in form of non-legible utterances. The music was composed by Tomáš Dvořák, and like what he did for the previous game, the soundtracks in Samorost 2 are pleasant to listen to.

All in all, this game as a single piece isn't so bad but neither so great. However, Samorost is a worthy series that fully deserves your support. You would like to play this one and the original game title before to really go for Samorost 3, a real masterpiece from the new era.

review_text:
I didn't really want to write a review this early, but I want to try and do my part to keep reviews above 70%. It's a great foundation to a well-crafted ARPG. Anyway, here are my thoughts so far.

Getting a huge hit of 90's-2000's Cartoon Network nostalgia from the characters and story so far. Right around that Kid's Next Door vibe. 

The OST falls somewhere between Phantasy Star Online and Crosscode. Chill sci-fi with certified bangers where it matters. 

The gameplay and mechanics have been great so far, and without spoilers, the game just opened up for me to an exciting degree. I don't think I'll have to worry about running out of content for another 40 hours. I unlocked the character roster, and where I thought I would just play one character I liked all the way through, I was pulled in by great class design. I want to level every single one of them to max just to appreciate their kits. 

There is a valid concern regarding multi-player lobbies and one person being able to end the run before everyone is ready. I haven't experienced those kinds of players yet, but I'm sure that it's probably getting looked at with so much attention on it.

As for the "Always Online" complaints, you can turn off matchmaking and play alone. It requires you to relaunch the game after setting your preference to "Private". It's still online, but that's because this is going to be a Free to Play, Live Service ARPG. 

On the topic of Early Access, reporting bugs is extremely easy in game. Just hit F3, scroll to the issue, screenshot, and write a description. Instant delivery to the team. There are bugs, so if you're going to pay to play before the F2P release, please take some time to make the game better instead of complaining about them. Blood, sweat, and tears went into this project, and you can really feel that.

review_text:
[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
[list]
	[*]Has combat that rewards adapting your equipment to the situation, but swapping equipment becomes increasingly tedious over time.
	[*]Combat animations generally have the proper wind-up, but the main character’s attack feels janky
	[*]Compelling aesthetic; if you like what’s on the store page, you’ll like what’s in-game
	[*]Well paced difficulty on “Recommened” level
	[*]Restart from the last save point or autosave point on death; no “corpse runs”
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Introduction[/h2]
  Lost Ruins is a metroidvania with methodical combat that emphasises adapting your equipment and weapons to suit the situation. It introduces small yet meaningful changes to its genre, but the tedious UI hampers its execution.

[h2]Pixel Art and Anime-Style[/h2]
  The most apparent aspect of Lost Ruins is its visuals — a contrast of clean, anime-styled characters in a grimy, somewhat realistic environment. It’s a compelling aesthetic for those who like both styles. With its pretty pixel art and portraits in gameplay and dialogue, if you like what you see on the store page, you’ll like what you see in-game.

[h2]Adequate Animations[/h2]
  Lost Ruins also has adequate character animations overall — both in visual appeal and for gameplay purposes. The main character’s idle animation is incredibly animated, in two senses of the word. Environmental lighting is also subtly animated, giving everything a glow that makes enemies and your character easy to distinguish from the background. Most enemies have the appropriate wind up before they attack, giving you a fair chance to dodge and counterattack all but the fastest enemies.
  However, similar to older metroidvanias, the main character’s attack feels janky. Every weapon has the same overhead swing at a constant speed, based on their speed stat, so there’s a lacking sense of heft in the heavier weapons.

[h2]Interesting Gameplay, but…[/h2]
  In spite of its combat animations, combat is still interesting enough to engage in. While the weapon swing and movement are simple, the equipment you obtain over time are diverse and situationally useful. It’s a game that rewards adaptability; swapping to the appropriate equipment according to the environment and enemies you encounter will make fights easier. Whether wading through water or killing fast monsters, there is probably an item that will make obstacles easier to surmount.
  As you get further in the game, overpowered combinations of equipment become available and I love it. After cautiously navigating every encounter up to that point, there was an incredible relief in simply rolling over every enemy that once gave me grief.

  The need to frequently swap equipment, however, also means you have to navigate the inventory often. It’s cumbersome.
  You have to press ‘down’ and ‘up’ to trudge through your extensive lists of items. Even though these are partitioned in helpful categories, these categories are each a single, long vertical column. Most of the items you’ll frequently equip or consume are in 4 categories: weapons, spells, items, and equipment.
  You cannot skip ahead by jumping several items at a time. You cannot use your mouse. The only QoL in inventory navigation is the ability to change the sorting order and marking items as “favourites”. Though it’s better than nothing, the “favourites” feature simply keeps your items at the top of each long list, and still requires many button presses since you’ll likely want to keep several “favourites” (maybe six per category). Furthermore, when you want to try new items, it’ll take a while to find.
  It’s a small frustration that grates on you as you keep playing on.
  Fortunately, the game took me about 10 hrs to beat — including all side objectives, some frivolous achievements, and grinding for equipment and healing items.

[h2]Metroidvania, but is it Hard?[/h2]
  Expanding on gameplay a little more, there’s the matter of difficulty. Having beat the game on “Recommended”, I would say I had a comfortably tense experience.

  You can pause to heal in the middle of battle, but these are two key limitations that hinder such boring brute force. Firstly, the most common healing items regenerate 1 HP per second. Secondly, instant heals are expensive and tedious to obtain in large quantities. Not impossible, but tedious.

  On the first encounter with a new enemy, you are given room to fight it on its own, allowing you to learn its behaviour and abilities. You are then continually introduced to new combinations of enemies, each addition a compounding threat to your life. Fast enemies allow slow ones to attack. Some hinder your movements. Nearly every enemy can kill you if you carelessly swing at them. 

  If you die, you lose your progress up to your last save point. In a strangely refreshing way, this classic way of handling death works well. Given the increasing prevalence of ‘running to your corpse to take back your money’ in newer games, I think I like restarting with all your money and items still on you. The consumables you spent before death will return, so you don’t have to worry about making subsequent retries unnecessarily difficult. Put in combination with the autosave point right before boss fights, I never felt unduly punished for messing up.

  There is a hardcore mode, and new challenge modes unlock after beating the game, but I have not played them, so I cannot comment on those.

[h2]Is it Good?[/h2]
  All in all, it’s rather [u]difficult to recommend[/u]. Lost Ruins’ most interesting feature as a metroidvania is that it rewards the player’s adaptability just as much as their skill with the controls. Yet, this very selling point is hindered by tedious menu navigation as you frequently swap out your equipment.
  Its difficulty is well paced. Its visuals are as you see on the store page.
  It’s not a must-buy, but you might like this.

review_text:
When games like Yooka Laylee or Armikrog pop up wanting to cash in on the fondness of an old franchise, fail to meet the standard set by their predecessors, and gets absolutely lambasted for it, I'm utterly baffled as to how this game ended up with an overwhelmingly positive rating instead.
The graphics are pretty and screenshots look like they could've come right out of JSRF, but that's all the positive things I can say about this.
The inundation of cutscenes is exhausting on top of being poorly presented, with characters just standing around blankly as they have no idle animations or facial expressions. The writing is downright amateurish and certainly couldn't get me to care about any of these characters. JSRF at least had some major characters be voice acted in cutscenes, here you don't even get that, you just get a handful of grunts at best.

Everyone disliked the tutorial segments in JSR and JSRF for being excessively long, but this game's tutorialisation period is even worse.  There are multiple boss fights early on too, each more awful to play through than the last.
But the worst crime the game commits is a complete lack of momentum in movement; you move at a slower speed on foot and a faster speed when on your ride, that's it, going downhill doesn't speed you up, going uphill doesn't slow you down, at best you can hold down a button to boost at a slightly faster speed or tap a different button for an instant direction change + speed boost once in the air. Everything about the movement here feels wrong, it's stilted, it's artificial, you touch a halfpipe and immediately shoot out at max speed, it's totally busted. The only bit of praise I can give it is that you boost your speed and combos by turning into corners when grinding, but this also means that combo scores are focused primarily on grind rails at the expense of other tricks, one thing you'd think they wouldn't copy from JSRF.
Adding to the lack of momentum is the graffiti system where you have to stop at every point to do a stick waggling minigame for each tag. JSR had this, but not for the smallest ones, and JSRF got rid of it to match the design being open world instead of stage and routing based. BRC brings it back, and the small ones don't have the minigame but still pause your movement to display the tag, so every tag completely breaks the flow. The game's areas are also huge and full of empty space, probably because they wanted to make the manual tricks have more purpose, but as a result the locations are just boring to look at and boring to explore.

Making matters even worse is the soundtrack, in the entire time I played there was only one decent song which was of course Naganuma's track that they used in all the advertising, while everything else ranged from dull to downright annoying. It wasn't as bad as Birthday Cake but some tracks damn near came close.

This just feels like another game that completely missed the mark of what it was trying to copy, and for the price they're charging you'd expect it to have much higher production values than it does. I'm just disappointed, man.

review_text:
[b]tl;dr -[/b] Truly a grotesquely dirty yet uniquely beautiful experience that tortures you the entire time. Must be played to be believed.


[b]In-depth -[/b] So imagine if HR Geiger and Alex Grey were the art directors for an atmospheric horror video game and you would get Scorn. Have played video games for the better part of three decades and I have never played anything quite like this game. From start to finish; everywhere you look, everything you do, every single step of the way you are confronted with horrifying imagery that keeps you unsettled and grossed out for the duration of the game.

Everything you think you know about video games is wrong when you play Scorn. There are no tutorials. There is not a single word spoken. There is no "music" only horrific ambiance that is used for dramatic effect and for unsettling you with shear silence. There is only a minute Heads Up Display and in fact it's more of a heads down display. Everything is unsettling and grotesque, literally e v e r y t h i n g. The weapons; the enemies, the viscera laden bio-mechanical technology all around you, the main character, the story, the actions you must undertake to progress, anything at all that you see anywhere at anytime might make you want to hurl.

On the other hand, after you really start taking it all in and noticing what the theme is, the game really starts to shine with an unforeseen splendor that you were too horrified to notice before. The cohesion of everything I mentioned above and how every single speck unifies with and adheres to the theme, transform this into a gestalt that was clearly crafted using an elegantly horrific design.

The story itself is also not traditional and you're going to have to make up your own mind about what happens but be forewarned that the ending is not for everyone. Other than that I truly enjoyed what it took to get through this game. It really feels like a task was completed after the emotional price I paid to progress in this game. The story does a fantastic job of elevating the main themes here by making you really feel the weight of your actions and it does so in many different ways. It is painfully emblematic of the famous Thomas Sowell quote: "There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs"

These non-traditional and unique choices will also likely turn off a lot of players and, I would almost recommend using a guide unless you are someone that wants to go in blind but, be forewarned you are going to be punished for thinking that this game is like any other video game. The games is not very intuitive or easy to understand so getting lost is a near certainty.

This.

I've been waiting for this for eight years, as many of you have. I've racked up hundreds of hours getting teams of young guns to reach the mightiest of prizes, the Great Lord Stanley's Grail. Countless nights of sleep were sacrificed when came the real season: so many sodas... so many chips (crisps, for our friends in the UK). 

Bathroom breaks were (unwisely) postponed when my Habs played the Bruins (almost systematically) in legendary first-round skirmishes. Meals were skipped. Assignments were botched. 

Life, however, uh, found a way.

And now, thanks to the dedication of the people at SI, I can rejoice (at long last) the return of the Prodigal Son.

I've only played a few hours thus far, but I am ecstatic! This is no beta test, this is a very polished, very stable game and it delivers. Plus, with the help of the just-as-dedicated people of TBL, there is a fresh, up-to-date roster pack waiting for you to be savoured. I don't think I could thank them enough for their generosity for the past eight years, nor would my words amount to their work. 

I will say that the resolution (fixed 1024x768) is my main irritant, but it is in NO way a major source of irritation; it is merely an attempt at searching for a "con" amidst a very impressive number of "pros".

You're a hockey fan? Get this. Now. 16,99$ (yeah yeah, the Canadian dollar took a drop) is ridiculously low for an early access of this quality.

review_text:
Been playing this since the beta. As a huge Star Trek fan, I loved this game for years as it was (and still is) one of the only good Star Trek games out there. It took what was at the time the new lore from the reboot movies and used it to create a vision for the future of Star Trek beyond what Voyager had given us. Played my Federation character up to the maximum level, and would come back to play new updates like those surrounding the Romulans. I only really seriously came back and started playing when they released the content surrounding Deep Space 9, the Dominion, and the Gamma Quadrant around 2018.

I played for a good while with my friends queuing for adventure zones and so on to earn reputation to get better ship equipment and what not. However, it is clear that as player numbers have fallen, Cryptic needs to keep making money, and so more and more of the game has become monetized. Once they monetized a lot of the endgame content, it became pay-to-win and I lost interest in continuing playing the game. It is because of this that I can't recommend the game to most people. A lot of the leveling is very fast now a days, and while the story lines are hit or miss, nearly all end game content has become a cash grab.

If you're a fan of MMOs, this will be a pretty average MMO. The ground combat has never been spectacular, and the game is really only worth it for the in-space aspects which it does well. If you're a big fan of Star Trek, though, you'll love the game. Although if you're coming in from the new shows, do know this game operates on a different (and in my opinion better) timeline.

After only a few hours on the first day i put it down out of frustration, I had difficulty figuring out some of the things i needed to do. I went out online and most information out there was out of date as the game is still in development and thus changes now and again. I found the discord and got help just by searching for my questions in the new player help area. Sure enough others had asked those questions and been given answers. I went back into the game the second day and started making headway. 
I will say that as of the time i write this review, the play feels fairly polished. The environment is great the story is largely there in notes and fluff text you find. Not sure they plan on adding in Voice Acting, but honestly I am not sure it needs it~! In short, IMNHO ([b]In My Never Humble Opinion[/b])... [i]It is a great game![/i]

Pros: 
1. good graphics and a creepy feel
2. Developers have their vision and are not going to change a lot of stuff willy-nilly just because a set of people don't like it. I admire a good strong vision from a dev team IMNHO it keeps the team focused . That is not to say things have not been adjusted or tweaked when needed (looking at change history) 
3. Brought to us by the Developers of "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" a STELLAR and creepy game.
4. With the absolute garbage being puked or shat out by the bigger game companies it is refreshing to play games from small teams who care

Cons:
1. the game is NOT easy, this may intimidate some but if you like a challenge this is fine. But fair warning if dying a lot as you learn a game upsets you I say Stay Away this isn't for the feint of heart. 
2. It's still Early Access! If you have not played an EA game you might not enjoy it. EA games can take drastic turns or even rests. I don't see this as a history for this game though. 
3. I can see some of the gamers I know not liking it. There is a lot of going back in to areas to farm things you need. Every time you level the map changes a little but not much. and once you learn Gnosis 1 the same map becomes more of a challenge. Some will call this "a grind" but I felt there was incentive and reward enough to keep me going back. 

Things i wish I had known from the start:
1. as of this typing when you find a map to access a new area it is accessed through the same portal you go to the first island through just switch the destination by choosing a different one along the top of the menu that comes up 1st when opening the portal. 
2. keep a keen eye out for Flora to collect and use at the base, and learn the right mushrooms to eat lol. 
3. no shame in holding off learning Gnosis 1 it does add new difficulties to the game once learned. I waited until lvl 25 and may have jumped the gun so to speak :)

TLDR: like the game but it is a challenge to learn, the rewards felt worth it. If dying a lot learning a game bugs you stay away.

review_text:
At the current price point its a waste of money. There is about 20€ worth of content in here and its not exactly all high quality content. For everything done right the game does something monumentally stupid. 
For example the game gives you a dodge to reveal enemy weak points, great idea solid way to reward accurate shooting. But then it binds said weakpoint mechanic to you having 100% stamina. So if you jumped, ran prior to battle or god forbid got hit a second ago that entire mechanic is effectively disabled. Worse yet weapons in this game have essentially 0 accuracy outside of scoped in mode so even when you reveal said weakpoint there is still a 50% chance to completely miss it because you did not scope in when shooting. 

Another example. [b]The game upgrades weapons and gear not just numerically but also via added special effects.[/b] So you get a challenge(kill x amount mostly) and then you can use a materials to boost your item. Neat idea that is completely invalidated by said upgrades being hidden from the player. Yes, you read that correctly. You are given no info on what the upgrade will do before you execute it, so you might easily waste an hour farming materials for an upgrade that in the the end you did not even want. 

Or how about this. [b]You have a limited amount of ammo and spells recharge very slowly so logically you need to plan your moves carefully ahead to not screw yourself. [/b] Great, I have to carefully choose my battles, except you cannot because the game will you just randomly spawn in enemies so you essentially cannot plan for shit because that one elite and five scrubs can easily spawn in additional two elites mid fight and even behind you so every encounter turns into effectively a coin toss as to whether you will be able to finish it. 

I could go on but I suppose my point is clear. The game is schizophrenic in its design. It does one thing and then undermines it for no gain whatsoever. It legitimately feels like half the design decisions were made to accommodate some future change or some cheese strategy that exists only on paper. 

Buy it on sale or avoid entirely.

review_text:
➤➤ Short Review: --Skip--

I "wasted" 4.7k hours in this game, hoping since launch (back in june 2021) that the game would improve as the foundation was really hitting that itch for me, but it's time to give up. After multiple world expansions (up to 3 new regions, 1 new randomized dungeon and a city exploration with timelimit), multiple class reworks, expansions and updates, after many "new enemies" to fight, player housing, a card minigame and after some new quest types, the game still isn't in an acceptable state. I played the game for this long mostly because of my alliance (guild) in the game and I had fun playing with them, even if the game itself wasn't good.

➤➤ Long Review:

- Story: The story of Base PSO2 is good, but it's majority cutscenes with some fights here and there. The story of NGS however, it's not great. It's slow, boring and somewhat predictable. It did however get somewhat decent with the latest story update, but it wasn't enough for me to say they redeemed the story.

- Gameplay: NGS gameplay originally was one of the stronger parts, but the longer you play it, the more you notice how empty it really is. It looks flashy, but there is no depth. The devs even realized this and added more customization to the attacks, trying the bare minimum to increase the build variety in the game, but for me, this is just a bandaid fix for deeper issues.. Another massive flaw was the overreliance on Dodge/Weapon Actions (A parry/counter unique for each weapon). The devs again realized this and added new mechanics to bosses such as Attacks that can't be avoided with dodge/weapon action, again, bandaid fix for deeper issues. Let's talk about the elements next. Usually, you would think Fire does something different than water or light, but in NGS, they all do the exact same. If the enemy has an elemental weakness, after hitting the enemy often times with that specific element, the enemy will go into "elemental down". That's it. There is no "fire deals damage over time" or "water decreases armor/damage resistance". Besides the "elemental down", there is also the "physical down", which is also the same as the elemental down, but it relies on physical attacks instead of elemental attacks. Now with all of the different classes available and lots of different weapons types, you could just play a different class/weapon combo to fight the boredom, but as mentioned above, the game heavily relies on Dodge/Weapon Action. Every fight with all melee weapons will be the same, the same goes for all ranged weapons and all tech (elemental) weapons. There are some minor differences for each weapons playstyle, but  these are really small. The gameplay also doesn't have the typical 3 roles system for the classes. Yes, you have classes that can "heal" or "buff/debuff", but they're extremely simple, Only 2 Skills that heal, either the same amount as a healing item or Full Life and Full PP (Mana) once with a massive cooldown and 1 buff skill. The Debuff isn't even a skill, instead it's a passive for one specific class which applies when you hit the enemy. Not to mention, all of the skills mentioned above aren't even necessary to clear any content. (Instead of them, the class called "Ranger" is necessary, as this class can apply an effect on an enemy that increases the damage of all people hitting the marked spot, basically making them necessary to have if you want to clear high end content when they launch.)

- Sound: The Soundtrack is actually decent and somewhat memorable. Doesn't feel out of place as well, but as with any soundtrack, you might start to hate them.

- Visuals: The game looks visually decent enough. The world looks nice and the effects are good, but the characters are bad. I don't understand how they thought this style for characters was in any way good. As an active player, you get used to the graphics, but for majority of new players, 90% of characters just look straight up awful and in some cases, it's not even the player's fault. They tried to "fix" this by adding a cel shading option to the game for all characters or just yours. This however isn't enough in my opinion. The foundation is already flawed and shows cracks. Just watch the reveal for the Atelier Ryza collab with NGS. The NGS versions of Ryza and co. look awful.

- Collabs: Yes, the game has collabs, quite a lot actually. From Eminence in shadow and Frieren to Atelier Ryza and Melty Blood, tons of collabs here, HOWEVER. The collabs are really barebones. In the beginning, all you got was "AC Scratch Tickets", (Real Money Gacha) for the cosmetics of the collab IPs. That's it. Now, You also get cardboard cutouts of these characters to place in your Creative Space (Player Housing), AMAZING! No quests, enemies, stories, nothing. The only exception being the Sonic "Collabs" if you want to call them that. Instead of "AC Scratch Tickets" with the cosmetics, we got Limited Time Quests somewhat Sonic themed. They were ok the first time, but they get boring really really fast.

- The only positive of NGS that no other MMO currently tops: Character Customization. The character creator in NGS is surprisingly deep and good. You have tons of sliders that actually change the character. You have the ability to mix and match outfit parts (which are separated into 3 layers, Outerwear, Base/Setwear and innerwear). You also can freely customize your whole character and change everything about it with no barriers. Want to change the Gender? Do it. Don't want to be a human anymore, change to a CAST (Robot). Now with all the years of NGS behind us, there are tons and tons of different outfits, hairstyles, accessories, motions and so on that you can use to create truly unique characters ... IF you either scratch (pay for the gacha) or grind yourself to death for the ingame money.

- I skipped so many other flaws and problems. There is no Trading between Players, the player market Search is horrendous, gear progression is boring, content gets repeated (especially normal enemies), the community is extremely horny and down bad, Rewards for "difficult" content is really demotivating, the game is p2w, the game punishes you if you play for free, The tutorials are bad (if there are even any tutorials explaining specific things), the open world isn't being used at all, majority of content gets obsolete in few months, and and and ...

I dropped my Hiveswap Act 1 review just now, so I'll follow up with my review Hiveswap Act 2 innit. The simple question is yes/no does the Archmage reccomen-Yes, the Archmagos Recommends. I WANT you to play this game... after you Play Hiveswap: Act 1. For those of you in the future reading this, I recommend you read up on the decade 1990-2000 in America and the rest of the world, and then play Act 1, and then play this.

As with Hiveswap Act 1, I was before playing it occupied with real life chaos, though only up to about a month or less than a month after this was released. This had a profound effect on me, and I'd guess also on the writing crew, so I missed a few features (the bee game) in that playthrough which hadn't yet been re-implemented. This playthrough was totally blind, note. I stuck with it to the end, I kept the orange blooded troll on the land ferry for the record.

Suffice it to say I was complete absorbed for a few days leading up to the Yuletide with it and every bit of narrative writing hits in a certain way. Maybe there's ways it could have hit harder, but then I wasn't on the crew and they did a good job of it anyway.

Pros-Deep, engrossing storyline that keeps you in it constantly until you finish innit bruv. This feels like a good Homestuck game and it feels like your actions have consequences, and serious consequences at that, and maybe you wish you had done something different but you don't know what you could have done different anyway. Alternia's a planet with brutal characters on it but there's also a lot of good characters on it and maybe the characters on it are better than those you'd find in your own neighbourhood. Maybe you'd trust them with your life before you'd trust anyone you know IRL with your life.

Cons?-I wouldn't call this a con because partaking in a trial is awful business as a human ANYWAYS. Alone in troll society that WILL happen, it's long and drawn out so if you're about to leave the Goldblood car make sure to save and come back for the long haul.

I don't really think there's any real Cons save for that one or three main characters ended up not being featured, though their residences and living spaces might have been.

Look just Play Act 1 and then get to this stage m8. Act 3? Wait a while and work on your patience innit, bruv.

I recently played Lucius, a game with an intriguing premise of playing as a young boy with supernatural abilities who is the son of the devil. While the idea behind the game was promising, unfortunately, the execution left a lot to be desired.

The game was riddled with numerous bugs and glitches that made it a frustrating experience. I found myself having to restart chapters frequently because NPCs wouldn't do what they were supposed to do, which made it difficult to progress through the game. The gameplay itself was tedious and repetitive, with a lot of clicking around and performing the same actions over and over again.

Despite the game's technical issues and lackluster gameplay, I pushed through and managed to finish it. However, I have no desire to play it again. The story and concept were interesting, but the technical issues and poor gameplay detracted from the overall experience.

The controls themselves were not problematic, and I had no issues with them. However, the numerous bugs and glitches made Lucius a frustrating experience. The game seemed rushed and underdeveloped, leaving me worried about what the next game in the series will be like.

Overall, while Lucius had a good idea, it was poorly executed.

review_text:
I'm 41, and I cannot recommend this game.  Despite others my age who've raved about how good this is. If you have an actual life - and enjoy seeing your playtime into a game recognized, avoid this. For the record, I'm not bad at FPS's. I loved Doom Eternal, Far Cry 3, Crysis, Bioshock. They say this game is like dark souls and destiny. Well, truth be told, I didn't really think Destiny was all that great when it came out. - Bungie really popularized the whole idea of cramming RPG mechanics into an FPS action genre. It just felt dumb and unnecessary - I worked at a gamestop when that game released. And I triggered quite a few kids sharing my opinion lol.  Shooting stuff and seeing negative numbers spew out of an enemy while depleting their health bar just looks so f***ing stupid, sorry guys.  So there's one big aspect that ruined this game for me.  Mainly though, this is just a difficult and punishing waste of time that reminds me that I'm way out of touch, more than any other game I've ever played. I don't really play many roguelites in general. But I do have a few favorites recently; battleshapers, Entropy Effect, and a few others.  Why did I buy Witchfire?  - It looked f***ing awesome.  Why question the purchase with so many rave reviews?  Well, I blame myself for reading just a couple of the sycophantic reviews of this game on steam before pulling the trigger. I think roguelites are one of the worst things to happen to modern gaming, aside from microtransactions and the GAS concept.  When did we decide that cutting content into a fraction of what would normally be required to be considered a full game was acceptable in a game?  I guess it's seen as ok, just as long as there's randomly generated enemies and a level-up system to feed the dopamine-addicted youth. Eat it up. This game has all that s*** and more.  There's a lot more to love here...
This game's atmosphere is amazing. The graphics are 10/10. As good, or better than any AAA game on the market. This is a bright beacon of light to see. I almost considered not requesting a refund just because of all the hard work the small team spent on this game. There's an amazing soundtrack/background.  Solid sound effects.  Smart enemies. I would have loved it otherwise, had it not been such a punishing game. Make it an open world game, or a linear story - either is fine. I would love this game.  But the difficulty level is obsurd!  Plus, paired with the fact that if you don't make it out, your entire time devoted is null; You loose all your "witch power" and progress/ power ups because you never made it out.  Nah. Sorry.  With 2 boys who constantly hound me to play overwatch, and a pretty healthy marriage I've kept going, this game offers nothing of value for me because it decided that my time isn't worthwhile, especially if I'm not up to the demands of this ridiculous game structure and its lore.  ANY Time invested into anything when you're 41 means something! Why the f*** do I want to die over and over getting my a$$ handed to me!?  For real. I could not make it through 1 f***ing quest. NOT 1. lol. 10+ tries. I guess I suck and this game. It wasn't designed for me. But for all you nerds in dire need of dark atmosphere who found dark souls and destiny to be "revolutionary", or if you're just a dopamine addict with some appreciation for the occult, THIS is the game for you.  If you're 41 and you have a life, I would say avoid this, but f***-it - give this game a try - or instead, find a good movie to see with your spouse. Your choice.  Big takeaway here is that your time is mostly useless unless you know all this fantasy RPG roguelite bulls***, or just need more of that sweet dopamine.

review_text:
This game may have smashing reviews from thousands of players, but I can't agree. It took me all of 10 minutes to realize that this would never be my thing. Why not?

- I don't like games that are all sneak. I like to be able to bash them around a bit, take a few hits, and come out on top.
- It's too strategic, too nit-picky, too mother-may-I...I found it limiting and annoying at every turn.
- I admit I didn't play it long, but I didn't see any kind of skills, level-building, or character development.

I like: adventure, sandbox, platformer, strategy (in a more forgiving way)...what would you do if a platformer game required you to jump off the edge of the screen and hope the ledge is there, then kills you if you miss? A space 4X game where you build your empire but there's an enemy which, upon contact with you, will smash you and you can't catch up because you're behind the curve; you've lost, but don't realize it for 20 turns. That's where Stars in Shadow failed. Or a strategy game which requires you to follow a specific path, then kills you each time you fail...which is what this is. Constant saves, back-ups, reloads...this game is just annoying. To be fair, the graphics are smooth and the sound is good. review_text:
A game I love, but can not recommend... still.  This game was unplayable when it launched, and 4 years later it's a great game foundation held back by the laziest level designs and predatory micro-transations that would make even Ubisoft blush.  

The character customization, player housing, and combat experience is S tier.  SEGA can make really great boss designs and mechanics.  I just wish most of them weren't recycled bosses from the previous iteration of PSO2.  Your creativity can run rampant if you let it. (to the detriment of other players)  Your ability to express your yourself through your player avatar is second to none.  You can create the most unique avatars or cosplay just about anything you can think of.  The player house building is just as good letting only your imagination be the limiting factor.

NGS has some beautiful open world areas with little to do, but you'll be asked to do it over and over until you hate it.  All the limited time content is confined to the laziest level designs consisting of flat blue "90's VR" style planes and boxes.  It's like after the open world areas were constructed they took away all the designers assets and gave them a blue cube to make all the live service content.

This game is "gamble to win" meaning every system uses RNG as a crutch to pad out any gameplay, progression, or monetization.  I'd like to recommend you just try PSO2:NGS, but then I'd also have to recommend you have 1-800-GAMBLER on speed dial.

review_text:
A very promising game

I'm sure a lot of people will find this game to be great. I am not one of them for the following reasons

The gameplay is stretched too much (for me) by being grindy. If you enjoy the gameplay loop, know that it's not THAT grindy but it was to me. I had to farm, and farming was done by kill x enemies, clear x areas repeatedly. I'm not a fan of it. I don't mind a little bit, but a big chunk of the gameplay was dedicated to this, which is why I am saying it has great potential but not atm (again, for me).

The lack of content
the repetitive nature of entering the map, clearing map, exfilling, the game pushed me away for a bit. More content would be the solution but as of right now, there isn't enough for me to justify spending more time into the game.

However the game gets a lot of things fantastic.

The gunplay is excellent
Great audio feel, especially on gunshots
Generally good balance of guns
The world is gorgeous (but you get used to it fast due to the repetitive nature)
The difficulty is high, and I love it.
Enemy difficulty is well balanced. They are punishing, but always fair.  I really have to use all of my tools and the game encourages me to.

Some of the things I wish devs would do
Early game ammo issues for some guns clearly make some guns better than others in the start. Why does angelus get 600+ rounds when shotguns get 50+?
That's about it though. the devs are passionate and they listen to community a lot. The project is headed in a very promising direction. Fow now, I will shelf this away and can't wait to get back to it a year later.

review_text:
As someone who really enjoyed the first act of Hiveswap, I gotta say that I was really disappointed with this one, especially with how long it took to come out after Act 1. A large portion of this game takes place on a train with multiple cars, segregated by blood spectrum. You travel between the cars trying to reach the front in order to switch train-tracks to get on the fast track to reach a party in time before its too late, that way you can get the info necessary to head back home. 

Unfortunately, the game really slogs down after a few carts in, and you do have to go back through the cars MULTIPLE times to accomplish objectives, and there's no fast-travel map of the train, so that means you have to go through multiple loading screens going through not only each car, but each section CONNECTING each car. Its something that would've been so simple to incorporate, but it wasn't, which adds a lot of unnecessary padding to this game's run time. There was also a section where I thought I could perform a little side quest as I was going through each train car in order to help out one of the troll's who had a sick/injured lusus, which I was excited to complete, but there was no point at any time where I could've gotten what I needed to help that troll before I reached the ending. I won't spoil the ending by the way, but it also wasn't worth all the extra fluff in between all the train cars leading up to it. 

Everything I did felt pointless at the end of it, as none of it really mattered. Three years of wait on this game and it most certainly was not worth the wait when compared to how much better the first game was compared to this one. No amount of Hiveswap Friendsim characters they threw in can make this game more worth it than it is. Don't pick it up for its initial $14.99 asking price, wait for it to drop or go on sale before you buy it if you want to continue the Hiveswap series. The first one is much better, and its only asking for $7.99 right now. I just hope act 3 doesn't take too long and we can continue the adventure, and hopefully it'll be a better entry in the series than this one is.

TLDR; Lots of loading screens when there really didn't need to be and the act ending isn't worth the fluff. Get it on sale or when the price drops.

16. Unsucessfully consults internet again.
17. Concludes that while I am not sure what I am supposed to be doing in this game, I am sure that figuring that out will take me more than two hours, thus:
18 Refunds game.

Verdict: Wait until it's done.

review_text: This Batman game will always have a special place in my heart. This game feels like an absolute love letter to the fans. Especially with the various cameos, easter eggs, and dialogue references that comic readers can easily point out. The vibe of the setting matches the chaotic open world perfectly, from large fires to thugs littered throughout the streets the city always feels like it needs saving. The story is filled with twists and really awesome fights throughout the game, stealth is just like the other games in the trilogy and is always fun striking fear into your enemies. Combat easily reminds you that you're playing as Batman and it's totally badass. Enemy variations leave you constantly planning how to take everyone down during the heat of battle. Overall, this is one of my favorite games of all time and it still holds a candle to a lot of single player games today despite it's age. The devs really cooked with this one and you should defintely check it out if you find yourself looking for a really great single player game.

Game is loads of fun, so I'll recommend it....
BUT it has some glaring issues. The biggest two being:
 1) Your goalie is cosmetic. Which, yeah, is whatever most of the time. You should be thinking about how to prevent enemy plays in the first place. However, I swear 90% of the goals gotten on me have been slow-moving shots from the blue WHERE MY GOALIE IS FACING. It doesn't feel good because you have no agency with your goalie, so it can leave you feeling helpless at times.

review_text:
You'll often find yourself losing games because of incredibly frustrating situations like a lone Specter Child slowly destroying your Farm placed far in the back without you noticing due to the lack of any indicators. If you don't have the warnings window open, you genuinely won't know a structure is taking damage without directly looking at it, and the window will simply say "a building is damaged" without even pointing you to it. Later on in the game, when you've got nearly 100 villagers, you will also lose them to random fights for this very same reason. It's difficult to tell if a fight is even happening aside from the occasional combat sounds, and trying to keep track of nearly a 3-figure count of villagers on your own is a feat, to say the least. Also, you can't pause the construction of walls, meaning your Builders will always have it as a priority on their list, even if you don't want those Crylithium Curtain Walls built because your Crystal Harvestry got destroyed by a random Specter last night and you want to spend your remaining Crylithium on charging your Essence Collectors (you can't stop them, and they will spend all of your Crylithium on those walls and you will lose because your towers will have no charge)

As for the tower-defense aspect, it's just a matter of time before you discover that spamming Ice Golems and Ice Bolt towers is the only way to survive the later waves. You can't determine target priority on towers, and Ice is the damage type that no monster in the game resists, as well as dealing bonus damage to Fire Elementals. There isn't any strategy to placing towers beyond the basics (line them up behind walls and make a maze). A couple of towers, especially the Tumbler-based ones, are left in the dust thanks to the lack of a target priority system, while AoE spamming towers remain the most functional. And what do you know - there's an AoE Ice damage tower. Why would you use anything other than it and the Golems?

All in all, it's a fantastic concept, but the game spreads itself thin among its many interacting systems and fails to convey critical information when it should be immediately known. Its cracks will show the more you try to experiment, but even if you're fine with sticking to the meta, you'll still find yourself at the short end of the stick when you eventually fail to notice a lose condition the game doesn't do much to help you keep track of.

review_text:
Probably my least-favorite LEGO game so far. It's just not very interesting. The teamwork puzzles are about on-par with other LEGO games.

The variety of character classes feels slightly lacking compared to Star Wars, Marvel or Lord of the Rings. Some of the puzzles are kinda dumb but in a very specific way. For example: there's one where you have to build something to help you jump up to a high platform. The problem is the characters can jump high enough without the built object. The game won't let them actually get up onto it but they CLEARLY jump higher than the top of the platform they're trying to reach. Just lazy level design and (like every single LEGO game) utter lack of playtesting.

As with several other recent LEGO games (Marvel Superheroes and LEGO Movie, for example), there's the absurd sexism of "only women can jump high and use a watering can, while only men can cut through vines with their knife/raptor claw."

So... if you really LOVE LEGO games, this is one. It doesn't suck but it really doesn't have anything unique like most of the other LEGO games do. It could be argued that playable dinosaurs are the unique thing but really they're just another character class like high-jumpers, explosive-users or super-strongs. It just doesn't feel like there's anything that makes this one a worthy addition to the collection. Yes, it was fun to play through all the JP movies and the LEGO humor is well-placed with (for example) the Tyranosaurus Rex snatching the lawyer into his mouth to brush his teeth, rather than eating him. Makes the games very family-friendly without making them stupid or childish. But of all the LEGO games, this one is solidly the worst I've played so far (okay, LEGO Movie might be worse but for VERY different reasons).

I'm going to try to keep the review as spoiler-free as I possibly can, because it's a game that the less you know about it, the better, but tldr; I would say IMSCARED is the best horror game I've played, but it's more like an incredibly unique experience that no other horror game I've seen has done, and is the FIRST horror game I would recommend to anyone interested in horror, outside of even just horror games as a whole. 

Most, if not all games I play that I thoroughly loved and enjoyed, tend to stick in the back of my mind for a week or two, and that's probably how it is for most people on here, too. And although I didn't spend many hours playing IMSCARED, as I do with most other games I love that live in my head rent-free for weeks, the limited time I had for it felt a lot longer than the number steam says I have in the game! 

Despite its age (2016 is the remaster afaik) the pixel style/art hasn't aged bad (In fact I LOVE it! Popular pixel horror is rare nowadays), moreso it retains the uniqueness of the game/experience. The sound design is simple too, making it complementary to the world. The most unique part is of course, the "external" experience outside of the game; the folders being created, the text pages leading you through the puzzles, on your computer etc. People seem to give a lot of credit to [horror] games that interact with the user/play outside of the games window, such as breaking the 4th wall, reading your pc info, saying the name of the owner of the pc you are playing the steam game in, Doki Doki Literature club is probably the biggest one that comes to mind. And don't get me wrong, I think that's a creepy and cool feature that they should use from time to time! But as far as I know, this game was one of the first to try this intrusive feature that some don't give credit for, and furthermore, making it the core idea of the whole game; a creepy, stalking entity that's like a sentient computer virus that wants to befriend and play with you.

[spoiler]The finale/end of the game was SO freaky, I won't go into details but I haven't felt my hair raise from a game in many years. For a moment I was contemplating even relaunching the game and waiting until the morning after to continue playing in broad daylight instead. As of writing this review, apparently the end of IMSCARED isn't over either, and I'm glad I finally got to playing this game when theres news of a part 2(?)[/spoiler]

Story
The backbone of this game is the story, which is mediocre. The main characters constantly tell unfunny jokes, and the plot isn't as poignent as everyone will lead you to believe. 

Gameplay
Just because the game is story oriented doesn't excuse the awful gameplay. The game requires you click randomly on everything in the room you're in to find the five memory items you're looking for, and then, and then play a tile flipping puzzle (which feels like a cheap iphone game) every level.

Graphics
I like the retro aesthetic as much as the next guy, this game has a very cheap, unpolished feel. The backgrounds and sprites are pretty, but many of the menus and puzzles look strikingly out of place. Many of the animations (such as the fight between the main characters) look like they came from a free flash game. 

Music
One of the redeeming qualities of this game, but its not amazing either.

If you ever played the original EHM then you wil have no issues playing this one since it is basically that game.

However there is one thing that should improve and that is the trade AI.
I did some testing for fun and literally not one team was willing to trade their "future franchise player" for Connor McDavid straight up. Show me one NHL team that wouldnt do that trade IRL. Im talking about Sabres not trading Mittelstadt, Canucks not parting with Petterson for McDavid and similar trades. LOL
This just illustrates a huge flaw in the trade ai and you will often bang your head in the wall for all the stupid offers and rejections you will see in this game. Lesson learned is to stockpile picks and build through draft. Just ignore whatever the assitsand GM is saying sinc ehe will say every trafde is really bad except the ones that are really bad.

but all in all this game is worth it if you want a hockey sim that is cheap.

For a PC game, Animalia Survival feels like a complete letdown. It's the kind of game you'd find for free in the App Store, and even then, it wouldn't be worth your time.  If you're looking for a survival game with any real substance, look elsewhere. This one is a complete waste of your hard-earned money.

review_text:
Graphically, this game is incredible. After that it all falls straight off a cliff. Glorified walking simulator, though you move more at the speed of a crawl (probably to artificially ensure that you break the two hour refund barrier). There are no directions or dialogue or narration or any markers to indicate anything at all, which a cynic might again suggest is probably to assist in nudging the player past two hours of playtime as they wander aimlessly searching for the next of about a dozen total interactive buttons that you left click to progress the vacuous, linear story (if we're being charitable this is an artistic decision to immerse the player in a confusing and foreign environment and allow them to put the story together on their own). Anyway, this game is basically entirely devoid of what an average game developer might call "mechanics". I would also add that it lacks severely in the horror department, there are some things which I would describe as gross or unsettling--but nothing scary ever happens.

Basically a minimally interactive visual novel about rebirth set in a weird futuristic biomechanical hellscape, but all of the budget went to the visual part.

tldr; $40 tech demo, furthest thing from a game or horror that I've purchased in a long time. Watch a commentary free longplay on 2x speed and have a look through the art book if you liked what you saw.

review_text:
[b]To the Moon[/b] is a single player adventure story game in the style of old spirited JRPGs.  You play as two scientists whose job is to implant memories to a dying man, fulfilling his last wish to have gone to the moon.  

The gameplay in To the Moon is virtually non-existent; while you do control the characters’ movements, the game is, essentially, on rails, sans occasional simple puzzles.  The graphics are sprite-based pixel graphics very familiar to gamers of the 90’s.  They are conventional and utilitarian, but not stylized or impactful.

So, the gameplay and visual elements aren’t fantastic, but what about the story?  Well, that is certainly the highlight of this game.  Without spoiling, the story is pretty interesting and effective and keeps you engaged.  There’s some good characterization and some interesting observations.  

This is a difficult game to “rate” - I’m sure that there will be people who really like this game, and I think it is to be lauded for its original story and scrappy origin of development.  Judging it for what it is - a very small indie game that takes 3.3 hours to play, it’s fine.  The biggest glaring flaw with it for me is that it just doesn’t need to be a video game.  The creator took the tools at their disposal to create a game that told their story, but really, this doesn’t need to be a video game, or gain anything from being a video game.  You could imagine the entire game played by a bot and just watching it, but in that case, it’s a mediocre movie.  Elements unique to gaming (chance, choice & agency, etc…) are just missing here, so it’s hard to feel like it is a good game to me.  But also, I mean, it’s a game that costs a dollar!  

If you’re in the mood for an interesting story and a very casual and short gaming experience, check it out!  I have not played the successors of this game, but I feel that if they incorporate more gaming elements and continue developing interesting and original ideas they could be could, and that their future is certainly worth paying attention to.

[b]Recommend?:[/b] No
[b]Rating/10:[/b] 4
[b]Value @ $25 (estimate)?[/b] 3.3 hour/dollar (excellent)
[b]Hours played for review:[/b] 3.3

review_text:
TL;DR for lazy people: Boring, confusing, horrible stealth mechanics. Decent story.

This game sounded a whole lot better on paper than it is in practice. You're a creepy mute kid who is apparently the son of Lucifer and you have to kill everybody in your house so your father can have souls, using diverse methods to knock off your targets one by one while making it look like an accident.

Unfortunately, finding how to do it is a hassle, there's only one way to kill each target and it's not always obvious. there are few clues and if some of them are usually simple and clear, you never know where to find the item, you have to search a huge, confusing manner to find said item and use it. Even after you found the thing, it's not always clear where and how you're supposed to use it. This game doesn't hold you by the hand.

Despite those problems, the game is rather interesting to follow as some drama starts because everybody's stumped and the detective in charge has no idea how all these deaths happen. But then comes ... The Betrayal. The one chapter that manages to ruin what little fun this game managed to offer. You have to cause a power outage so you can sneak around to get in the garage, which is on the ground floor, on the absolute opposite of your starting point. Here, you have to contend with locked doors and horrible stealth mechanics that barely work coherently. you can't see a thing but you don't dare use the flashlight in case this game actually makes you easier to spot when your light's on. All you do is try just about every door in the frickin' house while avoiding the adults patrolling with flashlight for no obvious reasons while your remaining satanic powers are drained because you manage to get spotted by someone who's at the far opposite of you in the corridor or by people you couldn't see or hear and open the exact same door you were planning to open.

This, this is what killed the game, that was barely alive in the first place. It'll probably end up being one of those curios I bought for a buck that I'll never finish, let alone re-install and that's too bad 'cause I'm rather curious about how the story ends. Oh well.

Some early bosses have insane super armor and dodge/spam grabs (looking at you Kugihara, Ogita). It would be fine if the blocking issue wasn't still present, or the fact grabbing is butchered cuz they time out 2x as fast (which ruins Shinada's combat), ON TOP of all of this? for some goddamn reason, the training masters can just PARRY YOU FOR EVEN DARING TO BREATHE IN THEIR GENERAL DIRECTION. Standing completely still? Fuck you, parry. The Komaki parry is so broken on Sosuke that he will just drag you through dimensions to parry you for breathing. Ayanokoji too with his insta tonfa tiger drops. Not to mention all the physics based games they broke due to physics being tied to FPS (same issue as every single remastered in the collection).
