review_text:
The game takes place in your family's mansion as you explore it for particular tools and interact with particular items in particular ways to kill unsuspecting people working in your house. The idea is pretty cool and the deaths are so ridiculous that it's almost like a horror/comedy game. That being said, the game feels like such a chore. You have to explore this huge mansion to find the particular tool and interact with the particular item to kill your particular target. This isn't really open world like Hitman with multiple ways to off your targets or you can do things in the order you want. Everything is really rigid and with little to no clues, you'll find yourself running around aimlessly looking for things to interact with.

As a result, I would say to avoid this game. Even with the interesting concept of being the devil's child who has to kill people, it's just so tedious. There's too much exploration with no benefit to it other than running around aimlessly until you happen to find a random tool and interact with the random, correct item to kill your targets. The only enjoyable part is watching the ridiculous ways people die but you'd be better off watching a YouTube video showing all the deaths than going through the actual game.

I've been a fan of Hakuoki for years (let's not say how many, LOL), and when they announced a 'reboot' of sorts, I was curious. Why fix something that wasn't broken? But now that I've played a few routes, I see that this isn't a fix, per se, but an expansion. The story line I'm so familiar with is still here, but with more details and more characters to get to know. I liked Shinpachi's route, and I enjoyed Sanan's route more than I thought I would. (Would it be cliche to say he's complicated?) I'm still going through the new routes, but I'm really enjoying myself. It's the same world, but it's bigger now. Later on I'll play the original routes to see if they've changed much, but even if they haven't, I wouldn't mind. I have no regrets seeing my bois again. Even the occasional typo or translation boo-boo isn't enough to dampen the fun.

I know the series since 2003. This is an excellent game, with an interesting story, beautiful landscapes and town hubs, enhanced by a stellar production team and incredible visual effects (for that time circa 2006) - - all of this, includes a dynamic and fast-paced combat system (one of the very best combat system I've seen up to now). 1) The voice acting goes from ''well done'' to ''just ok'' - (not impressive), and most of the time quite annoying. You can feel that the voice actors really did their best to incarnate the characters. The producers really chose sharp and high-pitched annoying voices.

You will see cutscenes at the main plaza, in the streets, at the Guild Hideout, when you interact with new characters and after bosses.

3) The dungeons get extremely repetitive ; there are only 5 distinguishable ''themed zones'' in the entire game. If I recall properly, in Volume 1, you have the Green Landscape / The Waterfall Caverns/ The Desert. Later on in Volume 2 and 3 you get access to the Desert zone and the Network zone. Yep - - that's it. Even .Hack/IMOQ had 8 zones all together.

4) Clearing the dungeons to 100% is an excruciating chore - - the distance between enemy groups is significant - in order to fully kill all the enemies in a dungeon (about 15 to 17 encounters, it will take you 45 mins to 1 hour, all depending on the circumstances and your strength level) - - And that's when you actually speed up your movement with spells and items.

review_text:
So! Get To The Orange Door just obtained a massive update and so I'm going to write a review for the game. I'll go over what I liked and what I didn't like.

Like: 

Everything great and fantastic about the previous version of the game (which is still accessible - Thanks, Andrew!), has been tweaked, reworked and incidentally - vastly improved. Controls are much more fluid and responsive, the shooting feels fantastic and the levels went from great to [i]Legendary[/i]. Honestly, if this was it, I'd recommend that the Developer raise his price or he'd be giving money away.

For bosses, I haven't run into the Legion Sentinel yet, but the Blade Sentinel has become an actual challenge, with a real boss arena that rewards outmaneuvering him as well as outgunning him. Since the previous arena was a couple of raised platforms, this is a major improvement and I'm excited to see where he goes for boss fights next!

Last, and certainly not least, the removal of the platforming sections at the start of every run. Normally, first person platforming doesn't bother me in the least, but I always managed to trigger some bug or cause an issue with the movement that made completing the segment either harder than it should've been, or outright impossible thanks to a bug that was impossible to fix.

Dislike:

The main draw of this update is the dungeons and...they're very basic. It's basically a railroad of the same set of rooms arranged randomly. Mostly, it's combat encounters that you clear, then move to the next area. This wouldn't be too bad, if not for two things that make compound to make this problem worse than it should be.

The first is that the game's difficulty has spiked considerably. This is both to due with the enemy's improved AI over the last version, but also to do with the Player's capabilities being reduced to make room for the Meta Progression System.

The second is that the Dungeon's are the fastest and most efficient way to obtain Jade Vines, the currency required to progress through the Meta Progression System. Which means that, if normal runs are giving you trouble and are nearly unbeatable, you wind up, as I did, grinding dungeons for several hours until you've progressed to the point where you've got a couple of extra lives, starting bits, etc...which means you're traversing the same set of 3-4 rooms with combat encounters for [i]hours[/i] just to be able to attempt a normal run. Considering that these rooms are not nearly the same quality as the massively reworked levels of the main runs, this...is not a good thing.

Also, I dislike dual-wielding. Not the concept, but the implementation. For your guns, you click the left mouse button to shoot the gun in your left hand and the right mouse button to shoot the button in your right hand. Now, in a controller, I imagine it feels a lot more natural, but on a Mouse and Keyboard, it just felt awkward. Also, when you reload your guns, you briefly hold onto the first gun with both hands for a second and then reload the second...and then briefly hold onto the second gun for a second before slowly bringing up the first gun. Kind of unnecessarily slows down dual-wielding's combat.

Fixes: I don't want to just cry and say 'these things are bad' because, while I dislike them, they aren't game breaking and, if the developer would care to listen, here's some fixes I think may alleviate the problems.

For the Dungeons, I think you want to focus on the two problems that compound. Number 1 is varying up the dungeon rooms, which I'm sure was going to be done anyway. I would like to see more than one exit to every room (similar to Hades) so that a bit of player choice is preserved.

Also, the difficulty I believe should be re-balanced to allow those who aren't godlike at shooters a chance to complete normal runs without feeling pressured to grind several hours of dungeons first. I understand this is already being done, so please take this as a word of encouragement.

Finally, for dual-wielding (specifically semi-autos), as much as it's cool to be able to fire one gun for a bit, then fire another gun, or fire both at the same time, I think expediency and automation would be a fine trade for a little bit of player expression: While dual-wielding semi-auto firearms, have the main firing mode be firing them one at a time, then have the secondary fire-mode be shooting them simultaneously.

For automatic firearms, I don't think any change is necessary, or if you have an auto in one hand and a semi in the other. Just while dual-wielding semi-autos. Also, please adjust the reload animations. Thank you!

Conclusion:

Get to the Orange Door just received a massive (and I do mean massive) upgrade in sheer quality. Buy this game. Play this game. It is a [i]bargain[/i] and well worth the money! I'd even call it a steal! Yes, I had some problems with the game, but what bothered me may not bother you and what bothered me the most is actively being worked on and will likely be patched soon!

This game is going to be legendary.

[h1] Tldr; Mediocre controls slapped on an otherwise great story with dull protagonists who won't shut up. [/h1] 

I was baited by the "overwhelmingly positive" reviews on Steam and it needs to be acknowledged that the story is emotional and deserves all the praise. But that's about the only positive this game has. Despite being a story-driven game, it's not justified if the game play is clunky and if the protagonists (that have 80% of dialogue) keep interrupting an otherwise smooth immersion into a heart-gripping tale. 

The puzzles are repetitive and get monotonous rather quickly as little is to be achieved from tile-inverting minigames. The pixel graphics may be good to look at, but with invisible barriers everywhere, it's a dumb click-fest just to get your character to move where he/she needs to so the story can progress. 

The protagonists are apathetic and constantly taking a jibe at the journey of the man whose dream they are supposed to be fulfilling which defeats the whole purpose of the story. The music is decent but the negatives of this game outweigh the positives which makes it impossible to recommend that someone pay money for this lackluster excuse of a video game. If you want to buy, make sure you pick it up during a sale, full price is undeserved. 

I may be in the minority in not recommending this game; I have no hesitation in paying for a 5-hour game focusing on a good story but if I had to drag myself just to get to the end and if the game itself feels like a chore, the payoff is not worth anyone's money or time no matter how good the story is.

If it were a movie (and the structure of Calisto Protocol uses cinematic narratives, aesthetics, and techniques), I would say it's a mediocre but entertaining product that becomes a bit repetitive towards the end and fully abandons the theme of the main character's personality breakdown as it approaches the end credits. I would also say that it is a slightly sloppy, spiritual successor to Dead Space with some great moments and ideas. If it were a movie, I would recommend it because I would recommend entertainment where you can turn off your brain and forgive a few things. But a movie doesn't make you watch for 14 hours and then not save your progress because of a bug. A movie doesn't make you play 3 hours of DLC and then not save your progress. A movie doesn't complicate your journey with a mediocre experience by throwing bugs at you that remind you that you're wasting your time.

review_text:
Lost Ruins is an excellent metroidvania, side scroller game.  Now this is the part where I talk about the story a little bit, but this is one of those games that talking about the story may spoil it for you so I'll just say it's about a young girl who has been teleported into a strange castle.

Okay then the likes, the story is really good at first I thought it was your simple stop the bad guy story but had plenty of twists and turns and well-written characters that just made the story phenomenal, especially when you play the game a second time and everything in the story just seems to click together.

The gameplay is really good it has a bit of a Dark Souls like feel to it, but with metroidvania-styled gameplay, it's tough but fair and when you die it is mostly your fault. It also has a nice balance of weapons and spells you can play with, you can also customize your character with different items to give them more strength or more durability or certain abilities. The weapons and spells are really good each one with their own unique look and power, some weapons and spells are better than others so this game gives incentive to mix and match to figure out which character build works for you. 

The pixel graphics are really beautiful, very well done with plenty of detail and nice little touches to it, I also love the character portraits it has a nice anime feel to it. The levels in the game are really good quite diverse with plenty of interesting locations to look at and explore, like a sewer to a castle to even a crypt, all of it well designed that makes you want to stop and stare at certain places in the level.

The characters are really good very well written even NPC characters with little dialogue are quite interesting. I really like the main character because she's generally a very nice, very caring and considerate person, I also like this demon Merchant she's also really cool character and generally very sweet and caring, also I really like this Dragon maid she's super adorable looking.

The enemies and bosses are really good each one with their own unique design and skill that keeps you on your toes, especially when playing a more harder difficulties. The music is really good with plenty of great tracks to listen to, that fits the game really well especially at the last level.

The game also has quests by certain characters you meet which can give you better weapons or access to areas you couldn't get to before. Now the best things in the game is the multiple endings and different modes to play, basically after you beat the game for the first time you are given different modes like which mode, assassin mode and boss mode both the witch and assassin mode basically makes you play with a certain type of build. While boss mode where you get to play as three bosses you defeated and in that mode we get a completely different story which I found it quite good especially with the interactions of the three bosses. There's also different endings in the game which encourages you to play the game multiple times to get everything.

There's also plenty of great references not just to other video games, but to anime and manga like in one scene it makes references to paper RPGs and berserk. The notes in this game I absolutely love as you know I like notes in video games as it can help build a story and these notes are very good they help build the world; these notes give insight to different characters and the villain of the game.

Okay then the dislikes, alright there is not really anything to dislike about this game, okay there are some things but really they're just so small compared to how great the game is, but here are just some small complaints I have.The platforming can be a little bit frustrating sometimes like you could miss a platform after jumpping even though you were very close to it the platform. The final boss is a bit of a letdown I mean don't get me wrong the final boss has a cool design and she can be a bit tough, but I thought she'd have a second form like all the other bosses but no she doesn't even, not even on more harder difficulties she's still the same, like I said I found that to be a bit underwhelming and a little bit of a letdown.

[spoiler] Also for the ending to boss mode while I did enjoy the ending I felt like the third boss that insect girl I feel like she needed a better ending like she gets to go with the other two bosses back to their old world.[/spoiler] I also wish the game had some DLC to buy because I think it would do really well to have a soundtrack, pc wallpaper and art book for the game especially pc wallpaper.

Alright now that I told you all this stuff, Lost Ruins is an excellent metroidvania, side scroller game. With a really good story, really good gameplay and really good characters and just so much more to love so I highly recommend this game if you like metroidvania games I recommend this game to you.

review_text:
This game is a ripoff, don't buy it, don't waste your money on it. On the outside the game looks great, they make it seem like an involving immersive adventure but I promise you its far from that. On the inside the game is horrible, most updates just make current bugs and issues even worse. All the assets in game are free assets, none of them are custom-made by any of the developers. This game isnt worth 20 dollars, it isnt even worth 5. Its very laggy, glitchy and the community is overwhelmingly toxic. 

I found a comment on here that perfectly explains alot of the games issues within the game itself. It goes as follows: 

Cons:
-There isn't an in-game map to help navigate the damn place. No set migration routes for herbivores to follow, no ways to truly mark out different territories that has been "claimed" to either encourage people to stay away from the place or find the alpha and fight for it.
-If you are trying to hide/blend into the foliage? There is a chance it's not there for players that have taken their graphics to a lower spec for performance, So you're just a dumbass standing out in the open to them.
- The servers are practically empty. No one is playing this game/the advertisement sucks so people don't even know about it.
-Better get used to lions, because that's all most people are. There is no limitation to how/when/who becomes a lion so they are overrunning the place. There's no sense of balance whatsoever which leads to:
-A review on here says it's an eat/drink/die sim. They are correct, there aren't any goals. Zero game play. Nothing to achieve, nothing to help shape experiences or build interest on. Hell, most people don't role-play out a basic ass child's game of "house" or "family" or any sort of pride/herd/group dynamic to make the game interesting.
-A review on here says it's irritating because people just want to sit around and talk. They are also correct. I spent time with a group for over an hour before I realized that we weren't just sitting around waiting for an admin to help out players or take care of problem players/server rule breakers. They were in a VC and just forgot to tell everyone else.
- The game is laggy, and buggy and I still haven't found out why. Animals clip through the rocks, but you can't see through the damn leaves if you're playing as a giraffe and get to close to a tree. You can be starving to death, or dying of dehydration but your button to eat/drink just refuses to work. Running with a herd -- or hell just a single other person playing the same species? Better get used to them jumping back and forth because the lag doesn't seem to know where they are either. That leopard over there? Yeah it looks weird because for some reason the body of it is vertical instead of horizontal. Game is a mess.

Please dont buy this game. Most of the time updates are missing information, or are completely wrong. There is so many reasons to NOT buy this game. Dont waste your time with this. I wish I could get a refund still.

THIS IS THE HOCKEY GAME YOU WANT. First off, stop holding your breath on waiting for EA to release an NHL hockey game on PC. It's been 7 years now and it's just not going to happen. 

Download this game play a round (it will create folders for mods), then exit. Then go into discussions and find Walt Jr's Legs comment on his mod and link and you can then play all the current teams, a few classics and all the current roster of players for 24-25 season. Walt has clear instructions on how to install the mods on his link to Nexus mods.

The mods are REALLY top notch. All the team logos and colors are spot on. 

The only thing this game is missing is a full season mode with custom teams and a full 82 games. It has a mini season mode with like 6 games, but I need more! 

Oh, and I'm playing on an Asus Ally ROG.  The cheapest model, and the game is flawless.

Probably pointless to write a review at this point but it's a hobby lol so .Hack//G.U. Last Recode is a game that has a heck of a lot going for it but is let down by certain aspects such as certain level designs and pacing along with a lot of side stuff that just takes too long that isn't rewarding enough and yet I still put it as a buy so I'm sure you're wondering why dood?

The game is split into 3 main volumes and a fourth extra volume that ties everything up nicely, the reason I say it's worth it is all that side stuff? you don't reaaally need to do, sure some of it can net you some genuinely nice perks, one that in particular will help with a post game dungeon at the end of chapter 3 no less, otherwise you can really just play the game and beat it dood.

review_text:
It is genuinely hard to describe how little there is to do in New Genesis. Anything I could say will sound like I'm leaving half of the things out. I'll instead make the statement that there is pretty much nothing meaningful you can do that doesn't just loop back into the cosmetics and social chat-room play style. You will be provided gear that is good enough for anything. You will be boosted to the max level through the story. There are the cocoons of course, but those are one-and-done. Once you're powerful, there's nothing to use this power on. There's nothing to fight. Duel quests are maybe the exception, they can give you a source of income, but then the only purpose of this income is to just buy things from other players to dress up your character with.

PSO2 is a completely different story and one of my favorite games of all time. My playtime on steam is less than half of my total playtime, as I played on the Microsoft Store when it was exclusive to that. I would barely recommend that, and if this game looks like it really interests you, go for it. Play the original. The character I've made in PSO2 I haven't changed the design of since before NGS came out, making the purely fashion-themed NGS worthless to me. 

Finally, if you are literally Just looking for a social chatroom and fashion game, I don't really think you'll find a better one than NGS, but they're very predatory with their microtransactions. Most interesting and desirable items are going to come from Scratch Tickets, which are exactly what they sound like. They're just lootboxes, and they cost a significant chunk of money per roll. You can buy these items from other players with the free currency in game, and it's honestly not an impossible task. You can certainly earn enough of the currency to make likely one outfit you really like, though it will be a considerable amount of work, meaning it'd give you something to do in the game. Of course, the best way to get this currency is through buying your own scratch tickets and selling the items, though...

review_text:
TLDR; A game that may be worth keeping an eye on, worth buying for £30 or £40 but requires improvement to become and stay competitive.

It sort of reminds me of early BF4, it has to look like arse (ass for those across the pond) in order to run, plays like arse at times, has it's own bug infestation (ironically), and has a couple of crappy game mechanics; namely the company system (more on this later), yet has a good game design at its core as well as a great sound (bar a couple of bugs) to it, and most importantly massive potential. 

Looks wise, it is decent. Higher resolutions and high settings will cause serious performance issues (even the NASA computer kids on reddit have problems), yet it still looks decent enough (and is immersive enough) on the necessary settings (namely 2560-1440 res, ultra performance balancing, low everything bar medium texture) that it doesn't cause me any major issues for long-term game enjoyment. 

Play wise it works well overall, there are some bugs that may cause a slight freeze (although I suspect it is more performance issues than anything, especially when the flammenwerfer comes out to play), sometimes the sound can bug out when rapid firing HMG emplacements, and there is the occasional crashing to menu/desktop. yet to be fair these are fairly rare (past dozen or so games it crashed once at the end of a performance intensive match). Overall it is great to play, especially due to the seemingly innovative and very fun decision to not despawn bodies and add physics and mass to them, filling a corridor at the end of a 10 wave horde fight is incredibly fun, especially in urban maps.

It's biggest issue by far though is the company system. It's (as others have pointed out) obviously a clone of the helldivers system, the issue is that unless you start your own company (and have 30 mates willing to play it with you at set times) you will likely have problems with it. Either because they (a company) don't want new players (level up is reasonably fast but shouldn't make a difference), are holding a spot for somebody else, can't be bothered to deal with sorting through join requests, or just simply aren't active. Whilst it doesn't stop you from playing, it does look as though there are certain rewards (and possibly a storyline of sorts) that you can't obtain. 

Personally I would have said the best way forwards was to scrap the need for being in a company (have it like Holdfast's and most other games clan/regiment systems (even war thunder has it's squadrons reasonably sorted on issues like this)), and have it so there is an overarching series of grand campaigns (as with Helldivers) you can join, either as a squad (of up to 25 people), regiment (of up to 50), battalion (of up to 100), or a division (up to 200), with the opportunity for larger armies if someone really cares enough to try and herd a playerbase like that (personally I would rather herd cats). Have it so players can either join a group on a more permenant basis or simply play with random squads/groups rather than having to group up. It could be fun to have an overarching campaign where players actions (especially the larger groups) influence the outcome and state of the galaxy as a whole, win or lose like in old (I won't touch the new with a barge-pole) BF2.  

Overall it is a fun game to play, I wouldn't pay more than forty quid, but I suspect (or hope perhaps) that it is going to be a game that sees some very interesting development. Should they go down the line of overarching opt in or out large scale campaigns/events, bug squashing, concept optimisation, and NON-DLC weapons and kit development this has some good potential, so long as the developers don't simply use it as a cash-cow. It seems like a bit of a labour of love (at its core at least) and like I said, is very reminiscent of early BF4 in that it has a rough-ish start but could skyrocket to become a much loved classic, definitely worth watching for now.

review_text:
It's not a bad game, but it's not a good game either.

Vehicle controls are floaty and imprecise, especially aerial vehicles, since the dumbed down mouse movements for the helicopters cause oversteer, and planes are really stiff.

That brings me to the vehicle weaponry.
Most weapons seem identical across categories, for example, the cannons across all vehicles, be it light tank or artillery truck, feel identical, with a comically fast reload rate. It makes everything feel the same, especially when the life-span of vehicles are about 10 seconds, which is extremely frustrating.
You also have the issue of the third-person camera's aim being offset, so if you don't have the target in the crosshair, the round might just miss by a mile. This is especially noticeable with the Anti-Air vehicle, which doesn't seem to be specialised at all. Restrictive elevation on the guns, low fire-rate (the same cannons as the tanks I believe, but 2), and compounded by the aiming issue mentioned, hitting enemy jets is nigh impossible. Helicopters, sure, about as easy as with a normal tank.

Physics bugs in vehicles are common in my experience. I can drive the artillery truck, and shake violently for a second and lose half the vehicle's durability for no discernible reason. I can also try to take off with a helicopter and just combust, immediately dying. 

There's no localised damage on vehicles on a broader scale, so if your landing gear touches the ground a little hard your entire plane explodes, sending you to the shadow realm. In a game solely about chaos, you'd hope the aspects relating to chaotic environments would be polished.

Finishing off vehicles, their designs. They have slowly devolved to becoming more bland and futuristic. Many military vehicles are smooth kludges, with boring paint schemes (grey base and red stripes). Resistance vehicles on the other hand are on the opposite side of the spectrum, they're excessively garish. Green base with neon pinks, yellows and blues, no cool-factor, just a visual south-pole.

From vehicles to weapons, they are in a similar place to the vehicles'. 
Samey from gun to gun, with uninterestingly vague designs, and restrictive ammunition capacity for the amount of enemies you're going to undoubtedly face. 
Most weapons now have a secondary fire, which is nice, but sometimes very unfitting. The sniper rifle for example has a homing missile attached to the foregrip. That makes me sad. 
There are no pistols in this game, probably due to the fact that aiming is now optional. There's little point in shooting people, since a new group of 4 are going to show up in 2 seconds afterwards. Ideally you would find a tank and just shoot wherever until it catches fire 5 seconds later.

It just feels like gunplay has been demoted massively. Little to no reward for using them in anything but emergencies, similar guns apart from the extreme outliers, poor accuracy on automatic weapons, poor ammunition stocks, and overall to arcadey a feel to them.

Stationary guns are also frustrating. Very boring designs once again, indestructible, so if you have to stay around and area to do an objective, you bet your sweet gourd enemies will not leave it alone, ragdolling you every other breath while dealing with infinite helicopters, tanks and planes from the enemies. Restrictive fire-arcs once again, making them hard to use as the player.
And worst of all, "mortars", both as stationary weapons and on vehicles, are missile launchers. Homing missile launchers? How do you get it so wrong? It would be wonderful to have an indirect fire weapon, but it requires line of sight, and automatically locks on to whatever, so it's about as challenging to use as your lungs. 

Many weapon attacks are also choreographed, so you will see where an enemy helicopter is about to launch a missile. Is this a 3d bullet-hell game? What's the point, it's so stiff in practise. Besides, it doesn't really matter that they signal where they're shooting, because you will be hit by random explosions every 5th heartbeat anyway.


I think I've vented enough about that now, on to the player tools.
The parachute is as reliable as ever, no real complaints there.
The wingsuit is trickier to make a verdict on though. Out of every arcade-like aspect in the game, the wingsuit feel the least so. It is punishing with your airspeed, being sluggier than a snail to control when you're not at max speed. It's hard to describe, but turning feels like you're rotating inside a tincan inside a BINGO-tumbler. It's hard to be precise when you're rolling around like a marble. 
Grappling while wingsuiting is also a science, as quite often you will just reel into the ground, despite being parallel and trying to pitch up at the same time.

The grappling hook is very fancy, with a lot of toys and functions. It's excessive for me, because they're hard to use reliably in combat with the weird input delay sometimes, hangups, etc., but I appreciate that you have a lot of options. We like that.

There is sometimes noticable delay or lack of response when quickly switching from wingsuit or parachute to grappling for speed versus trying to stop wingsuiting/parachuting. Sometimes it just doesn't respond, and you reel straight into a wall while going mach, which ragdolls you, and probably sets you up to be rocketed/cannoned by the mosquito-like enemy presence.

Graphically the game looks nice, but it lacks vibrancy, and has what I can only describe as a brown filter over it.

The world feels pretty sparse despite being so big. I have a hard time finding unique details, since most towns seem to be the same church in the centre, and the same few houses scattered about. I'm probably generalising, but it's hard to look for details when there's no reason to visit the towns. There are no stores, very few interactions you can make with the surroundings there, no collectibles I've noticed, so I just fly over them. The few times I'm in towns, I'm probably crashing into the ground trying to do a wingsuit stunt, or picking up vehicle A to drive into checkpoint B (which are right next to each other)
With a map so large and towns so uninteresting, it kinda forces you to fly everywhere if you're not just in it for the chill vibes of a driving simulator. Most cars do feel like hotwheels though, being so zippy and slidey they're hard to control, but I guess there's a demographic for that.

Missed oppurtunity?
The ocean is vast, and lakes are plenty, but boats don't really serve a purpose when you have all the tools at your fingertips to completely ignore them. I really like boats, ships, barges and ferries, and their arsenals and functionality has only improved in this game, yet there's no real use for them?
I can get into a zippy speedboat to cross a lake, or I could fly along the coast in my wingsuit and get there before I find or deliver a boat.
I could stage a beach assault with a tank on a gorgeous landing craft, but I have to slowly get out of the landing craft as I beach it to jump into the tank, because It's singleplayer.

From map to map challenges. 
This is a really big problem for me, as there are hundreds, or what it feels like, thousands of micro challenges all over the map, which is what you have to complete to seemingly finish an area?
What are these challenges? 
Jump of a cliff/building/smokestack and fly through 3 checkpoints with your wingsuit.
Find a vehicle of a certain type and drive 15 meters to a checkpoint (they have static spawns of the exact vehicle you need very close to the goal)
And rarely, something that forces you to activate your single neuron. I had one challenge where I had to grapple an ATV up to closed off bridge. Kinda fun!
Another where I had to destroy some glass blocking my flight-path, also more fun!
But those are rare, and you seldom have to think at all to do theses supposed challenges, which makes them as menial as laundry, in a piece of interactive entertainment about chaos.

2 mny wrds, goot bye

review_text:
This is a tricky one. As a Jet Set Radio Future obsessive, and later, Jet Set Radio, (the two left-field rollerblading, spraying, future-grinding games that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a direct homage to), I put off playing this for a bit. The possibility of disappointment was too great! But turns out this is a super fun game that kept me plugged in, and not just because of mis-placed nostalgia. That said, it has a high bar to live up to, and I don't think it quite clears it.

The start of this game is a goddamn slog. The game *does* have fun characters, but they sure aren't around at the start. The starting areas are drab and the cut-scenes are SLOW. The music hadn't grown on me at this stage, and I was pretty mad that they didn't just get 2 Mello (absolutely jammin' JSR-style music producer) to do the whole soundtrack. And skateboards? This is a goofy game, and having "cool" skateboards and bikes (with no futuristic add-ons) is jarring. For the first couple of hours I was having a pretty grumpy - but not terrible - time. I was sure that it was going to be nostalgia that pulled me through.

Then, not too far in, the game opened up, I'm unlocking tags, new areas, and hooking together combos like nobody's business. There are improvements in this game! The tag system is great. The flip-phone map and camera system is GENIUS. The cut-scenes are still boring, but you get to meet a claustrophobic masochist, who is always in tight spaces having a terribly good time. The police enemies are annoying (on brand for JSR). The main thing is that the flow is gooooood. I maintain that some of the level design is very poor, with some unlockables requiring specific backtracking or annoying hidden access points, but if you find yourself going for the unlockables and achievements that require combos, you will be in for a treat as you start to flow through the large levels. The soundtrack grew on me, and I have the soundtrack LP on order...

Overall, an incredible achievement. The team put this together with a lot of love, and without a big budget. Nailing the look, getting the soundtrack together, the tags, the amount of characters... an absolute lifetime achievement. It's not perfect, but I'll be damned if I would give this a thumbs down - if only because I want Bomb Rush Cyberfunk Future so badly! Get this, and get the Jet Set Radio remaster, and fall in love with a absolutely unique vibe.

Doesn't everybody dream about being an unholy terror that is above suspicion? No? Just me? Oh dear.

When I first tried this game years ago, I hated it. I wanted to carelessly run about the house causing mayhem and destruction. Sadly, this is not how the game is intended to be played. 

While there is still mayhem and destruction, it is more structured and stealthy. It made sense the more I thought about it. How else am I supposed to kill an entire mansion full of people if they already know I'm the son of Satan? By slowly picking them off one by one and driving them mad of course! 

I found much more enjoyment in the game this way. Sure, hamfisted homicidal tomfoolery has its perks. But there was a sophistication to combining common household items with a bit of telekiwhatsit powers to make things spicy. Thumbs up!

This game is the masterpiece of the series. The other two are a bit lacking compared to this one, but those are different reviews that I'll write later. :P 

I recommend purchasing the entire bundle on sale, since it's an older game.

review_text:
Updated 2020/09/30:

As usual. I'll start my review with TL;DR: Playing Shadow Tactics: Blade of the Shogun (ST for short) is like playing Mahjong Solitaire. In most levels there are a lot of guards between you and your objective. But you have to peel off the guards layer by layer or else you'll trigger an alarm. However, when playing ST you'll spend about 60~80% of your time just wresting with the control. Considering this game was released in 2016, [b]personally, I wouldn't spend more than 20 dollars on it. 25 tops[/b]. But if money ain't too tight, the art is indeed pretty good. It's just the control that's atrocious. Now I'll get in depth a little.

pros:
[list]
    [*]The core mechanics is kind of solid. Stealth and strategy was implemented in a really fun way. There are various NPC that have different types of behavior. And you have various characters each have their own unique flavor of abilities. creating various challenges where you have to figure out how to outsmart the enemy to achieve your goal.
    [*]Japanese voice acting created a really atmospheric environment. (provided that you choose the Japanese audio option, with English subtitles for those who don't speak Japanese)
    [*]The art is really flavorful. Both the graphics and the soundtracks are superb. Easily one of the top 10 I've seen in a decade.
    [*]Various in game challenges add a lot of replay value for those completionist.
    [*]The game features a quicksave and quickload system, one of the game's saving grace. The other being the art.
[/list]
cons:
[list]
    [*]There are a lot of in game dialogues and cutscenes which took place while the game is still in progress. Which makes it a lot harder to follow while you're trying to focus on playing the game. And that's one of my major complaints that loses the game some major point on the story department.
    [*]The game features a perspective camera at a 45° angle. While 45° angle camera shows off the game's many beautiful scenery, it's a poor choice for a tactical games. In some situation you'll end up with multiple transition or action point at the same area, and if you're so much as miss click by one pixel when issuing a command, all of a sudden your unit will charge up the hill and ended your game.
    [*]Lacks of proper pathing AI. This compounded on top of the previous camera problem. The game features a transition method where as if you want to move your character to the roof, up the ladder, into river, etc then you have to click on the transition point then the character will go interact with that transition point and transfer onto the new area. The problem is you'll have to basically hold your character's hand the entire time from one transition point to the next all the way to the next safe area. Which felt like you're babysitting your character and could get really tedious.
    [*]Enemy AI is sporadic at times. Certain NPC will for no reason go off script and does something it's not suppose to do. Even friendly NPC like Kuma will suddenly behave differently or crash entirely. Which happened to me once and I have to reload the last check point to fix it. Quite frankly speaking, without a quicksave/quickload system, this game would be completely unplayable.
    [*]The game lacks dedicated pause button. Which for a strategy game like this one is kind of a must have. There is a shadow mode that was executed weirdly in which you can [b]hold[/b] a command per character and tell them to execute simultaneously. However, it in practice when you have to enter shadow mode and issue a command, it is awkward that you need to enter shadow mode again to issue another command; what it should have done instead is to program it so that when you enter shadow mode you can issue multiple commands to multiple character sequentially and then exit shadow mode to execute simultaneously. On top of that, shadow mode doesn't freeze enemy in place so when you've finished setting the command the enemy NPC may not be in position for the command to function properly.
    [*]The game lacks a command queue to show what command it has registered. Again, something that would have worked really well for a strategy game like this one is the command queue which makes it that much clearer whether or not a command has been accepted. i.e: if I tell character A to do this to NPC X. Pause the game and show that in a queue so that I know that command has been accepted. Then I can move on to character B and figure out what to do with it.
    [*]The game imposes arbitrary and nonsensical restrictions on player to lengthen game time. Just to be clear, these restriction does not make the game harder or challenging, it's just makes more time consuming and tedious. One of the weird restriction is that Mugen can't not drop a body downwards. This is more prominent to me during mission 9 when one of the challenge requires you to hide all the bodies and you'll want to use Mugen as much as you can for it because he is the fastest character when carrying bodies and he can carry two instead of 1 for your three ninja unit.

    And then there's some weird AI detection restriction. In ST one of your ninja unit can disguise herself to fool the enemy, on the other hand there is also a unit that can see through the disguises so challenge you to path around the detector enemy. However, some of the later level features a snowy scene and character walking over snow will leave some footprints for a few seconds. What puzzles me is that the detector can somehow differentiates between friendly AI's footprints and your footprints, a setting which adds some arbitrary challenges that also makes no sense whatsoever.

   The most annoying of which involves the controllable raccoon Kuma. You can control a pet raccooon via another character. The weird thing is they impose a range restriction so that you can not placed Kuma too far from the raccoon owner. This is such a meaningless restriction that I'm sure on paper sounds like it adds more challenges but in reality, for me it only makes controlling Kuma more tedious. Because I figured out that you can interrupt Kuma when it moves by issuing a distract command. So late game I have to constantly move the character into position to move Kuma, then move the character back to stay out of view, then slowly lure the enemy guards away from their post to clear them one small group at a time. Which really, really isn't challenging for me, it's just wasted a lot of my time.
    [*]Enemy AI does not remove corpse upon discovery nor do they stay alert after discovering dead bodies. These are some of the questionable enemy AI behavior that breaks this game as a stealth game. Personally, and I can't believe I'm saying this, I prefer Hitman 2's AI behavior in which enemy AI will remove bodies. And in ST, since the game spawn a team of guard when they go into alert, it's possible to have it keep spawning enemy AI which creates more dead bodies and creates unnecessary burden on your computer.
    [*]Some of the level design were questionable. Especially the later level where the game gives you sparse disposing location, not even into river or down a mountain for no reason. It sucks.
[/list]

If you're still reading at this point, let me end with this for the time being. [h1]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/h1] is by no means a bad game. But there are major problems here and there that hinders the game from achieving true potential. TBH, I'm kind of hoping that I wouldn't have to downvote this game but then I asked myself if this game have zero story element (because it's hard for me to follow the story while trying to stealth around enemy) then would I still pay 44 CAD for this game? And the answer is a no for me. But if money isn't too tight and/or you don't mind struggle with the control a bit, because the game is really pretty, or you find this game on sale, like 20 CAD total kind of sale. Then give it a go. Otherwise, stay away from this game.

review_text:
With hundreds of hours in the game from 2017-current, this is the best form the game has been in and it continues on an upward trajectory.  The lead devs have been very active in both public discord and private conversations.  Through my interactions with them, I fully trust that they can move RHL from early access to full launch without straying from their mission and with Gearbox behind them as the publisher, I am not concerned about them wavering on their ethical monetization principles.

Gameplay is fun, builds are diverse, grind is relaxing.  That being said, if you aren't a fan of warframe or destiny-esque grinds, then skip this title.  Movement is snappy, the systems are simple enough to be broadly approachable, but deep enough to keep you coming back to further tailor your build.

Overall, would recommend -- if not now, then definitely on full release.

review_text:
[b]New York Style Pizza[/b]

14 g instant yeast
617g water - 95F
950g all-purpose flour
19g fine sea salt
25g granulated sugar
American Pizza Sauce and Toppings:
1 tablespoon (14g) butter
1 tablespoon (9g) extra virgin olive oil
6 cloves garlic, rough chopped
2 teaspoons (4g) red pepper flakes
28 oz (794g) can of crushed tomato
2 teaspoons (2g) dried oregano
1.5 tablespoons (21g) granulated sugar
salt and pepper to taste
Splash of olive oil
2 cups (227g) low moisture mozzarella, fresh grated
2 cups (200g) Monterey jack cheese, fresh grated
1/2 cup (26g) parmigiano reggiano, fresh grated

[u]Pizza Dough:[/u]

Preheat the oven and a baking steel or pizza stone at 500F for 45 minutes before utilizing it.

Whisk yeast and sugar into your water, and allow it to sit for 5 minutes. In a separate bowl, add flour and salt and mix by hand to combine. Pour your water mixture into your flour and mix by hand until you get a rough dough, then transfer to a work surface and knead until it starts to pull away from the work surface and is relatively smooth.

Place your dough in a greased bowl, then cover with plastic wrap and let rise for 1 - 2 hours at room temperature or until double in size.

Punch down your dough and dive into 300g pieces. Form those pieces into balls and place them in a floured proofing pizza box, cover with a lid, and proof at room temperature for 3 - 4 hours. (If you do not have a proofing pizza box, you can use a floured baking sheet, cover it with an inverted baking sheet and wrap it in plastic wrap.)

[u]American Pizza Sauce and Toppings:[/u]

In a medium sauce pot, add butter and olive oil. Set that over medium-high heat; once the butter melts add garlic, cook until fragrant, add pepper flakes, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the garlic begins to brown on the edges.
Add crushed tomatoes, oregano, salt, and a splotch of olive oil, boil over medium-high, reduce heat to low, and simmer for 12 minutes, stirring occasionally or until thickened and viscous—season with salt to taste and let it cool down.

[u]Assembly:[/u]

Place one of your pizza doughs onto a floured pizza peel, and flour your dough generously.

Punch your dough down in the center, working your way out to create a ¼” wide. Pick up your dough, place it over your closed fists, and rotate it around, gently stretching to 13” to 14”.

Place a couple of spoons of your sauce, starting in the center, spreading in little circles, and working your way to the edge until it gets evenly spread out.

In a medium-size mixing bowl, place mozzarella cheese, Monterey Jack, and Parmigiano; mix until combined. Sprinkle your cheese mixture to your desire and place in the oven onto your baking steel and bake for 5 - 7 minutes or until the edge gets golden brown and the cheese melts.

review_text:
This review WILL contain some Spoilers to story and gameplay!
I don't write a review often, but for this it doesn't deserve the hate it gets.
For my part i sadly (Or probably luckily) got finally around to play it over 1 1/2 years after release so most on launch bugs and crashes most likely have been fixed (I didn't have a single crash in my 13,2 hours of game time.)

Let's start with the negatives.
Combat: Combat is.. very simple and I found a cheese very early on in the game if you continuously press A and D while meeleing you dodge pretty much every attack. I very often looked at my second monitor and reading or watching videos on the side while I just kept fighting against multiple enemies.
Enemies: There isn't a big variety of enemies. Overall there are like 5 different types of enemies (I count the "fat" and blind ones to the nomral ones). Which is fine but I believe the game would have benefitted from some more one off big monsters that you might not be able to really fight, the 2 Heads are put as a miniboss in too many stages of the game imo and after the first 2 times they were more annoying then adding to the game.

Now to the positives.
Story: It is a great story. All the elements for a "Stranded survival" experience are there. Isolated on a dying station. No way to get help other then helping yourself. A very interesting plot with backstories to how the place came to be and an ending that leaves many questions behind that need an explanation in the future projects!
Graphics and Perfomance: Game is running very stable on my PC (I5 Processor, 16Gbyte RAM and a 3060TI), graphics are very beautiful. A lot of gore and scenes that straight up reminded me of Dead Space (Which is a huge compliment imo). 
Weapons and Creativitiy: I really like the weapons, there aren't a lot but they show some creativity in design (Still simple tho) and I thought the "frame" for every weapon to then switch out the top part was fun. I sadly couldn't figure out the point of the tactical pistol until the end haha. The Alt fire modes are pretty fun.
Overal atmosphere: Game captured the atmosphere of what it wants to be very well. A stranded experienced no help from authorities, isolated with some very strong minded NPCs in the game.


Overall opinion:
Is it a masterpiece? Far from it. Is it a bad game? Not at all. 
It is a very solid start from what could turn into a really cool universe with a cult that controls government bodies that want's to bring Humanity to the next stage of evolution by any means necessary. A resistance group that wants to stop them. It is a great concept with A LOT of potential and I hope we can see more in this universe to build on top of this!

My Score: 8.5/10

As much as I love the "Hakuoki" series (and trust me, I really do), "Kyoto Winds" falls a little short compared to "Edo Blossoms". Don’t get me wrong—the story, characters, voice acting, and art are still absolutely top-tier, but the structure of the game kinda holds it back.

The main issue for me is the repetition. Since most of the routes share the same base storyline, you're forced to replay the same events over and over again just to see minor differences depending on the guy you're pursuing. It starts off magical the first couple of times, but after a few playthroughs, it gets... well, boring. That emotional impact and immersion from the first run just starts to fade.

I really wish there was more variation and uniqueness in the early and mid parts of each route to keep things fresh, because when the routes do branch out and get personal, they’re incredible, but getting there feels like a chore after a while.

Still, it’s an essential part of the "Hakuoki" story. You need "Kyoto Winds" before "Edo Blossoms", and it sets the foundation beautifully. Just be ready to sit through some déjà vu.

The Fleets are interesting but Inactive after a short amount of time.
The Content wont last long so you will loose interest faster than expected (but the time it lasts is great).
You often have the feeling as if an update were going to be the last and the game will be shut down but it probably wont. It needs a complete rework, better graphics and more Endgame Content but since Paramount probably wont invest in it, that will remain a dream. Maybe the new devs will Change something.. please
The lore is rich and interesting for people with Star Trek interest but also for new starters i guess.
The Ingame Galactic Trade Network uh i mean The Exchange feels like the definition of inflation because you will have to own tremendous amounts of ingame money to get some ship, or weapon or whatever. In the case of ship weapons, you can often see the best weapons because their Prices are very high.
The Game does provide endgame ships through events but you'll quite possibly need some special item that is very rare or hard to get normally and extremely expensive on the Exchange to get a certain ship. Some ships even require you to be in a Fleet. And some ships are only available on the Exchange for prizes that again, might seem a bit too high but yea.. that's STO. And then there are the ships you actually want to play that are not even on the Exchange/the real life Money store anymore -.- . For Example because i really don't like that they are unavailable ingame for me to get: The Elachi Sheshar-class Command/Intell Dreadnought Cruiser, Saturn-class Intel Science Spearhead, Kelvin Timeline T'laru-class Intel Carrier Warbird, Eisenberg-class Star Cruiser and the list goes on and on. Please Make all or at least most ships available at all times. PLEASE.
Oh and the PvP is About as dead as it can get.
What i would like to see more of is something like the TFO called the "Crystalline Catastrophe". A TFO that requieres at least 10 Players and it felt quite good to have a big Group fight on the same Battlefield (sadly i was only abled to do it once because no one ques for it :/). It reminded me of the last Mission for Destiny 2's Final Shape, where 12 People work together, it just feels like a more Alive game in that Moment. Although it is probably horrible for the Servers and Devs.
And the Server Connection has been horrible and remains to be horrible.


And something that really makes me Angry. I hate it when a gigantic ship can turn 360 Degrees in a second or Speed through the Universe with 100km/ms. It's great that there are items that allow you to turn faster and make your ship faster in General, but big ships should (in my opinion) be slow. You should want to Play smaller ships because their faster and more manoverable but have less hull and do less damage. A big ship should be slow but hit harder. If a big ship hits hard and Speeds through, it's just boring. Your speeding around in a Hull/Shield Monster whilst obliterating EVERYTHING EVERYWHERE -.-


I hope this will help and inform about the game in an at least okay fashion.

Personally, i would like to see a STO 2 with the same ships and content but made with a new game engine, better graphics, more content, new features that make the game more interesting.. but that is quite unlikely to happen.

review_text:
[b]Tldr[/b]
After almost 4 years and 100 levels of 'content', I would guess that dev team's core philosophy behind NGS is something along the lines of :

Put in the least amount of effort, recycle content wherever and whenever possible.

Not too concerned about growing the playerbase, the priority is to squeeze the tiny amount of players who have proven that they will tolerate the above and spend significantly and regularly on fashion items.

This is a game that's not very important to us or the company. We just keep the lights on and can continue operating like this for 100's of levels to come. The players will allow us. Most of the proceeds from NGS are invested into other projects.


[b]Level 100 Cap Update[/b]
Sadly, but not particularly surprisingly, most of the things from the old review are still true. I talk about the new stuff here, check the old review towards the end to see more about the game in general.

There still exist weapons with absurd drop rates, but as of lately the devs have been ensuring that there's a weapon option that the player can work towards and grind the materials for. If you play casually, the cost of gearing isn't painful. If you're min maxing, it's not as costly as it was before but the caveats and rng associated with successfully pulling it off still exist.
They story so far in almost 4 years and 100 levels remains lackluster (to put it generously) and is only able to accomplish anything remotely interesting when it key jangles characters from or links to the old game. The new Urgent Quest (equivalent to a raid in other mmo's) is a fight against the Level 100 cap update 'Final' Boss and that along with the scant amount of story, are the only content of what the devs consider a major update. [b]Everything else is recycled content, business as usual for NGS.[/b]

The fight itself leaves a lot to be desired and I wouldn't consider it befitting of a major story update boss. I've seen them design better fights for what would be considered less important bosses in the past few years. For major new raids, mmo devs would usually have an idea of how each class would perform in a fight..for example how Class A will position itself during this phase of the fight or the possible ways Class B might upkeep their damage during this particular attack from the boss. The NGS devs? Well, they do know, what I'm saying is they don't give a fuck. They can't be assed to craft an enjoyable, worthwhile 'final' boss experience for all their players. The content has been getting lazier and lazier and they're always testing how much they can keep recycling. 

I wanna point out that I'm calling this bitch a 'Final' boss according to the presented story beats and heavy implication that there won't be any significant story updates anytime soon, along with the fact that the credits play after as well. Frankly, I believe that they can and probably will go on well past 100 levels in their typical lazy, scripted and soulless fashion of delivering content.


[b]Slightly Older Review[/b]

I can write an essay on this, but I'll keep it brief. 
The two best and most outstanding qualities of this game are its combat and its fashion/character customization. Everything else..and I mean literally everything else about the game is severely lacking and objectively bad, so much so that its frustrating because the aforementioned is really, really good. 
The dev team is very rigid and stubborn and are excrustiatingly slow to balance and update things related to gameplay.

The combat and fashion as I said are the only things the game has going, but if you wanna get into either of them and enjoy them fully, it will require a lot of irl spending. The fashion items and fun emotes and stuff are buyable with ingame money, but the amount of that you will make as free to play would require you to do a mundane activity in game for 8+ hours to afford one, maybe two, items you might be interested in.

If you enjoy gearing and min maxing, then I highly recommend staying away from this game. There are certain weapon drops that are on the level of myths. There's a thing called Fixa which every weapon can have attached to it and it comes in 5 levels and different effect types. They only [b]recently[/b] made it so that the player can recreate this on a weapon that doesn't have it, either by spending a copious amount of free to play resources you accumlate over the course of several months..(for just a rng chance of getting it on one single weapon in the end) or by whaling on the game obscenely hard. Fixa has existed since the game's release and has always been a major point of contention, which took the devs 3 years to even begin to address.

The only way I could recommend this game is if you intend to play it casually on and off. It's arguably perfect for that and can easily be picked up and dropped. The combat is fun and you'll likely find a weapon and class you enjoy playing. All classes function as dps, so if you enjoy playing support in games you might not be as interested. Raids, bosses and whatever else have no real mmo mechanics that require any team oriented strategy..most of the game's strategy is found in optimizing your dps. 

That's about it..and yes, this was brief for how much could be said about the dev team dropping the ball so hard on a game with this much potential. They will never understand the extent to which they harmed and lost the community and following they had going with this franchise. 
Thanks for taking the time to read my review.

review_text:
BEFORE YOU BUY PLEASE READ!

Please remember this is coming from an unbias opinion as I have never played this game till today nor been involved in watching it's progress. So I have been playing this game for 5 hours or so now and something has become very clear to me through my playtime. I have encountered more bugs than I ever have on a early access game; far more than The Isle, Draconia, Beasts of Bermuda, or other survival games with similar mechanics. I see that very recently crocodile was added as a playable and that there are two dlcs (christmas and skins) already. I think this is really horrific considering the state of the game and the fairly high price-tag of $30AUD/$20USD. I think it would be in everyone's interest if playable's development was halted for now and the basic concept and mechanics of the game were fixed and given some love. 

Here are some of the issues I encountered in under 3 hours of play;
- Leopard climbing insanely broken (Don't even understand why it was added in this state tbh it is horrific).
- Getting stuck in eating animation
- Getting stuck in drinking animation
- Getting stuck in lying animation
- Drinking not working in certain areas of water at all
- textures turning white
- textures turning glossy
- calls changing ??
- calls not working
- jump not working
- delayed jump/bite/run
- delayed damage
- hitboxes not being biteable 
- Unable to stick meat
- Unable to pick back up stick-ed gores
- Models turning insanely low poly on high end pcs
- Insane crashes/disconnects when ping/internet/FPS is completely fine
- Getting default skins from nesting w/ non default parents
- animation glitches w/ IK system
- Unable to pick up babies
- Unable to eat meat
- Unable to eat edible plants
- Group invt not working.
- Insane lag and rubberbanding
- Delayed footprints
- Leopard's tail kinks as it runs
- Bodies despawning after less than 2 minutes.

This is an absolutely insane amount of glitches for the very short amount of time I have played, and I would never endorse nor recommend an early access game this broken to any player. This game has amazing potential, but the devs need to have a look at what really matters and focus on that to a serious degree.

review_text:
I like it.

Combat is clear and responsive. Audio helps the player understand what is happening around them. Because of the hectic nature of this game Directional audio is important. Each weapon has a distinct way to use it beyond just the handling. Spells can be unlocked for some additional firepower. 

There is no story incentive to go to A > B > ... > Z (Fin). Instead as you play through each map you find things you can't access. Which hints you into doing something to grant you access. So it's much more about exploration, Which I love, and the experience of finding something new that keeps you moving forward. 

There are 3 types of progression in this Rogue lite game. 
Meta-Progression, Which have you unlock new guns, relics, Totems & Spells between each run. This Progression doesn't necessarily make you stronger but allows you to change your play style or find one that suits your particular skills. Some of these Meta-Progression you can unlock can be found mid-run. I am currently running a pure fire spell build, which under some circumstances can Mowe down hordes of enemies. But I started with using a more defensive ice build to slow enemies down giving me the upper hand. 

Story Progression.
Some of the Meta-Progression also unlocks new areas you can access, which helps paint the story of what has befallen the lands. In my opinion this is currently lacking. However it doesn't take anything away from the gameplay. 

Mid-Run Progression.
During a Run you find and fight a node of enemies. When you clear one of the nodes you are rewarded with a Giant Crystal. Which grants you 1 out of 3 potential upgrades of a specific type. The types available varies based on the equipment you chose for the run. If you have no way to do Fire damage you will not find a Fire based upgrade. These upgrades range from utility like an extra potion slot, to "Deal increased damage to Elite enemies". If you die or leave a run you loose these upgrades.

The combined above things keeps me coming back for more. I want to see what is behind Genesis 4, in the Pyre puzzle in the Spire of the Island of witches. The combat keeps me engaged. So I very much like this game.

review_text:
This game probably broke something in my brain. Try as I might, I really can't think of a game that has eaten my brain quite like this one (and the game it is a re-telling of), and I think that the amount of time I've spent in this game could probably be used as a diagnostic criteria for something. 

Although only one route is currently out (along with a short story from the Bachelor's perspective) and some aspects to the story are not fully explored as of yet, it is still complete and satisfying, and you don't necessarily need to have played Pathologic Classic in order to understand it, although I highly recommend playing it at some if you haven't already (either before or after this one). 

The Haruspex's route is about life, death, survival, and sacrifice, as one might expect, but it's also about family, love, belonging, rejection, time, childhood, adulthood, duty, and the devastating effects of settler colonialism, among other things. The story is unique, surreal, and engaging, and something you can dissect from multiple angles over and over again, extracting more from it each time. 

None of the characters in this game are normal. Everyone is interesting and at least somewhat strange in their own right, just like the setting. Artemy is a character that can be played in multiple ways, as many aspects of Artemy's character are meant to be in conflict with each other. It feels realistic for someone attempting to find one's place after a period of estrangement from their community and while trying to mend things that were broken, especially during a time of crisis. 

I wouldn't necessarily call it a "horror" game, but it is certainly unnerving and anxiety-inducing at points. The choices posed are difficult, and the evolving and unforgiving gameplay accentuates the struggle for survival against seemingly impossible odds. You can adjust the difficulty, but it's intended difficulty can be pretty grueling on a first time playthrough. However, the game walks you through the mechanics with straightforward tutorials and has a mind map that helps point you in the right directions, which sets it apart from its predecessor. This game also allows you to heal when you sleep, unlike Pathologic Classic, so that's also helpful. 

The only issue I'd say the game has is that it's not very well-optimized at times, and if you're playing it on a hard drive, you'll experience long wait-time lags at transitions between indoor and outdoor environments and loading screens. Using an SSD will reduce this issue significantly. I'm able to play it at max graphics settings on a gaming laptop that's relatively average specs-wise and get 30 FPS, which is fine by me, but your mileage may vary if you feel like a game running at anything but 60 FPS is unplayable. 

Some people might complain about the combat being difficult (although you can get into the rhythm of it if you practice enough), but I'd argue that fighting people in real life tends to be very high risk and sometimes the only reward is coming out out of it alive. However, unlike real life, you only really take a hit to your reputation if you decide to steal someone's liver - to make medicine, of course. 

Overall, it's a fantastic game. I'm waiting excitedly (but patiently, as the team is pretty small) for the next route.

review_text:
Witchfire is a really weird game. I think the word I would use is that it feel directionless, and has no spikiness. The pitch of "FPS Rogue/Souls-like set in a dark fantasy world hunting witches" is right up my alley, and I was ocassionally looking at the dev logs, but like... it just doesn't work? And I don't really understand what I'm missing that so many people seem to adore about the game.

I'll note up here, right now, the performance of the game is really, really WEIRD. It runs at 120hz for me (3080, 3850x), but it's so jittery. Sometimes I open a menu and the game freezes for multiple seconds. The game drops frames and hitches constantly, sometimes up to 1-2 seconds at a time. It's not quite unplayable, but it's super noticeable and you will have to ignore it if you want to play more. I'm not sure what it'd run like on worse hardware, but if it's more jittery, it was already pretty close to intolerance for me.

But spikiness. What I mean by spikiness is, think of Tarkov. The difference between a TOZ-106 and a HK 416 is gargantuan. If you're sneaking around with a TOZ, get the drop on someone, and grab their rifle, you feel like a god, but also this massive sense of anxiousness until you get out safe with it. Gunfights are short and brutal, and every shot could be lethal. You open a cache, and you know that it could contain something worth millions. There's these spikes of fun.

Think of Hades. The difference between your power at the start of a run and the end is massive. You're whizzing around leaving blades everywhere and lighting is coming down and your gun now shoots five grenades and the bullets track enemies. Your difficulty can also increase so you have to absolutely perfect the game to get under time and not get hit. Spikey.

Think of Dark Souls or Elden Ring. That moment of "Oh shit what is that fucking thing" or "Oh cool a new weapon, oh it looks cool" or "Finally, I can upgrade four levels of my weapon and dump on enemies". The spikes of joy at finding a chest, or beating a boss.

Witchfire is bizarre because it feels like it has no spikiness. When you kill a camp of enemies, you get a level-up and a buff! But the buffs are all boring; do you want +20% stamina? +3% damage per 10% of your health you're missing? Perhaps +1 potion slot! They're all so... dry and mundane. I unlocked four weapons, and they all felt like they killed enemies at roughly the same rate, in roughly the same way; point at the head and pull the trigger. You would think the shotgun would be so much more effective since it's close range, but it just kinda wasn't? I upgraded a weapon; it does ~50% damage on undamaged enemies, so on the first shot! Yay?

Like there's this strange lack of joy in the game's meta existence, and it feels like there's a bunch of alpha-level cool mechanics, but none of them really come together to form a whole? The movement feels great, but I never really feel like I need to or should move much (and you run out of stamina REALLY quickly). The guns feel solid and kinetic, but they all do kinda pitiful damage; my bolt action takes 2-3 headshots to kill the weakest enemies, I can't imagine what the automatics feel like. They also have really weird range; damage drop-off from range goes to basically zero, and it's not like at 100m, it's closer to 10m using a revolver.

There's portals you can use to leave the map, and there's a timer! Oh no, you'll have to... stand there and do nothing because it doesn't trigger enemies or anything. I found a key, I can go use it to open up that chest I found, and it.... has some ammo and 2 pieces of gold? Ok? I came back from a run, so now I have enough to level up! I can buy one skill level. Ok, are they meaningful? I mean... you can get +3% stamina! Or perhaps +2% more money. Or +10% health?

Like I can't quite explain this properly if you haven't played, but it just felt like everything was kinda a dissapointment the moment I unlocked it, and that left me with no drive to see more things. Like every moment the game had to go "Look at this cool new thing! One more run to test it out maybe?" or "What an amazing find; what else could be out there?", it just threw me a couple coins and told me to fuck off. 

I dunno. It's kinda bizarre. Maybe if I played a couple more hours the game completely opens up and it suddenly gets better? I stopped because I got inside of the first tower, and the game told me that I didn't grind enough to progress, so I went back home, and it told me that I needed to grind more to progress. It was just strange. Like I feel like I needed to absolutely love the base gameplay of the game and be OK with it just being that forever. And the base gameplay is OK, but I never really feel like I needed to do much other than click on enemies and sometimes dodge a sword.

The game doesn't feel like unsavable or like a mess, it just feels like at least to me, none of the parts fit together in a fun way? I have to imagine after this long, this is the feeling the dev wants in the game, but I just can't really see why. Like taking a tiny case study; is the emotion I'm supposed to feel after finding a chest, not being able to open it, finding a key, and going back to open it confusion at what I got, and a sense of "Oh I guess it's more than it's sounds like?", only to go back to base and realize, no, it is indeed pretty much meaningless? Is that the intention? Because it really permeates every element of the game.

review_text:
Sometimes games just don't vibe with you, but you play them anyway, because they were in the Humble Choice selection and looked ... interesting? Touted as a 3D action platformer by users ... 

What it really is is "Tony Hawks with graffiti grinds and bad combat".

You go around the stylized world to grind on rails and smear your graffiti over the graffiti of other crews. You do tricks, boost around, and fight the police ... and read the terrible dialogue to get the "story" moving. Grinding isn't really anything cool, though, the game does everything for you automatically. There are no "tricks" to speak of. You just press B,X,Y alternatively to accrue points. For nothing. 

The first part is actually not that bad, but it doesn't feel impactful, because actually doing tricks is meaningless. It only fills your "combo" meter, which in turn gives you boost. The real reason to do all this is to grind, pardon the pun, REP. Earn enough REP and you can challenge a rival crew and progress the game.

While you do that police keep endlessly spawning the more you "vandalize" the city. You can defeat them in melee combat with your "tricks", so you keep pressing B,X,Y, sometimes spraying them with paint to momentarily blind them ... or you just ignore them, because they seem to keep endlessly spawning, as I said, and can't really do much, at least not at first, I'd assume. The foot soldiers really are powerless.

I'll give the game points for some originality, and for sticking to its theme, and also for its selection of music, which isn't really my genre, but it's obviously fitting, and that's that. I remember vaguely that there's a series of games very similar to this. Jet Set Radio, now that I've looked it up. If you're the kind of person that has played these games and really enjoyed them, and you're desperately looking for an unofficial sequel, then this might be it. Personally, I just don't like grinding fucking REP as the main activity in any game. Definitely the weirdest game I've played this year, though ... or one of them, at least.

If it were focussed more on the tricks, I might actually not dislike it that much. BUT, it's overwhelmingly positive, and most likely that means that fans of this type of game got EXACTLY what they wanted, so I'll give it that. Just take this review from someone who apparently wasn't a Jet Set Radio fan to begin with before you buy a "3D action platformer" fpr 40 bucks!

Let the Jester awards commence, because this game's "fan base" seems to not take criticism well. ;)
