review_text:
a disjointed and messy experience.
the game tries to be many things at once and it doesn't shine in any of it.

a half-assed roguelite system
fishing (cause every game needs it for some reason)
a movement system that got worse as the game kept getting updated
stuff not being explained to the player on how they should progress or an in-depth in game guide

enemy recognition: you cant tell which enemy you should shoot first when you're flying all over the place because everything is black and neon bright which leads you to dying more often than you should've. bosses are also pretty lackluster.

movement system: sticks and stones felt good and snappy. after trying out the recent update it felt night and day. it's slow, floaty and has no weight or momentum behind it. 

hit detection: i've had this happen a couple times where i just randomly get hit and die for no reason. pretty annoying

level design: stop and go. it doesn't flow well if you're blasting enemies and the next second you're hunting for a goofy aah key for a bunker just to upgrade your gun for example.

weapons: either they're balls or they are just alright. melees suck a lot and it just ends up with you restarting the run if you even dare try to go melee only (atleast in my experience, feel free to correct me). atleast the animations are pretty good. wish the same could be said about the next point.

art style: again, since everything is black and neon the only way to describe it is colour vomit. everything blends into each other and in general it's just painful to look at after a while.

soundtrack: it's alright. nothing amazing just alright. sticks and stones had a better roster of songs but he had to remove those cause of copyright as far as i know but this is entirely subjective.

i know i brought up sticks and stones and yes i could just play that version instead of the latest but the game could be so much more but it's held back by a dev who doesn't know what to do with his own game.

Combat was improved, stealth was improved, story was even better than the first, bigger open world than Asylum, amazing voice acting as always. review_text:
[b]An extremely story-driven JRPG about people playing an MMO, where the worst part about it is the actual game you're playing.[/b]
This consists of 3 HD remasters of the .hack//G.U. games released back in the mid-2000's, and a brand new 4th volume included in this bundle that gives this whole saga a real conclusion.

The story is probably great. It's hard for me to take a plot seriously though when most of everything that happens occurs in the video game within this game. The world outside of the MMO and general lore of this series as a whole is far more interesting and incredibly vast, where the timeline takes place in the futuristic years of the mid-2010's and a lot happens on the outside just because of an MMO.
I think they expected you to have played the previous .hack games and watched the prequel anime though, as they make loads & loads of references to both, and I didn't figure a lot of it out until I watched the backstory videos and searched things up myself.

Ironically, despite the game being about another video game, the gameplay itself is the absolute worst thing about this. It's tedious, repetitious, has loads of pointless mechanics, and so on.
As a JRPG, there's little thought needed into actually playing the game. There are elemental weaknesses, shield breaking, status prevention methods, and all that, but you can go through the whole thing using the same "mash A to kill thing" strategy over & over again while the more complicated-sounding stuff can be completely ignored altogether. The only thing you'll have to worry about is finding equipment with bigger numbers than what you're wearing, but even then you can still get through the story with equipment a hundred levels lower than you so long as your character's level is at the appropriate level for a monster/dungeon; even upgrading said equipment is pointless as stats barely get a boost at all and stronger equipment comes by fast.
The only enemies that can actually give you trouble are the late bosses of each game, but even then you can overcome them fast by doing a quick grind prior to gain a few levels.
I believe they're aware of how terrible the gameplay is in this since they added a "Cheat Mode" to every game that pretty much allows you to breeze through each volume and focus only on the story.

Its storytelling is also pretty obnoxious. Too many times, they want you to log out of the MMO and check your mail to progress the story. Other times they want you to go through a pointless dungeon and/or quest that has absolutely nothing to do with the plot itself, as if all it is is just to pad the time you play.

Each game lasts dozens of hours to go through first-hand if you play them "normally", except for the latest volume which only lasts a few hours and serves pretty much as the epilogue to the whole thing.
In the last volume, they still make you go through practically pointless dungeons even though you no longer need to do much or any leveling by that point, and the gameplay's pretty much the same as the first 3, which is dull.

If you really wanted to just go through the story, you're probably better off watching playthrough videos, or watch the .hack//G.U. Trilogy movie that covers the 3 games and maybe play the short 4th volume yourself.

Found another and it took three shots, then another was two, it simply kept bouncing around like there's clearly "something" that considered "damage" but considering one hit on the protagonist takes between three to four bars of health, I wasn't experimenting around to find out, more so when ammo and health is scarce. - The combat seriously frustrated and zapped all my enjoyment out of this game. 

Then the game will just straight up harm or if you're low on health like me 99% of the time straight up kill you because the parasite is harming you, and this becomes a constant and worse factor towards the end of the game, where it took me probably longer than it should because the game kept killing me for trying to figure out what I'm supposed to do whilst panicking.

The positives:
+ It's a hockey sim, a market that is in dire need of a good product.
+ The stats are believable.  Scoring and penalties may be slightly inflated but I grew up watching hockey in teh 80's so I have no issue with the increase in scoring.  A 4-3 game is more entertaining than a 2-1 game.  :-)

The negatives:
- Issues with CPU GM's (players getting put on the trading block but when you inquire you get a message that says the player is untouchable; teams with cap room waiving star players, not overly common but it does seem to happen and in the major case that I saw it was said player from the trading block being waived the next day after my inquiry and said player was the scoring leader at the time)
- 2D match engine could use some work, there are some times where the penalty being called doesn't seem to fit the situation or the play being made by the player with the puck doesn't make a lot of sense or for that matter the play made by the defender
- The UI could use some work, takes a bit of poking around to find things

review_text:
(34hrs) - It's a VERY "Japanese" VERY "Anime" type game where the story and dialogue are weak and the characters are annoying, but the core of the gameplay is pretty fun if you like flashy grinders and the character creator is absolutely awesome for all kinds of "psy-fantasy" aesthetics. I've been digging it more than I thought I would after years of never playing it due to the things I've heard.

(400hrs) - Old fanbase is trippin' balls. You can still play PSO2 you just gotta click the thing on the loading page.  I am really enjoying PSO2NGv2, I've only been subbed for 2 months, but I really love the fights and I keep finding subtleties in the combat that I really enjoy.  Vital information is hard to come by and I had to do way too much research on my own to figure out what to do, so I'd strongly recommend finding a guild and chatting with people to answer your questions.  

YouTuber Keroppi makes daily videos that have helped me understand what's going on, highly recommended.

I find the complexity in combat very simple, but in a way I really enjoy. I'd say it's a bit more complicated than Genshin Impact, and a bit less complicated than Black Desert, both of which I also really enjoy.

If you're reading this and want to try the game I'd recommend following these directions: *please note these are my suggestions for how I play, there's no reason to follow this if you'd rather just run around the open world in cute outfits or whatever*

1st- Skip all the cut-scenes and get to max level as fast as possible. Focus solely on the "Main Story" quests and tasks - but don't skip any of the learning!  There will be a little "info window" that pops up with a short description pretty frequently and it's important to read and understand what those are trying to tell you, even if they do a poor job of illustrating the very info they are trying to convey.

(Don't switch classes at first, but do try all the weapons to find the one you want to level first and do the story quests.  You can swap "classes" at any time and having at least one fully leveled will make it a million times easier to swap to any of the other -or all others if you really want- later on)

2nd- You will get free gear as you level as part of leveling a new account, this gear you will use for a long time. I believe it gives you the stuff you will keep at level 65. Current level cap is 100. (3/24/2025)

3rd- Once you hit max level, get your free gear, and finish the story - do all the "cocoons" and "tower" missions to get all of your skill points.  Your "gear score" is what will lock you out of certain missions and you will get some score by *spending* skill points, so make sure you collect and spend all the skill points. There are 47 skill points at present. This will take you approx 15hrs. 

4th- There is a TON of gear and weapons that are "leftovers" from previous expansions and nearly all of them are entirely useless.  Depending on how far into the future you're reading this you'll need to identify "what gear and weapon I should be working on acquiring and improving?"  

At present, the armor is level 10-star and has 3 improvement tiers:
Ektasis - base
Dostasis - 1
Trestasis - 2
Akrotasis - 3 (final at present)

Doing the dailies and weeklies will give you most of the mats you'll need to improve your gear, other things might come from the open world or different challenges, but nothing was hard to find.

At present, the weapons are level 11/12-star and has 3 improvement tiers, with one extra thing to know:
Exelio - base
Duo Selio - 1
Tri Selio - 2
Akroselio - 3
Eredim - (contains a set of 3 unique EX Augments you'll need)

(Ignore Twaalv and Windard type weapons unless you actually roll one - which you won't - at which point just ask someone, lol)

Eredim weapons will always have a group of 3 EX augments which you can transfer to your 
--Selio weapon, but you must always move all 3, no picking and choosing, therefore a set of 3 that compliment one another are more valuable. They offer a bunch of different playstyles so I'll let you figure out which ones you want to use. (I prefer Shortage, Turnover, Maintain Balance if you care to know, I don't recommend it to most players.)

5th- Augments - as you play you'll get augments that you can apply to weapons and gear. Augments that end in "LC" are a weaker variant, but significantly easier to get and apply.  The vast majority of the game can be played and enjoyed with the free gear you'll get at 65, but the "reason to play" if you want to upgrade your gear will be the long tail of getting a set of weapons and armor to upgrade and replacing the augments with stronger and stronger versions as you go.  At the upgrade kiosk you can combine many augments into more powerful ones. These are hard to get and take a lot of time and can be a lot to learn, so take your time.

There are many strategies for augments, preset skills, and weapon potentials.

I don't want to get into the various strategies to do this, but I don't mind farming, so for me - I just bought the base weapons and gear that already had the "Preset Skills" I wanted and went from there to apply the augments I wanted.  Rather than rolling "Preset Skills" after I've already upgraded the weapons and armor.

At present day I have a bit over 400hrs into the game and have a 99.8% complete weapon, and one of the three armor pieces pretty much fully decked out, the other two have LC augments still and one still has a level 4 Preset Skill I'm still deciding what to do with.  I'm providing this information for context in how long it takes if you don't want to just buy stuff with cash, which is also an option for some people.

If you want to buy loot-box cosmetic items and sell them for cash and just buy the best stuff, that is an option if you've got the cash and don't want to care about improving a weapon and gear. Many people do this, I am not one of them.

Notes:

-I do not recommend starting new characters if you can help it.

-Make sure to start on the same server "ship" as your friends.

-If you get two copies of a cosmetic item, the first use will unlock it for your current character, the second use will unlock it for your account.

-Read the challenges and quest information for the dailies and weeklies - don't try to use slam attacks on crit-combo day, for example.

-There's usually not much reason to go crazy and burn yourself out on event tasks, this is maybe the most respectful-of-your-time game that I've ever played considering how easy it is to get enough gear score to do everything and how many "seasonal  points" I've been able to acquire during seasonal events.

-You will make 2 Star Gems (currency) for the first 5 people you "like" their character "lookbook" that resets every day.

-Learn the different shops - there's a lot of info on the page of each shop including how many of each item you can buy each week and how long until the shop resets. There's too many shops and each one has too many items, just take your time.

-There's a yellow "treasure" item in each zone that always spawns at the same spot each day that gives a decent amount of money. It takes less than 10 minutes to get all of them each day once you have the teleports to each zone.

-The grinding zones (Dext Base for money for example) have different levels based at what level your character is. You can select the different levels at the teleporters on the map for each zone. Do this for different drops, money, xp, or whatever you're looking for. Usually, for money you'll want the lower levels for higher total kills, for xp you'll usually want the higher levels for more exp per kill.

Good luck on killing Ruine Masquerader at level 100!

review_text:
[h1] The Best SAO Game [/h1]

[b] What I Liked [/b]

I'll start this off by saying the point of the game isn't the story.  The story isn't bad.  There are only so many ways stories in SAO can play out.  The story is the only way they could justify bringing in characters from the anime over.  That being said, if you're a fan of SAO, then you'll like the story.

The combat is where the game shines.  I've tried a few SAO games over the years, and none of them felt quite right.  This one though makes me feel like I'm in SAO.  The characters move and play like they would in SAO.  The enemies behave as if they are their counterparts in the anime.  The combat is great.

Of course, the point of the game is the grind.  It's a huge, huge grind.  It's all about leveling up and grinding for gear.  Doesn't make it bad at all.  With 21 characters, there is a ton to grind for.

The graphics are good, and again, I feel like I am in SAO.  I wish more locations from the anime were in the game, but it's good for what it does.

[b] What I Did Not Like [/b]

I'm an old guy, so the game hurts my hands after awhile.  There is a bunch of button mashing.  More than likely I'll have to give it up because it's too hard on my hands.

Playing online is the primary point of the game.  Doing co-op dungeons and boss fights.  The problem is that will get boring after awhile since there isn't a huge variety of areas.  The other issue is that the player population is low, and half the time bots filled in for a live person.  But, they were decent bots who fulfilled their role decently enough.

Day one DLC is also a downer, along with microtransactions.  They aren't required though.

[b] Why I Stopped Playing [/b]

Haven't yet, expect I will once it bothers my hands too much and I tire of the grind.

[b] Disclaimer [/b]

I have been a gamer for over 30 years.  I tend to play mostly PC games.  I also bounce around between games A LOT.  I may purchase a $60 game and play it for 2 hours or spend $10 on a game and spend 50 hours on it.  Even if I played a game a short time, it does not mean it is bad.  It just means another game caught my attention.  I also complain about flaws in games a lot, even about the littlest of things.  Keep that in mind when reading my reviews.  If I do not have a complaint, then the game must be special!

review_text:
Picked up this game blind and boy was that a mistake.
The screenshots look fancy. The video adverts look fancy too.
When ya play it though, it is just... a hub-based mission-after-mission game.
It does not feel like an MMO, it feels like a mobile game.
The game came out 3 weeks prior to this review (according to steam), and its already on v1.1.0 with DLC episodes and gacha up the wazoo.

The last SAO game I played was Hollow Realization (alicization doesn't count).
You play Kirito, and do Kirito things I guess, except there is no real skill tree or anything.
The first few hours you just go to the same one or two maps, listen to dialogue, kill some monsters, listen to more dialogue, and then rinse and repeat for the next mission... and the next mission... and the next mission.

The game explicitly tells you "you should probably do all the main story before multiplayer", and as you can see I only spent 4 hours on the game before I realized I was just playing a glorified mobile game- gacha and in-game-purchases included.

The game talks about crafting and stuff, but its really just more gacha- with a daily limit.

I saw in other reviews that people enjoyed the combat, but honestly it felt rather clumsy to me.
I played on a controller, and it was... okay?
When characters only have basically "attack", "heavy attack", and "skill 1/2/3" and "super skill", its just... repetitive.
The flying was just clunky, nevermind "flying combat" lmao.

I'm grasping at straws to talk about anything positive in this game.
I guess it looked nice?
The story could've been interesting, but is dumped hard on by the glaring gameplay flaws otherwise.

If you want to risk buying it, do make sure you watch actual gameplay videos or streams or something to make sure its your cup of tea, because I wish I would've done it ahead of time as I would've never bought it in the first place.

Take my opinion for what its worth, but this was my first steam refund request in over a decade.

review_text:
I've been trying to think of how to review To the Moon for several days now. Part of me wants to approach it chiefly as the vital piece of indie-game history that it represents. Another part wants to completely set that reputation aside and look it at as a game and narrative by itself. But I've struggled to make much progress through either angle, and part of why might be that I don't like To the Moon as much as I remember liking it.

To be clear, To the Moon is broadly successful and even more broadly a good game. It's plotted well, decently pretty, has a great soundtrack and is surprisingly good at tugging on the old heart strings. All that said though, it's still clearly the work of someone who is still far from mastering their craft.

Much of the dialogue is - for want of a better (or less online) word - cringe as hell. Most of the attempts at comedy fall pretty flat and leave To the Moon's tone feeling more uneven than it should. I'm all for levity in sad stories, but where the more emotional side of the storytelling has aged surprisingly gracefully, the comedy feels extremely 2011 in the worst way possible. It's not agonisingly bad, but there was more than a few eyeroll-inducing moments throughout its short runtime. And as well written as some of its more touching moments are, certain revelations feel more than a little rushed and a little contrived. There was obviously a strong desire to have big reveals and shocking twists and much of the story has been mangled around to better accomodate them, perhaps at the expense of the relatability that it could have had. Also, the slightly naff puzzles present only to fend off the early 2010s "not a game if no gameplay" crowd really don't need to be here and I'm glad they get dropped about two thirds of the way through.

As much as these flaws do work against the experience and prevent To the Moon from being a masterpiece, they do add a certain charm. Games like this aren't really made any more. You no longer have to manhandle a shitty engine like RPG Maker to make a touching, narrative-driven, no-combat game like this, you can just press a button on Gamemaker and it will all but generate one for you. While game development getting easier is great for accessibility, there is now a certain level of homogenisation in indie games as less sacrifices need to be made to accomodate certain limits. To the Moon works as a great time capsule for the early days of the indie boom, and I imagine I will return to it again someday not too far into the future. In part, I'm glad I wasn't so enamoured with it on this revisit, as it will make it easier to approach the two sequels that I've put off playing for so long. If you haven't played To the Moon, it's not the absolute, unrivalled must-play that it once was. But it is an excellent time capsule and will probably get a good few tears out of you by the end of its four hour playtime.

By the end of the scene I hated all the characters involved (excluding the two main characters)

If you're a fan of homestuck then you might enjoy the game , if not I'd give it a miss

review_text:
Rise to Ruins is a fairly brutal village building god game, if played as intended. In fact its basically quite unfair, and the game pulls lots of tricks to ruin your village and any fun you're having building a village. There are thankfully modes of incremental difficulty for the less masochistic gamers, and the core difficulty curve can be learned in relative safety in a Traditional Mode. The issue is village AI is fairly dumb, and you have no control over them except in an obtuse sense. Villagers will walk into enemy land while "wandering" outside of the village, starve to death with a massive surplus of food, and generally bug out and not do their job even if you have set up everything to be as efficient as possible. And this is working as intended, apparently.

You build a little pixel village under threat from a spreading corruption that decays the land and spawns bad guys. You are a deity with a fairly comprehensive set of powers, both destructive, creative, healing, and utility in nature. You have no influence over land that is corrupted, so cannot attack it directly, and for the most part the corruption cannot be conquered or destroyed, only endured. The point of the game is to simply survive for as long as possible, through defenses and arming of your villagers and judicious use of magic. 

There is an overworld map, and each region on the overworld is a biome to survive in. The only primary victory condition is to survive a year in every region, which you have to spread to organically from each village you form via migrating villagers you select to leave for the new region.

And that is Rise to Ruins. You are a deity to a small group of people trying to simply survive an unstoppable, albeit partially containable, corruption. If you enjoy god games and village builders, and a have a taste for lite tower defense, this is a very fun and addicting game. Be warned, on Survival and higher difficulties it can be brutal, and even on Traditional difficulty a few too many mistakes and setbacks late into a village can doom it. There are many "features" to enemy AI that will essentially ignore established rules to circumvent your defenses, and added to this are "random" disasters like earthquakes and lighting storms that target your village. Pretend its just the corruptions angry god throwing its own spells at you if it helps justify it.

No matter how slow you are, half-pipes carry you to the same height.
People made fun of Sonic 4 for this stuff.

The manual ability and the existence of closed loop rails trivialize scoring. You can't even fumble a trick by inputting it at the wrong time, like before landing. I thought this game was about movement but it's actually a collectathon.
You can also only wall ride context sensitive billboards which is really lame.

There's no failure condition for the graffiti so you can just spin the stick in a circle, making the graffiti feel like an afterthought that's just there because JSR did it.

This is the kind of game I'd expect to have replay value.
Very forgettable outside of modding, not worth the asking price.

Worth your time half off.

review_text:
I've always been in love with movement shooters and just fast paced FPS games in general, Quake and Titanfall were and still are the games I'd point to for my fascination with this genre. I've followed GTTOD's development and finally decided to try the game myself and shell out the cash, and needless to say given the current state of the game I'm not disappointed. 

This gameplay scratches that itch of the niche that I love, the movement is sleek and quick and the gameplay, although somewhat tedious given the lack of enemy types ranging from cannon fodder to a slight threat still gives you that adrenaline filled rush of slide hopping and air strafing combat constantly. While the average player new to the movement shooter niche might struggle for me the game felt immediately responsive. Not to mention the art style and design is top notch. Every weapon feels powerful and tailored in design and gameplay to a mark.

But enough about me praising the game, lets go over some issues that I have encountered and would like to make anyone reading this aware of.

Glitches and bugs, while the game for being early access is expected to have bugs it should be noted that you will eventually run into something that will ruin your run. For me I lost my 10k kills run due to entering the battle portal a second time believing it was something new to find a weapon or piece of content, instead it resulted to softlocking my run and forcing me to restart, in all honesty I was quite livid to losing my run and therefore progress to the achievement but its to be expected. I can easily break the record of where I left off, but I'd prefer to not have to worry about my time being turned to naught. Any other glitch you may encounter tends to be quickly remedied and doesn't harm you, I just was particularly unfortunate in the timing. But to to the fact it was present and finding that I'd consistently phase into walls in some occasions due to the sheer speed I was propelling myself with slide hops I don't doubt for a fact that the issues are still greatly present. It is early access and I can fully understand if these are present, but it is something to be aware of when purchasing.

Content, at the time of writing the game is quite small given the 15 dollar price tag, its quite fun however unless you are like me, a person who can't seem to fill their addiction to anything fast paced then I must be blunt and say to consider your purchase carefully. It is a fun game, but until it gets more content outside of around a half a dozen levels I can't give a 100% recommendation in good faith to anyone who isn't fluent in the genre.

Graphics, the default bloom is, to put this rather bluntly hard on the eyes, after a hour of gameplay I had to turn it down to half of default due to it harming my target acquisition. However everything else is perfectly fine.

Those are the issues that come off the top of my head, I've greatly enjoyed the game and looking forward to the continued development of GTTOD.

review_text:
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is Jet Set Radio meets Philip K. Dick with the most satisfying, tasty, and STYLISH fine tuning needed to make it my GOTY on launch. Fun plot with the levity and stakes balanced like the OG Jet Set games, but with controls that feel tight and delicious to actually get your combos in to beat other ciphers. Amazing soundtrack goes without saying. Visuals mimic the OGs but with the flexibility of modern hardware and software to really make it shine as a style and not related to any possible limitations. 

Base game is fantastic, but the modding community and ability to have that exist on PC in an accessible way is also amazing; both in the shitpost factor and a constantly rising skill ceiling to scratch that combo-hungry ADHD brain.

To the bitter end.

And you'll then agree with me that the only thing that matters is how pretty it all is.

One day, also you will have played the game. And you'll know that it's a gigantic exploration of a world so nightmarish, so alien, that nothing makes sense anymore. A slow exploration, a confusing exploration, an exploration that you'll at times despise.

And you'll then know that the game offers a handful of puzzles. Some of those puzzles are hard, some are easy. But all of them will annoy you in some way, frustrate you even. Not having solved a puzzle will frustrate you and solving a puzzle will frustrate you.

And you'll come to know that the game offers a little bit of combat: combat against a small amount of enemies with a small amount of weapons. And that the combat is frustrating, annoying, slow and that you will come to fear it. Hate it? Yes ... I think hate is the right word.

And you'll even come to realise that the game is telling you a story. A story without words. A story that makes no sense. A story that you'll never quite grasp. Because everything is so alien that even the story is too alien for you.

But none of it matters. Because you'll also come to learn that the game is even prettier than what you see here on the store page. It’s pretty because it is ugly and pretty at the same time. Observe my brother!

Yes, you are going to despise the game, scream at it, rage at it, hate the puzzles, despise the exploration, fear the combat. You'll view upon the game with [b]scorn[/b]. Because the game also views upon you with [b]scorn[/b].

And you'll then *see* that you hate the game and the game hates you not because the game is bad, but because the game wants to hate you and wants you to hate it. The scorn *must* be mutual, for love cannot exist without hate and vice versa.

And despite all of this, you're going to continue playing. Because it is just so pretty. Your senses will be so overwhelmed that you'll not feel the torture anymore, you endure, you want even more scorn.

Those are the things that will be. And for us, those are the things that are. We know. Oh yes, we all know.

Become one with us. You know you cannot escape my brother, it's far too late for that.

I see you soon.

review_text:
An intriguing colony-sim/tower defense game with a steep difficult curve created by a solo developer.

I started off really enjoying this game. The colony management aspect of the game is incredibly deep, with the need to manage food, water, and even trash while building defenses and holding off increasingly difficult waves of enemies. Random events, starvation or poor planning often ends up with your village getting overwhelmed and having to start over. But a nice level up mechanic allows you to gain experience to unlock ability chests that improve everything from your towers, to spells, to how fast your villagers work.

My biggest complaint with the game, is that once you've successfully figured out a defensive strategy and stabilized your economy, your offensive options are extremely limited. In fact the game actually punishes you for pushing the enemy back by increasing the spawn rate of hostile units when reclaiming territory at all. While I understand that the idea of the game probably isn't to defeat the "corruption", I would have preferred a goal or some way to finish the campaign. As it stands you can only upgrade your units a limited amount, while enemy increases in strength every night, which basically ensures defeat eventually.

[b]Overall: 7/10[/b]

review_text:
It's tough to give this a binary "Recommended / Not Recommended" review here, but ultimately I think I have to give it a Thumbs Down. The continuation from Asylum was great. I enjoy the combat, even if some of the later brawls were just a ridiculous amount of enemies in single rooms. The rooms where you sneakily take down sentries one-by-one is fun, even if they copy/paste that formula repeatedly in the same rooms. The story is exactly what I would expect from a Batman game, and I enjoyed the inclusion of classic Batman characters throughout. I really liked the idea of the open-world map, and while I think Asylum's smaller map led to tighter segments, expanding that to a full "city" was a cool to see.

That being said, I think the city kinda collapsed under it's own weight. Movement was incredibly unfun. In a post-Insomnia Spider-Man world, it wasn't nearly as zippy enough, nor was it particularly dangerous to move between regions. It just felt like a slog. This was made worse by there being a large impenetrable wall in the middle of map, forcing you to go the long way around constantly throughout the game. It didn't take long to make this feel like a chore instead of an engaging part of the gameplay. It obviously wanted you to interact with the collectibles along the way, like the Riddler trophies, but so many of those require gadgets you get later, it feels bad to try and remember ALL of them to return to later. Once I decided I wasn't going to get them all, I didn't care to stop and explore the map.

This really was just made worse by the Catwoman DLC. Since I'm playing the GOTY version a decade after release, I didn't realize this was bonus content and just played her segments as part of the base experience. She shows up so infrequently, and her segments are so underbaked, it ultimately felt really bad to play her (especially since she had practically no upgrades by the end).

While I did find the story serviceable, I did think the ending was very underwhelming, especially since it cuts right to a Catwoman segment. I felt like I was missing a good ending or something due to how abruptly things resolve. I guess they're hinting at the third game in the trilogy, but it still felt like it's missing something.

I think at this point, you've made your mind up on whether you're playing this decade-old game in a lauded trilogy. It's definitely worth a shot if you want to experience the Arkham games. But I couldn't really see myself returning to this in the same way I might revisit Asylum in the future. Just too much busywork and not enough pay-off.

was made worse by there being a large impenetrable wall in the middle of map, forcing you to go the long way around constantly throughout the game. it didn't take long to make this feel like a chore instead of an engaging part of the gameplay. it obviously wanted you to interact with the collectibles along the way, like the riddler trophies, but so many of those require gadgets you get later, it feels bad to try and remember all of them to return to later. once i decided i wasn't going to get them all, i didn't care to stop and explore the map. this really was just made worse by the catwoman dlc. since i'm playing the goty version a decade after release, i didn't realize this was bonus content and just played her segments as part of the base experience. she shows up so infrequently, and her segments are so underbaked, it ultimately felt really bad to play her especially since she had practically no upgrades by the end . while i did find the story serviceable, i did think the ending was very underwhelming, especially since it cuts right to a catwoman segment. i felt like i was missing a good ending or something due to how abruptly things resolve. i guess they're hinting at the third game in the trilogy, but it still felt like it's missing something. i think at this point, you've made your mind up on whether you're playing this decade-old game in a lauded trilogy. it's definitely worth a shot if you want to experience the arkham games. but i couldn't really see myself returning to this in the same way i might revisit asylum in the future. just too much busywork and not enough pay-off.

review_text:
This game is a masterpiece even during its limited EA content state. Yet, as with any product, it shares moments and design approaches with tinted flaws. Individual people are going to have their unique gripes, and here are mine...

- Gas attacks (e.g. flung by the Gravedigger) are unfairly overpowered. They can be precisely dropped or planted around your current location. Yeah, I know. You have to keep moving, but f*ck me for taking a moment to, you know, shoot an enemy. The gas obviously lingers. Yet most egregiously, they do massive instant damage followed by additional uptick damage. I can't recall a previous game in my library history that has made a gas attack this damn powerful. I hate it.

- The spiders [spinner], are ridiculous. They're weak and relatively manageable if you can anticipate their encounter or manage to find safety in distance. However, they can also just spawn around you unexpectedly (when above ground, cause obviously you'd expect to encounter them within their sewer domain) or dart unannounced around the corner. If you're swarmed by 3 or more, expect to be severely punished, or killed. 

- The townswoman. How is it she can teleport vertically in either a descending or ascending direction without limits? If you spot her, she can be dealt with easily enough and even baited into a vulnerable whiff pose. However, the reason why this character makes my hate list is because I haven't yelled more at anything else in a game (and I am a SoulsBorne veteran) than when I'm fighting a powerful enemy, then suddenly I'm hit by someone who wasn't even on the radar, and confusedly look around to see it was that f*cking townswoman b*tch again! Like, an instant cheap shot move that I didn't even know I was supposed to be ready to dodge. 

- "We're heading to the party and we're going to have a real good time." ~ System of a Down. That is, unless you immediately spawn into a max leveled (skull with long horns) enemy region. Fight and die, or run and maybe only get mangled to the point that you want to die. Oh, the glorious choices.

Okay. Thanks. I feel better now. There are several additional frustrating moments, but mostly become manageable and the sum of the good parts far outweigh the bad.

I've seen some complaints about the gameplay that I just seriously do not understand. I find this to be one of the most entertaining titles I've ever encountered. The mixture of being a single-player extraction shooter, provides light RPG elements, is a roguelike, and provides unique mechanics behind its weapons--is pure bliss, when you're not being swarmed by spiders. 

I bought this game during its Alpha launch before it was released on Steam (so I have far more hours into the game than my profile leads you to believe), and have obviously reinvested into this madness. If you check my achievements for Witchfire, you may notice I've unlocked the same achievements on multiple sporadic dates. This is because I reset them using the Steam console just so I can relive unlocking them again. That's how much I adore this game and showcases what a masochist I apparently am. I don't understand how this game hasn't become more popular than it currently is and sincerely hope the finished product will remedy the lack of current interest. I want this game to inspire similar products or sequels. 

If you haven't played this yet, don't let the difficulty intimidate you. It's punishing. Very, very, punishing. But, it's fun enough that hopefully you'll enjoy yourself even while the game is smashing your face into gravel laced with radioactive hate.

review_text:
If I had to put the priority of the game types this would be most in alignment with assuming you play it in standard / traditional mode and not "peaceful" mode, it would be sim management, tower defense, city builder, godlike.

Sim management, this is almost I daresay the bread and butter because so many things can go wrong.  You don't just build a population like in many city builders.  You have to wait for either nomads to come along, or wait for your sims to have children, and then grow up before you can use them.  After managing to get some additional sims aside from your starter, you need to keep them alive and manage their task types.  Messing up this part will fundamentally screw you over.

Tower defense comes in a very close second, because at the end of the day (literally each day), monsters come to your base, if you don't protect it and your sims, you won't get far.

City builder comes in third, but also only ever so slightly, because it lays the foundation for the rest of your game.  You need to make sure you upgrade your buildings along the way and not just build like a fanatic because see #1 about sims (you don't have a very big population to work with at the start).

Godlike, comes in last but is surprisingly VERY effective for whatever you need it for.  Whether it is to keep regenerating resources or to spawn new ones, or summoning a temporary golem to keep your base alive, this one covers it all in the forms of utility, offensive, defensive and aiding spells.  Problem is, the only way to keep increase your "mana" is to maintain high population (see again #1, sims).

TLDR:  the game is rather intricate if you take the time to learn it and very rewarding once you get a feel for all the mechanics.  Plays like an old school city builder, but with much more depth.

review_text:
4/5

Pros:
- Very adjustable. There's not just a difficulty setting, but a bunch of challenges (hunger, sickness, taxes etc) can be turned on or off fitting your preferred playstyle.
- Artwork. At first I was sceptical, but I came to quite enjoy it. Seasons and weather are nicely done. I like that winter is more dark, and the lighthouse with its waves is really pretty.
- I actually like the food decay + hunger thing. Makes a nice challenge, and cooking has an actual purpose.
- Family helpers. Having my spouse and kids do the watering and weeding is actually so much better than getting a bunch of sprinklers. 
- Aging. The village feels much less static with people dying and people being replaced by younger generations.

Cons:
- Its very woke. I don't mind homosexual couples or them adopting children, but it got to a point where heterosexual couples became a minority and more pregnant men than women walking around - not fitting the 1700's setting at all. I don't mind people wanting to play like this, but I do hope the developers make it as adjustable as they made much else. I would suggest making the third gender optional, another option to regulate who can get pregnant and who can adopt, and for those who'd like a historically accurate game, another option of who can marry. Note to the devs: adding those options would make the game more popular outside the US - there people might feel violated by a historically accurate option set, but it goes the other way round too. So please, make it optional.

review_text:
*I HIGHLIGHT BOTH WHAT I THOUGHT WAS GOOD AND BAD IN THIS REVIEW DONT THINK IM JUST DUNKING ON IT FOR NO REASON*

i didnt think i would be ready to leave this game iv been waiting 3 years for after 7 hours,
there is a lot of good here, but the bad is fundamental imo. i think this game would be a 100% recommend at a lower price

the combo system is too easy
i havent felt very challenged trying to go for combos in this game, my highest combo is only a 3.4m because getting to that number felt really underwhelming and meaningless, your trick timing doesnt need to be precise, you dont lose anything by doing long moves and interrupting the animation, and spamming tricks is slower but there isnt really any punishment for it. i think manuals are a great mechanic for this game, but it also has pretty much no drawbacks, just that after a certain amount of time you cant hold it. these mechanics need a little spice, especially when things like crew battles depend on it so much. and i dont like the way the score multiplier works, leaning into corners and doing wallrides for combo multipliers seems fine because it forces you to do a lot of stuff across the map, but in combination with a limited trick list, it just starts to feel like cheese when you are going for high scores. you pretty much just spam x y b on rails with some jump tricks inbetween until you leaned into every corner and hit every billboard. the combo system feels void of skill and meaning as soon as you fully learn how it works. I love, and still play thugpro for those juicy combos, 14m means a lot more there than it does here. this was clearly designed for a more casual player (which is fine) but it isnt fulfilling to me

some maps are too large and linear
some maps (like the mall) add few exceptions for original lines, and it feels very limiting, the best jsr maps were the ones that were compact and full of different options. i feel like i havent been happy with a map past the mall to be honest. a lot of maps are abundant in some places, and void in others, its as if someone marked a spot to be finished later but just never did. the segmentation of maps feels awkward and limiting to traverse, it feels cool when you just unlocked a new section, but it usually doesnt flow well afterwards

aside from what i didnt like,
the animations are great, like seriously amazing
outfits/recolors are cool
ost is nice
artstyle is executed very well
the story is fine, pretty repetitive after a bit, but it isnt difficult
some characters could be more interesting/memorable but i overall like their designs
combat is eh, needed more time in the oven
different sports to choose from while tricking across all of them feels consistent to one another, whether that be for better or for worse
day 1 dlc is not favorable, but it doesnt cost much

in conclusion,
this game has just enough depth for the casual, but not enough for some others, and i think thats alright. i expected more of this game, but maybe thats just on me

review_text:
TL;DR: THIS IS WORTH PLAYING IF YOU LIKE OTOME GAMES. It is professionally made with well produced music and pretty art. Personally this isn't worth the normal price though! Wait for a sale! (I got both for like 10 bucks I think).

Review: This is a review of boths games. I do this because, as many have expressed here: this is just the first half of the game and it is not (in my opinion) enjoyable without the companion game Edo Blossoms, which gives the actual ending. You should know what you're getting into before you spend the default price.

Why the thumbs down? Because this is NOT a feel good, nor particularly romantic game. I play otome games for the romance man. Heated moments of passion and nice writing. Preferably with a true happy ending. I could deal with tragedy if the romance was super developed... WHICH  IT ISN'T HERE. Not to say there isn't romance at all, but rather the romance that exists is sparse as hell and doesn't affect the direction of events. 

The story, namely the basic historical events of the fall of the Shogun, is what takes front here. Which again would be fine if the story was... GOOD. But it really isn't. Its obvious that the fantasy part was just shoved in there to make it something other than pure historical fiction and is thusly not so well developed. There are so many ways they could have given the player more control or added more tension to the romance. But they didn't. every single thing that happens in this game is anti-climactic.

And if you're waiting for good romance moments in the second... Don't get your hopes up. Reviews here made is sound like this was build up and the next one was full of romance (I love slow burns!) so I was excited.

I was horribly disappointed. I get the impression that the happy endings were meant to be bitter sweet, but it severely lacked on the sweetness part. Like eating a lemon rind when you thought you were getting lemonade.

A lot of this game was boring. A lot of the big events in history were text dumped on you. It's so boring it was hard to sit through the text dumps so I'd walk away and forget it was on (which  is why the play time is so long!) It was a struggle to get through without yawning. This game is older now and pretty much seemed to set off the shit ton of otome Shinsegumi games, so props for that BUUUT.... Let me tell you: THERE ARE MUCH BETTER SHINSENGUMI GAMES. Voltage has one that really tugged my heart strings and did it without some stupid poorly developed fantasy sub plot. And with a reasonably useful lead character, I might add.

So buy it, on sale. If you're bored.

I can really recommend this game, its super cute and addictive

review_text:
Beat the game in 5 hours here's my review and opinion

Lets start with the basics and what i knew when going into the game
- Bonelabs is underwhelming compared to boneworks
- Bonelabs is more like a modding engine then a game
- Bonelabs has "the best" physics

Here's what i felt when i beat the game
- Campaign is alright its like people said underwhelming the campaign is mostly based off of minigames then a actual deep story.
The puzzles in the campaign i often accidentally skipped instead of completing them... Oops?

- The modding integration is kind of ass? It uses Mod.io i already dislike Mod.io for how it always crashes or spits out errors compared to Nexus mods and here it didn't even automatically log in compared to blade and sorcery and it didn't even allow browsing mods. Is that a luxury or something? To browse mods in game...

- The physics are honestly not that crazy for my feel i often even disliked it.
your character is fully physics based getting hit by a fast moving object in the chest will cause you to be flung by it which makes sense. HOWEVER my character would REFUSE to climb as he would be kicking the walls for no reason and i also managed to soft lock 5 times during my 5 hours. (Technically 7 but i managed to glitch out of the softlock) The reason why this happened was cause my hand somehow clipped into the wall and there is no way to reset it once that has happened apart from making it pick up a weapon while its going crazy

In general you could say this is a negative review.
And you WOULD be correct however the reason i am giving it a positive is mostly cause i lack knowledge of any actual good vr campaigns then anything else if i played a FUN and GOOD vr campaign then this would easily have been a negative

So here's the positives
The campaign allowed a decent variety of approaches. I often found a side route that i used to either get rewards or skip a part of the game which was funny in my opinion it felt like doing something unintended

The world has a nice vibe. 
I always liked watching boneworks and labs for its world, its got this hint of virtual reality X realism that makes it fun to watch and explore FOR ME atleast.

The death mechanic is cool! 
Sounds weird but i like the fact that you can be dying and still survive by killing a enemy just like in borderlands! Makes battles a bit more intense when everything slows down and you HAVE to kill a guy or you die.

Avatars with their own skills.
While in this game it was more of a gimmick then a actual "yeah we give you the tools figure out this puzzle goodluck" even the puzzles where you did have to swap it was plainly OBVIOUS what they wanted you todo so like. Eh... But apart from that its a cool CONCEPT, now to see it actually get utilized properly in a more interesting manner.

now the negatives.
The physics for me were Super wack. I don't know if i had something wrong but if a item would be on the ground i could not crouch and pick it up as my hand would move away from where i guess you could say my feet are and into where ever the void is. So i would have to avoid crouching physically and instead crouch using the joystick then walk back a bit and THEN grab the item like ??? You have a force grab but like cmon i just want to hold the items in a specific way while doing it with just one hand. And of course my hand would often clip through objects for reasons that i cannot explain as i still don't know how it happened

Controls were fucked too
I would get very off putting movement like getting stuck behind a wall and then launching forward
Very "ice like" movement i would slip and slide around. Holding a item would make it try to calculate how i grabbed the item through my hand position AND compare both hands which made a bunch of items like a bat break whenever i tried to swing it compared to swinging it with one hand. Also you always needed a start up with running in order to jump otherwise you would do the most pitiful jump known to man. Running is also confusing as its barely noticeable if you are running or not (That's probably a me issue though as i prefer physically swinging my arms in order to run in game then standing idle)
THOUGH after i played a bit i got used to all this so its just something you gotta get used to i suppose.

Now after ALL this i am not done with the game yet. As there is infact a port of boneworks for this specific game, and there's also a bunch of mods which make their own campaign that's the one advantage bonelabs has its a game about modding. So who knows what could be created given enough time

review_text:
TL;DR.
If Dark Souls and Destiny 2 merged in the best possible way — you’d get Witchfire.
Incredible gunfeel, moody atmosphere, and endless replayability. Worth every cent.

 Gameplay

The shooting feels phenomenal — easily on Destiny 2’s level of precision and impact. Every weapon hits hard, and just firing feels satisfying.
Each gun comes with unique perks and upgrades, keeping combat fresh. The balance is perfect: no overpowered builds, no useless ones — you’re always just slightly weaker, which makes fights intense and strategic.

It combines Destiny’s silky-smooth gunplay with Dark Souls’ deliberate rhythm and risk–reward feeling. The result? Combat that’s both thoughtful and thrilling.

 Balance & Challenge

Witchfire keeps you alert at all times. You can’t just rush through — timing, movement, and cooldowns actually matter.
Bosses hit hard but fair, rewarding focus and adaptability. The game punishes carelessness but never feels unfair — it’s always your fault, and that’s what makes it fun.

 Visual Design

Absolutely stunning art direction. Even the base area looks beautiful — you just want to stop and take it in. Every environment feels handcrafted, detailed, and alive. The atmosphere is dark and oppressive, but not horror — just the right amount of tension.

Exploring

Exploration is genuinely rewarding.
Hidden doors, events, minibosses, puzzles, and those little glowing fireflies leading to loot — there’s always something new to find. The game constantly rewards curiosity and careful observation.

 Sound Design

The sound work is exceptional.
You can pinpoint enemies by footsteps, locate secrets through distant whispers, and feel the tension build through ambient noise.
Play with good headphones — it’s immersive on another level.

 Verdict

Witchfire blends Destiny 2’s perfect gunfeel with Dark Souls’ challenge and atmosphere.
Every system — shooting, balance, exploration, sound — fits together flawlessly.

review_text:
Okay so, in the interest of presenting a fair review lemme just list the things I liked about this game: the music. The music was super good. Okay that's it. Now I'm going to tell you why this game is actually pretty fucking terrible!

So I heard about how great the story this game had was and how I'd fall in love with the characters and when I started, I super wanted to! I really did! But they're actually shit! Neil and Eva are fucking terrible dicks and the "funny" moments aren't really funny, they're just long and fucking boring. Neil is supposed to be the "silly guy with a heart of gold" but actually he's just a giant nerd who is a dick, and his "jokes" and "humor" mostly amount to shit Sheldon would say in The Big Bang Theory. Eva, on the other hand, is supposed to be "a tough guy with a heart of gold" but actually she's just a cold bitch who takes everything super seriously. Basically the two main characters are cardboard cut out cliches that you'd see in a middle schooler's first story.

On the topic of stories, this one is a fucking garbage fire! So, if you don't want spoilers, probably stop reading now! Okay, you've been warned, so here it is: the big twist that Johnny had a twin brother named Joey who died when he was like five is something I'd personally expect from one of M. Night Shyamalan's lower tier movies. There's nothing in the story that hints at this twist and it comes out of left field; it seriously feels like the writers wrote themselves into a corner and couldn't figure a way out so they just pulled some middle schooler shit.

Hey, notice how I've brought up middle schooler twice? This is something I like to call foreshadowing (something this game could've done with, bazinga!), because hey, guess what? I'm a teacher so I read a lot of shitty stories! What does this have to do with my final gripe with this game? Well, mostly its gotta do with the treatment of what I assume is autism (its never explicitly said that River and Izzy have autism, but I'm gonna say they do because of CONTEXT CLUES); I work with a lot of autistic and special needs kids as a teacher and holy fucking shit I've never once seen anyone treat autism like the characters do in this dumb fucking game! They act like its some sort of shameful secret and that they dare not say the name, lest God strike them down with it. Literally no one talks like this and it makes it very hard to connect with these already terrible characters.

Also the ending implication that they're all just in a ~simulation~ like Johnny is dumb and I called it like 30 minutes into the game once I fully knew the premise.

Oh also clicking to walk is dumb and I really wish they would've told me I could use the arrow keys to move instead of finding out I could do so by trial and error.

In conclusion, this game blows, you're idiots for saying the story and characters are good, and the controls fuckin' suck. Peace out nerds, go play a better game like Rakuen!

review_text:
Left 4 Dead – A Nostalgic Dive into the Origins of a Legendary Franchise

The Left 4 Dead series holds a special place in my heart. After recently diving back into Left 4 Dead 2, I decided to play the original for the first time, and I’ve got to say—it was a strange but truly incredible experience.

While the sequel includes campaigns from both games, there's something unique about playing the first installment on its own. It’s fascinating to see how much the series evolved, yet how well the original still holds up. The gritty, suspenseful atmosphere that made the franchise so iconic is fully present here, delivering that same heart-pounding tension I remember from years ago.

And of course, the original cast of survivors still shines. Their chemistry, dialogue, and the desperation of their journey make the story unforgettable. Whether you're navigating dark corridors or fending off a relentless horde, the experience remains gripping from start to finish.

review_text:
As a retro hockey game, it works pretty well. Feels like an old Nintendo game. As a modern game with a meta structure for replayability, it falls pretty short. The game also feels like it wildly missed opportunities to embrace it's theme. 

It just feels very shallow. I realize it's still early access, so maybe there's a lot more coming, but there just isn't that much going on past the core gameplay. There's only about 4 skills unlocked with about 4 more you can buy, but even they don't feel terribly different. Hit the puck off your opponent's face or hit it off your teammate's face, the end result is pretty indistinguishable. Despite the game's aesthetic, the gameplay pushes very little past what is realistic. There's no fireball shots or barbarian whirlwind attacks, just some minor puck manipulation. 

The decision to go with a rogue-like path structure over a "league" format is kinda mind boggling. Lose even one time, and your team is gone forever. It doesn't fit the sports theme, where occasional losses are expected even for the best of teams. There is a create a skater mode, but no ability to use it in the campaign; you are stuck playing the same character each time. There are hints of a storyline involving him being a golfer playing hockey, which I found impressively unoriginal considering all there is to work with. 

Just so many missed opportunities, and so little to ultimately stick around for.

Upgrade your weapons by collecting pointless objects, or by doing pointless side-missions -- don't worry, there are two different types of side-mission for maximum entertainment value. There's some attempt to invoke nostalgia for 1980s action movies, but they forgot to take the good parts of those movies, and instead just put in horrible dialog, neon colors, and music that is surely in violation of the Geneva Conventions.  Adding insult to injury, the cut scenes attempt to invoke nostalgia for 1980s action movie games, most of which were shoddy cash-grabs in which the pixel-art "cut scenes" were the only tie-back to the movies these games were based on.

In conclusion, I'd recommend burning your money over playing this game.

review_text:
To save time, I'll summarize the experience I had with Pathologic 2 in bullet-points. These will cover points of contention I initially had with the game (and how they quickly turned into features which improved my experience) as well as the "best parts" of the game as a whole.

Learning Curve: I had Pathologic sitting inside of my library for nearly three months before I decided to play more than 30 minutes into the story. Before you gain an appreciation for the slow-burn timing of the game, it's going to feel somewhat agonizing. However, once you immerse yourself in the story and characters, you'll actually feel pressed on time: As though the world is moving too fast for you to keep up. Combat mechanics are straight forward but asset management takes some getting used to - The latter being essential to succeeding on a playthrough. 

Writing and Storytelling: Only second to *maybe* Disco Elysium and Knights of the Old Republic. Nothing short of fantastic, as long as you take your time to appreciate it. The story is *extremely flexible* too, with your actions having drastic consequences on the story depending on your dialogue options. What's unique about Pathologic 2, is that the consequences are *on-going* in the story, not something that arbitrarily effects a set-ending as in Disco E or KOTOR. You are altering the story, cover to cover. Also, the doesn't spell out important decisions or comments you make with obnoxious "persuasion check" or tacky coloring. Like all real-time conversations: Once it's out there, it's out there and you have no idea how it'll turn out.

Atmosphere: The game has aged amazing, given when it was made. The atmosphere can be terrifying and tranquil depending on where you are. Interactions with the characters will leave you with a sense of sonder - Craving more and more insight into who they are and what they might be thinking as they interact with you. You truly feel like an entity separate from the world around you. In the best way possible: You feel utterly out of control and helpless. More playtime rewards you with a lessened sense of helplessness, encouraging you to master the game and your playthroughs.

Overall, the game stands as one of the best titles I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. A great gift and recommendation to people who enjoy storytelling and crave that feeling of emptiness upon completing a game. A feeling which beckons you back, again and again, because you know there's nothing quite like it out there.

review_text:
I don't have much to say besides that Hakuouki is a classic that must be played by all otome game lovers. I don't really understand why they split the game into two parts at all, so keep in mind I'm talking about the whole game (both halves) when I say this. 

The new characters are really charming, got my gripes with some bullshit storyline aspects in some of them both new and old actually, but they're amazing. Switching from other otome games to this I really felt this as more involving at least character-wise. Like for example Code:Realize's story is way better constructed than Hakuouki's but the characters aren't as layered as Hakuouki in the long run (and here I'm also speaking of the sequels/alternate stories), so the romances turn a bit too cringy and cheesy for my liking, because of how "perfect" (in different degrees, I really like Saint Germain and Impey, but Finis took the crown =w=), most of them seem to be, while characters in Hakuouki aren't dislikable by any means, but they got flaws, like Kazama's cynicism, Okita's sassiness and emotional dishonesty, Souma's tendency to always self-guilt, Sanan's ability to not talk and get misunderstood often (though some of his grey morals really ain't helping either) etc. 

This is also one of those old-fashioned otome games that tend to not be made as often anymore, where you have to really struggle to get the guy you want by using the trial and error of multiple choices adventures, you don't have a main menu where you can choose a route, and I really REALLY miss that gameplay aspect of it. (Edo Blossoms does but it's assumed you played Kyoto Winds which is where the work is mainly focused on)

Another thing I really like is how they made it easier to obtain all CGs and endings, not by save/load files that you had to make yourself at convenient places, but by allowing you to directly load the chapter you need with the stats you need. There's some charm in figuring it all out yourself, games like Heart no kuni no Alice heavily rely on save files, but that can become often tedious and most Hakuouki's endings aren't that worth it to go to that extent in my opinion (besides the Good ends obviously, with some exceptions, mainly Okita Souji. *insert a biased cough here*).

Some downsides would be the already mentioned bulshit storyline threads, like sometimes I just feel like the writers had no idea what to do with certain characters so they went on crack one day and were like "ah yeah, this totally makes sense!" (Hachiro and his whole arm situation comes to mind right now, like what. why. how??, Shinpachi to me was another problem, but in the opposite way, while Hachiro's route tended to be complicated and eyebrow raising af, Shinpachi had almost nothing going for him besides a "big bro/little sis" dynamic between him and Chizuru and while that doesn't necessarily have to be bad I also wondered why the story needed to be told in the first place besides just ticking him off the checklist of available samurai bachelors). 
That said, the second downside is Chizuru herself. While not entirely aggravating at all times, she unfortunately joins the dull, useless rank of otome heroines that expresses the wish to improve but she never does. Probably one of her best versions was in Yamazaki's route, where she expressed how while she found she was bad at fighting, she tried her best to fight in different ways, like using her medical skills and I could really see how hard she tried, besides just being the guy's emotional support as she's usually reduced to. I liked her attitude when in pair with Kazama or Okita too, maybe those sort of personalities just make her twitch enough to show that she's got character, which is always a plus for me lol.  However I think most of the guys and the story make up for it enough, especially if you're a history nerd or have interest in Japan's last samurai time period. 
 
Anyway, the game (+Edo blossoms) ain't that expensive at the time of this review, so I really recommend trying to go for it if you like otome games but never had the chance to try out Hakuouki. Also excuse my chaotic review, I'm really just writing this out of nostalgia and wanted to express myself somewhat. I might edit this later on. 

PS: I hope Idea Factory will stop milking this series. Unless they localize stuff like Hakuouki Reimeiroku and all the other Hakuouki mini games lol (Idea Factory, if you're reading this *wink wink*). But if they don't stop i'm sure we're gonna fall back into it like the trash we are. lol

review_text:
I really, really wanted to enjoy this game. It just felt like it wasn't actually ready to be released. 

The unique factor about that attracted me to this game was the generational aspect. Yet, the NPCs get married to random other NPCs so quickly that you don't even have time to romance them. I wasn't even able to stop the wedding, despite standing there and insulting the bride through the entire ceremony. There also weren't enough characters available to romance at baseline, and I didn't want to get started with a legacy game with a second choice character. Interacting with the characters was very flat and didn't offer much to keep me interested in learning about them. They each have three traits, but that didn't really seem to affect anything about their contributions to the game. 

It was also extremely difficult to survive. There was not much available to forage and the hunger bar goes down quickly. Food also decays after a certain time period in your inventory. I'm a cozy gamer and the stress of having to worry about dying/my game ending led me to turn off both of these functions. But it was either all or nothing and then there wasn't any challenge at all. 

I really just wanted to request a refund and move on without having to leave a "bad" review, but because I played over 2 hours, my request was rejected. The main issues I had with the game aren't things that would be obvious with only 2 hours  of game play. Now I'm stuck with the game, so hopefully these are issues that are fixed in the future. 

Positives: the music is beautiful, I loved the sound effects of the NPCs, the emotes are fun.

review_text:
For those with a short attention span the TLDR is:
Some good mechanics and Ideas, lore rich with a well written narative. Had alot of fun with it with friends in coop. Nice range of ships and races to play. Horribly monitized with a huge chuck of the features behind paywalls with alot of forced grind and a huge amount of pay to win features and ships. So much so its more like a hidious mobile game with predatory slotmachine like lootboxes, so those of you who at risk with gambling or have small children who want to play, then this game is not for you. I have put alot of hours into this game and have enjoyed alot of the elements and if it wasn't for all the lootboxes, would likely recommend

For those of you still reading, thank you.

Pros:
*Excellent Story elements with a nice enough blend of the different series enough to please most fans (Unless die hard)
*Nice ship choices with some good refitted models for those who love their chosen series
*Well designed and plentiful loot options (Excluding pay to win items)
*Graphics have been updated well over the years to still warm your gpu up despite the aged engine
*Enjoyable mechanics with some excellent but rather simple gameplay for the space combat
*Great range of abilities for each of the specialisations with good build options for your character
*Huge range of choice when it comes to factions you can play which matching shipsets for your chosen race
*Good range of cosmetic customisation, rarely see two alike.
*Devs do sometimes throw you a bone with some free items, which is always nice
Cons
*For a free to play game, its incredibly expensive with some packs costing as much as £300 for a couple of ships. Owners are whale hunting hard.
*Lack of parental controls to block in app purchases on the website
*Much of the best loot to be got is from lootboxes which have slotmachine like random chance drops so those of you with a gambling addiction or have younger kids i recommend you steer clear
*Alot of fear of losing out mechanics used here, Waving it in your face that the guy stood next to you just got an epic ship you can only get through a purchase of such an item or a ridiculous grind.
*Ground combat mechanics are incredibly clunky and without any polish since release
*Ground missions also just feel like busy work, just grindy variants of actions that just take time ("Go here talk to him, walk here press this and then come here stand on this and kill these")
*Confusing number of currencies, alot of which are not interchangeable and some which can only be acquired through lootboxes.

With all thats good about this game, from its amazing stories and wide range of choice for things. Too much is spoilt by the greedy store. With all the talk about regulation laws coming to lootboxes I think this game could potentially suffer in the future as they rely too heavily of the lootboxes for everything. I just feel a fairer system would go a long way to making this game so much better, as if you wanted to get every item for a character you would literally have to remorgage your house and with the lack of any droprate information being readily available either I feel it lacks transparency too.

review_text:
Survival Tips for those looking to pick up this game

 - Speed is always better than power, because stun locks make everything one-sided. This also applies to you. 
 - The healing amulet is your friend
 - The shield is your good friend
 - The roll is your best friend.
- Healing amulet + Belt is the game's internal easy mode as it means you can't die unless you're really bad at dodging. 
 - Combat for stronger enemies is the really boring process of roll-attack-repeat. This is probably what's causing people's complaints for this game. It's slow. Especially when it comes to area hazards where you have to burn them away, and then wait for the fire to die down. There are trinkets to counter this, but, until you get them, its a lot of waiting. 
- I managed to beat the game fairly quickly once I switched my build to shield + dagger. The shield is great and even works on bosses in ways that make them stupid easy. The dagger's speed lets you get in hits without getting countered, but the range means you'll have to space and time your rolls so you're close enough for a hit. 
- If you want to use magic, you can...but only if you like constantly going into menus to restore your MP or swap to another consumable wand. Magic Sucks. Get the Knife.

Overall, the game is okay, but I wouldn't call it great or even very good. Its short, its simple, its awkward, and its the kind of game where you're constantly looking for the quick kill on otherwise mundane enemies and bosses.

review_text:
Fairly simple action game that's somewhat on the short side but is bursting with charm. Visuals are top-notch. I especially like the giant monster girl boss art. Gameplay is pretty fun. The story however is predictable and nothing special, but there are giant monster girl bosses. More games should have giant monster girl bosses.
Combat is quite good for how simple it is. Equip weapons and/or spells and press button to use. For the most part (boss mode has some special attacks when jumping) no fancy combos, special attacks when crouching, jumping or dodging, just swing your weapon or cast your spell. There's a fair variety in weapon and spell types with different attack speeds, reach, damage and status effects which when combined with the accessory system that allows you to further affect those offensive as well as your defensive capabilities leaves a plethora of approaches all perfectly viable. Experimenting with different builds throughout the game was pretty fun. Enemy design is done well and encourages that experimentation with various builds; you can't always just run up to all the enemies the same way, attack and back off, a somewhat common fault of more simple action games.
