review_text:
I should start by saying that I really don't want to write a negative review of this game, because parts of it are very good. The Art, which everyone has already touched on is one of the best uses of particle effects and lighting that I've seen in a 2D game, and the level design is, for what it is, actually very good. I did enjoy myself when exploring, both while going through the first time, and when going back for all the chests that I skipped (There's a reason to do so, it's explained in game). 

Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the combat, and for a game that is so heavily based around it, it's a deal breaker. To put it simply, it feels as though the players move-set and the enemies where designed for different games. The player has a simple move-set, with slow weapon swings even on fast weapons and a dodge that has I-frames but also a very long recovery, which indicate that the game is one based primarily around spacing and avoiding enemies with similarly long windups and cool-downs. 

Many of the enemies however didn't seem to get the memo, and attack so fast that in the time it takes for some of the player's slower weapons to swing, they can finish the recovery on their last attack, start up a new one, and finish it before the player can hit them. This more or less results in a combat system that encourages not skill, but finding the cheesiest possible strategy and then spamming it regardless of how boring it is to play, and make no mistake, standing out of range of enemies, hiding behind a shield while the enemies get killed by spinning swords isn't fun.

Perhaps this kind of clunky combat would work if the game was based primarily around avoiding enemies, and indeed many horror games achieve success in this way quite well, but this game is a different beast, as it has fairly involved 2 or 3 stage boss fights, in which the sub-par combat is left to fend for itself, devoid of any good level design to hide behind.

To compound this, the game has a fairly significant number of smaller design issues that make it quite frequently a chore to play. On that front, the rest of this review is just going to be list of my more minor issues and some of my ideas on how they might be resolved.
[list]
[*]Due to the way healing items are distributed, I sometimes found myself farming healing items, since I had no where near enough money to buy them. Just add an Estus flask, or failing that, at least make healing item drops more consistent in late game areas. I know it's a bit of a cop-out to just steal a mechanic, especially one from Dark Souls but From's been using it since Dark Souls 1 for a reason.
[*]A fairly early game item allows the player to get a full heal more or less when ever they want so long as they have access to a portal ([spoiler] I'm talking about the purifier [/spoiler]), but requires just standing there for upwards of 40 seconds in the later parts of the game. A mid game item that gave the player a full heal when a portal is interacted with would quite handily resolve the issue.
[*]The game's combat often requires the player to switch equipment and weapons in order to deal with changing circumstances, as many enemies are markedly easier to fight with certain weapons/spells/passives. Loadout hot-switching would be very useful, or failing that, at least the ability to favorite items in the menu such that they always sort to the top
[*]Checkpoints only save the first time you pass them unless you fully unload the area. While I understand why someone would want to avoid a save in certain circumstances, not being able to re-save at all is very unhelpful when for example, fighting a boss and wanting to go in with a specific loadout that makes the boss more manageable. An easy solution here would be making it so one could reactivate checkpoints manually after they've been activated.
[/list]

Samorost 2 is pretty cool. People will go on and on about it, out-snobbing each other with cries of BURRR THIS IS A FLASH GAME IT SHOULD HAVE BEEN ON NEWGROUNDS, REAL GAMES FOR HARDCORE GAMERS ONLY PLEASE!!!!, but ignore them. They're dumb.

I love the way Amanita Design makes their games - a lot of love clearly went into the worldbuilding. You're a little man in his PJs exploring floating mushrooms that have been uprooted from the ground and left in space! Your spaceship is made out of a discarded can of weenies! There's a sewage tank and the water stains look like a pastoral farmscape! So many little beautiful details that are worth the price of admission alone.

I'm not so much a fan of the puzzle-solving. Most of the puzzles are fine and are nice little breaks from the art, but sometimes they are a bit of a pain when trying to decipher context clues in a small Flash window. (FYI, this game was released ten years ago and it holds up well, though it's hard to see things sometimes.) Sometimes, there's areas that you need to click on that weren't clickable before and the game doesn't bother to tell you whether or not they're activated. It's not a perfect system, but it's fine.

Samorost 2 is uneven but overall fine. If you want something with more difficulty, check out their games Machinarium and Botanicula. There will be a sequel for this one coming out very soon, too.

review_text:
It really sucks to have to say I don't recommend this game, but it's just not very good. The campaign is a complete mess with what feels like the majority of it being a series of forgettable mini-games. What little that has actual care and effort put into it is surprisingly good, but those moments are few and far between. The first hour of this game sets expectations very high but the rest simply does not deliver.

The developer's excuse is that Bonelab is supposed to be more of a modding platform or pseudo-engine like Garry's Mod or Little Big Planet, but those games give players full access to the ultimate tools for creating anything and everything. They can be excused for having a lack of built-in content because the ease in which players can create their own has resulted in an overflowing cornucopia of free to download addons. Bonelab lacks built-in content and its mod tools suck, as they lack functionality and are not intuitive or fun to mess around with. This has caused a content drought, which is a death sentence for any game attempting to survive off community creations.

At the end of the day what we have here is a game without enough valuable content to warrant the price tag, and that's pretty much the end of it.

game is reworked into a pile of unplayable shit with a huge favouritism towards killers with unbalanced p2w killers and perks that render gameplay into nothing but frustration and more unbalanced bullshit

killer miss their swing? nope, its lingering hitbox so they flail their mouse like a special ED kid with the class pet in their grasp to do a 360 hitbox for that half second and hit you regardless of accuracy or precision

killer knocks someone? gen pops - pop goes the weasel perk

looping the killer and need visual queues if they'll turn around? they walk backwards at max speed and catch you anyways

anti camp mechanic to prevent being camped on? doesn't fill up regardless to if the killer is 20m 10m or even 5m away. 

want to attempt on the hook with default 4% if you're aware that you're guaranteed to die or go into 2nd stage before anyone saves you that game? they reworked it so you cant attempt unless under specific conditions

pallet rescue or flashlight rescue? reworked so that its frame perfect the very second they finish picking them up although they can counter flashlight by literally looking up or down or facing any structure to prevent shining it in their face.

use the structure to hide yourself? half the killers give dumb visual highlights and audible noises anyways. if you're in a bush some can just see your outline anyways. behind a wall? ghost face and micheal myers just reveal you anyways and they find you although they couldn't see you for shit under normal circumstances

survivor knocked and on a pallet? accidentally throw down the pallet because the option to heal is practically not there because of camera angles without the use of a med-kit

is movement created equally? FUCK NO! killers don't have a slow or fast vault or different interaction speed, they all have the same rapid speed which only quickens with perks or depending on the killers ability too. survivors have to literally have to interact with things in the right direction and angle or else its a slower version of what should be your fastest movement while sprinting although half the stuff you interact with are smothered by a corridor meaning you cant get the fastest vault and costs you the chase all while most of them have ranged harming abilities which go through walls, double dash which catches you immediately and also rapidly fast vaults anything you can vault or some dumb structure where if you drop, vault or loop there's a shortcut designed purely for the killer to just take and close that distance immediately since they suffer no drop penalty or can traverse a small gap that survivors cant. Killers have their movement tied to any direction as well meaning they can face any direction they want and not suffer movement loss while survivors have their movement tied to their facing direction so when it comes to turning corners or evasion during chase especially by looping them around something circular you go to turn and your character has to turn around completely before moving the other direction so if its small they catch you immediately

audio of any use? to a degree but audio is purely one thing other than lobby music, the music still blasts as a survivor and half the stuff like entity or terror radius completely shut out any useful audio like hatch when you're last survivor with no way to reduce the other less important audio. I don't need the loudest thing playing being killer radius when I LITERALLY CAN SEE THE FUCKER CHASING ME! it also obstructs the stealth killers a lot since there's literally audio that they make when in stealth but its so smothered by lots of awful and excessively useless noises and music 

fairness? none existent... vampire and DND killer literally have everything a killer can have and more. they have ranged attacks that go through walls, don't have to vault anything since their flying abilities are busted and have some way to counter pallets by preventing them from being thrown down. id say they don't have stealth out of everything but i'm pretty sure every killer is considered stealth now with perk selections giving them 0 terror radius under certain circumstances - dark devotion, trails of torment, machine learning, tinkerer and furtive chase - killer perks

What I DO enjoy is that murdering everyone just gives me a sense of.... contentment? Murdering the same person 5 times in a row the same exact way to forcibly grind out achievements however, makes me wish I too was burned alive by a malicious satanic six year old with a tricycle that controls like a drunk two legged horse in a one wheeled wheelchair. I kid you not, it's unusable, and spoiler alert- it's the big "ultimate" reward for doing all your "chores" AKA- Fetch Quests.

The best/worst part about this game is the achievements. I feel like the developers released a game they knew was at the most 8 hours long (if you're playing blind like me, and by blind I mean literally blind and you've just consumed copious amounts of alcohol) then decided to pad the playtime by forcing you to kill half the people in the game 5 times, drive 10Km with that god awful tricycle, and oh yes.... playing for 40 hours...... #IdleLife

AGAIN I ACTUALLY LIKE THIS GAME! Seriously- for some reason wasting my time with this game just fills me with nostalgia, or that may be the psychosis talking. I hear the second game (oh yes you heard right they made a part 2 and part 3, mwuhahaha have fun future me!) takes place in a mental institution. review_text:
First of all I want to say that this was my first time playing a Hakuoki Game, 
so I can't really speak of that disappointment many experienced players speak of, since my own experience was a completely different one. 
Someone mentioned that "there wasn't even a kiss scene" which is true as far as I am aware of (only played three different routes so far one main and two of the treasure box routes), however I kind of feel like reminding people to think of the time (or era) and place. It's not like today, where you're already smooching each other's faces and dropping your panties on the second date or something. Though, even today (as far as I know) Japan isn't all over that public affections thing, so that's something to keep in mind when playing a game like this one. You need to learn to appreciate the small things like the character of your choice choosing to hold hands with you or just standing closer to you than would be considerate "normal". That 'complaint' of many people was something I really wanted to get off of my chest here. However, like I mentioned before, this was my first time playing a Hakuoki game so I'm unable to say if the rage over there being too little romance in the game is justified or not.

For someone like me, who was new to the world of the Hakuoki Games, I can say that it's totally worth to buy the game. The plot is nice, the characters amazing and I found myself often lost in the game for hours without realizing it. Don't let yourself be discouraged by the whole "there's no romance so don't buy it" comments from actually buying this game. Since, the only two things I can really complain about myself is the fact that at some parts the voices quited down a bunch so I couldn't hear them over the music (when they were mostly murmuring to themselves, so maybe that's partly intentional?), but then there were voices like Shinpachi's at times when I felt like I needed to plug out at least one of my earphones to make sure I wouldn't take the risk of possibly going deaf from his next line. The second part is more of a personal thing than a real flaw of the game. The treasure box supposedly gave you more possible romances with more characters, but there were two characters I had a huge interest in for they could possibly have opened up two completely new paths or points of views to the game and situation the MC was in, but instead I found myself thinking that we were offered characters that only differ slightly from some others in personality even if the whole stories behind them are all interesting in itself. 

Long story short, if you're new to the Hakuoki games and keep the time and place of the setting in mind in regards of the 'lacking' romance (seriously, I found myself wondering where said lack was after reading some reviews and then playing the game myself 'cause it's subtle, yes, but plenty) then go ahead and buy this and most likely enjoy it, asking yourself what all the negative reviews are about. 
If you're an experienced player of the Hakuoki games then maybe you should stick to said negative reviews of those other experienced players and wait for the "full" game to come around or just.. buy this to support the idea of games like Hakuoki coming to Steam or Hakuoki and the people behind it anyway? 

Either way, can't agree with the people who say to not buy this game
since instead of feeling frustrated I ended up looking forward to the next and how all the MC and I as a player experienced so far wil carry over into a new experience and story.

review_text:
[b] The game is not worth it anymore.  [/b]

Base PSO2 was fun, story was actually good with decent delivery and plenty of content, amazing soundtrack, lots of variety in gameplay, game modes, combat and the amount of photon arts, different areas and location, and even miscellaneous stuff like inviting NPC or player avatars to quests, recognizable cast of characters even if they're just NPC or bosses (Never thought I'd be saying this but I miss you Dudu and Monica), lots of concert varieties, events, decorated lobbies, interactions and such which [u] NGS lacks [/u] despite having a more fluid range of movement, better character models, good looking graphics, freeform house building and good soundtrack, it honestly can't compare to what base PSO2 has to offer.

They even went so far as to remove the SG rewards from Base PSO2 Challenge Quests and moving it to NGS game modes (Which is reasonable to a degree imho), but it isn't really much fun and engaging compared to PSO2 Challenge Quests.

NGS had its good moments in UQ/raids but thats only that, aside from Fashion which is where most of the players are mainly doing. it honestly falls way too short compared to the original PSO2. The lack of content, variety of Photon Arts and in gameplay itself, there have been some reworks on classes but there's hardly any difference. Game is already at lvl 100 cap and the amount of PAs hasn't even increased and to make things worse, were still in the same 4 regions where we began. The story at all isn't really that good even despite having an interesting concept, its way too short and the delivery of it is really lackluster and way worse. All updates are focused on the microtransactions, mainly fashion items.

I've stopped playing around 3 years ago however, I kept in touch with the updates via my friend who got me into the game and after said 3 years, I would honestly say that its honestly a great idea to do so considering the game still hardly has any content and such. Either just stick to playing base PSO2 or play Warframe, Dragon Nest, Black Desert or any other MMO would be much more worthwhile, any other games even could do in my honest opinion as harsh as it sounds. Its sad to see that a game I've loved end up being like this.

Don't get me wrong I really love PSO2, but NGS? [b] No. [/b]

Ngl at this point, I'd rather just see a remake of Phantasy Star Portable & Portable 2 Infinity in a newer game engine or just a HD port with better multiplayer features in all honesty.

- The graphics are cute 
- The game is challenging
- Its an excellent city builder and a good take on the god genre
- The tower defence aspects keep the game moving
- There is a nice difficulty curve to work your way through

- larger map size (it can feel too restrictive sometimes)
- Maybe some monolithic structures that give a bonus to your current map and a small bonus to other maps in the world, they'd cost a lot to build, it'd be a great endgame task
- Animal training, would unlock mounts and pack mules for your gathers
- Maybe some sort of magic training for villagers that could be cool

Message to the dev: Make some DLC for the game or an expansion pack or something, people will pay for extra content if its there and decent.

I'm personally a rather interrested book reader, I read alot of books in my life and..I do NOT paly games to read a story, I'm sorry but when I play a game I want to have influence on the game and that is exactly what the game lacks, you have zero influence on anything, you seem powerless as you are just walked trought the checkpoints of the game, you collect notes on stuff, but there seems to be no impact on anything and than I see all the praise and awards this game gets and I wonder if half of those are not faked.

review_text:
Just Cause 4 – Bigger, Bolder, but Not Quite Better
Rating: 8/10

Just Cause 4 builds on the explosive sandbox foundation of its predecessor but stumbles slightly in the execution. While it introduces impressive new weather systems and visual upgrades, it loses some of the charm and chaos that made Just Cause 3 a fan favorite.

Visuals & World – 9/10
The fictional country of Solís is visually stunning, featuring diverse biomes like jungles, deserts, and snow-covered peaks. Dynamic weather effects — including tornadoes and lightning storms — are genuinely impressive and add spectacle to the mayhem. Technically, it’s a leap forward from JC3, with sharper visuals and more environmental variety.

Gameplay – 8/10
Rico still has his grappling hook, parachute, and wingsuit, but now with customizable mods that allow for more creative chaos. However, the destruction feels less satisfying, and the mission structure becomes repetitive. The emphasis on faction-based territory control doesn’t fully land, often breaking the game’s pacing.

Story – 6.5/10
The plot tries to go deeper into Rico’s past and the mysterious weather tech, but it’s largely forgettable. Characters lack depth, and the writing doesn’t carry the self-aware energy of earlier entries.

Sound & Polish – 7.5/10
The sound design is solid, especially during weather events, but the game launched with noticeable bugs and AI issues (many later patched). The overall experience feels less refined compared to the more cohesive fun of Just Cause 3.

Verdict:
Just Cause 4 is a visually superior game with ambitious ideas — especially the extreme weather mechanics — but it doesn’t recapture the pure, explosive joy of Just Cause 3. It's still a fun sandbox if you’re in the mood for destruction, but it feels like a step sideways rather than forward.

Score: 8/10

review_text:
Bear in mind, at the moment of this review the game is in early access and has already gone through 1 major overhaul of stat system and progression. Will likely update when game fully releases.

First of all, this is a single player game. No playing with friends, that is probably the only "bad" thing I've come up with so far but I can't really say it is bad because I can not imagine a way to make this multiplayer anyway so I won't consider that for the review.

The graphics, sounds and environment are amazing. The design of enemy models, weapons and random events and things you find around the map are amazing (currently using RX7700XT to play 2k and goes smooth). 

There will be moments where your heart is racing during progression because the zone you are into is giving you the middle finger and I am all for a game that doesn't grab my hand on everything. And the nice thing is that once you think it is getting easier and you progress even more it gets harder again...

The game has a very very wide range of spells and weapons that you can mix and thankfully now there are easier ways to get them upgraded quicker (shadow orbs seem to spawn more often, used to barely have one sometimes now i've some sitting on my inventory waiting for me to finish the current one).

The upgrade system of weapons is straightforward; kill enemies, get new power, use new power X times and kill X enemies, repeat. But the effects you get from the new powers get more and more fun for a lot of the weapons. Spells are just "hit X enemies with spell" which is honestly fine. Nothing convoluted, no need to rack your brains there.

Leveling works like any souls game, you kill enemies and they drop witchfire that you use to level up. Easy, but this will change the maps layout of events too which is a nice addition to not make this feel like routine.

The new stats are more obvious to what benefits you get from them, feel free to experiment a bit since there are stat reset items in the game. They also added beads which make nice interactions with stats and weapons to improve builds even further.

Again, this is in early access right now but so far it has been worth every cent I spent on it and more. If you want a first person shooter survival game where you burn the wicked and the heretic this will do.

review_text:
This game has a unique Save game feature. If you die, you are punished by getting a debuff. You can't remove that debuff. If you reload your old save, that save will have that debuff. All of your saves will have that debuff. 

That is amazing and not seen before. However there's some other major issues with the game that prevent people from experiencing that save system and prevent the idea from being added to other games.

There is no Save & Quit. There is no Save & Quit. What is that? There's no harm in adding Save & Quit. It only benefits the experience of the gamer.

You can't quick save. You save at various undisclosed points in the game. You discover these, seemingly randomly, by inspecting every item in every house. 

That's too punishing. No Save & Quit. Going to miss an opportunity to save. I die i get a debuff and have to reload a save from possibly 60 minutes ago.

The save games use GMT to list the time they were saved. Not a big deal
There is no Cloud Saves. THAT is a big deal. Pathologic 1 has cloud saves.

Beyond saving the game. The performance of this game has to be one of the worst I've ever seen in recent years. Even on a 4080 and 7900x. I have to set graphics quality to minimum to stay above 60fps most of the time. The game is poorly made. I don't know why so many 3D games use Unity when Unreal has always been the better of the two for 3D. The small added cost of the engine is worth it and always has been worth it. Heck Unity doesn't even provide customer service or properly support their engine, but Unreal does. You get what you pay for and the product here with Pathologic shows they didn't put the extra work needed as they cut costs on the engine by using Unity and cut costs by not giving enough time to create their engine.

I'm seeing the same stories in this game as found in the first game. Like the burning of the person at the stake, then the people watching. As they walk away they all say 1 by 1 they should've done something to stop it. In Pathologic 1 I murdered all of them for murdering this innocent person. In Pathologic 2 I can't do that as the save system prevents trying it, but more so I have zero rep and can't trade and need to trade to get food to survive. It makes me more passive and a watcher of the story created by the devs.

A unique save system, poorly designed and a badly implemented game. I feel Pathologic 1 is the better game, however graphically Pathologic 1 for sure shows its age and this one is easier to play only for that reason.

This game has zero voice acting. You're reading what everyone says. They do talk, so there is voice acting, but it's random words it seems, so it's just voices, no acting.

Ultimately the lack of Save & Quit is the #1 and only reason I can't recommend this game.
If there's a way to mod Pathologic 1 to make it look modern, I'd for sure recommend that.

review_text:
*Some JC3 to JC4 comparison talk
Get it on sale. Otherwise, no.

Pros

-If you mess around with the settings, you can get some rather beautiful landscapes. The draw distance for foliage and such is not great, no better than JC3 I guess, but this doesn't really kill the pretty views. It's a different lighting compared to JC3, not as much glow and maybe more shadows but certainly beautiful in their own rights. The lighting change between regions can be off putting but it's quick so eh.

-Some abilities from JC3 are just standard in this one (no more having to do challenges to unlock abilities). 

-The map is massive (the rivers are small). It's a large map with a lot of verticality and areas with updrafts near cliffs (not a lot though).

-The tethers easily make this game. 3 different tether load-outs each able to customized (activate via tap/hold/automatic), 3 different tether types (balloons, tether, and boosters). Each have mods and can be used in clever ways, balloons to make cover from aerial attacks or to just fly away those threats, the boosters can just launch people away BUT they can overclock to be used kind of like in JC3, and the tethers....well, they can do a power yank otherwise the same. I've had a blast realizing I can attach boosters in the right spots on the mech to fly around with it with perfect control, mild control with a flying limo.

-The freedom of movement. I have been enjoying this game mainly for this fact. I got the DLC, get when on sale, and even without the jet boost and the hoverboard it's still crazy fun. The tether to pull yourself around in the wingsuit is as satisfying as ever.


Mixed:

Challenges Gone:
-Challenges are pretty much gone. Replaced with "pass through x going x kph", "pass through x in x", "wingsuit through 3 rings in x time", and maybe something else as dull. They're easier to do which is nice and do enough of a type and you can unlock tether mods or wingsuit mods. I think some other stuff but nothing I can remember right now. So if you liked challenges, sorry. 


Wingsuit:
-The wingsuit has been reworked so it feels less "flighty". Because when flying with a wingsuit, one doesn't want to be weightless like a bird in JC3 but as a real Rico. 
-If you get the DLC to have the jet wingsuit f you will be sad to know that you cannot take off from land or sea and the minigun is gone replaced with missiles instead. NOTE: If you have all DLC you can just use the hoverboard to surface fast and then wingsuit when jumping, you will get a good amount of air.
-Airbraking looks and handles awful, if you stall too long you just cancel out of the wingsuit. It just felt more sensible in JC3
-The missiles you get are not lock-on and do not even go where you exactly aimed, it's an area attack with 4 missiles with decent aoe. The problem is attacking air targets or anything not exactly near a large flat plane making you have to get pretty close to hit with a missile or to kind of cheese the aim to get one missile to hit where you want.

-Destruction is mixed. But I think it's because the physics are just wonky, you'll notice it a lot with tether+reeling things. Not everything breaks in a way that looks right, a feather light giant satellite dish for instance...

Cons:

-The game is jank. I had to reverify my files, a common need, because my DLC didn't appear in the black market drops. Thankfully, only had to do this once.

-No pistols. Stuck with 2 weapons. Resupply!

-The map is massive, but it's still barren. The devs get how to do landscapes, but cities they just cannot seem to understand that they need more. Solis is 80% barren and 100% black hand everywhere. The game is kind of a good example of getting the big picture but not all the small details *map still pretty.

-No distance is reflected when setting a waypoint or tracking an objective. Just kills the scale.

-No running.

-The "cutscenes" are just awful. I've messed around with my settings but I just cannot fix the sharp light, lip sync issues, and character faces looking awful. They don't look bad in game, even though the cutscenes are in-game (maybe that's why?). They are just poorly optimized

-Tom Sheldon is not Tom Sheldon, the character looks nothing like him.

-The tethers (yea they suck too). The game's combat really wants you to go fast and move. So when trying to make quick tethers to boost helis/tanks into the atmosphere (because I have no explosives), sometimes the tethers just don't deploy fluidly, I have to hold to deploy and let go to deploy the end of the tether, same as 3, yet it gets buggy. I'll try to do it and Rico just doesn't shoot the end of the tether so I have to press the button again and it just cancels the tether out. Sometimes I'll try and I'll reel myself into certain death. It's just as if the game cannot handle wanting to shoot 10 tethers in succession.

-Chaos is meaningless (from how it was). Chaos can be gained from pretty much anything, and in fact, you get it more from doing ANYTHING other than blowing up enemy structures. There's no sense of accomplishment from destroying bases as things will just repopulate (kind of like when you beat JC3 and you can select to do that but you don't get to choose). 

-So little to blow up, no grenades or c4 to even do it with. They're just gone, enemies have grenades but you don't. The lack of this forces one of your weapons to always be an rpg or another reliable explosive. Or using tether mods for balloons and boosters to handle them. While you never need to blow up anything big anymore (sad) I'd think you'd still want some explosives to help with that tank or helicopter making you hate life.

-The water near or inside Solis looks so awful. Waterfalls look anti-climatic, calm river just goes into a gushing waterfall, they all do this. The mixed to this is the water outside is really nice. So I am not sure how much of this was deliberate but couldn't be realized how they wanted perhaps.

-Wanted Forever. If you get on alert, honestly, just call a pilot and fast travel to the same spot, it cancels the alert lazily... Can't really escape by air because the helis go the speed of jets and the jets are already shooting at you, go on the ground? They will hunt you down hard. I will go into the mountains and just as they call off the the search there's always a heli just a moment away from actually spotting me. It makes doing some things just a pain.

The enemies, so many enemies and they all know exactly where you are. And they all have grenades and decent aim and blend into the environment because the devs didn't give them a highlight or outline silhouette to help you distinguish them beyond their muzzle flash or all the red and green dots aimed at you. It gets worse when you have to stand in a small area to complete an objective and the enemies just keep coming and building up

-Resupply is tedious beyond all reason. Do you need to resupply your 2 guns and get a vehicle to bail out? Easy, call in 3 separate pilots and wait for 3 drops one by one to do so :) 

Rebel Drops / Pilots: (Kind of sucks)
-Rebel drop and fast travel beacons have been reworked into Pilots. Pilots can call down ONE thing or fast travel you to a location. Afterwards it's a several minute cooldown to use them again. You can have a good amount of pilots, so no more having to get more beacons, yay. BUT pilots can only call down one item at a time AND pilots wait for each pilot to drop off their supply one by one. I haven't timed it but, opening comms link, going to resupply, opening their options, selecting the option, selecting to call it in, selecting where I want to call it in, waiting 7 or so seconds to fall (+ however longer until it is settled on the ground), then grabbing it. Only to wait 7 or more seconds again to get my next resupply drop or my getaway vehicle. You can sit in the comms and this does speed the timer for the resupply and pilot but...why not make it that fast always?

review_text:
TLDR: The game is finished, not abandoned. Are there better similar-themed games? (Not quite like this one) Yes, but you wouldn't be looking at this one if you wanted to pay their price, or, you already own them. So buy this at 50% off and have some fun.

Lots of reviews complaining about the game being 'abandoned.'
The game was finished. It's as complete as initially intended.
BUT, could it use some more updates to round some things out? Sure it could. It'd be nice to get those updates. But without them, (and especially on sale, like, 50% off) the game is a great value. It has an amazing progression system, but I will admit that after (384 hours) the basic gameplay is getting a little stale. So, I started trying to 'trap' the corruption and do more risky gameplay things to make things more fun for me. It would be cool if we got some new updates to round out end-game boredom, but like I said, there's still a lot here and the game is in a finished state. It's like if a game leaves EA and it's now '1.0' status. Some games continue to get content updates after 1.0. This one 'hasn't really' gotten those updates, and we might never get them. Doesn't mean this is a bad game. Just weird that I'm seeing negative reviews for lots of complaining reasons that don't make sense.
The game is a little slow on higher-population built-out areas. (I like to run it in the background while I do other things, which slows it down even more.) But I still like coming back to it now and then to progress the progression perk system.
Are there better Colony-Survival-Management games out there? Yes. And they're generally more expensive. review_text:
Bonelab is a wildly ambitious VR title that pushes the boundaries of physics-based interaction in virtual reality. Developed by Stress Level Zero, it acts as a spiritual successor to Boneworks, expanding on its ideas with a mix of experimental levels, sandbox gameplay, and modding potential. Rather than focusing on a traditional narrative experience, Bonelab is more of a platform—a physics playground that encourages players to discover and shape the world around them.

The campaign, while present, feels more like a guided introduction to the game’s systems than a self-contained story. Each level presents a different theme, showcasing climbing mechanics, driving, puzzle-solving, and combat across various stylized environments. There's a surreal, almost dreamlike flow to the progression. The body-swapping mechanic, which lets you change your avatar's physical traits on the fly, adds a unique twist that’s tightly integrated into gameplay. However, the campaign can feel fragmented or unfocused, as its primary purpose is clearly to prepare players for the open-ended experiences that follow.

Where Bonelab truly shines is in its sandbox and community-driven content. The game offers a powerful physics engine that supports a massive range of interactions, from wielding medieval weapons to flinging enemies across rooms with makeshift contraptions. It thrives on emergent gameplay—moments that aren’t scripted but born from the systems interacting with each other in unpredictable ways. The inclusion of mod support from day one means the game evolves constantly, with the player community contributing everything from new levels and characters to completely custom game modes.

The VR implementation is solid but not without its challenges. Movement is fully physics-based, which makes for immersive, grounded gameplay but can also lead to awkward climbing or locomotion quirks. There’s a steep comfort curve; newcomers to VR may find some of the motion nausea-inducing, especially during high-speed sections or more chaotic environments. Still, for experienced VR users, the tradeoff is worth it—few games offer this level of tactile control and player expression.

Combat and traversal feel more refined than in Boneworks, but they’re still rough around the edges in places. Melee fights have a satisfying physicality, and gunplay is responsive and detailed, but some mechanics—like enemy AI and environmental interactions—can feel inconsistent. Fortunately, the game’s modular design and constant stream of user-generated content help smooth over these issues, providing fresh challenges and tools long after the campaign ends.

Bonelab is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be: an experimental, mod-friendly physics simulation wrapped in a VR framework. It’s not trying to compete with tightly scripted action games or deep RPGs. Instead, it hands the keys over to the player, saying, “Here’s a box of tools. Go break stuff.” While not for everyone—particularly those who crave structure or are sensitive to VR motion—it’s an outstanding example of what sandbox VR can look like when it fully commits to player agency. For fans of Boneworks, modders, and VR tinkerers, Bonelab is a chaotic, fascinating, and ever-evolving experience.

Rating: 8/10

review_text:
Strong start, the plot and me got lost in the end. 
     Story started compelling but quickly became rinse and repeat of the same thing. Isaac! i mean Jacob! you gotta get here right now! oh shit the door is locked and you need a keycard. Then 15 minutes of walking around aimlessly looking for a keycard. Got it? ok now go through the door. Fight for a little while then do it all over again. The lack of the locater beacon thing from dead space makes it very hard to figure out where to go sometimes. I found myself lost for many minutes of gameplay, it all starts to look the same after a while. Very easy to get turned around.
     There is a stealth portion of the game and it is very VERY boring once you get the mechanics down. You then spend the next 40 minutes sneaking around just in case the same type of enemy is present in your new areas. The overall variety of enemy is somewhat lacking, I think only a dozen total different enemy types exist, including one off bosses that you only see during specific moments. The weapon variety is pretty equally poor, two different shotguns are distinguishable only by the number of rounds they hold in one magazine. There are two different pistols and one assault rifle which is really the only gun worth getting in the whole game. The upgrade/progression mechanism is nicely streamlined, you only ever have to worry about having credits, no power nodes or other crafting components which is very nice. The guns do seem more powerful when upgraded and feel good to shoot, again both good things.
     The Story is something like an above average fan fiction combining dead space and resident evil and it's only ok if I'm honest. It starts as a boiler plate space pirate/merchant picks up cargo and follows a gripping arc for about the first third of the game. It quickly devolves into meaningless nonsense and wishy washy motivations interrupted with flashbacks and thinly veiled twists. The universe is well thought out and very cohesive but the main story arc got a bit lost along the way.
     Overall I would recommend playing the game but save yourself some money and buy it on sale or humble bundle, don't pay full price for it. I know I would be deeply disappointed if I had. It does a good job at tasting similar to dead space but still falls quite short of recapturing the essence of the original. The gameplay and movement are very close, but the atmosphere and overall uncertainty are lacking. I feel that the weaker melee of dead space made everything more stressful as you fought mainly to keep the enemies at bay. This game almost incentiveizes you to be within melee range. The dodge is very powerful and you have almost no fear of the enemies once you master it. If it wasn't for my childlike love for the original dead space title I don't think I would have enjoyed this as much. Prefacing my review i want to write, that i am not really horror fan, but that didn't stop me from playing all of Dead Space and most of newer Resident Evils. While having quite good fun from them.

Now, going back to the meat of this text - Callisto Protocol.
It was hyped as something akin to Dead Space. Setting was there, scenery, welp, maybe too. Graphics? IDK, it was stable, looked decent, but i don't care about them since this framegen shit. Game ran pretty stable at high FPS and crashed only once.
What was not there? 
- any kind of dread (literally i was not scared for even a while),
- any real challenge (i was literally selling all my ammo and healthkits to upgrade weapons and it was still easy)
- any enemies with good gameplay design (most of enemy encounters is just spam with melee and finish of with gun/ start with gun for some advantage. some enemies are just more annoying than challenging - bugs that jump at you, heads in cocoon that grab you, even final boss was sheit)
- any real character building (no real motives why characters would start trusting eachother and grieve after death)
- any good combat system and weapon upgrades (it's just repetitive, generic and boring)
What else was there but i would like it to not be here?
- DLC (it makes bad story worse and puts together worst parts of the game)
- main character slowing down from sprint to walk - just because. add to that too much narrow spaces to squeze through that slow you down
- linear game design - i despise it. when there was any fork i always went 'good way' first and then had to backtrack to collect stuff i left behind
- cheap jumpscares
For this game to be worth playing there would need to be major overhaul of most of its systems and some rewrite of story or addition of plot points. And it still would not be worth it's price, as this is game i finished in 11h while 'licking walls'.
I don't regreat getting it at discount, since i wanted to see if it was as bad as i hear. And it was. I really hoped to be proven wrong, since I itched for good game of this kind, and nothing scratches it since years. Sadly, too many bad decisions were taken during development.

The game takes place in feudal Japan and follows a group of five assassins who are tasked with overthrowing a corrupt government. The game received critical acclaim for its challenging gameplay, detailed environments, and engaging storyline.

The game's visuals are stunning, with beautifully rendered environments and detailed character models. The characters are all well-developed, with distinct personalities and motivations that make them feel like real people rather than just game characters.

I have to admit I knew going into this game that it isn't the type of thing I'd normally play, but the amazing reviews and tantalizing plot premises demanded my attention. In the end though, I wish I'd stuck with my gut feeling... Feel free to downvote my review, but if you do please leave a comment as to why you didn't find it helpful. I'm trying to provide an honest and meaningful review, so if there are issues with it I'd really like to know!

[b][u] TL;DR [/u][/b]
There's very little game play, and what there is, is mostly bad. The story has promise but becomes overly predictable and gets tripped up by out of place humor. The graphics and audio work for the game but are nothing special. That's not to say it's all bad, again the story really does have a lot of potential and the repetitive puzzles are fun the first few times. 3/10.

[b][u] In-depth Review [/u][/b]
[b]Gameplay:[/b]
There really is not much gameplay. Besides clicking your way through episodes and then solving the same type of puzzle in between said episodes, there are only a handful of cheap, cheesy game like moments tacked on. While that is frustrating enough in itself, the lack of gameplay is worsened by the terrible interface, the whole game is pretty clunky, I can't believe how off the mouse detection seemed at times. 

[b]Story:[/b]
The story is the only saving grace for this game, and even it has some really weak areas. The serious story elements are actually quite good and can make one stop and think. However, those moments are almost always ruined by the asinine dialogue of the main protagonists. Supposedly you are controlling two doctors, but they sound much more like middle school children. I don't mind having some comedic relief especially in such a somber story, but the balance is off and it usually feels way out of place. Additionally the last half of the story felt quite predictable, it starts of pretty decently, but as you delve further in it becomes fairly easy to see what's going to happen next. It's possible I was just making lucky guesses, but I think more likely it was some cliché elements and excessive foreshadowing. 

[b]Presentation:[/b]
As for the artistic aspects of the game, I'd say sub-par at best. The old-school graphics are fine for the purpose of the game, but a lot of it is very ugly and plain looking, sepia tone is definitely overused. There are a few cut-scenes with a different art style and there is just no redeeming quality to them either, no unique artistic style, nor charm, nothing. There's also a sequence with a “closeup” of one of the doctors and rather than create a new sprite for the closeup it appears they used the same little sprite and just magnified it, causing the whole sequence to look really terrible. I don't understand how the music receives so much praise, while it's not terrible and fits well with the game it's repetitive

[b]Summary:[/b]
I have hope for the story. I really think it would make a great premises for almost any other form of media, and honestly hope to see a well done book, movie, etc. with this premises at some point. From a gaming standpoint though there is almost no redeeming quality. I give it 3/10 for the following, I encountered no bugs, the story does manage to get it right about half of the time, and (honestly) I did enjoy the first 3 or 4 puzzles.

Echoes of the Plum Grove is a cool life simulation featuring a novel generational system extending beyond typical farm gameplay. Aside from constructing a farm, one also prepares the farm for winter and makes lasting decisions that shape their family's future.

Strengths:
✔ Adorable papercraft visuals with sweet touches
✔ Intricate generational system: individuals age and die, leaving an inheritance
✔ The combination of farming, town life, and survival keeps things interesting
✔ Dynamic seasons with actual repercussions

Cons:
✖ The start can be trying for newcomers to the series
✖ Less romance interactions than other farming sims
✖ Occasionally sluggish pacing

For life sim fans seeking long-term inspiration and a dose of survival, Echoes of the Plum Grove is a good recommendation!

review_text:
For as long as we have existed, there has been one fact of life that has stood the test of time: kids love dinosaurs. Always have, always will. So for TT to make a game based on the Jurassic Park IP, a series all about said dinosaurs, is a no brainer. I've only ever seen the first film and played 1998's infamous FPS game Trespasser, so I have very little connection to the series beyond that, but that didn't stop me from having fun with this game. 

It's your fairly typical LEGO affair, covering the first four films in the series. There's a large collection of characters that are unlocked by completing each film's levels, although if you asked me who most of them were I'd be clueless. Each minikit represents the bones of a dinosaur, which become playable once you unlock them. The stud multipliers are very easy to get, with me being able to achieve x3840 pretty quickly, which makes purchasing everything a breeze.

When you unlock different dinosaurs in each level, you can customise them to your liking, making entirely new species to roam around the park with their own abilities which are convenient for Free Play. I even made one based on my cat. The standard 1M stud level is present as always, although this game's catch is that you won't actually be able to play it until you reach 100% completion. Instead of that as the bonus, you will find bonus levels across the different parks, although most of these are just taken straight from the actual levels.

There may be some expense spared in some areas, but I'm sure this is one park LEGO and Jurassic fans alike would be happy to endorse.

review_text:
This game is very entertaining and is able to run well on many systems, however, due to the number of effects, unoptimized configs and lockdown of graphical settings, it is not as customizable nor optimized as older Source games, such as Half-life 2, Counter-Strike: Source or even Team Fortress 2.
At this point, pretty much all Source games support OpenGL rendering, which is much faster than the proprietary renderers such DirectX (or Direct3D), even the decent DX9 and 8, however, this support is only included for Linux (and other operating systems similar to ones using Linux); while I would definetely understand gatekeeping this performance (and security) to make people more attracted to free operating systems, I do not believe this is something done for activism/raising awareness, rather just a decision for convenience, which costs basically 75% of performance for Windows users and, even if the Windows version also used OpenGL, Linux, BSD and other free oprating systems would still vastly outperform Windows.

I see this game to be vastly superior to its sequel (Left 4 Dead 2), containing more cohesive and better visuals, better performance, better characters and better campaigns. The darker visuals are ideal to the slower (when compared to Left 4 Dead 2's) gameplay.
Left 4 Dead lacks some additions later implemented into Left 4 Dead 2, however, not to its detriment. Such as lack of melee weapons, less zombies and less special infected, it makes Left 4 Dead much less of a zombie killing sandbox and much more cohesive with its lore and ambience. The disparity between difficulties is not obvious and might be subjective, but Left 4 Dead is less ridiculous than its sequel in relation to that; they both are definetely unfair, technically, considering you're one man (or four if you count your team) fighting hordes of zombies, but zombies in the first game are less janky, lesser in number, while still being threatening since you have no OP melees.

review_text:
Let me preface this by saying I love shooters, melee games, ARPGs and Soulslikes.

This game is actually terrible.

Levelling is extremely boring and weird. The enemy count increases a lot while you only get a tiny bit of HP and/or stamina if you choose optimally. The weapons do not deal more damage while levelling, yet the amount of enemies on the screen increase 3-5 fold while their HP also increases.

I had a 'long range' bolt-action rifle and could not do more than 5 damage to enemies far away. Enemies took about 300-600 damage. Consistently shooting headshots up-close with it still required 5 hits to kill most enemies at Level 11/12. What the...

I don't see the point in levelling, nor do I see the point in playing the game at all, with skills and melee on such massive cooldowns and weapons shooting wet noodles.

It honestly just feels like such a huge slog. There's so many weird design choices in progression that it actually makes me feel annoyed just writing this feedback.

Imagine levelling Souls gain 10 times, gaining no character power and like 20% extra Souls gain, while scaling the total enemy HP per map to like 9x. This Souls can then be spent on... Making the game even harder while not gaining any weapon damage? I don't even know what devs were thinking with this weird enemy scaling.

The game itself feels very floaty, slow, arcadey with huge AUDIOVISUAL indicators for enemy attacks. 

I don't recommend.

review_text:
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. 
When NGS first came out, I was actually pretty excited - I thought it was really fun. If I remember correctly, it would've been a few years after BOTW had came out - so the hype for that was still pretty fresh in my mind.

That being said, within just a few weeks / months, content completely ceased up. There was nothing keeping me from playing or logging in. And with NGS now getting all of the love and PSO2 now been effectively KILLED(1) off entirely, the entire game had nothing for me to do at all.

Fast forward a few years. I've decided to reinstall the game, and wow, um, I guess it has content? Sort of?

The game didn't slow down on cosmetics(2), but the story is as much dog water as it was when I last played. 


This next part is not meant to be a 'review'. It's more so a vent I wrote up, that I'm going to paste here since It carries over a lot of my thoughts.

- Bulk UI

Navigating the UI is a fucking chore. With 8 to 10 menu buttons (I don't remember if its 8 or 10, but it's definitely something on those lines.) cluttering the bottom of the screen, and with each menu itself having a plethora of things to fucking pick from, it’s an overwhelming task to locate anything specific.

-Overwhelming Pop-Ups and Tutorials

Nearly every single login will tell you something. Every. single. one. nearly. When I returned after a year or two, I had so many NPCs that could not stop telling me things that made literally no sense to me.

- Tutorial Accessibility

For those returning after a break or who may have inadvertently skipped a tutorial, revisiting these guides is a challenge. Although there’s a feature to access old tutorials (I think.) actually finding it or the specific information you need is like searching for a needle in a haystack, compounded by an excessive amount of text. There's so much fucking fluff. The only way I could find a reliable tutorial on getting my grips with the game was to replay the beginning of the story.

- Storyline Quality

The narrative quality is dog water. Actual dog water. The story lacks anything that makes it worthwhile going through, and the characters fail to evoke any sense of connection or believability. Yes, the game is a science fiction universe, but the world-building doesn’t resonate or feel plausible at all. I know this is a very heavy anime game, but that doesn't excuse the characters from being nothing more than just caricatures of anime girls doing anime girl things. What I've experienced of the story so far was: Threat appears --> Kill threat --> Characters have a party -- > Loop. The same thing each time. 

- Economic System and Shopping

The game’s economy is absolutely fucked up. The only thing I can think that comes close is Gaia Online's economy, and that was due to a fucked up mistake they've done their best to fix. The value between items is just...w t f. Some items are fetching tens-of-thousands while others in the same scratch (which means, the same % of getting each item) reach into the millions. Unless you're some reason addicted to this game and want to spend at real money to HOPEFULLY get things you can sell, you can forget about making any money. 

Actually, you literally cannot make money unless you spend IRL money. You can't get a private shop (unless you can with Star Gems. Not sure.)
I don't know how PSO2 was doing by the end of it's life, because I wasn't around for it, but back when I played back in... I think It would've been 2013 ~ 2016 on JP servers, I  actually had fun with the OG PSO2. It was alive, well, thriving. 
Weapons in that game felt like they were varied, but In NGS  weapons don't feel like they have a playstyle to them at all.


Citations:
1 - Technically, PSO2 Is still alive. You can play it, there's just no one to do things with. 
2- The cosmetic team and content team are not the same. I am aware of this. I am not faulting or putting any blame on the cosmetic team, but the fact they're making so many cosmetics for a game that barely has any players OR content, is wild.

review_text:
I got this game gifted a few years ago and I finally decided to play it. I was pleasantly surprised when I saw that the topic of autism - specifically Asperger's Syndrome - is brought up in this game and depicted in two women. I am a woman who has been diagnosed with Asperger's and the way River is written felt very authentic and relatable to me. I was diagnosed rather late at 18 years old - although I could've gotten diagnosed earlier, as it was already brought up by teachers in elementary school, but my parents didn't want me tested. This late diagnosis has left quite a few scars on my development, and this aspect is also emphasised in this game. 

Apart from Josh from Watch Dogs 2, I've never seen another character in a video game who is meant to be on the spectrum. That was very nice to see and aside from that, the story as a whole is very good and touching. The music and world design really enhance the atmosphere. There are also quite a lot of funny moments. Only downside is that you have to control your character by clicking with your mouse for 95% of the game but for whatever reason, you can finally move around with arrow keys in the last 20 minutes - this should've been a thing from the very beginning. Overall, a very fun and emotional experience that you should look into. I regret not playing this game way earlier.

This is not a good game.

I'm several hours into this thing and I have to say it's more frustrating than anything. The puzzles aren't intellectual, they're stumble around until things work out sort of thing. They're a very few clues to tell you what order you have to do things. The visual aesthetic is fun, but the monotone colors and unrelenting textures means you can miss a lot very easily because nothing stands out. I've missed an important tunnel several times just because it's a small hole off to the right and I just didn't see it.

The puzzles give you vague clues of what you're supposed to do, but on the whole it's mostly just trying everything until something works.

Combat is useless. The enemies are pretty dodgy as well. I've had them disappear, and then reappear behind me when there was no way they could have been there.

The most frustrating thing for me though is as I'm going through the game I'm wondering what the point is. Who are these idiot aliens who have designed even the most simple systems to be complex puzzles that they have to solve. It's no wonder they don't seem to be doing very well. This game is attempting to create "difficulty" with its save system, but all it does is create frustration. A limited-save system to add difficulty makes sense for games where you complete one level at a time (fail the challenge and you're punished by having to waste time, e.g. Dark Souls), but for an open-ended game, where you can't predict how much time the player will waste, it's simply inexcusable.

A shame, I really expected it was better from the dozens the positive reviews I read before trying this out!

review_text:
Samorost 2 is short. It's going to resonate differently with each individual. I personally found nothing particularly fantastic about it. The original Samorost sets itself apart by using close-up photographs of various objects, mostly forestial, to create the illusion of large landscapes. Samorost 2 relies more on a traditional hand-drawn approach, and struggles to be as visually interesting as the first game, which is available for free on the Amanita Design website.

Samorost 2's music, as usual for an Amanita game, is top-notch, and one of its highlights.

There are only a handful of puzzles in the game, and the design is problematic in certain areas. For example, the point-and-click interface allows you to click anywhere on the screen to interact with any object - yet for certain objects, it requires your little hero character to be standing in a certain area, making it easy to dismiss something as non-interactive when in fact you were just incorrectly positioned.

And the very last puzzle of the game is a frustrating chore - it's a timing-based puzzle, already something I don't care for, and if you get it wrong, which is highly likely as it takes a bit of trial-and-error to figure out, you have to grind out the game's previous puzzle to get back into the situation needed to try your luck again. The previous puzzle involves collecting animal farts. Of the 90 minutes I played the game, I spent maybe 30 minutes collecting animal farts. That kind of pisses me off.

So I can't really recommend the game. It's not exciting, challenging, or visually appealing enough to merit even a short playthrough, and spending money on it seems silly. It should have been a free flash release. Skip this and play the excellent Machinarium.


4/10

I want to enjoy this game, the concept is pretty sound. Unfortunately a lot of your ability to micromanage situations is based on your god abilities. Most of which you cannot have readily available on the quick selection tabs to handle the various situations that arise. 

Your villagers seem random in their affinity to help out. Normally I see my villagers attacking nearby monsters, other times they simply run back and forth in the same small section of land until the monster kills them. 

The corruption is a neat concept, an enemy village that slowly spreads. Unfortunately this too you're not suppose to fight in any meaningful capacity, it seems to be there only to hinder your ability to expand. If you decide to try to fight back the corruption they begin to fight back in constant spawning groups. You can slowly manage this with an absurd number of towers, but it feels the only genuine way to combat this threat is immensely unsatisfying and without reward. 

The game is too random with it's meteor shower events, I don't mind losing when I have the ability to learn from my mistakes, but to lose simply to bad luck feels as if I'm robbed of my time rather then enjoying it. I had 2 back to back meteor shower showers that devastated a good portion of my production and then further cemented it by spawning several fire elementals that I could do little about with my limited god power pool having been drained by trying to mend my buildings. Population is also a meager struggle, which is again limited further whenever the game decides to kill off a number of your people due to random meteor showers.

There's a good game in here, but some design choices seem to take away from the fun to the point it's no longer enjoyable rather then add to it.

Nice game for anyone who likes the LEGO style games. Personally I like the LEGO games and have quite a few in my collection. There are elements of combat in the game but nothing too difficult and an endless supply of lives anyway. The game is more about exploring and collecting items rather than fighting. There is a story that vaguely follows the film franchise with some comedy elements included.

On the positive side the game is large with lots of areas to explore. The game has 4 different worlds to explore. As with all LEGO games there are a large number of characters to select.  

On the negative side there is no ability filter for this game which is found in other LEGO games. This makes selecting the correct character harder than it needs to be. I also found the auto selection of characters in free play could be improved to select all the required characters for the level. The game also contains a few bugs that I had to search and fix manually. Fortunately there are a few pages out there with details of each error and fix. 

None of the bugs were too bad and I would generally recommend this game for those that like LEGO games but a more recent LEGO game will have game play improvements.

I spent the whole time playing and repeating the same phrase to myself, "What happened?" I had no idea that Square Enix had made a fourth Just Cause game until I found it on sale.

Instead, players now have to complete tedious quests like guiding prisoners who walk too slowly to an extraction point. There are even demons in the game now. 

Not only has the gameplay been downgraded, but the graphics have also taken a hit, making it look like a bad console port. 

I would highly recommend that if you're looking for the Just Cause experience, you return to the third installment in the series. That's what I did, and I enjoyed it very much. 

Overall, I would rate the game 2/10 and would not recommend it.

review_text:
Blood Dragon is easily the best game Ubisoft has ever made. A beautiful blend of 1980's nostalgia, from the tron-inspired graphics, to Michael Biehn voicing the protagonist with an endless supply of one-liners, through the over-the-top setting of the apocalyptic future of 2007 (after Vietnam War II). The story and Easter-eggs are a blast. 

The game starts out strong with an intro having you empty a chain gun into an enemy base while music is blaring. A Predator-handshake follows not long after. You soon find yourself facing wave after wave of cyber-soldiers. The fun continues like this all the way through the end.

Pros:
++ Fantastic retro story, characters, and setting
+ Great audio, including SFX, 80's action-movie music, and voice-overs to accompany the game
+ The one-liners are hilarious, and frequently break the 4th wall, especially about how boring the collectables are in every Ubisoft game
+ Fun weapons which become increasingly over-the-top overpowered (in a good way) as you gather collectables for unlocks
+ The trailers for this game were also hilarious nostalgia trips. 100% recommend watching them all before playing

Cons:
- Difficultly is a little too easy. I'm fine with playing an intentionally over-powered super soldier but the AI is dumb and its extremely rare that you will feel even a little bit challenged.
- More on the above, the "bases" located around the map that you have to liberate are just way too easy. It's always the same thing- kill 10-ish enemies (or more if you set the alarm off) to liberate the base. Very little variety in this activity; you really have to force yourself to tackle the bases in different play styles to make your own fun
- Collectables are usually just sitting somewhere unguarded. Would have been nice to tie them into actual side missions or something

review_text:
Echoes of the Plum Grove, developed by Unwound Games and published by indie.io, is a beautifully melancholic and surprisingly complex take on the farming and life-simulation genre. At first glance, it looks like another cozy countryside game about planting crops, befriending villagers, and enjoying quiet days in a small town. Yet beneath its soft, watercolor aesthetic lies a system of survival, legacy, and mortality that turns this gentle world into something far more meaningful. It begins with a shipwreck that strands your character on the shores of Honeywood, a rural island village surrounded by forests and fields. What starts as a simple story of rebuilding a life slowly evolves into a generational saga in which time passes, families grow, and the choices you make ripple through decades of village history. The result is a game that feels both intimate and enduring—a blend of comfort and consequence rarely seen in its genre.

The foundation of Echoes of the Plum Grove rests on its blend of traditional farming sim mechanics and life-management systems. Players plant crops, tend livestock, gather resources, cook meals, craft tools, and build relationships with the townsfolk. The daily rhythm feels familiar to fans of Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon, but Echoes adds layers of realism and tension. Seasons are not just visual changes—they dictate the rhythm of survival. Crops wither if planted at the wrong time, and food spoils if hoarded carelessly. Winter, in particular, is an unforgiving season that tests how well you’ve prepared; without sufficient stockpiles of firewood, preserved food, and warm clothing, your character and their family can grow sick or even die. These mechanics give the game a grounded, almost historical tone—it’s less about endless productivity and more about sustainable living in a community that feels genuinely alive.

The game’s most distinctive feature is its generational system. Unlike many life sims that freeze time or loop endlessly, Echoes of the Plum Grove allows your character to age, fall ill, and eventually pass away. When that time comes, you continue the story through your descendants, inheriting the land, the family home, and the reputation your ancestor built. This sense of continuity transforms small decisions into lasting ones: how you treat your neighbors, how you manage your finances, or how you nurture your children all echo forward through the years. If you ignore your fields or neglect relationships, your descendants may face harder beginnings. If you leave behind wealth, strong social ties, and good health, they inherit an easier life. This mechanic turns what could have been a simple farming simulator into something contemplative and almost existential, making you consider not just how to live well, but how to be remembered.

Honeywood itself is one of the most charming and well-realized settings in recent simulation games. The village is filled with distinct characters, each with their own routines, preferences, and temperaments. Some are warm and friendly; others are prickly, gossipy, or downright unpleasant. Relationships must be nurtured through conversation, gift-giving, and mutual respect, but Echoes doesn’t shy away from friction. You can just as easily insult or alienate villagers as you can befriend them, and some quests even encourage mischievous or morally questionable behavior. This social realism keeps the world dynamic—people respond to your behavior, and friendships, rivalries, and even grudges can persist across generations. It’s a rare example of a cozy game that acknowledges that small-town life isn’t always idyllic. There’s gossip, jealousy, and tension, but also warmth and humor in equal measure.

The art and sound design elevate the game’s emotional tone. Visually, Echoes of the Plum Grove has the look of a handcrafted storybook—lush green fields, soft pastels, and charmingly simple character models. The gentle lighting shifts with the seasons, and the animation carries a quiet rhythm that mirrors the passage of time. It’s not flashy, but it’s evocative, managing to make even mundane actions like chopping wood or walking through the snow feel atmospheric. The music is equally understated, a collection of melodic and pastoral themes that shift with the mood of the season. Birds chirp in spring, wind howls in winter, and soft piano notes accompany your daily routines. The result is a world that feels warm but not saccharine, contemplative without being somber—a tone perfectly suited to the game’s themes of growth and transience.

While the core experience is rewarding, Echoes of the Plum Grove is not without its flaws. The social systems, though ambitious, can feel underdeveloped. NPC dialogue is often repetitive, and some villagers lack depth beyond a few simple lines or predictable routines. The AI behavior can be inconsistent—characters sometimes stand still for entire days or fail to react meaningfully to your presence. The quest design also wavers between inspired and underwhelming; while some storylines carry emotional weight, others feel like filler or lack satisfying resolution. The pacing can occasionally drag, particularly when managing the minutiae of daily survival, such as tool maintenance and illness recovery. These rough edges don’t break the experience, but they do reveal the growing pains of a small development team aiming for a deeply systemic world.

Yet, even with its imperfections, there is a sincerity to Echoes of the Plum Grove that makes it memorable. It does not rely on endless grinding or artificial goals to sustain engagement; instead, it encourages you to find meaning in small victories. Seeing your crops survive the winter, watching your children grow into adults, or witnessing your family’s home stand for generations carries a sense of permanence that most simulation games never attempt. For players who want more than escapism, who crave a farming sim that values emotion and consequence as much as routine, it delivers something rare: a world that feels both cozy and alive, where the passage of time is not just a mechanic, but the heart of the experience.

ST:E presents you with moments of fun fights, but is hindered by glitches. RUBBERBANDING. When the screen is full, enemies are there, then back over there, then pause, and actually still way back there. WTF and that’s if they’re not walking in place. It is also easy in late game to get stuck or lost in a pile of bodies, and/or broken base pieces. The base is sometimes enemy restrictive and other times an enemy clip-fest. Furthermore, you can climb the base wall until later when the glitches/lag make you fall. 

To add insult to injury are the cosmetics for sale with incessant popup reminders. This is disheartening considering all of the existing issues and initial price point. Even I, a Starship Trooper fan with an admittedly low bar, think Offworld should fix the game first, then ask for more money.

This game is a Free to Play title, overlaid with a marketable IP, priced to hoodwink the consumer, and chased with a couple extra nut shots masked as "Supporter DLC.”

This is not worth its base, nor sale price, but maybe around $5 and only if these issues are fixed. 

Thankfully I found Helldivers 2 and you should too.

review_text:
Fun for maybe a couple hours, like barely beyond refund timing.

Having enemies constantly spawn around you, who can spawn behind you and knock you back into a pit of instant-death, is completely stupid.
Timers popping up all the time on top of the constant spawns is also not fun.
The UI makes no sense. It seems like they randomly chose click to hold and on release of a click to do various interactions. For example: if you try to upgrade a weapon, you have to click on it, then click to hold on the upgrade button. If you try clicking both it won't work on the second and clicking to hold won't work on the click release. Another example: out in the field, some things you pick up with click to hold, and others are release of click. And they can be part of the same pile.
Then they have a nice menu system where it shows you what you can do before your run, but then you actually have to walk over to the stuff to do it - this is a bit frustrating in the case of the merchant that randomly sits around your camp in some random corners once you unlock him.

The guns are nothing special. I've tried about 8 or so and they are fairly standard. Maybe it gets better, I don't know. The first hell gun was interesting, but it has only 3 shots. My biggest gripe here is the long range weapons. Short range is in your face short range, and everything else is mid-range. The enemies have no problem shooting you 2-3x the distance you can shoot with a long range weapon, and you can't shoot very far. Apart from one upgrade, they've been pretty disappointing.
There is some other gear, but it doesn't matter enough to make me care if I wear it.
Spells are interesting, until you realize they charge back up on kills and can't actually rely on it being ready when you need it. I always have to look at the tiny icon for it in the bottom left of the screen before a fight, and I can't really look at it during a fight, perhaps because of a wide screen monitor. It really needs something to tell me it's ready instead of an animation pretending like it is gonna cast then doesn't, making me wonder what the heck just happened.

This is definitely not worth $40. It might be worth $5, but it is no where close to being good as a souls-like with guns. It's very indie, low quality, with dumb design choices holding it back.
