review_text:
I recommend this game because it has very strong points, and Hakuouki as a franchise is definitely worth it, but it has issues that really take away from the enjoyment.

[u]The issues[/u]
- Well it's only half of a game. I think it was a mistake to split the game in two, because in this first installment you are left with a lot of unresolved plot threads, unanswered questions, and an ending so open it doesn't feel like an ending at all. (Because it's not ; it's the middle of the story.)
- It's not an actual PC port. I'm glad to be able to play on PC, but the UI shows only the original commands and does not adapt to keyboard, mouse or controller. You have to figure out the controls yourself. If you play on fullscreen the image will probably be blurry because PC screen resolutions aren't supported. Play in windowed mode if you have this issue.
- While it's good to have an English version, the translation is terrible. Speech is overly interpreted (making it unnecessary vulgar and misogynistic) with a few sentences being complete inventions, some are just plain wrong (they mean the opposite of what is said), there are typos (missing letters, missing words, misspellings)... A lot of sentences don't feel very natural in English either.

[u]The good points[/u]
- The game is very good at making you feel emotions. Even just the prologue will make you nostalgic for a time a place you don't even know yet. Everything tugs at your heartstrings, from conflicting loyalties to reticent betrayals to tragically unbreakable friendships... I think it's the game's strongest point.
- The music is great, and its use greatly enhances the gameplay. The headquarters music will feel like home to you. The complete silence will impart how scary a scene is. Another stong point.
- The voice acting is amazing, with great voice actors <3
- The illustrations are beautiful, especially the CGs.
- Despite the high number of routes and several mandatory events, each story is very different and each character fulfills a different fantasy. There is definitely value in playing all the routes, even if a character does not interest you at first.
- The game teaches you an incredible amount of things about the bakumatsu and the Shinsengumi, which is nice if you don't know anything, and great if you're already a fan of either.

All in all more good points than bad, but be sure to play Edo Blossoms too in order to get the whole story !

review_text: I absolutely love this game, but it has a lot of problems in its current state. The biggest being the difficulty and progression. There is a lot of RNG going on behind the scenes determining what the run will be, however it comes in one or two flavors, tediously easy, or outright unfair as hordes spawn on your location, curses rain down on you spawning endless enemies, with you armed with weapons that simply are not powerful enough, or with ammo reserves not deep enough to handle the sheer numbers getting thrown at you. The further and further I get into the game, the more and more I am succumbing to unfair deaths. The stamina system does more to leave you hobbled, rather than act as a crucial resource to manage, as when in combat, keeping tabs on a thin line, at the out most edge of the screen isn't viable, when you have to actively time dodges as not to get hit from every conceivable angle. With most enemies having ranged attacks and being surrounded being the norm, use of cover often isn't possible, leaving you to dash to dodge incoming attacks, leaving you slow, and absurdly vulnerable when your stamina inevitably depletes. Spells are largely useless with how ridiculously long they take to recharge, you either have to save them for something big, or just get used to not having them. The progression system feels meaningless, as each level, your upgrade is so minuscule, that it takes a dozen or so levels specked into a single stat to have any tangible impact on gameplay. With most equipment progression gated, you are woefully under equipped to actually progress through the game, leaving you to grind out the same couple of levels for basic resources to level up, which become exponentially more expensive each level, meaning even more grinding. There may be a far more optimal gameplay loop than what I have found myself in, but the game does little to guide you outside the most utterly basic information, leaving you to grope about for meaning behind everything getting thrown at you. Again, I love this game, but it doesn't do much well, and poor design choices bog down what should be a stellar experience into frustrating tedium.

I think in order to fairly and objectively review a game, you need to look at it in four section: Graphics, gameplay, sound, and story. These four elements make up a game. By this reasoning, let me review To The Moon.

Graphics - N/A
Graphics are arguably the least important aspect of a game, in my opinion. To The Moon is created in RPG maker, so graphics are even less important. 16 bit, familiar animations, etc.

Gameplay - 3/10
TTM is not a game, per se, but more of a collection of cutscenes. This is fine, because it is heavily story driven.

Story - 5/10
Unfortunately, I was disappointed. The story is creative, but no where near the level of depth and emotions that I was led to believe existed here. The dialogue is boring at best and the majority of time incredibly cringey. References to Animorphs feel out of place. The dialogue is full of colloquialisms and phonetic spellings which are awful.

Sound - 10/10
The soundtrack for this game is amazing and it's only saving grace. Mostly piano based, which works nicely with the dialogue and triggers an emotional connection. Unfortunately for TTM, that's the only good part of the game.

I paid 1.99 for TTM and finished it in two sittings in about 3 hours. I feel like that's a fair value for what I paid, but I wouldn't pay much more. In my opinion this game is completely overrated and feels more like a high school play than a 'brilliant' game.

Overall Rating - 6/10

8/10

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a really solid stealth game with a fair amount of tactical/strategy elements, and I really enjoyed playing it for a few weeks on my Steam Deck. Where most stealth games use more of a first-person or a third-person view and concentrate on a single character or maybe a pair of characters, Shadow Tactics takes a larger isometric view of the map and uses squads of 2-5 characters with varying special abilties. I really enjoyed that this large-scale vision allows you plan an approach towards your mission goals, especially in conjunction with its planning/execution system. Shadow Tactics allows you to plan and set up moves to be executed at the same time, so that a character who is in disguise and talking to a pair of guards can stab one guard while a second character sneaks up and stabs the other guard, while a third character throws a shuriken at the guard on a rooftop who might see the other two getting ganked. This really enables a lot of skillful tactical planning and execution, presenting you with both difficult challenges to figure out how to approach, and a reasonably wide variety of skills to try to resolve those challenges. 

The game's story wasn't anything special, but I did enjoy the presentation, especially the animated scenes between each mission. There was one particular scene when the entire squad is reunited that I thought was particularly impactful, aided by how the scene physically unfolds. I would've been interested to see some gameplay mechanics that maybe tied into how you decided to accomplish each mission, perhaps making your decisions a bit more impactful in subsequent missions. Absent any such impacts, I just played the whole game as a full-on murder machine, making sure none of my foes lived through any mission. There was one particular vignette that occurred during the mission at an invaded village that I went far out of my way to try to prevent from happening, and I was pretty disappointed that the game didn't support my heroic intervention. Adding some minor elements like this could've really helped elevate the game, to add "small stories" to the game's larger narrative. 

Shadow Tactics was a fairly difficult game, even on "Normal" difficulty mode, which did make it a little grind-y at times. Overall though, I think its a really good addition to both the stealth and the tactical strategy genres. The core gameplay loop of watching, planning, and trying to pull off your plan works really well, especially because the game generally makes it very easy to try again (at least on Normal difficulty) if something goes wrong. I've always enjoyed the watch/plan/execute cycle in other stealth/assassination games, but the squad-based strategy element really elevated the gameplay here. If you enjoy either of the stealth or strategy genres, I think you'll find Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun to be worth your while, especially if you're playing on the Steam Deck.

review_text:
[h3]It's been nearly 6 years since the Kickstarter campaign happened, but the game is finally here! Sort of...[/h3]

Relic Hunters Legend is a coop top-down looter shooter that currently features 5 characters that each have their own set of abilities and passives, with each being able to choose between a select list of equipment types along with a primary and secondary weapon with up to 4 players.
[b]Please note that the game requires an internet connection at all times.[/b]

Your main goal will be to uncover the story's secret through quests and some occasional cutscenes (especially the animated ones) that makes you feel like watching a cartoon, while trying to find the perfect gear to fit your characters and the guns you'll be using.
It feels fast and fun to play. If you're somebody that try to become the fastest man alive in video games, you'll be happy to hear that gear and skills can give you extra movement speed, reload speed, or just give you the extra punch you need to sweep an entire room full of enemies in a blink of a second. All while trying out all the different sparkles that may come out from your tools of destruction and making your characters look as fly as possible. A very simple concept, maybe too simple even...
You may find your journey "too easy", "too hard" or just right depending on your skill level and what the game may hand to you. As with every looter shooter, the game will make loot rain from the sky to the point where you might even find more items than you shot bullets every now and then.
Even for looter shooter standards however, the inventory is extremely clunky which makes getting items sometimes feel overwhelming and may cause you a headache while hovering over dozens of guns just to see if they have the stats you're looking for.

It's noteworthy that this is an Early Access game in every possible way. A sizable chunk of the content is still missing, the interface makes you feel like it just came out fresh from an alpha build and your adventure will be riddled with bugs, both in form of monsters and technical issues. It's also important to note that the game can become quite repetitive after some time.
[b]Despite being a coop game, you will encounter a lot of story mission that are weirdly designed with forced singleplayer.[/b]
In the dozens of hours spent in beta tests, I would sometimes wonder whether the game would be ready for a full release and if all the bugs will ever be fixed due to how broken the menus feel like. In my time in the Early Access build so far I've seen some fixed but a lot of them still remaining and really hope that Rogue Snail will be able to patch most of them, if not all.
For some people though, this might be enough to make them not try out the game just yet and reasonably so. This game is FAR from being perfect, but there's something very special about shooting bad guys in a (mostly) joyful world with an adorable cast of characters that will make you want to keep coming back.

Relic Hunters Legend feels like an unpolished gem.
If you are someone that might be easily irritated when encountering bugs, I would advise to wait for the full release of the game before playing (it will also launch as a F2P title).
However if after reading this review you are still interested by the game and willing to invest your time in this game, for 15€ (10€ with the current launch sale), this game may certainly entertain you long enough to make your purchase worth.

[b]TLDR for people that are too lazy to read through the full review:[/b]
[list] Pros:
[*]Fun and satisfying gameplay
[*]Cute art style and universe
[*]Simple to get in and addicted to
[*]A diverse list of equipment that makes you wonder why Starfield couldn't do better [/list]
[list] Cons:
[*]Can feel repetitive after some point
[*]A barely functional UI
[*]Lots of bugs
[*]No multiplayer support for story missions [/list]

review_text:
It's fun for a few hours but it quickly becomes repetitive and frustrating.

* The campaign is very short and quite easy for a rogue-like. I've beaten it on normal difficulty on my second try and quite a few times after that; might be just luck with starting stats though.
* There are too many unskippable animations. The whole experience would be so much smoother if you could turn them off for menu transitions, winning/loosing, getting stuff after games etc etc. (There's a setting to skip goal replays so hopefully they will add more of these.)
* [Offensive] AI can be pretty dump at times. Your teammates often opt to chase the puck you are holding (so you cannot pass), or cluster in front of you with defense (so you cannot pass and you cannot shoot). The opposing  goaltender is more likely to keep the puck when there is nobody in front of him - but he will pass every time you are standing right in his face (and of course with 0% chance to intercept).

Hopefully it will get better in some next release (still an early access), I'd like to give this another try.

review_text:
OK, yes.  I can, VERY tentatively say, "Yes, I recommend."  However, I am having several complaints that I am not entirely sure will ever be addressed.  And so, I am going to make a list of gripes, likely get hit with a "jester award" or fanboy wrath, and hopefully give someone who isn't "diehard" some insight.  I will start with....I am NOT a "Souls fan".  Personally, I find the entire genre to be, essentially, "unnecessarily difficult as a means to artificially pad your game".  That isn't to say I haven't played and enjoyed some.  I'm just saying they aren't my "first pick".

First off, the "souls-like" tag is pretty fairly earned, though not as bad as it could be.  If that seems like a problem to you, if it makes you "nervous"...probably move on.  However, I never felt like my ire was aimed at a "tough enemy".  Instead, it was aimed at terrain placement, or inconsistent AI, or poorly explained mechanics.  The game punishes you...fine...very "souls like".  However, it's got enough annoying me without being shot through walls or my dash being stopped short because of a small obstacle that shouldn't even be noticed in a gunfight.  It's infuriating enough to round a corner and get mowed down in one blast, losing all your loot.  Now imagine losing all your loot because a skull on the ground "blocked" you.

In that same vein, the camera has "its moments".  While it hasn't been frequent, it has been frequent enough that I made note of it.  Usually because of said "terrain", but the camera has gotten stuck in something several times or otherwise "glitched out"...spinning around and shaking with no way to see anything.  Again, in the midst of a heavy fight...not something that should be happening.

Secondly, the "familiars" or whatever the "boss-like" characters are....specifically the one of the Island of the Damned...are infuriating.  Not specifically because they are "hard".  Fine.  However, their behavior is inconsistent.  Some runs I'll come across him, spazzing out in his corner of the map and as long as I don't hit him; he's fine.  Other times, I'll be in a fight, nowhere near him, and he'll come over and "get involved"...usually wiping me out because I'm getting hit from behind and not at "full health".  Please do something about this.  It's really annoying to be doing some casual farming run and suddenly "Grunthok the Flatulent" comes out of left field and vaporizes you when you weren't even fighting the damn thing.

Thirdly, I feel like health drops need to be slightly more frequent.  I can go entire expeditions and not have one health serum drop.  Most I have ever seen is in one run is three (which admittedly for that run was PLENTY).  Still, to open 7 chests, kill every bad guy on that main map, and beat "Grunthok the Flatulent" and not get one health drop...even with the pitiful 1% Arcana boost chosen...seems a bit stingy.

Perhaps, there are all manner of explanations within some aspect of the game I haven't found.  The point is, these things are not exactly spelled out.  I still don't fully understand how "mysteriums" work and where to farm those.  The dungeon is annoying the crap out me with Sanity being introduced and I'm not entirely certain I understand THAT mechanic; but it seems to basically be just another way to drain your health in a game that is already doing it plenty....which just seems asinine.

I do enjoy the game.  And I can certainly hop online and find all manner of walk-throughs and guides.  The gunplay is pretty solid and the different guns I've used have each had their charms.  I WANT to like this game.  It's acting like that antisocial kid, though, berating you and being a general jerk every time you try to get close.

Maybe, instead of a "dash"...we can get a "teleport".  Perhaps make one of the traits tie in to "ease of traversing obstacles" so that, for instance, more mobile characters don't have small obstacles blocking them.  Give us more control over how "challenging" or "casual" we want a run to be (perhaps toggle if we want the extra bosses...and therefore extra loot chances....we've already beaten to be there on a certain run).  I saw another review mention tying calamities more into the loot you pick up and I can get behind that.  As it is, the game seems to either "kick you when you're down" or "let you roll over it".  "Feast" or "famine".

...And could we play "dress up" with our "Preyer"?  Sure, he looks badass; but, some customization would be "badasser".  Perhaps it's later and I haven't gotten there, yet.  I like making my character my own.  Sue me.

I really hope things get smoothed out on here because I am worried these issues I have will only get worse as I progress and fights get tougher.  I'll be PRAYING for the days that "Grunthok the Flatulent" was inexplicably getting drawn into fights a quarter map away; as I now curse "ZorZlub the Incontinent" for somehow nuking me across the map with a melee attack or something.  There is so much here and so much that COULD be here.  I just hope it doesn't end up alienating me and others before it can get there. with silly overlooks and mistakes.  As it is, while I can recommend it...I'm uncertain how long my own patience will hold out.

Edit:  I felt it was only fair to address my gripes with additional play time and research.  Firstly, I should NEVER [i]have[/i] to look up walk-throughs and forums for your game.  Much love and appreciation for the community that has stepped up to fill this gap; but, it was a task that the developer should have taken on.  This is a serious oversight.  There needs to be better explanation within the game.  Many of my complaints stem from the game not being clear about something and you either have to figure it out yourself or hope someone else has and is willing to explain it.

However, eventually, things do start clicking into place and, if you are willing to...the game is "eventually" a lot of frustrating fun.  Just be prepared, it almost feels like the first few stages and ascensions are nothing but a hazing.  The early game doesn't feel "right".  The "Gnosis" levels are the biggest walls and it isn't until Gnosis III and beyond that things seem to "normalize".  At least, that's how it was for me.  It wasn't until this point that things like "healing potions" began dropping with any frequency (though still, some runs, I'll have NONE......HOW?!) and my character has access to a mostly full compliment of abilities, skills, and weapons.

That's the biggest takeaway for me....this is a game that requires you to put the time in to experience it's best.  I'm 40 hours in an I still have only a "solid" grasp on everything (and there is still Gnosis IV and all that comes from that for me to learn).  I can say that, yes, small issues compound so if there is something that annoys you early that's a legitimate issue (say, the terrain posing serious problems)...it will only get worse as the hordes get nastier and bigger.  However, if you are willing to educate yourself a little and put in some extra work...this really IS a solid game.

review_text:
In the current state of the game it is not worth your investment.  The game holds promise of what could be but failure by the devs to properly curate their game and improve it has led to a state where there are many obscure mechanics that make no sense.

Issues I find present with the game current


- The common warrior bug which can spawn an endless swarms can one hit kill you if you are not the guardian class during its charge attack, two hit kill otherwise and send you flying with a single hit.

- Bombardment effects
                 1: Bombardments from plasma bugs come from straight above you and have zero hint as to where they are landing unless you look straight up.  This means you are not looking in front of you and die to the one hit/two hit kill warrior bugs.
                 2: Explosive pill bugs can spawn anywhere and launch themselves at your constructions as an engineer (and note, they only launch themselves at your constructions or medic stim machines, no one else), make a noise that sounds like mortars falling from the sky and are barely the size of a basketball on the ground.  They are hard to react to and even if you do shoot them to try and save your buildings it blows up the bug anyways blowing up your structures.  A single pill bug is enough to kill you and instantly destroy your engineering structures.  It even can fall out of the cave roofs on maps with such.
                  3:  Inferno bug bomardments kill you before you can even stim yourself given the delay on the stim.  They kill faster than you can react to it.

- Engineer bugs and mechanics
                   1:  You get to make 1000 resource worth of buildings that also have a limited count, including only 1 turret and 1 turret ammo dump.  That is fine on paper but if for some reason you are unable to make it back to the buildings you made, they are there for good and counting against your maximum building cap for the rest of the mission crippling your CLASS ABILITY.  So then you cannot make another ammo dump or turret for example if you have one elsewhere on the map.
                    2:  Engineering placement for their personal building is very finicky with only being able to be placed on extremely level surfaces that half the time ends up far enough away from the objective that its useless or the only place you can place the stuff down is where the bugs spawn from surrounding the objective.  Good luck manning a turret when a tiger and multiple warriors spawn on top of you.
                    3:  The engineering flamethrower blinds you and team mates turning your entire screen black.  In some cases its been reported that it makes their entire screen black for the rest of the game and it has caused headaches due to the visual effects.

- Extraction from the base at the end of the mission sucks for anyone but mobility classes as they commonly leave everyone behind to extract alone.  It leaves a sour taste at the end of your gameplay when you die constantly unable to extract alive and meanwhile that sniper which spent the entire mission up on a tower someplace in no danger is on the ship alive.

My biggest complaint however would be the community on discord including its moderators hired by the Staff.  They are some of the most close minded people when it comes to quality of life features, changes, or anything that would help improve a new players experience.  

I brought up concerns some friends of mine had with trying to get into this game and my response from them was along the lines of "Skill issue, get better, join a large group and only play with them" among other reasons as to why they should gatekeep the game from new players.  Like why have a quickplay feature if you can only properly enjoy the game in a large group?


In the end the its a game that holds great promise for a niche of large PvE coop gameplay but fails to meet the mark after being in early access for a year, failing to maintain a minimum of 1000 active players, and continue to fail to curate their toxic community which wants to keep the game in a state of an 'old boys club' where only they can enjoy it.

review_text:
After playing through just over a year in game, I can thoroughly recommend Echoes of the Plum Grove.
It's an incredible game with so much character, the artstyle is gorgeous and adds to the warm feeling of the game. Its dynamic, never knowing what might happen the next day. I adore the fact that you can play through generations, and the overarching story is lovely. 
I do however wish certain things were tweaked, like a way to water all your plants at once, the ability to use dresser furniture as a storage for clothes. I wish certain things were more obvious, such as how to smelt bars/get the recipe to smelt bars, and other small things like that.
One massive pro for me is how adjustable the settings are. The fact you can turn on and off taxes, aging, diseases, decay, energy, hunger and tool durability is a massive plus, as games where these are a non-negotiable option can be tedious and frustrating. I love that you can also remove the fishing minigame so its just a simple click to catch fish, and that aging can be adjusted to be slower or faster. 
I do, however, wish there was a way to look back on your family tree, to see how you got to the character you're currently playing. I would also love if locals could comment on your parents, grandparents etc if they were friends with them. 
One major major plus is that ALL the animals can be pet. And I mean ALL of them, which is so important to me.

review_text:
[i] Originally posted on October 28, 2013 [/i]

To The Moon's core concept, a dying man trying to fulfill a final wish through memory-based technology, is simultaneously compelling from a science fiction perspective, and deeply sad. I bought the game because it was well reviewed, and because that concept intrigued me. However I found myself unable to finish it due to several key frustrations.

Chief among these is the game's uneven tone. The game's writing constantly alternates between inappropriate or ill-conceived humor, and scenes that are supposed to tug at your heartstrings in a frankly very sappy manner. But that sappiness is what we're playing for, and buying into, so it's very disconcerting to have so many flat attempts at humorous asides completely break the mood. While there were some charming moments that made me laugh, and I certainly appreciate the proper and necessary usage of comic relief, the game's designers took it several steps too far. Furthermore, the game's retro art style and JRPG interface really limits the emotional impact of the narrative, and doesn't really bring anything to the table on it's own.

One particularly frustrating aspect of this is the asinine gameplay, involving fetch quests, idiotic "memory-breaking" activities, and totally inappropriate JRPG-style fight scenes. What little gameplay is present is not really very enjoyable. It's enough to make one question whether this story would be better told in a different medium. Dear Esther, another game that was very short, focused on narrative, and had minimal gameplay, at least existed in a 3D engine and had some really beautiful visuals. Dear Esther also didn't force you to play silly minigames in order to advance the narrative.

A bright spot in To The Moon is the soundtrack, which, if you're in the mood for sentimentality, really hits the spot. However it's better enjoyed without the game getting in the way. To be honest, I would recommend that people simply watch an LP of the game rather than play it, and skip over the "gamey" sequences. Or just read a plot summary while listening to the soundtrack, and maybe look up a couple of key sequences on YouTube. Either option would be far less frustrating than actually playing the game.

review_text:
After spending more than sixty hours in Witchfire, I can confidently say it is one of the most satisfying shooter roguelites I have played. Developed by a small team, it delivers AAA‑quality visuals and a deep gameplay loop. As a preyer, I hunt witches with forbidden guns and pagan magic, and the game lets me decide whether to pick off enemies from afar, study encounters tactically, or combine firearms and spells into my own brand of mayhem. I am a long‑range enthusiast, and the time I have invested has been rewarded with memorable head-shots and tense cat‑and‑mouse encounters across the game’s richly detailed maps.

The July 2025 Webgrave update is the most transformative yet. It adds a brand‑new region called Velmorne, a blighted town full of secrets and new enemy types. This update introduces the Rosary, a system of passive skills that lets me tailor my build and share configurations with other players. The Workshop has been overhauled so I can control the research path of my gear, and the old stat categories have been replaced with an RPG‑style system using Flesh, Blood, Mind, Witchery, Arsenal and Faith. There are also new Gnosis levels and a redesigned Ascension Shrine, with a special item to reassign points if I am returning to the game. Webgrave even adds a proper tutorial via a prologue level and an in‑game handbook. For snipers like me, the highlight is the Oracle, a new sniper rifle that can ignore walls. There is also the lever‑action Nemesis and the quest‑locked Koschei. These additions, coupled with the Rosary and refined stats, make character builds more rewarding and combat more tactical.

This update builds on March 2025’s Witch Mountain update. That patch added a sprawling descent into Witch Mountain, the game’s largest level to date, and introduced Fallen Preyers 2.0, semi‑autonomous allies, Shadow Orbs that offer high‑risk, high‑reward challenges, and a suite of new gear. Earlier still, the Ghost Galleon update in April 2024 added souls‑style classes, new Calamities, a Calamity meter that teaches you to avoid mistakes, and the Gnosis system that lets you slightly over‑level and unlock hidden paths. These patches show that the Astronauts team listens to feedback from us and continually expands their world. They released a huge update just two weeks ago and released an updated patch today on Aug 13!

[b]The maps themselves are masterfully crafted and gorgeous to look at and run through.[/b] Early regions like Scarlet Coast are a study in melancholy; broken flotillas litter the shoreline, a blood‑stained beach and an abandoned fishing village give way to a quarry. Irongate Castle radiates corruption with its foul aura, labyrinthine dungeons and three separate ways into the castle! Witch Mountain’s labyrinth requires careful navigation and is filled with traps and Fallen Preyer allies. Velmorne offers narrow streets, blighted courtyards and new enemies that will surprise even veteran players. Each level feels like a mini‑dungeon; they are semi‑open but interconnected, giving me multiple angles to line up long‑range shots or retreat when calamities hit. The design encourages exploration with hidden Vaults, Shadow Orbs, Witchmarks, navigation charts and events that reward curiosity and precision.

[b]Weapons and sniping mechanics are a standout.[/b] The game already features excellent marksman rifles like Hailstorm, which has the highest base damage of any non‑demonic weapon. Landing three consecutive critical hits refunds bullets to the magazine and, at higher upgrade levels, improves handling, increases zoom distance and even unleashes a freezing shockwave. However, misses reset the buff and there is a stamina cost for aiming, so disciplined shooting is essential. Hypnosis, another bolt‑action rifle, rewards patience by charging extra damage the longer I aim. Now, with the Oracle’s ability to shoot through walls, snipers can set up truly spectacular shots in Velmorne or Witch Mountain. Mixing these rifles with spells, for example freezing cones to control mobs or shockwaves to knock enemies back, enhances the sniping loop and stacks the damage. Even demonic weapons like Vulture and Hailstorm act as panic buttons or boss‑busting tools, but I find myself returning to precision rifles because of how satisfying the critical‑hit system is. Stack that with electrical shock on top of fire...the damage numbers roll...

[b]Visually, Witchfire is jaw‑dropping.[/b] The game uses advanced photogrammetry and post‑processing to build gorgeous semi‑open world levels. The developers took their photogrammetry pipeline beyond The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, shooting objects at high resolution, using drones for large scans and compiling tens of thousands of photos to create assets. They then optimized these scans so the game looks stunning without sacrificing performance. Details like natural dirt, weathering and unique compositions give each environment authenticity. Even after dozens of hours, I still pause to admire the sun piercing through ruined arches or the way light dances off wet stones in Velmorne.

Witchfire has evolved into an exceptional roguelite FPS. The developers have continually expanded the game with new regions, systems and weapons, and the Webgrave update addresses onboarding while giving veterans deeper build options. If you enjoy sniping or methodical long‑range combat in atmospheric, dungeon‑like maps, Witchfire will scratch that itch. My 60+ hours have flown by, and with the Rosary system, new maps, gnosis levels to unlock and the Oracle in my hands, I'm not stopping.

TLDR, Service guarantees citizenship.

Fresh out of boot camp, I stepped into the roaring chaos of the 1st Mobile Infantry Division, one of the most elite units in the galaxy. Barely 48 hours into my first deployment, I had already dropped into twelve battle-ravaged planets, facing legions of the Arachnid menace. My kill count? An astonishing 2,673 bugs.

I had little time to process the whirlwind of events. One moment, I was stepping off the troop carrier, the next, I was knee-deep in combat. Every movement was fluid, every command instinctive.

On Zeta-Prime, I faced a swarm so dense, it seemed to blot out the sun. My pulse rifle spat fire, cutting down bug after bug. My training took over, and I moved through the battlefield with deadly precision. “Keep moving, apes!” sergeant barked through the comms, but I was already ahead, pushing forward, determined to carve a path through the chaos.

Dropping into the deserts of Omicron-Six, my squad faced tunnels teeming with warrior bugs. It was a claustrophobic nightmare, but our resolve held firm. Grenades cleared the way as we moved deeper, the mission to destroy one hive. Explosions echoed, and the bugs screeched, but our focus never wavered.

On the ice plains of Rho-Tau, the 1st MI skills were tested to the limit. The cold bit through our armor, and the bugs had adapted, moving with terrifying speed across the frozen landscape. But our determination was a fire that no ice could quench. I fought like a veteran, each encounter adding to my growing legend.

The words of my training sergeant echoed in my mind: “Service guarantees citizenship.” But it was more than that. It was about survival, brotherhood, and a fierce determination to protect humanity.

As I looked out over the battlefield, the bugs retreating under relentless assault, I knew his war was far from over. But I was ready. I'm a Mobile Infantry trooper, and would fight until the very end.

TLDR, Service guarantees citizenship.

review_text:
10 Major Failures of The Callisto Protocol

1. Overly rigid melee combat:
The dodge system tied to directional input feels imprecise and clunky, making encounters more frustrating than genuinely challenging.

2. Poor pacing:
The game relies too heavily on narrow corridors, forced walk segments, and unskippable cinematic transitions that repeatedly break the flow.

3. Lack of enemy variety:
Most enemy types behave similarly, causing combat to feel repetitive halfway through the campaign.

4. Overly linear level design:
Despite its promising setting, the levels rarely offer meaningful exploration or alternative paths.

5. Badly placed checkpoints:
Death often sends players back several minutes, sometimes including repeated cutscenes that can’t be skipped.

6. Technical issues at launch:
Stuttering, frame drops, and visual bugs—especially on PC—seriously harmed immersion (with some issues still lingering).

7. Underdeveloped narrative:
Characters lack depth, motivations feel shallow, and the world-building doesn’t reach the potential the premise suggests. And on top of that, you have to pay for a horribly written ending...

8. Restrictive and awkward inventory system:
The small inventory forces constant item drops, undermining pacing and strategic choice.

9. Limited actual horror mechanics: 
The game leans far more into heavy action than atmospheric horror, failing to deliver what many players expected from a “spiritual successor” to Dead Space.

10. Repetitive execution animations:
While visually impressive at first, the kill animations become repetitive and slow down the gameplay experience.

Reflection

These ten points outline how The Callisto Protocol struggles in execution despite its strong production values. Most of the issues stem from design decisions that prioritize spectacle over fluid, satisfying gameplay. Ultimately, even a visually stunning title can fall short if the player experience suffers. Video games should be an engaging and enjoyable escape—games are meant to be fun, not frustrating.

It didn't surpass Dead Space.

review_text:
This JRPG 4-pack is an incredible journey; very few games can take this many hours of my life without garnering a sense of resentment, but this was special.  I can't say that I was left wanting more, but it didn't wear out its welcome, either.  Keep in mind that as big a fan of the genre as I was back in the Fourth and Fifth Generation (I didn't play much else back then), I've really fallen out of love with the genre, so there may very well be better ones out there that I just never picked up.  I also probably didn't play this the way that I was supposed to, so keep that in mind, but that also means that I had the freedom to even do that in the first place.  With most of my biases out of the way, let's get started.

The gameplay was pretty refreshing, and I don't know why more games of the era aren't like this.  Devil May Cry came around and revolutionized 3D Action, but it took other genres a while to try their hand at this type of combat system.  Like my beloved Rogue Galaxy, these games have a similar, but watered-down type of combat; you run around and slash at things in real-time, and the mechanics, while not all that deep, are pretty solid.  You've got your standard combo, your charge attack, and your over-the-top specials, and while that's mostly it, you can get enemies into a special state where your special moves do more damage and give everyone a bonus in experience.  Doing all that, you also fill a bar that lets you go into berserker mode.  There are tons of options, and your main character's warrior class is a jack of all trades, so you'll have access to several different weapon types over the course of the 4 games.  Your companions are controlled by AI, and you have a few basic guidelines to give them, which isn't a whole lot of control, but they mostly act intelligently.

The basic structure of the game allows you to dial in an address out of hundreds or thousands of possible combinations; dial it in to a level appropriate to your party, and go on an adventure!  There isn't a lot of variety - most of the areas are pretty cookie cutter - but all of the outside areas have different times of day, and what's there is designed beautifully.  Even though a lot of the areas look the same, I found myself getting really absorbed into the scenery, though mostly outside; the dungeons are neat, but not as pretty, and they're a lot longer.  Each area gives you a rank once you finish, but thankfully, how quickly you cleared it is not a factor; you can just take your time and do a good job.  Most equipment can be customized with extra goodies that give you benefits such as status ailments, elemental damage, and HP drain.  You don't really have to worry about grinding, either, because your levels skyrocket with little provocation; if you're looking for a challenge, keep on walking.  That said, there is so much to do: the game keeps track of which items you've possessed, which monsters you've battled, etc., and the more you do, the more your guild grows, which gives you extra benefits.  With that and all of the different quests available, there's plenty to do, and honestly, I found it fun just going on adventures to random areas, maybe even more than the story missions.

The actual story... well, it grew on me.  At first, I hated all of the characters (except the one who established early on that she's just OVER IT), but by the end of the third game, I found myself even getting attached to random NPCs that wandered around town.  I became genuinely happy for my extremely stereotypical shounen protagonist when people showed a genuine interest in his wellbeing.  Even some of the more annoying characters grew on me by the end, and with a cast this big, and an attitude as cynical as mine, that's no small task.  The actual plot has a lot of weird things happening, and not having played the other games or watched any of the anime, I was pretty lost at times, but almost everything comes together in the end.  If nothing else, it's a thematic departure from the usual settings of a game like this.

The environments, as I've said are beautiful, and the more unique elements of the game generally look pretty cool.  Most characters have some form of tribal tattoo on them, and they all look pretty neat.  In typical anime fashion, the main character's outfits get progressively more ridiculous, as do the weapons, but once I started to lean into that, I began to enjoy myself.  The monsters look very unique, especially the avatars, and even though some of them are a bit outlandish, they are very creatively designed.  Special attacks, spells, etc. are all appropriately flashy, and usually not too hilariously over-the-top.

The audio is pretty good; nothing really blew me away, but there's a lot to like here.  I didn't notice too much of the music, but the fields have appropriately serene music by day, and somewhat unsettling music at sunset.  A really nice touch is that at night or in the rain, there is no music, and you can just enjoy the atmosphere.  Most of the voice acting is good and not only fits the characters, but also frames them in a way that makes them work, not to mention that Liam O'Brien plays one of them, and that man is a national treasure.  You have a couple of duds now and again - one character sounds like a little girl making fun of how little boys talk [b]all the time[/b] - but they aren't too common.

If you're looking for something that's going to let you just pick up and go on an adventure at a whim, this might be up your alley.  I'm not a big anime fan, and despite that, I found myself really getting really into it.  I can't recommend it just for the extra fourth game that's never been released before; it introduces a few cool new things, but it's shorter than 5 hours, and in terms of plot, it doesn't add much.  That said, if you're looking to play these again, or are a newcomer (like I was), it's a pretty good value, and is pretty fun once you finally get into it.  See you in The World.

review_text:
While this game is certainly not bad, it's not exactly good either. But since most reviews are positive anyway, I might aswell tell you why it just didn't work for me.

-The story
In it's core I thought the overall concept was actually pretty original. You pay as two scientist who travel back through a dying man's memories in order to grant him his last wish artificially: taking him to the moon (roll credits). Though during the story, your original objective is often questioned, as you begin to understand that this wish is not what would make your patient truly happy.
So, it's really not the story that set me off, it's rather...
-The dialogue
You'd think that in a story that's supposed to make you sad and teary, you wouldn't need a character for comic relief. But damnit, the second main character suplied you with a steady ammount of jokes in all the wrong places. I just couldn't take the game serious anymore. At the first half of the story, whenever there was an emotional moment, that same guy, messed it up over an over again. And by the time the game was starting to get deep, it was just too late for me. 
You see, the sad moments of the game largely depend on how you attached you grow to the characters over time. And maybe it's just me, but I hated both of them.
-Gameplay
Well, interesting gameplay is virtually nonexistent. But that's really not an issue in a story driven game. As I mentioned before, it has a great outline, but it just feels so unrefined at some places that it just wasn't enjoyable for me.
-The length
You'll probably finish the game in 3-4 hours. And while I don't want to badmouth the content, you may think that it's been a short ride if you don't even have all the trading cards by the time you are done.

All in all, I'd say it's okay if you can pick it up during a sale. But I really don't think it's worth the full price if you take a look at what it offers. Just about 4 hours of gameplay which aren't even amazing. But I assume that most people have a far better time, given that they don't dislike the main characters as much as I do.

Uff.. at first I gave this game a recommendation... but after playing for longer it jsut became unbearable.

The Good:

+ It's a great game with a superb atmosphere and good story.
+ Bizarre, confusing and not always easy to follow plotlines.
+ Graphics and Sounds are fitting.
+ Fully adjustable difficulty settings let you customize the game so the most annoying parts (like hunger and thirst) that dont really add to the game can be minimized.

The Bad:

- Dialogues arent voiced. Which makes for a tedious read.
- Gameplay is.. well crap. Gameplay consists only of running from A to B and talking to people. Rare (and annoying) fights happen... as well as other elements that are in the game but are either so rare or entirely unrelevant to the game (autopsies, lockpicking....)
- Layout of the Town is atrocious. When your gameplay consists of running from A to B you should make the level design accordingly. its a pain running around with tiny fences blocking your path, forcing you to take huge detours nonstop.

BUT .... Fazit:
This is what breaks the game for me:
All the atmosphere is useless if you create a game where the player has to literally SPRINT every second to have a glimmer of hope to get MOST things done. even on a second playthrough I couldnt do it.

Even worse: 
Dialogue Options have NO impact on anything. You will notice this on a second playthrough: it doesnt matter if you are nice or an asshole, ask them about A or B: The response is the EXACT same thing.

This and some other bad design choices made me abandoned the game

review_text:
When BioShock first surfaced in 2007, it wasn't just another first-person shooter — it was a seismic shift in how narrative and gameplay could intertwine. A bold blend of dystopian storytelling, atmospheric world-building, and moral complexity, BioShock raised the bar for what games could be. Nearly two decades later, its legacy remains intact, even if some of its mechanics show their age.

An unforgettable setting. The underwater city of Rapture is the crown jewel of BioShock. Dripping with Art Deco decadence, rusted machinery, and eerie silence, Rapture feels like a living character — beautiful, broken, and full of secrets. Every corner tells a story. Every audio diary, sign, or shattered storefront adds to the slow unraveling of a society that once believed it could escape the constraints of morality, government, and god.

A story with real weight. BioShock doesn’t just ask players to shoot their way through enemies; it challenges them to think. Through the philosophy of Andrew Ryan, the tragedy of genetic excess, and the unforgettable mid-game twist (you know the one), it deconstructs the illusion of player agency in clever, meta-textual ways. The “Would you kindly…” moment remains one of the most powerful narrative gut punches in video game history.

Gameplay with flexibility. The combination of conventional firearms and plasmid powers allows for creative combat. You can set traps, freeze enemies, ignite oil slicks, or hack security drones to fight for you. It’s not a run-and-gun shooter — it’s a sandbox of cause and effect, and the game often rewards experimentation.

Moral choices that matter. The Little Sisters — genetically altered children who harvest a substance called ADAM — present one of the game's central ethical dilemmas: do you save them and gain less ADAM, or harvest them for personal gain? The mechanic is simple, but it adds real tension and feeds into the game’s themes of control, consequence, and free will.

Combat can feel clunky. While the variety is impressive, weapon feedback and enemy AI don’t always hold up to modern standards. Hit detection is occasionally wonky, and some enemy types can become repetitive by the game’s latter half.

The final act stumbles a bit. After the story’s mid-point crescendo, the last hour or two feels more traditional and less inspired, culminating in a final boss that lacks the nuance of the narrative that precedes it.

Visual aging. While the art direction remains top-tier, the original textures and animations (in the non-remastered version) show their age. That said, Rapture’s design still shines through thanks to exceptional style over sheer fidelity.

BioShock isn’t just a game — it’s a philosophical experience wrapped in a shooter’s clothing. Its questions about freedom, power, and the illusion of choice linger long after the credits roll. Though some mechanics may feel dated today, the core of BioShock — its ambition, storytelling, and atmosphere — is timeless.

If you’ve never explored the depths of Rapture, now’s the time. And if you have, there’s always something new to discover on a return trip.

review_text:
While I wouldn't call myself a Left 4 Dead fan, I am very passionate about this game and the sequel, even to the point where I've played all of Back 4 Blood for some reason. In general, Left 4 Dead 2 is one of my favourite video games of all time, would be my favourite zombie (or infected, whatever) game if it weren't for plants vs zombies garden warfare, yes I am being serious. I love almost everything about this duology, from the gunplay to the artwork to the story to the mods to even the menu design, it is all impressive. Not my favourite duology because of reasons mentioned two sentences ago, but still very much up there. Here's the thing however, one thing I have intentionally excluded from the list is the characters, which are famously what makes L4D so good in so many of the playerbase's eyes. And I agree, most of the characters are reasonable, emotionally deep and realistic characters meaning you can sympathise with them, understand their struggles and make yourself feel like you truly are fighting alongside them in a chaotic post-apocalyptic world. But notice how I said "most". Now I don't have a unique or witty way of saying this so I'm just going to do what every other over-dramatic person in this situation would do, that being to say it as it is but with caps lock on so that I can emphasise my point: ZOEY IS ONE OF THE WORST VIDEO GAME CHARACTERS EVER CONCEIVED BY MANKIND AND I WISH SHE WAS THE ONE THAT DIED INSTEAD OF- whoops almost just spoiled the end of a 15 year old  game everyone has definitely already played by now there, remind me not to do that again when I do another negative review. Anyway here's why.

I don't know if saying that Zoey is a badly written character is an unpopular opinion or whatever, but I do wanna say no offence to the writers or voice actor playing Zoey in the slightest, the writers did an incredible job in other places and the voice actor did a great job in general. Zoey just feels like a side character in an 80's text-based adventure game, so whether the writers were being overworked with 2 hours of sleep when making her or she was made by a 12 year old on a "bring your son/daughter to work day", I wouldn't be surprised either way. But what makes Zoey such a bad character? Well I promise I will actually answer that question this time in the next paragraph.

I want you to consider the other characters in Left 4 Dead 1 to start. You've got Louis, a successful business man with no combat experience in the slightest, and who probably has a pill fetish if the L4D community is a reliable source. There's Francis, a biker dude not used to working in a team with strangers, but is still willing to lend a hand to the group of survivors he has found himself in. And then there's Bill, a war veteran who clearly has a lot of experience with combat and gunplay, but zombies is a whole other story for him. Now try and describe Zoey's character. This is problem #1, Zoey is a boring character with nothing unique or distinct about her. She's just some random person who ended up in the zombie apocalypse alongside three other far more interesting characters. Now I get it, complaining that she has little backstory and saying that that alone is the reason why she is a bad character is a harsh thing to say, which is why I would also like to bring up the fact that she has basically no character development at all, both in changes to her as a person as well as traits she adopts throughout. Now admittedly, this is a part of Left 4 Dead 1's story that was lacking a bit, there is barely any character development in general, but in this case, you'd think they'd go all in on Zoey having the character development, but in the end even Francis ends up having more than her. Zoey is more one-dimensional than a Back 4 Blood character. In fact, look at Left 4 Dead 2: pretty much every character is unique and changes their attitudes to the zombies, each other and the impact of the apocalypse on their futures, something Zoey seems to be physically incapable of doing. Now I'm going to change the subject out of fear of repeating myself again.

Whether Zoey also looking like a really boring character as well as playing like one was intentional or not I don't know because I'm not a secret agent at valve trying to see whether people would care about Zoey dying in Left 4 Dead 3 coming out in around 20 years time. I know it sounds bizarre, but hear me out. Just by looking at the characters you can see how equipped or unequipped each character is for the zombie apocalypse, from the one in a business suit to another in full army uniform. Zoey is wearing a bland red jacket and jeans. Again, I get it, maybe her looking like a regular person was intentional to show just how unpredictable the outbreak was and how any one of us could be in such a situation any day now. Still though, what are we supposed to make of that? That she likes wearing that particular kind of outfit? The plain features don't say much in terms of her non-existent personality or her interests of literally nothing, unless it's meant to represent youth? In which case, ok, but why make that her entire character? Anyway, you're probably wondering why I mentioned earlier about her playing like a  boring character given how the character difference is completely cosmetic and each character plays the same. Well no offence to the voice actor once again, but the actual lines given for Zoey really don't help with character building or establishing her as a human being capable of doing human being things. Also I don't know if anybody else experiences this, but why does the Zoey AI absolutely hate me? No joke, when I play singleplayer, Zoey always shoots the witch whenever possible, shoots gas canisters when teammates are nearby, uses the only medkit on herself when she has the most health of the entire team (usually in the green too) and completely refuses to revive teammates, even when all the infected are dead. As if hating Zoey couldn't get any easier.

I think one of the reasons I hate Zoey so much is just seeing how well the characters in Left 4 Dead 2 were done. L4D2 probably has my favourite cast of multiple main characters of any video game due to just how contrasting they are in addition to how well they go together. watching as Roachelle basically becomes like a mother to the entire group despite clearly having no experience with that kind of thing before, or seeing how Nick goes from being a snide asshole to everyone to really letting his light shine through in their darkest moments is really heartwarming, even in a grim zombie-ridden world. Coach and Ellis' humour despite their worst fears coming to fruition is also charming, making these characters not only easy for each other to love, but for the player to love too. It's a shame that Zoey never got this treatment, sure there was not much potential when you really summarise her character, but considering how much less inspiration there might have been for other valve characters, I know they could have done so much better.

I understand some people might defend Zoey or whatever, well good for you, more power to you in fact. I just wanted to complain about how terrible of a video game character Zoey is in my opinion, and not even for valve's standards, I'm comparing her to characters from games like Far Cry 6 and Saints Row 2022. If you think Zoey is a good character, that's fine, just know I am going to disagree with you unless you actually give a reason or reasons as to why, because I am seriously struggling to think of a single one. I know valve won't see this because they despise listening to their community, especially on the topic of their games, but at least they lay the foundations for wonderful communities to sprout in their wake. If only I could bring myself to give this beautiful game a positive review, unfortunately Zoey exists. So yeah, TL;DR: Zoey sucks.

review_text:
STO is unfortunately not a very good game.   It's a collectors hobby with some esoteric niche content for people who have spend the time, effort, and money to build a collection that allows them now to continue to find ways to play.  

Pretty much all the ships you want to fly and use are locked up in gambling boxes that require you to purchase "Keys" to unlock.  You pay to have a near minuscule chance to get what you want.  It's a frustrating nightmare.   Other ships are available for purchase directly, but you're still having to pay money... and rarely are they the kind of ships you nostalgically lust for being a Star Trek Fan... which honestly is the only reason why you're half interested in playing the game in the first place.

Gameplay starts out decent.   with a slow game pace and limited skills that slowly start to ramp up with level unlock.  Equipment is simple and generally intuitive at this point, but once you achieve high level what once was a rather fun game of timing, maneuver, and position is now a skill spam dystopian nightmare of overly complicated traits, equipment, and ability interactions that requires you to build chaining macros to properly activate in sequence to fire off... and the game honestly devolves into having spent enough money for the right 'special' consoles and skill traits, and smashing your macro spam button of choice fast enough.  

Not only this, but game play at the end is so radically different from the start, that leveling to max is nothing more than the prolonged starter instance before you're playing the  'real' game. 

For the good sides, there is an element of puzzling out good combos, trying different set ups and builds on different ships, and the joy of seeing them work... Very little of it feels like Star Trek.   

The ship design is superb, and the design creative and wonderful.  Good enough that many people just collect ships and fly them around purely for the artistic value.   Most of my critic is what you're meant to do with them... and sadly a number of very well known ships are essentially useless for actually playing the game.

There are a number of really engaging story arc missions and narratives that do rise to the occasion.  That are engaging and feel like immersing yourself in a season of Trek... albeit more in a Discovery sort of way with entirely too many epic wars, galaxy ending events only you can stop, and far fewer of the more interesting but more mundane sort of missions that appeal to my personal sensibilities and sense of grandeur.  

End Game Content severely lacks any real prize or reward structure to incentivize or encourage elite content.    Everything you really want is behind a pay to get your chance to play Gambling Monolith known as the Lockbox.  And its all the things behind those paywalls and gambling monoliths that let you play in the only real Endgame... which are the player created DPS leagues.

The greatest single piece of STO was the Foundry, which allowed players to create their own playable missions for other players.  It created a near endless stream of content from truly talented and creative people who were passionate about Trek... and could allow you to build your own piece of the universe as well.    IT was removed when Cryptic became unwilling to continue to keep it up to date, and with it ended the best of the game.

STO was a buggy and unfinished game when it was released... and it's never really recovered from this.  You will find a few individual pieces on the whole that can give you enjoyment, but on the whole it's just flat out not worth it... if you aren't already invested in it.

review_text:
I hate rom coms so this is what I play instead of watching them when I'm feeling sad or hormonal. This game may be for you if you like angst, blood and emotional repression. Also, maybe Stockholm syndrome... 

This is the first part of a two part story (the second is in Edo Blossoms) so don't expect much explicitly romantic stuff or a satisfactory conclusion at the end of this game. Also, you should probably use a walkthrough if you want to get a conclusion with a specific guy. If you do what I did the first (just load up the game, pick whichever options I felt like, see what happens), your character will end up sad and forever alone (but then you can figure out which one you're most interested in). After that, I went back with a walkthrough to follow each character's route (haven't finished all of them, though).

One of the great things about this game is its interactive glossary. It's very interesting and means that you can try and convince your friends that you are playing this for educational purposes. Ignore the not-vampires, demons and anime boys!

Overall, I think that this game is beautifully made and makes me feel things. I never skip the introduction because it is so spooky and perfectly sets the tone! I think that this game works so well for me because it blends together horror and fluff... As in, each seems more potent because it's contrasted so strongly with the other. If it was only one or the other, I would probably stop caring quite quickly.

review_text:
PSO2 Base: It is good to come back to this game and enjoy online play finally. My original intro to the series was on Gamecube for PSO.

I am an MMO player and a MOBA player. This game is very cool. I played the heck out of it, and as long as I am not focusing on 1 thing too much, i find the general growth pacing satisfying and rewarding.

NGS: I also feel that the System's and Utility features offered in the shop are valuable, and don't seem tacked on in any way. I am especially fond of Batch Movement and the re-done menus. Crafting has been revamped and makes a lot of sense now. The growth and pacing are balanced so that you're always going to find people who are willing to purchase your materials for their gear! And finishing a piece of equipment is also satisfying.

Combat feels very fluent and requires practice to utilize. There are always several more ways to increase your Battle Power. There's always something you can work on to get more and more power.

If you should decide to pay for in game currency, you aren't overwhelmed with so many different kinds of currencies as in other MMO's that the value of your Purchased Currency doesn't diminish with newer added types of currencies.

While it isn't perfect, yet... It is a very well put together game and borrows elements from both Phantasy Star RPG games and Phantasy Star Online games. The union of the 2 game styles hasn't been fully embraced by patrons of the PSO series, and you will get some variation in opinions of New Genesis. For me, coming from other MMO's and having been an avid RPG gamer for handhelds... I assure you this is a very polished concept for a game!

It has great potential. I can't wait to see what the Funding Boost is going to provide for us in the future!

review_text:
To the Moon is one of those rare games whose reputation precedes it, a supposedly devastating emotional journey wrapped in the aesthetics of a retro RPG. And while some of the praise is absolutely warranted, approaching it with clear eyes reveals both its brilliance and its limitations.

Narratively, it’s a quietly ambitious piece. The premise - two scientists diving through a dying man’s memories to fulfill his final wish - is undeniably compelling, and when the story lands, it lands with a thud straight to the heart. The writing has an earnest, almost handmade quality: sentimental but not manipulative, quirky without tipping into outright cutesiness. The relationship at the story’s center is layered, messy, believable, and the final act is genuinely affecting.

Mechanically, though, To the Moon is barely a “game”. Interaction is extremely shallow: light exploration, trivial puzzles and the occasional connective mini-game that feels more like padding than meaningful engagement. The experience succeeds in spite of its mechanics, not because of them. Some jokes also overstay their welcome, and the script leans heavily on quirk as a way to smooth over pacing dips.

But even with those caveats, the emotional core is potent. The soundtrack is exquisite: simple piano themes that burrow under your skin and elevate every moment. The pixel art, though modest, supports the tone with warmth and clarity.

To the Moon isn’t flawless and it’s not the transcendent masterpiece some describe. It’s a touching, sincere narrative experience with rough edges and a remarkable heart; more interactive novella than traditional game. If you meet it on its own terms, it rewards you with something gentle, human and quietly unforgettable.

review_text:
After a rough ride (starting as a F2P, losing a publisher, mostly switching to a paid single/multiplayer game), Relic Hunters has been released from EA. And it's almost great. Almost. It's held by a small number of design decisions ranging from annoying to catastrophic.

Pros:
The 6 characters feel pretty unique and most are fun to use. The skill trees are interesting enough that there are plausible routes to good build diversity, too.

Art style and direction is good.

The gunplay (you know, the main thing in the game) is actually good and fun. It's a looter shooter, and the looting and the shooting both have their high points. Weapons feel different, and definitely play into build variety.

The exploration missions are pretty great - it's fun to wander around, and most bosses feel different and have fun mechanics to interact with.

The animated movies are pretty good!

Cons:
It's a looter shooter with the single worst inventory management system I've ever seen. The small inventory is shared by every character. If one character equips a piece of gear, all have to carry it around. This is idiotic. There is a stash, but it's literally pointless.

The majority of the missions are not exploration. 80% of them are some version of "keep the bad guys out of this small circle." Sometimes the circle moves, sometimes you clear one circle and have to go to another. They all suck. It's a terrible mechanic, and it's literally most of what you do in the game.

Charge skills/jumping. Initially, these feel cool and fun to play with, but given that in almost every encounter enemies will be able to interrupt your skill charge up and your jump (making you fall straight down and waste the skill), these become annoying and a detriment, so you don't use them.

Falling off an edge - you take a little damage and you respawn pretty quick, but you keep a little momentum from when you fell. Meaning, sometimes you just keep respawning and falling over and over. It doesn't work well.

Grinding. The F2P bones of it are still obvious, and it's the bad parts of F2P. Did you love rep grinding in WoW Classic to get those items you need? No? Screw you, it's in here anyway. I hope you like territory control (*insert Xzibit meme*).

Mid - the plot and writing. It... exists.

TLDR; it's a pretty good game that's almost great. Almost. Except for some design decisions, some of which are fixable (enemy interrupts), some of which aren't (the F2P bones).

review_text:
[i]Preamble (added for clarification): Liking Pathologic 2 is completely legit. This game was simply too hard to recommend for me. This is a review about why so many people like it expressly for the reasons that make it hard to enjoy. Please stay respectful and read at your own discretion.[/i]
----
This is more of an artistic experience than a game, and therefore the perfect example of critics contrasting the average consumers. I think this game is fantastic; but not as a game, and certainly not for most, hence [b]I do not recommend by default[/b]. The braveness of direction and design earns its laudatio, but it is hell to play. Very hard to describe. If you enjoy this, you are probably pathologic.

I dropped the game, twice. (Edited again for clarification.) I kinda hated playing it. Following others' advice, I played to the 2-3hr mark and since it didn't click for me by that point, it likely wouldn't ever since the rest of the game doesn't change. In order to understand the positive reviews I consumed hella deep dive YouTube content on it, so [h3]here is my analysis on why reviews are [i]raving so hard they could be a club in Berlin[/i] whereas actual gamer completion rates for Pathologic games are low.[/h3]

1. As most reviews will tell you, this is an incredibly niche experience for a hyperspecific kind of people. Namely, theatre-minded (not general art, specifically stage plays) folks who vibe with cryptic weirdness and anarchic breaking of styles and conventions, even when resulting in inaccessibility for a general populace. Literally the entire appeal of this game is its [i]performance[/i] - not a literal benchmark, but a performance of pathos and meta breaking. A lot of Pathologic analysis YouTubers also did stuff on mindbending shows like Neon Genesis Evangelion or Utena, if you care for comparisons. Which means the target audience for this is not gamers, but a theatrical audience that is looking [b]to be played instead of to play[/b]. You can't be good at Pathologic. You cannot get better at Pathologic. You can not enjoy Pathologic as a game in its most fundamental, ludic sense. It forces you to give up control. If you're in this cerebral niche, you will love this game all the more and 100% write a review on it; hence the amount of raving reviews not being proportional to the amount of players actually playing the game. And that is fine. Liking Pathologic is fine, but it is also niche.

2. Pathologic 2 has amazing narrative direction moving between layers of player consciousness, that however also requires a high cognitive investment and intrinsic motivation to actively want to experience that. The gameplay is neither rewarding nor good. Saying that it's not good (it's extremely punishing and slow-paced) does not negate the fact the game can still be good for people who weren't looking for that in this game anyways. Saying that this game design being 100% intentional does not negate the fact it will still drive away most people, understandably so. People expect different things out of games, e.g. not going through an existential crisis and not sitting through a performance. I'm not talking about the story or philosophy, but the literal gameplay (or rather, its intrinsic and unbearable dependance on story hooks to keep players tolerating it).

3. Pathologic is one of the most unique "games" out there. However, all prior points combined, in order to acquire its unique writing one has to go through such sluggish, stressful gameplay that it should be understandable when people don't like it, it doesn't mean they didn't try to like it or didn't understand the game. The more you like Pathologic, the more you will agree it is not a game meant to be played as a game, and therefore scare off most.

4. Lastly, a ton of comparisons to classic Russian existentialist and/or nihilist literature are drawn in comments and reviews. I will end by saying that the people who enjoy this game would probably all enjoy Dostoyevsky, but not all who enjoy Dostoyevsky will enjoy this game - and that is fine. I'd rather someone drop it respectfully than anybody being disrespectful about others "not getting it".

I cannot recommend Pathologic 2 to the absolute majority of people. However, let it be known I will absolutely be buying Pathologic 3 too just to support the developers and their creative vision. I hella respect indie devs going off the trodden path.

review_text:
I sadly wouldn't recommend Scon to the average player as its gameplay just doesn't feel fun to engage with but if you're looking for a beautiful world to look through and admire then Scorn might be for you.

To put it simply, Scorn is fundamentally a piece of artwork that has a game slapped onto it. Scorn involves elements of combat that feel out of place and unnecessary with enemies feeling like more of an inconvenience whether you engage with them or not. There are plenty of puzzles that usually feel fine and aren't too challenging to complete but feel used incorrectly as they tend to push you through a linear world when I feel they could have been used to feel like  they are opening up this strange world to you. HOWEVER Scorn is truly one of the best visual experiences I've had in a game as its clear inspiration from H.R Giger creates a disturbing and foreign world that ingolfs you in its atmosphere that unsettles you with the fear of the unknown in an alien world. There is little narrative or lore which I personally feel works in its favor as it feeds into this feeling of fear of a world that you don't understand. It's a world that clearly has a story to tell but wants you as a player to create your own understanding of the world that makes sense to you. Scorn is an extremely flawed masterpiece that tries to be something that it isn't and shouldn't be but still manages to be one of the most beautiful games i've ever played.

review_text:
I have a flashing weak spot for looter shooters. They hit my critoris in just the right way. But it wasn’t until relic hunters legends that I realised theres practically no top down twin stick options that scratch the same itch that Destiny managed too back in it’s hayday.

I played the beta for legends a few months ago and I’ve been itching to tell you about it ever since. But I wanted to get a little further into this early access title before giving it my seal of approval just in case three hours into the campaign it tries to offer me NFTs or something.

Well fund the Taliban and call me a Clinton it turns out it’s actually pretty good.

For an early access title it sure feels finished to me. Shooting guns is finger licking good, the campaign feels all there and there’s enough to do every day to keep me entertained for a while.

So what have we got. A main hub area to trade with other players and test out weapons. A campaign. Various levelable relic hunters with stats and ults to level which all feel different. Instanced mission nodes. And Guns with more random buffs than a gay porno.

I particularly like the loadout screen which was lifted from Destiny, and you rely on a gear score to know whether or not a challenge is right for you. You can upgrade your favourite gear, and the games lets you know ahead of time to not be shy about upgrading parts your into, because you can always merge that gear into newly dropped stuff just fine.

It has drop in co-op and it isn’t rare to land into a public mission already underway. You can play solo just fine but it’s always sort of a relief to have random friendos helping you in a public match. Oh yeah there’s ingame chat and emotes too.

Levels have secondary goals of random resources sprinkled around and chests of extra loot tucked away as a reward for poking around.

Rogue Snail have managed to create a toit little product. I’ve heard about polishing turds before but they’ve managed to compress a turd into a diamond.

If you were wanting a new game to play with your 3 friends, or just something to turn your head off for as you get into the zone of dodge iframes and killing tons of dudes then you should probably check out relic hunters Legends.
