review_text:
This is my first Sword Art Online game. I'm not a huge fan as you can tell, but I enjoy playing role-playing games. As someone who has never played the previous titles I'm not very knowledgeable on how well the others did.

- Controls -

The camera settings are terrible.

- Combat -

You're expected to guard and dodge a lot.

Combat is a little clunky, flying around can become irritating, getting stuck between/inside things is fun, and taking damage sucks even from trash mobs.

- Loot -

Terrible. With cosmetics feeling non-existent.

- Progression -

Abysmal. Crafting is limited since it's not supposed to be the main source of getting gear. I'm also not sure what the purpose of making character ranks so high was for except wasting your time. It could've been halved giving something each rank. The character rank also boosts their stats but it's very minimal.

- Co-Op and Free Roam -

Matching in NA region is slowly taking longer and longer to fill up. If no one's matching please just let me play with bots. It shouldn't take 5 - 20 minutes for the quest to actually start. If the reason is because you need one real player on each team then makes the bots a little smarter at clearing their objective.

Co-Op Earning points:
Players earn points by successfully completing mission objectives, dealing damage to enemies, supporting teammates, and achieving specific in-game actions during combat.

I've played Woods of Recollection enough to know that if you get the escort and cave objective you're not getting MVP 99% of the time. Those objectives take a very long time, and give very little points. The same can be said about majority of the other co-op maps. Most teams, especially strong ones will just zerg rush to the main objective and camp there to receive the most amount of points.

Free roam is nice because you can leave whenever you want. I also feel like it's a little more reliable when trying to find epic and legendary pieces of gear outside of crafting.

- DLC (Downloadable Content) and MTX (Microtransactions) -

Disappointed, but expected. Hopefully the battlepasses remain free.

Overall, if you're a Sword Art Online fan you probably find my review unfair. That's fair. I don't think Fractured Daydream is a bad game. It has its flaws sure, but I still enjoy it.

review_text:
I'll start like many other reviews and say that I loved Boneworks (BW). The story in that game was somewhat veiled, but it gradually became more apparent as the story went on. BoneLab is nothing like this. When I watched the promotional videos and whatnot, I thought it would be a story-driven sequel to BW, with similar writing. That is almost the exact opposite of what actually was released. There were some good parts to the game, but they all occurred in about the first hour of play through. I'll divide up my review to (hopefully) make it more readable.

[h1] The Good of BoneLab [/h1]

-It introduces new weapons that are somewhat interesting
-Introduces native support for modding
-Includes an updated physics engine from BW (more about this later)

[h1] The Bad of BoneLab [/h1]

-Absolutely horrible story
           This game started strong, but quickly made me want to toss my headset in the trash. As other reviewers have gone into detail, I won't write much here, but suffice it to say, they suck. The minigames that are forced into the campaign ruin the flow of the story and add nothing to the game. The body changing levels simply make no sense other than showing how well the devs can integrate that system into the game. After playing through the rest of the story, I can confidently say that I didn't use this system more than once. Maybe it would have been better if the system wasn't introduced with only about 15% of the story left.

       The story here was nonexistent and seemed to be a bunch of different ideas all compiled and shoved randomly into a cash-grab disguised as a game. 

-Weird physics system
       While BW had a wonky physics engine sometimes, it was undeniably better than BoneLab's most of the time. In BoneLab, half the time you'll go to climb something, or vault a ledge, and you'll find your legs will catapult you in the opposite direction. This causes you to repeat part, or all, of the level. This is especially tough since you cannot do anything about your leg position, when crouching either doesn't work, or makes your virtual head be glued to the floor, making you unable to move. 

-Overly simple level design
       Once again, BW shines much brighter than this game. BW allowed you to explore every nook and cranny to find hidden items and ammo (more on this later). If you wanted to, however, you could progress through BW fairly quickly without the exploring. BoneLab provides almost no exploration, and even when it does, the "hidden" areas provide essentially nothing. One level specifically has you find a "hidden" spot just to find two chairs and writing on the wall. This makes exploring basically useless. Most levels just force your down the story path as it is literally THE ONLY path you can take, with no dead ends or anything to make people curious. This makes even longer levels seem extremely short and underwhelming. 

-Ammunition/guns
       One question: Why make guns and ammo stay through the levels and remove the option to purchase items with ammo? I basically was extremely stringent on shooting enemies because in BW every bullet mattered. You could buy different weapons, and at the end, you could buy dev tools with your saved ammo. BoneLab lets you keep ammo through the levels, and doesn't give you a way to do anything except shoot things  with it. I wound up finishing the game with large amounts of unused ammo. You will get enough ammo to essentially run the whole game doing nothing but shooting enemies. I could have probably avoided 1.5 hours of game play by simply shooting everything and not worrying about how else to kill things. Also guns are perpetually saved as well, so you can keep the guns you initially get throughout the game. Gun spawns later in the game seem to be worse than those in the earlier levels. 
        Also, the final level gives you a ton of guns and lots of ammo to choose from/pick up. I thought from all these items it would be a huge battle like the clock tower in BW. I get to the end of the level and maybe shot 20 bullets to kill 6 enemies. Unlike in BW, where you either had to buy or find weapons to survive tough enemy waves, BoneLab hands you enough guns and ammo to play through the story five times in the first level. (You can also just play as the heavy and kill everything with one punch)

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
       I really wanted to like this game, but it just does not meet even my lowest expectations. If I had known I'd be spending $40 on a compiled list of tech demos and concept ideas, I would not have bought the game. There is almost no story development or reason to continue playing. In BW, even if you didn't understand the story right away, you felt an urge to lay simply to escape the world. Here it just seems like the developers wanted to show off their programming abilities and get a bunch of money from people that simply wanted a playable game. When I first got into the game, as the levels progressed, it felt more and more like a beta or early-access game. If you have BW, do not waste your money on this unfinished cash-grab.

[h1] TLDR [/h1]

This game is barely more than a compilation of mini-games and bugs. Barely any story, bugs, and little improvement over Boneworks left me feeling disappointed and like I was playing an early-access title. Boneworks was much better in several aspects, and this game takes the franchise back several steps.

If you like games with strategy, teamwork, and clutch moments, DBD delivers hard. Survivors have to outsmart the killer, manage objectives, and stay calm under pressure, while Killers get the thrill of hunting, predicting moves, and mastering their powers. It’s super rewarding once you learn the mechanics, and the skill ceiling keeps it interesting even after hundreds of hours.

The devs constantly add new content—new killers, survivors, perks, and events—so the game doesn’t get stale. And honestly, some of the character designs and lore are just too good. Whether you want a competitive experience or just chaotic, funny matches with friends, DBD is perfect.

If you’re looking for a multiplayer game that’s scary, strategic, and hella fun with friends, I definitely recommend giving Dead by Daylight a try. Just be ready for adrenaline, mind games, and some salty lobbies.

review_text:
I softly recommend Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon.

A few parts of this have aged like milk. Opening with a forced tutorial full of jokes about how annoying forced tutorials are is, in particular, a joke that kinda misses the mark given it's just as frustrating as it's telling you it is... maybe needed a rethink, that one. And compared to other similar open world games, this is pretty small in scope; a fairly small map, small range of enemies and weapons, a small set of side missions with little variety between them. Everything here is open world lite.

But that's also kind of the beauty of it. If you can pick this up cheap, then this gives you that rarest of things; a bite sized open world game. You can 100% this in a day without much difficulty. There are no filler weapons, no weak pistol you throw away when you get a stronger one; there's one Pistol, one Shotgun, one Sniper Rifle etc., and they're all fairly decent. Money is so plentiful, it's doubtful you ever won't have enough to buy everything you unlock. There's nothing, tutorial aside, between you and just playing the game.

The aesthetic obviously needs to be discussed. This is a game with neon palm trees, cybernetic panthers, guns that can be upgraded to fire lasers instead of bullets. It's a game where a level-up is met with a wailing guitar riff, as you throw the devil horns with your robot hand, electricty arching between your fingers. It's a game so filled with pulp 80s sci-fi energy, it finishes with a Miami Connection reference, for goodness sake; cuts don't get much deeper.

If you want to spend 10 hours blasting cyborgs with quad-barrel shotguns and watching 8-bit styled training montages, or if you want that open-world style of gameplay without the time investment or complexity that usually means, Blood Dragon is for you.

Another amazing installment in the Yakuza series, this one seriously expanding the scope of both the game and the story. Seriously, it feels like the developers were given as much time and budget to add anything they wanted to the scope of the game. 

This game, above all else, was the nurturing and carrying on of dreams and honestly I love this game for it. The passing of the torch for the next generation as well as honouring the dreams of those that have come before, I found the story griping from start to finish. Another part that amazed me with the game's scope was how each character was given their own totally optional side story. Why is there a fully fleshed out hunting side story for Saejima? Why is Kiryu now a taxi driver?? Why can I play Taiko no Tatsujin??? Honestly, peak. 

The combat was nice and varied, I never felt tired or bored thanks to the variety of characters and their unique fighting styles. Everyone felt like they hit hard, had their strengths and quirks that you can use to maximise their damage. 

That said, there are a few sore points with the game that I had. One being that the cutscenes for majority of the game are really nice remastered cutscenes, then some were randomly looking like the original PS3 ones. And the tonal shift from going from Saejima's part to Haruka was... something else to say the least. 

If you've made it this far into the Yakuza series, you'd be doing yourself a disservice by skipping this game. Definitely get this game, and if it's on sale? Even better!

review_text:
At first I wasn't sure if I was really into this game. It very much starts off as every other farming type game does and felt pretty repetitive.

Then half my town got smallpox and died. The calendar was just funerals for WEEKS. And I was like, "Oooooh. Okay, I'm totally into this." So, haha, do with that as you will. 

But seriously, the generational mechanics are really interesting, even if the romance/marriage feels lacking. I get not making things overly complex because everyone is one cough away from death at all times, but it still would've been nice to have some more depth to those interactions. 

I do love that the NPCs are also living their own lives. Several of my first pick spouses were snapped up before I'd even gotten my feet under me.

Also, I really appreciate the ability to modify the game and turn features on and off as you want. It makes it easy to tailor the game to your playstyle.

Despite the fact that I've seen the credits roll, I don't think I'm [i]quite[/i] done with the game yet. I haven't actually gotten to play as my heir yet, so there's a bit more of the game I'd like to see. And I also like the fact that with the randomness of marriages and diseases, each playthrough can be very different. I can see myself popping back into the game to start a new save after some time.

Between the unique elements and the adorable art style, definitely recommended.

These issues sincerely need to be addressed and fixed before anyone even considers spending one dollar on this game. You may not get what you paid for, and there is nothing that anyone can or will do about it if you don't.

Until these issues are fixed, steer clear.

review_text:
The visuals, artistry, the mystery world, all of that is awesome, but... 
And that's a big but; I still would not recommend it. Here's why.

Apparently, the game has been released unfinished after more than 10 years in the making, and the gameplay mechanics, especially combat, have been made clunky and too hard on purpose to make the game feel longer: 
- The dodging action has been cut on purpose to make the player dodge by strafing only or avoid combat entirely by sneaking around the enemies
- The [spoiler]health recharge tanks[/spoiler] have been made less than half empty on purpose
- Checkpoints (and that's what grinds me most) that fit the world's lore are missing, where the player could safe his progress, but instead the checkpoints are invisible, arbitrarily placed and too far apart. When the player dies, they never know where they spawn again and what needs to be done once again
- Exploration takes unnecessarily long just to show that something bad happened to the world without anything actually meaningful to discover other than striking landscapes and visceral visuals

Placing fewer, more unique enemies and making them harder, or longer to defeat would have made much more sense and would require the player to be more strategic, analytical and patient. I would have imagined unique enemies having some nasty, gory, gigeresque visceral attacks, as the world's alien biology seems to be out of control. Instead: shout the ugly spitting things in the face; repeat until dead. Some enemies look like they weren't initially planned attacking the player at all, hence the only attack they use is spitting; very easy to implement, much more annoying in combat. Either the combat was slapped on the otherwise fascinating game, or it was left finished. It isn't fun and feels out of place.

I am [b]very[/b] disappointed. Unless you are tolerant to frustration and enjoy games like Dark Souls that game will not be fun. You have been warned.

review_text:
Ahh, Hakuoki. The game I postponed playing for a very long time simply because of its price. However, I have to say that if you can spare the money, then it is absolutely worth it. 

A lot of otome games don't take the time to really develop the characters of the love interests, however, that is not the case in Hakuoki. It really takes the time to explore and develop the characters of the boys and all of them are quite pleasant and charming in their own way. 

The story is also very interesting and doesn't allow you to get bored easily. I'm not sure how historically accurate it actually is (as it is supposedly based on true events), but I do know that I enjoyed the story a lot. 

Contrary to popular belief, I actually found the protagonist decent. (for otome games standards) Yes, she was physically weak and perhaps not very intelligent, but she also showed a lot of bravery sometimes and there were moments where she showed a lot of emotional strength and made some insightful observations. She was definitely better than the protagonists in some other similar games I have played or at least that's how it seemed to me.

review_text:
You know what you need in a touching, sentimental story about a dying man's wish? Jokes! Lots and lots of jokes! Just put them everywhere and it won't ruin the tone at all!

I had read a lot about how this game was supposed to have a great story, one of the best in modern gaming. I'm thoroughly baffled by these reviews. The level of writing of the game was on par with, say Final Fantasy 2. It read like a poor translation in a number of places and just had too many winks to other games. 

One of the main characters (you control one of two Rosencrantz-and-Guildensternesque scientists) is just constantly poking fun at things that are happening in the dying man's memories. It's as though the writer is trying to keep you from getting attached to the characters. A lot of the time the characters will start to explain something ("You mean you think it's...?") but then they don't finish their sentence, which makes you wonder why they bothered saying anything in the first place. The music struggles to keep the tone maudlin, but the writing will not give up its ceaseless buffoonery enough for you to invest any emotion.

Now that that's out of the way, here's what's wrong with the rest of the game: 

The controls are bad. They are minimal, so you'd think they'd be handled well, but no. You have the choice between keyboard or mouse. With you mouse, you can mouseover things to see if they can be interacted with. Unfortunately, the zones in which you place your mouse seem to be not placed well on the items they're representing, so you may need to move the mouse around to find them. Also, after clicking someplace to make the character move, the character may or may not move there, OR they may just stuff halfway there.

The keyboard controls are a little better, but you use the interactivity indicator, so you just walk up to everything that looks interesting and try it out. That wouldn't be so bad, but you walk very slow. Not all the time! Just most of the time. There doesn't seem to be any logic to when you can run and when you can't.

There are little puzzles thrown in that have nothing really to do with the plot. There is an "ideal" number of moves to solve each puzzle and a total number of moves you've made in all puzzles to that point, but once you finish the last puzzle, you never hear about those again. Irrelevant.

The plot has a gaping hole in the beginning, and there's really no reason why the wish can't be fulfilled at the get go, which negates the reason for the rest of the game.

The music is not bad, but it's honestly all kind of samey. It also doesn't seem to fit the mood in certain places, but how would you be able to tell anyway, again because of the writing.

This game should've been a film because all the interaction is either completely irrelevant or just poorly controlled. You're not going to glean any emotion from those tiny pixelated faces anyway, and the writing won't help you either. Pass this one up.

tl;dr Dramatic narrative is ruined by overly jokey, low-quality writing.

review_text:
It's fun, but lacks a hook.

Witchfire is one of those games that you get when the devs are talented but directionless fans. Instead of something that's great and unique, Witchfire ends up playing like a list of the games that these developers love.
Souls/Remnant games, Apex, Hades perhaps, and a dash of extraction. While it's a great time killer, there's nothing to really draw you in and keep you playing. Just to list off a few fundamental issues that I have with the game:

Same maps on repeat. While this would be fine in a BR or extraction game due to other players providing the variable experience in matches, this is just a single player game. So it turns into a repetitive grind that only changes when you unlock gnocchi [sic] which opens up more of the maps with challenges, albeit very small extra areas. I feel like this just induces burnout more than anything in a single player game. 

Great Apex-like movement, no reason to use it. Seriously the long, fast slides feel very Apexy. Apex, as you might recall, is strictly PVP. I have no reason (or at least, haven't yet) to be taking these risky high-pace movements. I made great use of sliding in Apex, often grappling for momentum and flinging myself behind them to come out ahead. I am failing to see a reason to slide myself into a bunch of enemies that will stun lock that shit out of me.

The inventory/stash system???? What even is this? Why do unused keys go there and why can't I bring them with me?? I've got 30 useless keys in there. 

The level up system is just a mockery of a Souls game. Like it's maybe 12% endearing that you took inspiration from Fromsoft, but 88% embarrassing and kind of insulting that this is how you chose to show it. There is one single offensive stat that reduces spell cool down. Two supporting/ancillary stats to make the game a bit easier (one gives more souls, one increases item spawn) and then you have vigor, endurance, and a "heal more from your potions" stat. So what is the build here? Either vigor or endurance dump, or maybe cast spells a bit more often. No damage, no real variation, and therefore no purpose or reason to care about it. 

It does look pretty good though, animations are nice, guns are detailed, environment is fairly pretty and gives kind of an open world feel which is necessary, especially considering it's a hub-based game. But as long as it remains a mish mash of influences it will only be maybe a 5/10 game for me. I can see how some people enjoy it, but I truly believe most of these positive reviews will actually burn out within 10 hours of game play and change their minds. 

1 Year check in: 
Virtually the same, a lot more content, stats system reworked a bit, a few other knick knacks added... ultimately still just mediocre. Same awful game mechanics that turn the game into a grind fest, same awful sound engineering that play random ass zombie sounds all around you, make enemies that are standing in front of you sound like they're attacking from behind... It sucks because this is put together much better than the recent counterparts in the genre, but just isn't that fun to play.

I think this game is decently fun for about an hour right now, I hope as they keep working through early access it becomes the "deep and rewarding" hockey exp they claim. 

It's easy to pick up and play and the humor is pretty funny (for the most part), the arcade element has more than a little NHL 94 in it. What I wish is that they took more queues from games like NHL Hitz in adding depth to attacking and defending play. The passing/shooting can be inconsistent at time with players having very odd hitboxes to receive passes, the goalies for the AI will always somehow be massively better than yours no matter how you try and spec. 
The customization itself is just very lacking. You get whacky powerups but since the players you start with on your team has such indecently low stats, giving them any abilities is basically a waste since they can't skate or shoot well enough to take advantage of most of them. You only every upgrade the main character, angus, so spending lots of effort "building a team" as the trailer suggests just feels awful. Whether you have a good run or not is completely dependent on the luck of who you roll for teammates, it would be nice if after completing a boss you got to keep any other player and build a full team over time that gave you more options. Why don't we have a bench deeper than 5? Let us keep a player every time we beat a boss and then over time we have to make strategic decisions on the lineup card based on the region we are trying to clear and the teams there.
Right now it can be fun enough playing short term, but the longer you go the more it starts to feel pointless. This game lacks strategy right now and that is a shame.

Charming graphics, delightful characters, interesting and open RP / storytelling; This game is perfect if you ever wanted to insert yourself into a small costal town with plenty of investing elements such as marriage, children, and bloodlines! 

At first I was concerned this would be another wash and rise farming game with set plot points and a pre-determined cast but no-! I was instantly surprised with sickness and death only to have new faces enter the town with their own quirks and values. On seeing a child I had grown fond of turn into an adult and retain and renew some of their personality was so rewarding along with seeing how these characters progressed in their own bloodlines.
Safe to say I got all giddy on seeing invitations to weddings, sadness on seeing funerals, and pure curiosity when a new face entered the town. 


Outside of social events I enjoyed the slow yet steady pace of the game where it didn't feel days were dragging on to no end or that they were too short, it was a amazing middle-ground for me on default settings. The best part- I could change the pace of the game!! So many farm games don't have this option and it really adds to the balance this game perfectly captures for me. 
There is a bit of a grind, but hey, that's pretty much all farming games and this one was rather enjoyable. Building your farm up from nothing and gaining new tools and friends was a rich and rewarding experience I intend to sink many many more hours into.

TLDR 10/10 good game.

review_text:
I consider this game to be an improvement over Hiveswap Act 1, but ultimately it should still appeal to the same people (and most of those people will want to play act 1 first).

As before, it's effectively a visual novel disguised as a point and click adventure. However, despite most of it being literally on-rails this one has more legitimate puzzles and requires you to think a bit. The focus is almost entirely on social interactions with the trolls you meet, rather than "use item X on background object Y", which is a great change from traditional point-and-click fare and really plays to the author's strengths.

And yes, Andrew Hussie is in peak form here. The characters you meet are all fun and quite varied, the scenarios they place you in are creative, and several puzzles have more than one solution you can find. The story is focused on the parts of Homestuck's lore that everyone already found most interesting. The worldbuilding holds up with or without knowledge of the prior work. The comedy and character development is on point. There's plenty of silly secret remarks you can get from using every item on every person or talking to people at different points in the story, but since you're actually TALKING to people it doesn't hurt the pacing much this time. And the change in format renders it 100% immune to the pacing problems that Homestuck itself suffered from.

That being said, the brief portion at the start of the game where there AREN'T a lot of characters around suffers from the same slow pacing as Act 1. Maybe even worse since not much is happening.

Don't worry about difficulty. Most puzzles can eventually be solved by just talking to everyone about everything, and the one section with deeper puzzles (the trial) has a hint button that starts vague but will hand you the answer if you hit it enough times. There's no other skill-based minigames (one got removed and if it gets readded it'll probably be skippable) so anyone should be able to beat this game.

The game is longer than Act 1. Took me about 13 hours to complete (with moderate reloading to explore other options), compared to 8 on the first game. For replay value, there's a lot of hidden achievements based on the multiple ways of solving certain puzzles, on preserving certain items for the whole run, etc. In fact you'd need several full playthroughs to get all acheivements since some are mutually exclusive. But since you can't fast forward dialog I have a hard time imagining myself doing more than just a second playthrough (not counting reloads just before a part I want to retry).

Some people on the forums complained about bugs and softlocks, but I didn't see a single one in my play experience.

Overall, anyone who liked Homestuck, or even liked parts of Homestuck, will probably love this game. And Act 2 is better than Act 1. But I'd still suggest playing Act 1 before Act 2.

review_text:
I was drawn in by the setting of this game and then sold after seeing it win one of the Top Indie Games at MomoCon's Indie Game Awards. I felt lucky to receive a free key for attending the Indie Game Awards. The game was very fun in the beginning, but after a while serious bugs came to light. Some were just minor animation clipping issues. Others were much bigger, like plot events not firing as they were supposed to and a very easy to recreate issue where if you stab some and pick their body up in one move and then try to cary the body off during the pick up animation, the character will move to the spot but not drop the body if you still have the action button still held down. You also had to get the exact right view for navigating in narrow spaces, because raycasting did not pass through invalid objects.

Load times are also too long. I don't have a beast of a machine, but it is a better than average computer. Load times for some of the first few levels were over 4 minutes.

The story is great! And, I love Takuma's witty comments. I may be a too nit picky about somethings, but major control issues are a no-go for me in any game. If you can get past unresponsive controls in a game where timing is essential, go for it. I promise you will be amused.

Maybe it is worth purchasing during a sale, but I don't think it is worth full price.

review_text:
TL;DR This honestly would have been a more enjoyable experience if it was a VN like Friendsim.

Act 2 plays and feels like a product of significantly lower quality than Act 1. 
In short, it hardly feels like a sequel at all, at least in regards to gameplay. Act 1 was a pleasant surprise following its tumultuous conception and development. Charming and well polished, it gave me high hopes for the next in the series. That was a long wait, and unfortunately I can't rightly say Act 2 lived up to my hopes.

As I understand it, the original team that worked on Act 1 was majorly laid off after Viz acquired Homestuck. I was hoping this wouldn't result in too much turbulence when it came to continuing the Hiveswap series, but going from the first act to this game gave me whiplash. 

This game is presented as the sequel to Hiveswap: Act 1, obviously, but it plays more like a sequel to Hiveswap: Friendsim (The 0.99$ VN's that were released episodically after Act 1, and before this game).

Instead of playing like a point and click adventure game, like the previous game, [b]this plays a lot more like a VN[/b]. 

You retain your inventory from the first game if you carry your save over, but for the VAST majority of the game you don't use anything and you spend most of your time going through dialogues with characters from Friendsim. Each screen from the first game had plenty of objects that you could interact with in different ways with your items and abilities; In this game, there are hardly any items in the background to find or do anything with, and it makes them feel much hollower. You only interact with characters for the most part, and most screens consist of walking back and forth between characters until you exhaust their dialogue and the game lets you proceed to the next screen. 

Some of the longer sections of the game are just long because you have to walk all the way from the front of the train to the back, and then to the front again. At one point you have to walk from the VERY FRONT all the way to the back, just to have your character say "Well I didn't need to do this" and have you walk all the way up to the front again. And strangely enough, the walking mechanics are... spotty? You have to mash click to keep moving, and sometimes you will just... stop. It's a weird thing to mention but... This is the "core gameplay". so it's worth mentioning.

There are two significant sections of the game that I would say actually constitute "puzzles"; The trial, and the finale in the front car. Keep in mind this game is [i]very[/i] short. I think your mileage will vary when it comes to these; Personally, I did not think either event was very good by adventure game standards.

[spoiler]The outcome of the trial is apparently decided by an unrelated dialogue from an unrelated character BEFORE you board the train; If you don't select a certain option, you will not be able to access the "Good" ending to the trial. I'm not a big fan of that. The trial itself isn't exactly going to be putting Phoenix Wright out of business anyway. As mentioned below, keeping track of your items and the timeline in the trial is inconsistent and un-intuitive.[/spoiler]

The game falls short of Act 1 in other departments as well:
There is a real inconsistency to the quality of the assets in the game. Some backgrounds can be very quality, but others will have very obvious artifacting, or just be way lower resolution. 
Example: Moving from the indigo car to the purple car. The indigo background is very nice and high quality, but the transition between the cars and the purple car are much lower resolution, and some places have very harsh artifacting present.
One of the worst and most obvious discrepancies in quality is in the final sequence; Using Byers in the final sequence releases him and he has a flying animation, but when he lands again his sprite reverts to an asset from the previous game... But it's not properly cut out. The sprite is surrounded by a spotty white pixel halo from it not being prepared properly for transparency. This is very confusing because it's very obvious, and I'm pretty sure nearly anyone could fix this problem in under an hour in photoshop.
These are just some specific examples, these kind of discrepancies are present mostly throughout the length of the game.

There's also small general inconsistencies in miscellaneous areas of the game;
- Some items you acquire (Namely for the trial) go into your inventory, but some don't for whatever reason. It can be hard to keep track of what you actually have, because you can't even check the trial timeline/suspects/etc. until actually starting the trial. Sometimes you can't even check the timeline while questioning a witness, which is very annoying.
- Your interactions are commonly inconsistent: Some doors you just walk through by clicking, some open a little Look/Exit menu and you have to click again. 
- Some characters will talk very slowly, which makes me want to click to fill out their text box so I can read it. But when you are in a dialogue with multiple characters, sometimes one can speak VERY QUICKLY, which will cause you to skip over their text if you're in a rythm. The VNs avoid this problem by letting you go back through dialogue... And again, this basically plays like a VN. 

These are clearly very small criticisms, but you have to remember that these are basically the mechanics of the whole game. It gets annoying over time. The VNs were 90 cents, and also focused on dialogue... And they don't suffer from the same QoL problems.
You feel the minor annoyances a lot more because there's just not a lot else going on.

This is a very nitpicky example to mention, but even the achievements are arguably lower quality. The first game has unique little icons for each achievement, but this game uses the same icon for all of them. It might not mean much but to me it does illustrate a difference in the level of care this time around. 

I hate to say it, but this episode makes it harder to recommend Act 1, which is already a pretty niche title. I hope that the next installment makes some improvements, or at least reclaims some of the good aspects of the first game.

Since there's no neutral option between a Negative and a Positive review i'll stick with a Positive one because even with some flaws here and there, overall this game was still a fun experience at the end of the day.
So here are some problems from the top of my head that makes me not have loved playing this as much as i wanted to:

First, here's the biggest problem of them all, the constant need to open the inventory menu every 10 seconds as you end up needing a different type of weapon in order to fight an specific enemy that's unfair or too hard with your previous set.

Second, with the help of the previous problem, the dull combat gets highlighted further as you start to notice the tiresome pattern of opening your inventory, searching for a specific weapon in a mess of an order, dodge the enemy attack, kill them and then in the next enemy repeat the process, including switching weapons.

Third, this is kinda underwhelming in my opinion, but the resources of this game are actually LIMITED, you'll get off a boss fight or a difficult corridor section and you'll reach a save point and feel safer until you realize that your HP and you MP don't recharge for free at all, never, the only way to recover basic resources is by either using weapons that heal you or buying potions, which takes us to the problem that you'll interact with a vendor and notice that you can only buy from him 20 bombs or something and then never anymore, it's gone, if you waste every dynamite in the game, then that's it.

There are some other minor things that you can choose to nitpick in this game, but honestly i'm fine with the rest, and even with these problems i've stated, i've had fun and seeing the endings and the entire journey made me happy to have played it to begin with, it's a cool game to play if you like it's type, there's some very nice music tracks here and there, mostly to the ending parts, and the biggest seller of the game is definitly it's BEAUTIFUL pixel art mixed with some modern lighting and other post-processing VFX, just don't expect TOO much of the game and you'll enjoy it, that's all.

review_text:
This game has something for all fans of Star Trek. While the bulk of it might reference The Original Series, The Next Generation and it's spin-offs and Enterprise, there are definitely elements of the newer installations of Star Trek whether you as the fan, love it, hate it, or somewhere in between.

I will warn anyone considering to play this, that depending on how you game, this game can be difficult to learn without the proper guidance or research. While the in-game store makes it look like it's absolutely pay-to-win, it isn't.  However, the player can grind to achieve better builds for their ships if they decide to buy the latest Tier 6 ship, or stick with their free Tier 5 upon reaching level 61. It seems the PvP in this game died, but the PvE Task Force Operations are alive and well.

There are some glaring bugs that never got addressed, like the changeling in the "Jabberwocky" mission, the target in one of the Klingon missions for Klingon recruits (active during the KDF recruitment periods), and probably others as well. Depending on how your perception is, this may or may not turn you away from this game. Still, however, life persists in this game, and the community is live and well. Many things have changed over the years with Star Trek Online and unfortunately, I cannot share any experience to compare what type of game Star Trek Online was to the one of today. Be prepared to die a lot depending on your missions. If you're a masochist like me, but love Star Trek, then this game just might be for you.

As with many games, this one also comes with problems on top of bugs. As all die-hard Trekkies know, it should be possible to cross-faction or team up with different factions in this game, as cooperation is the foundation of the United Federation of Planets. Clearly, it isn't possible. Sure, if you want to play a Federation Klingon, you have to pay to unlock the option, but you cannot play a Klingon teaming up with a seemingly honorable Starfleet warrior or play a Starfleet Vucan who knows that it's logical to team up with Klingon Empire aligned people to face bigger threats, because that's the basis of Infinite Diversity in Infinite Combinations.

The space battles is where it's at in this game. If you pay attention to the detail of each ship and the writing, you can tell that the people who put time into this game love Star Trek, despite it's problems. At least, I can attest that this game is playable. If you want something fast-paced and something you don't want to put money into or a lot of time (or a bit of both), then this is not the game for you.

Easily 3/5 for me. It could be a lot worse and it can be better. The community still thrives and there's a lot of life in this game despite it's age. I recommend this game for any patient Star Trek fan who loves games.

I've been a fan of hockey for the majority of my life. And I've become a big fan of rogue-lites and indie games over the last few years. This is one of those mashups that are perfect for me. I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game, and while it has some flaws (like the traditionally frustrating rubber-banding AI and a lack of customization like line changes, as well as a pretty bare bones campaign) it's a very solid game. I think some people might not be able to overlook some of the issues other reviews have pointed out, and they're completely valid. But I'm looking forward to seeing what the campaign rework is like, and I'll be excited to dive back in as soon as it is available outside of the beta. This is one of those easy recommendations if you enjoy playing hockey games, but are frustrated by the lack of options on PC. And frankly, as much as I used to enjoy the EA NHL series... it's become an Ultimate Team riddled mess anyways. So I'm not really missing much. 

It has a goofy art style and presentation that doesn't take itself seriously. But underneath it plays like a hybrid of the newer style hockey games and NHL 94. To me, I think it's fun as heck. In it's current state, I'd wait for a sale to pick it up if you're not entirely sure. It's not one of those games that you'll probably sink 80 hours into but you'll likely get bang for your buck. It has that one more run feeling that most good games in the genre have.

So in short, has its flaws, still engaging, the challenging aspects will appeal to some but it won't be for everyone.

review_text:
I'm a massive fan of the dot.hack original series. I played it back when it released decades ago. That being said, this weird continuation/re-do is underpar by miles. It feels like some very generic story line and even cliche moments that would make even the biggest fans cringe. I get it, it's a jrpg.. but good god is it awful. If that is the point, then fine. But, this game suffers from ALL of the basic game mechanic problems. Scripted events that make you lose interest because all the "leveling" that the game says you should do is pointless. Leveling up does not matter unless it's a random battle before the "story" elements. It's awful.

The countless times you have to go back to check your mail, meaning leave the "game" just to click an email that can't be checked while you are "playing".. is just disgusting. I hate playing the game now, it's boring. It has small hints of complexity.. but is ultimately lost on the lost immersion from leaving the game or constantly back tracking to the main menu to "check" something.

The skills, combos, specials and even avatars battle systems are one dimensional at best. Spam attack, wait for dumb animation, hit other attack button. The word combo is muddy in this game as well, you ALWAYS use the same animations in attacks, no matter how you press your buttons or change timings.. the rest is point and click. Everything combat-wise is unrelenting garbage. A five year old could probably come up with more in-depth system than this. Items are even more generic, the 4 combat stats, and 4 defensive stats are effortlessly shuffled around on items to show "variation" in rarities.. the depth of a raindrop on concrete.

I know this seems critical, but any jrpg fan will cringe at how ungodly slow, unnecessary and boring this story and combat system is. The nostalgia I had disappeared about an hour in, as you effortlessly slaughter enemies by stun-locking them with basic attacks until they die. Anytime an enemy does something remotely dangerous, you can counter it from anywhere in the battle INSTANTLY! It's lame and critically bad. I wouldn't recommend this to my nephew, who will play anything at least once. I can't bring myself to play anymore.

The only thing that makes me laugh above all else.. is that your characters are about 20 polygons anywhere in the game. But during scripted videos/CGI moments.. characters have more detail, more polygons and even JIGGLE physics on breasts.. What kind of lazy ass development team could stomach this cheesy and lame attempt at an RPG? I'm ashamed of them. I really am. I'm glad this was on sale when I bought it. Wasted time, nostalgia and effort.

Next I'll add that the game has been changed dramatically. Gaining EXP is so super easy you can cap your level in just a couple hours without even trying. The PS2 version at least had a bit of a grind to it. If you combine an item to your accessory, such as an "Amber Dragon Eye", you'll increase your EXP gains even further so this kinda kills the game in itself.

It's a shame really... Such an amazing game was butchered as they do with all reboots and remakes. If they would have simply done the graphics update and left the rest of the game alone, that would have been fine in my book. It's obvious this is a PS2 port as MANY of the PS2 glitches and bugs are still in play, especially the bike missions in volumes 2 and 3. During a bike mission, the millisecond you run into a King Chim, hit Select to open your map and use Circle to back out, rapid tap circle and you'll spam King Chim counters for an instant mission win. You can also walk through the walls in two places in Mac Anu which was a funny bug on the PS2.

My personal assessment... Stop rehashing games if you're just gonna ruin them anyways. This game is so simple now a preschooler could clear it effortlessly. I'll continue to clear it simply for the achievements, but after that I'll be uninstalling it and should I want to play the GU games again, I'll just do so on my PS2.

review_text:
* I initially gave this game a thumbs down, but in retrospect, it probably was meaner than I intended. The bug persists until I reset the game data, which means some achievements are harder to get because those achievements require me to start from the beginning again, but it isn't, like, the end of the world, and the more people who play this game to give the devs more information, the sooner it'l be solved.

This game is tons of fun, and if you are playing hardcore mode, it is unreasonably hard. I really enjoyed everything the game had to offer, though hardcore mode is just annoying. Nothing I love more than ruining a 4 hour run to some unfair RNG. Of course, I wouldn't change anything, the challenge is part of the fun. Okay, maybe tone down the hardcore difficulty just a tad. It's just too unfair. But I don't expect a change just because I'm old and have the reflexes of a sloth in a cryogenic freezer. No, the reason I am not recommending this game is because it is plagued by a very strange, very frustrating, and very hard to figure out glitch where the video just stops working, but the game still plays. I was able to get most of the achievements with no issues at all, then all of a sudden, the game starts glitching out, and is getting progressively worse. It will start by crashing maybe once every several minutes, and usually when you are attacking an enemy, but as it gets worse, it will crash just shortly after getting into a saved game. Somewhere in the process, my Xbox 360 controller stopped working in the game, then the game just plain refused to close. The gallery section just doesn't work, I go to visit it, and it just kicks me back to the main menu. Finally, it wouldn't even get to the main menu, freezing at a loading icon. I've been trying to narrow down the issue, but it doesn't seem to be a driver issue, as I can reproduce the issue on several versions of the NVidia driver, and it is very strange how creating a new user profile seems to fix the issue for a period of time before it happens again. For the record, no other game I own has any issues whatsoever, and I've ran a tons of benchmarks just to see if anything else has issues, but nothing else seems to break at all. I know the devs are aware of the issue, and I'm sure they are trying everything they can to figure this mess out, but please be aware of this issue. If you can manage to play the game with no issues, then it is definitely worth your time, I mean if you like hurting yourself.

review_text:
I'm not finished with the game, so I'll update it later, but here's my review so far--if you want to read something this in-depth.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Definitely not your typical otome game. There are a lot of politics--none that you really HAVE to keep up with, but it helps understand the storyline--and lots of action. Which I love. I thought at first it was strictly historical fiction/romance, as it takes place in 1860s, but you quickly learn that there is a strong streak of fantasy/paranormal [spoiler] including demons and scientific experiments [/spoiler], which is very fun. Honestly, romance is not the top priority of this story, so if you're looking for something strictly lovey-dovey, this might not be for you. It's a really great read for those who like reading, the characters are pretty diverse given how many there are, and the art is very tasteful. The voice acting is great (it's in Japanese. Translations are a bit off or simplified at times, but they get the point across), and the effects are pretty good for a visual novel. The blood splatters really set the mood, haha. I advise using headphones because the voice levels do vary depending on the character and tone, so at times it can be hard to hear.

I will warn: Like most otome protagonists, the MC is pretty helpless. She supposedly has been trained to use a sword--and has one--but never uses it? If you can just pretend in your mind that she DOES use it at times and isn't totally incompetent, it's a great game.

review_text:
Animalia, currently it's fairly fun if you're lucky and meet fair players. The solo play is very lacking and you can only live a full life on multiplayer where you can find a player as a mate and then birth real players as your offspring and raise them. One of the most popular servers is pretty bad to play on, but one has enough active friendly mods and admins who are fair and the rules are pretty clear and make the game more fun. 

I love that you can climb trees as a leopard which I have wanted a good playable leopard in a game for a long time. And they added scavenging from carcasses to be easier. 

 Animalia still feels like a work in progress, but much of the game is good and since the last time I played I definitely see the improvements, of course making the foundations of the game are most important, so bugs and imbalances should be the devs main focus.
However, I know solo mode would be a huge thing if it was improved.  Like when I think of a playable singleplayer, make the world more immersive with intelligent ai where you can have a completely ai family and ai prey and predators living their own lives and dealing with eachother as well as the player, and also hope in the future they implement more african climate where there is a rainy season when most prey have babies, and also a dry season when things are more difficult and water sources dry up. Building homes would be cool too, especially meerkat colonies. And with warthogs, african wild dogs and hyenas to be able to repurpose old burrows and expand them to their needs. 
Please make group limits per species an admin setting, as well as character slots. More admin settings in general to better customize servers or control your solo save would be a huge thing to consider. 
Perhaps make the points also be able to go towards perks/abilities instead of just improving basic skills, for example burrowing animals be able to make a burrow on their own without needing to use an old one, another perk/ability could be for scent tracking to be easier, or small herbivores being able to turn and evade easier or jump farther, ect. 
I wish this game had a feedback space but I understand why not. But their roadmap setup on trello definitely makes things easier to understand, it was fairly difficult to find a discord link that wasn't expired to get more information on this game. 

Despite the new games coming out, Animalia is still the best african species survival game so if you can handle dying to unfair players and natural reasons on occasion and a glitch or lag here and there, go ahead and get it. I have fun more than not in this game when I do play, just be sure to read the rules of the server you're joining. 
Actually I haven't seen a fun african animal game like this since I, Predator. If you remember that game, this one is for you.

review_text:
To the Moon is all about its story, so therefore I will not summarize the plot apart from this: the story is about two doctors trying to fulfill a dying man's last wish of getting him to the moon.

As mentioned, the focus with this game and its greatest selling point is the story. The plot is pretty good; it has a few twists and the way the doctors try to help their client is interesting and well written. Also, the characters have real depth, which is the more impressive as To the Moon lasts but a few hours.
However, the story is also completely linear, the player is never presented with a meaningful choice and the levels are really small. Furthermore, the game tries to deliver an emotional experience but as you - due to plot reasons I cannot explain - are an outsider for the majority of the game the things happening on screen sometimes fail to deliver said experience; there is too much detachment.

Gameplay is threadbare and consists for the most part of walking to location/person X and clicking through (sometimes quite a lot of) text. These grant orbs that you need to combine with an item you need to find, after which you need to solve a very simple puzzle to continue the game. Repeat the above for almost every level. As mentioned, the levels are very small so you spend the majority of the time reading the dialogue. The gameplay fits in with the story, though.
What's worse, gameplay is bugged. The characters sometimes don't respond (well) to clicks and sometimes get stuck. Moreover, the mouse is rather imprecise during the puzzles and that is annoying as it leads to more missclicks.

In conclusion, I feel this game has nice characters and at its core a good plot but it lacks choice for the player and the story is completely linear. On top of that, it has bugged, threadbare gameplay that gets really repetitive a few levels in. Due to this, I cannot recommend To the Moon.

Let me start by saying that I've spent several hours playing many different games and this is the first review I've ever left. True, there are many games that are much more deserving of a first/good review, but I somehow feel like this game hasn't gotten the attention it deserves. 
 I bought this three-game series on sale, for like 6 bucks or something. I wasn't expecting a whole lot, but I love getting underrated games on sale for cheap, because a good majority of them I've REALLY enjoyed. Some of them get uninstalled and refunded immediately.
This is one I REALLY enjoyed. 
The graphics are outdated and the controls can be a bit clunky but overall this game held my attention for 7ish straight hours, I couldn't put it down. Even when I got frustrated in the chapter where you're running around in the dark, and I got spotted and forced to restart the whole chapter - over and over and over...I rage quit for like ten minutes and went right back to it. 
You play as an evil child and basically go around and murder everyone in your giant fabulous mansion - in some pretty amazing and graphic ways. I even enjoyed the side chores which do reward you. 
If you're bored of the same old games you always play, and can get a laugh and kick out of virtually murdering people - this is the game for you. The "puzzles" aren't difficult - true I did use a walkthrough once or twice - but I get impatient. Most of it is straight forward and you know what you need to do even before leaving your room - and if you don't, you almost always run into someone running through the halls that will steer you in the direction of what you should do. There's also the Ouija board on your desk that will give you task-related hints as well. 
I HIGHLY recommend buying this game on sale and giving it a fair chance. I found it extremely entertaining and WELL worth 6ish bucks.

review_text:
[h2]I Don't get It[/h2]

I don't think I understand the point of the game. It was investing and enjoyable but I felt confused a lot of the time. The way that the memory time-travel device works doesn't make sense to me. I didn't care about whether it made sense during Act 1, even though the game was trying to explain it to me. But after Act 1 it felt like I needed to get it to understand the story. And at the end I was left doing things that I didn't understand.

[spoiler]At first I hated the mechanics and thought the art style was boring, but I got used to them and really enjoyed Act 1. I was invested in the story and found the backwards storytelling interesting. But the story gets taken over by time-travel memory link stuff that was confusing and took away from the weight of the story. Suddenly there was a different "what could have been" plotline that I didn't understand the point of. If the story had ended when I discovered the reason Johnny doesn't remember I think I would have been satisfied.

I loved the music, and the story was investing; it could have been simpler though. the movement was annoying but there were many fun and interesting moments.

I don't know why the game even tries to explain the logistics of the time-travel memory stuff, especially if I ended up confused anyways. It reminded me of when horror movies try to come up with a supernatural backstory for the monster instead of just letting it exist and be scary. The game could have told me that I need memory links to go back in Johnny's memories and I wouldn't have needed more than that. i don't care about the more complicated function of the machine. I guess the story wouldn't have existed without the explanation. And if the machine was explained as little as I'm suggesting then what is the point of backwards storytelling? It still would have been interesting I feel. So my main complaint is that I don't understand what the game is trying to say about memory.

Also Act 1 confused me with the discussion of River's "condition." It seemed important and I thought a major revelation was coming but it was never mentioned after Act 1. I think I know what the condition is. Maybe the point was just representation; I did find River relatable. But the story treats the "condition" in a weird way that gives it so much weight. It is kind of treated like a terminal illness that will change the course of her life and the way everyone around her is able too relate to her when the "condition" is just that she thinks a bit differently from what is considered the norm.[/spoiler]

It is hard for me to tell how clever the creators of this game were being. I'm just confused. I enjoyed it though

review_text:
What is a game if not a mirror of life? Yakuza 5 Remastered is not simply an upgraded title—it is a sprawling, ambitious reflection of human struggle and perseverance, painted across the diverse landscapes of Japan. It is operatic in scale and yet deeply intimate. Few games have dared to go this far, and even fewer have succeeded in making every step feel meaningful.

Five protagonists. Five cities. Five personal odysseys. This is no ordinary sequel. It is a meditation on identity and purpose. Each character walks a path riddled with ghosts of the past and dreams deferred. Haruka, especially, stands out. To make a pop idol's journey as emotionally resonant as a former hitman's path to redemption? That’s bold. That’s new. That’s art.

As a person who believes that gameplay should echo the philosophy of the narrative, I was impressed by how Yakuza 5 Remastered handles tone and variety. The shift between combat, racing, dancing, and managing an idol career could be jarring in the hands of less confident developers. But Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio pulls it off with finesse. These transitions don’t feel like detours—they’re vital arteries of the game’s emotional and thematic structure.

What I admire most is the meticulous worldbuilding. Each city—Fukuoka, Sapporo, Osaka, Nagoya, and Tokyo—feels like its own character. The snow crunching under Saejima’s boots in Hokkaido. The neon pulse of Sotenbori. The modest shops tucked away in Nagoya's alleys. These are more than backdrops; they are living, breathing environments that root the drama in reality.

Technically, the remastered version sharpens the experience without losing its soul. The enhanced visuals honor the original while respecting modern standards. Frame rate improvements smoothen the pacing, but it’s the storytelling—always the storytelling—that elevates Yakuza 5 Remastered to something greater than nostalgia.

This isn’t just a game about yakuza. It’s a game about dreams. About people trying to hold onto something—honor, family, truth—in a world constantly trying to tear them apart. It is, in many ways, a game I wish I had made.

No numerical score can capture the layered beauty of this title. Like a good film or novel, it lingers in the mind long after the credits roll.

In Yakuza 5 Remastered, the fight is never just physical. It is always—always—about the heart.

9/10

review_text:
It took about 11 hours to beat the game for the first time. The Callisto Protocol really feels lacking in some areas, TLDR: Bought it for $19 on sale, and it felt about right for the quality. Not worth the $60 price tag.

Positives: 
-Offers big nostalgia for people who enjoyed Dead Space.

-More of a CINEMATIC style of game. lots of post processing effects, fixed animation elements, and cut-scenes. Less control over Jacob does make a lot of things look and feel immersive (even if you lose some control to accomplish the look)

Neutral points:
-Has a LOT of the jank associated with Dead Space (character feels slow but impactful, camera doesn't always prioritize visual clarity so jump scares come across better, etc.)

Negatives:
-It really loses points for lack of creativity. If you're going to basically swipe the entire idea of Dead Space, do it well. Striking distance really didn't add much to the formula other than a cinematic feeling. they removed probably the most fun mechanic of dead space (shooting a limb off immediately makes something less deadly) You KIND OF get the same thing when you knock off a limb, enemies shorten their combos. this really feels like a worse version of a game that came out almost 2 decades ago and somehow they couldn't figure out WHY it was good.
-It really isn't as scary as it should be. If its 90% jump-scares, it feels like only 10% effort. Aside from an early point where you're in  a small cave full of blood/goop and the mental asylum section of the Tower chapter, never really uncomfortable. 

-Really doesn't nail the difficulty well. Enemies are either brain dead easy (most enemies in the game) or near impossible to fight efficiently (anything that prevents you from fighting at close range) If you run out of ammo on the wrong part of the game, you can basically softlock yourself. ( I had half a mag RIGHT before a boss fight that you cant use melee attacks on, so I HAD TO cheese it by baiting it to an edge and provoking an attack so it would fall out of the map and die) They added special modes where they fix the guns (but make the game almost entirely too easy in the process) don't worry... bosses are still stupidly hard, since most bosses in the game will 1 or 2 shot you. and if that's not hard enough, you can play the game with next to no resources!

-Guns Feel bad at all points in the game. They never get better, and fail to capitalize on the fun part of survival horror (a gun that feels impact-ful with very limited use)

-so much content is LOCKED BEHIND A PAYWALL!!! you beat the game and OOPS, its still not over! only $20 to see what happens to Jacob!

Hoo boy, this game was mediocre.

review_text:
This game isn't good. The developers tout 'difficulty' but its clear that they use that as an excuse for an atrociously balanced game. Either that or their design philosophy was to intentionally cut as many corners as possible.

They created an open world that they DO NOT want you to explore: Fences, fences everywhere, for no reason. Oh look a fence blocking my path, dare I follow alongside it and HOPE an opening appears or do I go against common sense and try to find another path in the complete opposite direction? 
Made worse by the idiotically implemented stamina meter. Most of your time in this game will be spent waiting for your stunted stamina meter to refill. This is one of those games that has a stamina meter for the sole purpose of having one, and whose sole purpose appears to be to annoy the player.

They want this game to be known as the game of 'investigation and intrigue', but you will spend literally the LEAST amount of time experiencing those two things! Instead, you will spend the MOST amount of time being hungry...The hunger mechanic is nonsense. It doesn't add anything to the 'atmosphere' of the game. This whole droll concept of "Oh its SUPPOSE to be annoying! This game is SUPPOSE to not be the least bit fun!" Hmmm, okay, then why should anyone spend their time and money on a game that by its own admission and by people who claim to enjoy it ISN'T enjoyable (How can they even claim to enjoy it if it isnt suppose to be enjoyable? Doesnt that mean the game failed?)
If they wanted to have a sort of depressing mechanic to laud over you, then why not one that actually has to do with the THEME and STORY of the game? What the heck does hunger have to do with investigation and infection? 
As it stands now, this game is solely known for being 'Oh that game where you have to look for food'. If the developers seriously cant see how self-defeating this is for the story and atmosphere they are trying to present then there really is not much hope that they will deliver.


As for the story? Predictable. Very predictable, with story beats you see coming a mile away despite this games attempts to be 'surreal'. As a matter of fact, it seems the developers only tried to make the game surreal in a desperate attempt to make the game less predictable. Didn't work.

Its worth pointing out that there are a vast number of positive reviews that desperately claim this to be the 'Best Game Ever' whilst proceeding to fill their review with nothing but excuses instead of actually praising the game. If this game is really as good as they claim, then why do they need to make excuses for it? Funny how in their attempt to defend the game, they only end up making it look even less attractive, talk about self-defeating!
The simple fact that they go as far as to claim this to be the best game ever made is an immediate dead-giveaway that they're overcompensating for something that the game is severely lacking...

Would otherwise recommend this to HR Giger fanatics and graphics nerds, but it's a reluctant thumbs down from me.

review_text:
LONG REVIEW (CONTAINS MINOR SPOILERS)

This is not a good game. I remember having fun playing the trilogy 10 years ago on my PS2, but I guess I just had more tolerance and patience for these types of games. That being said, I remember that even back then I found the game far from perfect and somewhat boring, but now I find it extremely boring.

The biggest problem is the pacing of the game. The gameplay is constantly interrupted for the sake of the plot. Usually, I don't mind that. I'm not the type of guy who hates story-driven games. I do mind it in this game, though, because the plot is served to you in a form of long, badly written dialogues in which characters just stand still and only camera angles change. Every one does that 10-second pause after each sentence. No one is straight forward about anything. They say something cryptic, wait for someone else to ask about details and then go into them. If that wasn't enough, sometimes one of the characters ends up saying a simplified version of what the other one said, making the first half of the dialogue completely pointless.
Example:
-We are Epitaph Users.
...10 seconds later...
-Epitaph Users?
...10 seconds later...
-Yes, that means we...(starts blabbing for 3 minutes)
...10 seconds later...
-Oh, so you are basically this and this?
...10 seconds later...
-You can put it that way.
Couldn't the character say only the simplified version?
Also, there are these long exchanges that lead nowhere.
Example:
-Haseo!
...10 seconds later...
-What?
...10 seconds later...
-You have to save him!
...10 seconds later...
-Why me?
...10 seconds later...
-Because he said to contact you!
...10 seconds later...
-Me?
...10 seconds later...
-Mhm.
90% of the dialogue is structured like that and most of the game is dialogue. I played it for over 20 hours and I feel like 15 of them was spent on it. I know you can skip it, but I do want to know what is going on in the game and that is the only way to find out. The game takes place in an MMO and in order to progress in story you often have to log out in order to read an email and log back in. Sometimes you have to log out, read an email, log back in just to have a dialogue with a character, get another email, log out again, read the new one and log back in. It seriously seems like the devs went out of their way just to make the game boring. There is even a quest that you have to do in order to progress in the game in which you have to walk up to multiple NPCs scattered around the hub world just to listen to them talk. After the quest is done your character makes a comment on how boring it was almost as if the devs were aware of it. If you acknowledge that something is boring maybe you should fix it or get rid of it completely.

Story isn't that great either. Like I said before, the game is happening in a game, which in my opinion isn't a very good setting for a story-driven game. Everything ends up being less powerful and less meaningful since it all happens in some silly MMO. There is a character who gives people lectures about morality and treating others well, but since it is just a player in a video game, it is hard to take him seriously. He's just some guy who gets back home after work, puts on his VR headset and gets too much into the game. There is a scene early in the game that shows a character being killed. It's meant to be dramatic but you get pulled out of it with a line like ‘I love PKing those noobs. LOL’. You quickly realize that it's not a person being killed. It's just a character in a video game being PKed. Every battle that is meant to be spectacular is also diminished when you are aware that the ones who fight in it aren't meant to be people, but some 3D models controlled by a bunch of teens who scream stuff like ‘BONE CRUSHER!’ and wake up their moms downstairs. That makes the story very unreliable since people end up being hurt in real life through the game, but no one thinks of logging out or taking off their headset or turning off their PC whenever something like that happens. There are news about people ending up in a coma from playing the game all over the internet but nobody cares. People still log into it; mothers still let their kids play it. The relations between characters aren't very credible either. There means to be some kind of romance between some of the characters, but again, it's a video game. These people go grinding together a couple times and fall in love with each other without ever speaking with each other or seeing each other in real life. If that wasn't enough, the protagonist is often mean to his comrades to the point they cry (about someone being mean to them in a video game) as if he was meant to realize that he's unnecessarily rude, swallow his pride and apologize, but that never happens. His ‘friends’ eventually come back to him and they end up apologizing instead.

I can't really say anything bad about sound and visuals. The game looks nice till this day. The character designs are fun, memorable and fit the MMO setting. The same goes for the music.

There isn't much to the gameplay, but it is fun. Like I said, visuals and sound are nice. The battle theme gets you pumped up and the particle effects and sound effects make it satisfying to hit enemies. It is kind of repetitive, but as you progress through the game your character learns to wield different types of weapon so it isn't that bad. Also, each weapon has it's own visual design and their attacks varies a little, even between the ones of the same type. Unfortunately, the combat is pretty easy. You can tackle enemies that are 8 levels above you and gain levels very quickly. You collect healing items to help you during longer adventures and there's also a mechanic that lets you slowly regain health when you stand still. Both of these things are completely useless in this remaster. They added a new mechanic. When you lose a fight you can press ‘retry’ and you begin the fight that you just lost at with full HP and SP. There is no punishment for losing. If anything, you are REWARDED with full HP and SP for losing. Why would you ever use healing items or stand still for few minutes when you are dying, when you can just rush into a battle, get yourself killed, press ‘retry’ and regain your HP and SP for free? That being said, going to various areas to beat up monsters and collect new loot is the best part of the game, so I have no idea why they do everything to stop you from doing that. Of course you can go grinding whenever you want, but you will quickly become too OP for the story quests which will make them even more boring.

I didn't have any technical problems with the game. I see people posting about crashes, freezes and corrupted save files. I never experienced any of these. Either I'm lucky or the game got a proper update.

I never made it to the new content and I probably never will, but I saw the trailer on steam and I'll say this; for god's sake stop intentionally rendering CG cutscenes at low framerates. It looks awful. It looks especially bad in this since previous cutscenes form PS2 era run at smooth 60FPS. They seriously added choppy 5FPS cutscenes that look worse than the original ones form 11 years ago to this remaster.

Overall, if I had to describe .hack//G.U. Last Recode with one word it would be ‘boring’. The gameplay, visuals and music are ok, but in the long run you won't enjoy this game due to it's focus on mediocre story explained in form of badly written dialogue. I cannot recommend it to anyone. Not even nostalgic fans of the series.

pride and apologize, but that never happens. his friends eventually come back to him and they end up apologizing instead. i can't really say anything bad about sound and visuals. the game looks nice combat is pretty easy. you can tackle enemies that are 8 levels above you and gain levels very quickly. you collect healing items to help you during longer adventures and there's also a mechanic that fight that you just lost at with full hp and sp. there is no punishment for losing. if anything, you are rewarded with full hp and sp for losing. why would you ever use healing items or stand still Lost Ruins is a pretty darn good metroidvania with focus on exploration and using your items/spells/consumables to your advantage. Game is also rather hard and you most likely will need some time to get used to it.

Combat is slow and methodical, which can be bad for players that are used to lightning fast combat from other games in the same genre, but I personally very much enjoyed it, despite loving fast games. OST is alright. Some good tracks, some average tracks. Liked OST of the last area, very chill and melancholic.

Art style I absolutely adore, it's great. You can unlock bunch of artworks for gallery mode and I must say, they are fantastic. Game is looking pretty cool in general, lighting system is fantastic.

There is also bunch of custom modes, including boss rush mode, where you can play as 3 bosses in one character. Seems pretty fun, tried for a bit, can see myself getting back to the game later to complete it. 

Overall good package for its price, very much recommend to anyone looking for a challenging metroidvania.
