review_text:
[h1] After The Fall is NOT Left 4 Dead [/h1]
[b] However, this doesn't mean it isn't like Left 4 Dead [/b]

After The Fall is a really fun VR CO-OP Multiplayer shooter (there is a PVP mode but it isn't the main focus of the game). I'd say this is a good game but not a great game. The main thing to know is the core game play loop is fun, getting kills is satisfying, teamwork pays off, and the novelty of something being like L4D in VR is nice to have.

[i]So to put it simply, all my issues with the game don't come from the core game play but rather lack of what could be.[/i]

The issues I have are the lack of variety in the special infected and lack of maps.
Before I go out on a limb here, I just want to say I have hope that the game will be updated and hopefully most of my problems will be fixed but as of 12/11/21 these are my opinions.

The lack of maps isn't a huge issue currently but once I get into that ~24 hr mark I'm probably going to be wanting more from this game. The levels are replayable to some degree and getting kills is satisfying but a reason why I and so many others keep coming back to L4D is the fact that it has community made content and a plethora of maps. I'm not saying this game will get community made content nor do I think there will ever be support, but its wishful thinking to have hope for a tool set that would allow such.  Therefore, having only a few maps is definitely going to get stale pretty quickly.

Next, the lack of variety in the special infected makes runs underwhelming. The current roster of what they have is fine but c'mon, we neeeeeed moooooore! To add insult to injury, there are two special infected who do nearly the same thing, there is a brute who is a tanky MF with a whole lot of health. Then, there is a charger like thing that can run pretty fast and also tank quite a few bullets. Then there is the eater who is similar to a boomer, but that is it. More special infected designed around VR interaction would be really awesome and definitely spice up the game play, especially since a whole lot of stuff in this game is just shoot shoot shoot. 

In conclusion, After The Fall is a game that is fun, but if not updated to add more content and variety, will probably sit up on the old retired steam games library shelf after hitting that ~50 hr expiration date. I am enjoying myself at the time and I have faith in Vertigo to be able to update the game to extend its replayability beyond its current capacity.

This game is just so impressive. The world building is fantastic, the story has got me hooked, and the gameplay is engaging. It is a reading-heavy game, so that's something to keep in mind. I'd consider it something of a "survival novel". It's not exactly a forgiving game, I ended up restarting after hours of gameplay. But my experience felt even more rich understanding all the gameplay mechanisms and how to approach the world (e.g. when a guy pulls a knife, do you what you would do irl, run lol).

Even so the second time around there are still things I missed due to not knowing. But I like the world and characters so much that I could see myself playing this again with further knowledge of the "lines" to line myself up for a good ending. I'd say it's somewhat of a "wiki game", but I'd recommend limiting the amount of Googling and letting the world and game unravel to you naturally. Even when the world is unfair, through will, you can shift odds in your favor.

I dread to think how many people just want to buy a game and play it, and are not computer literate enough to grapple with this. Those people will have simply lost their money on a game that is not fit for sale. With no patch planned, it looks like this game will remain in an unplayable state.

At the moment I cannot recommend you buy this. All you're doing is gambling your money on the off chance you'll be able to play it, either before or after the worst tech nightmare in years. To be honest, I think it should be pulled from the store until the issues are fixed.

review_text:
The much touted “spiritual successor” to Dead Space, but to be honest, it doesn’t hold a candle to that franchise, not even close.

The Callisto Protocol’s beginning is pretty strong and rather intriguing, at a first glance it does look like a decent spooky time is waiting for you and the first half of the game is not bad, pretty decent, it does have great action set pieces and it keeps you on your toes for new monstrosities around seemingly every corner.

Then comes the rest of the game after the mine drilling section, which then becomes a repetitive and tedious slog when the developers literally ran out of budget and start to recycle certain enemies and even some levels.

The game keeps promising an amazing payoff at the end, but once you reach said payoff… You’re left with the feeling of a rushed wet fart and one of the worst final bosses in a horror game, ever, both on a plot and mechanical standpoints.

The graphics are amazing and it runs great I guess, not a single stutter in my entire playthrough, although I did get a couple of crashes and the main menu's "continue" option completely disappeared, making me think my save was gone, but it wasn't; starting a new game and IMMEDIATELY hitting "Load Save" took me back to where I left off, or rather before the game crashed. 

Alas, good graphics and good performance can only carry you for so long; all the good will and strong narrative from the first half are completely gone by the time you’ve reached the final boss and the ending only makes it worse due to how disappointing that payoff is. I only played the base game by the way, screw that jazz about adding another ending through paid DLC, f**k that.

I guess the game is good enough if you manage to find it SUPER cheap, especially with the first half being legitimately decent, but honestly I’d recommend you buy the Dead Space remake instead, heck, buy the entire franchise and yes, including the third one. Am I implying Dead Space 3 is better than Callisto Protocol? F**K YES it is! At least that game has better combat mechanics and co-op, this one only has missed potential and disappointment waiting for you.

6/10 - Much better games out there, get as cheap as possible.

review_text:
"Lucius" - игра, которая заслуживает внимания благодаря своим множественным достоинствам. Она не только обладает хорошей оптимизацией, что позволяет насладиться плавным и комфортным геймплеем, но и пропитана атмосферой жестокости, которая позволяет испытать настоящий адреналин от совершаемых действий.

Игра также известна своими интересными головоломками, которые требуют сообразительности и логического мышления. Разнообразие этих головоломок заставляет игрока постоянно придумывать новые стратегии и решать трудности, что добавляет дополнительного остроумия и увлекательности в игровой процесс.

Важным аспектом "Lucius" является захватывающий сюжет, который привлекает внимание и не отпускает до самого конца. Фасад идеальной семьи, скрытые тайны и шокирующие открытия создают атмосферу загадки и непредсказуемости, что поддерживает стимуляцию интереса и желание узнать, как развиваются события.

Игра дополняется возможностью кататься на велосипеде, что добавляет разнообразия в игровой процесс. Это позволяет не только передвигаться по игровому миру быстрее и эффективнее, но и встречать новые интересные места и открывать дополнительные возможности.

Наконец, "Lucius" радует приятной звуковой составляющей. Звуки окружающего мира, музыка и голосовое сопровождение удачно подчеркивают атмосферу игры, создавая более полное и погружающее впечатление.

В целом, "Lucius" станет настоящим увлечением для поклонников жанра, предлагая хорошую оптимизацию, множество жестокости, интересные головоломки, захватывающий сюжет, возможность кататься на велосипеде и приятную звуковую составляющую. Эта игра не оставит равнодушным ни одного игрока.

review_text:
"Don't mind me, just disposing of a body."

This game is a ton of fun with impossible amounts of enemies around forcing you to employ stealth mechanics and tactics and also sniping skills. Crucial weapon unlocks are tied to challenges which ensure you must play each level at least twice and each level is a huge open map with a half dozen missions.

That said the draw backs of the game mostly come from the limits of the AI. Patrolling guards are so regular you can time your movements to the second, getting spotted is tied to proximity to a hit box rather than line of sight of the NPC's face, and some sounds are easily heard while others sound just for the player. Alarms and explosions are not reacted to more than a few hundred meters out even if the call goes out over the radio, and NPCs will never leave their AO even if they see you sniping from a tower. And once the alarm goes out the guard's ability to detect your sniping spot becomes superhuman. Once you know the exploits you can pull off impossible stealth missions, knifing guards and hiding their bodies in the bushes IN PLAIN SIGHT.

Other potential downsides are the graphics are good enough this game won't work on an ordinary PC, you'll need a gaming PC or console. Also it gets glitchy sometimes with weird lag spikes but nothing major.

What I'd recommend for the game is instead of a barebones multiplayer they do a PvPvE match where first man to get the bounty target's dog tags wins.

review_text:
It’s not a terrible game, but I can’t see it being worth 40 Euro in its current state. Since this is the end of Early Access, I hope the devs can polish it more.

The bad:

- Weapon balance is all over the place, some guns are amazing, others useless.

- Enemies deal too much damage, with too many insta-kill mechanics. Even with full HP investment it feels like you still die in 3 hits instead of 2 hits.

- Enemy difficulty is inconsistent, some are pushovers, others absurdly strong.

- Maps feel extremly repetitive.

- Roguelite mechanics are weak. Most buffs are random and borderline useless. If I had to choose between +10% dmg/+10% HP or all other upgrades combined, I’d still pick the first.

- Some mechanics (like the Vestal Flame), feel meaningless.

- The rewards for the map events are laughable.

- Ammo... holy shit, I actually like the idea of weapon switching and looking for new ammo, but later maps are just stupid. Enemies turn into sponges that eat all your bullets, and even if you skill mostly for extra ammo, there’s still way too little.

The good:

- Itemization is fun,  there are many items for different playstyles.

- Weapons and gunplay feel great, even if the balance needs work.

- Graphics are solid, and the art style is at times exceptionally beautiful and haunting.

Conclusion:
There’s a good foundation here, but the balance, progression, and roguelite elements really need improvement. Not worth 40 Euro..

review_text:
Some good things about it, the space combat is great at the right times. I really feel immersed in the startrek world when I log on and get into some nice good ol space combat! The space combat really is the magnum opus of the game. Also this game runs on a very good F2P model. 

Now, onto the shitty part of the game. Lets get into the story/lore. This is for the regular starfleet line, where you work with Tuvoc and the old VOY crew for a good portion of the story. The first bit is nice, you fight some romulans, klingons, everythings coherent. Then you get later on, to the iconians. The Iconians really just ruin everything. They are presented as all powerful beings, yet need to use pawn races to get shit done. Why can't they just wave their hand and kill all the leaders. They had a chance to kill the main character, AKA you. When you kill that one Iconion on the flagship, they have a chance to kill you, but they don't, because.... reasons?  On top of that, the Heralds and Iconions don't really seem to be advanced, they seem to just have magic. They literally use staffs that shoot shit at you, and there are these random swirls that show up and explode and it all just looks like magic. I feel like I'm playing some lord of the rings shit mixed in with people with phasers and star trek uniforms. They can also spawn in these Solar gateways, which are just complete bullshit. All of the AI seem to agro on just you, which is annoying and unimmersive. I wish the Iconians, instead of being arbitarily powerful, instead be weak, almost defenseless creatures, that use these other races to do their bidding. Their weapon wouldn't be their bullshit magic. It'd be their brains, so they can manipulate other creatures to fight for them  over the centuries. But no, that would require a good storyline, and good lore. They are just overall really terrible villians. 

This leads into a bigger issue, the ground combat. The ground combat is just ass... it's awful. It's so bad. There are entire portions of the game, that are primarily ground combat. I almost called it quits when I was on the new romulus level. Ground combat could be good! Your away team people use little gadgets, like mobile shields, or healing node things. They can even spawn little turrets. Tac officers have grenades, and other cool abilities. However, this is just negated by the ass gunplay, terrible AI, and buggy gameplay. 

Bugs. The Bugs are not really a bug anymore, but they are features. Triggers fail to activate, so you sometimes have to just restart ENTIRE MISSIONS! I had to spend 2 hours on just 1 fucking mission being something failed to trigger.  This game is a buggy mess. 

In conclusion, this game could be good, but it simply is not. The story is bad, the gameplay is bad, the bugs are everywhere. I get why some startrek fans adore this game, but as a startrek fan myself, this game is awful. It's not worth your time, it's just fucking awful. The plot, gameplay, bugs. All are bad.

review_text:
Flawed? Certainly. Bad? Certainly not. Worth the full $60 price point? Fuck no.

Callisto Protocol is, in essence, Dead Space. I know pretty much every other review here says that, and it's true. You show up to a prison where some sort of infection has gone rampant around the facility, and now you must escape while fending off hordes of deadly enemies, forming tedious friendships with acquaintances, and facing down a greater evil. It's the Dead Space formula.

But I'll start with what I like about Callisto Protocol.

The in-game performance, graphics, and art style are really fantastic, which I was surprised by given it's a modern AAA release, especially being made in Unreal. Typically I'd expect to see my high-end computer struggle to even scrape 50 FPS in intensive rendering situations, but the game is really well optimized for what it is.

The combat, looting, and upgrade system is well done, though it certainly has room for improvement. I love the brutally fast paced melee combat paired with the quickdraw firearm combos the game lets you chain, but I feel it's heavily subdued by most enemies being trivialized by your ability to dodge left and right. Once you gain a basic concept of the dodging system, you're good to go. With that being said though, I can understand how some people would find the combat repetitive after a time.

This is a super small thing I liked, but I really liked how the game actually shows where/how you store your weapons. I hate it when games have the player character just sort of stuff their guns up their ass or put them into some pocket dimension when not in use, but I appreciate the attention to detail here.

Some things I really don't care for/could've been improved upon? Firstly the GRP Module (basically a telekinesis module that allows you to pick up and throw things) just feels really weak. It has a battery, okay fine I understand that so players can't abuse it and spam it on environmental hazards for enemies. But using it AT ALL on enemies sucks energy so fast that I found myself ever hardly using it.

Another thing I feel the need to comment on is the separation of side-exploration paths, and what leads to the primary objective. Throughout the game you can find side paths that lead you to extra lore or loot, which is cool, but the game LITERALLY DOES NOT TELL YOU IF WHERE YOU'RE GOING IS PART OF THE STORY OR NOT. I had SO many times where I was worried going down one path or another in a split in the road would lead to a point-of-no-return, or would just be a place for me to check out, and is incredibly frustrating, but not something I'm going to count against it.

This isn't a complaint, moreso being a general critique, but the game also likes to push the idea of the GRP Module being a crowd-control tool, but it has no *real* utility for that. I would have LOVED to have seen a function for it where players could quickly push enemies back with a burst of energy from it, in exchange for high-battery usage. Without any function besides just tossing enemies into spike walls or into machinery though, I just feel it was very half-baked.

Another thing I would have loved to have seen were more suit options/upgrade options. For the first half of the game you're in your prisoner jumpsuit with bare minimum health and storage space. Then later on you get a tactical/environmental suit with upgraded health and access to all your storage slots. I feel a sort of intermediary suit would have been good, like maybe a leftover guard's uniform or something.

Narratively, Callisto Protocol is VERY close to Dead Space, and a lot of ambiguity is left to form for the first half of the game, before it really begins to make sense and explain itself. The latter half of the game gets really good though, and I thoroughly enjoy some of the narrative elements and story points that the writers implemented, especially when it comes to Jacob's involvement in the whole situation.

Now onto what I didn't really like, the big part of this section namely being the enemy variety.

You have your basic slasher-grunt type enemies, with the only variant of them being a fatter one that has more health. You've got other enemies, like ones that sneak around with camo and try to ambush you, ones that explode when they get close, ones that spit at you, etc. All fine. But unfortunately there just isn't a whole ton of variety in threats. 

Almost all enemies just run at you and start swinging, and the ones that DO have ranged attacks can be turned into basic slashers by blowing their heads off, at which they'll engage you in melee combat. There's no enemies that force you to use guns (yes, including the aforementioned exploding enemies. Your GRP Module can deal with them), no enemies that are actually a hazard to engage in melee combat with (assuming you know what you're doing), and no enemies that really made me go "oh fuck", besides MAYBE the Security Bots, of which you only encounter once or twice throughout the entire game. This goes for the bosses too. The final boss is fine in a general sense, and actually got me moving. But unfortunately, like every enemy, his main melee attacks could just be sidestepped.

As for the scare factor of Callisto Protocol, it really just isn't scary, at least in my opinion. I fear the developers leaned on the "loud noise = scary" trope in horror, and while the atmosphere is sort of unnerving, it was let down by the fact I could expect to see a loud noise or something kinda creepy pop up on my screen. I think probably the only time I actually got sort of scared/unnerved was during the final boss ([spoiler] when Ferris is giving you a monologue in the tower and starts to mutate and transform suddenly [/spoiler]).

I also feel Callisto Protocol suffers from another problem Dead Space had; turning the player into an errand boy. You'll ALWAYS have someone giving you a "Go here", "Do this", or "Find this" order, where it feels Jacob is just sort of a drone and can't figure out what to do without instructions. 

Overall? Certainly not GOTY material by any stretch of the imagination, but definitely not as bad as many people say it is. I welcome anyone to give it a try during a sale, or if you're just that certain this is the game for you.

gain a basic concept of the dodging system, you're good to go. with that being said though, i can understand how some people would find the combat repetitive after a time. this is a super small thing i liked, but i really liked how the game actually shows where how you store your weapons. i hate it when games have the player character just sort of stuff their guns up their ass or put them into some pocket dimension when not in use, but i appreciate the attention to detail here. some things i really don't care for could've been improved upon? firstly the grp module basically a telekinesis module that allows you to pick up and throw things just feels really weak. it has a battery, okay fine i understand that so players can't abuse it and spam it on environmental hazards for enemies. but using it at all on enemies sucks energy so fast that i found myself ever hardly using it. another thing i feel the need to comment on is the separation of side-exploration paths, and what leads to the primary objective. throughout the game you can find side paths that lead you to extra lore or loot, which is cool, but the game literally does not tell you if where you're going is part of the story or not. i had so many times where i was worried going down one path or another in a split in the road would lead to a point-of-no-return, or would just be a place for me to check out, and is incredibly frustrating, but not something i'm going to count against it. this isn't a complaint, moreso being a general critique, but the game also likes to push the idea of the grp module being a crowd-control tool, but it has no real utility for that. i would have loved to have seen a function for it where players could quickly push enemies back with a burst of energy from it, in exchange for high-battery usage. without any function besides just tossing enemies into spike walls or into machinery though, i just feel it was very half-baked. another thing i would have loved to have seen were more suit options upgrade options. for the first half of the game you're in your prisoner jumpsuit with bare minimum health and storage space. then later on you get a tactical environmental suit with upgraded health and access to all your storage slots. i feel a sort of intermediary suit would have been good, like maybe a leftover guard's uniform or something. narratively, callisto protocol is very close to dead space, and a lot of ambiguity is left to form for the first half of the game, before it really begins to make sense and explain itself. the latter half of the game gets really good though, and i thoroughly enjoy some of the narrative elements and story points that the writers implemented, especially when it comes to jacob's involvement in the whole situation. now onto what i didn't really like, the big part of this section namely being the enemy variety. you have your basic slasher-grunt type enemies, with the only variant of them being a fatter one that has more health. you've got other enemies, like ones that sneak around with camo and try to ambush you, ones that explode when they get close, ones that spit at you, etc. all fine. but unfortunately there just isn't a whole ton of variety in threats. almost all enemies just run at you and start swinging, and the ones that do have ranged attacks can be turned into basic slashers by blowing their heads off, at which they'll engage you in melee combat. there's no enemies that force you to use guns yes, including the aforementioned exploding enemies. your grp module can deal with them , no enemies that are actually a hazard to engage in melee combat with assuming you know what you're doing , and no enemies that really made me go oh fuck , besides maybe the security bots, of which you only encounter once or twice throughout the entire game. this goes for the bosses too. the final boss is fine in a general sense, and actually got me moving. but unfortunately, like every enemy, his main melee attacks could just be sidestepped. as for the scare factor of callisto protocol, it really just isn't scary, at least in my opinion. i fear the developers leaned on the loud noise scary trope in horror, and while the atmosphere is sort of unnerving, it was let down by the fact i could expect to see a loud noise or something kinda creepy pop up on my screen. i think probably the only time i actually got sort of scared unnerved was during the final boss spoiler when ferris is giving you a monologue in the tower and starts to mutate and transform suddenly spoiler . i also feel callisto protocol suffers from another problem dead space had turning the player into an errand boy. you'll always have someone giving you a go here , do this , or find this order, where it feels jacob is just sort of a drone and can't figure out what to do without instructions. overall? certainly not goty material by any stretch of the imagination, but definitely not as bad as many people say it is. i welcome anyone to give it a try during a sale, or if you're just that certain this is the game for you.

review_text:
I've only just scratched the surface of what this game has to offer, but I can give it a thumbs up reccomendation without hesitation or doubt already.

What an experience!

Comparing it to Left 4 Dead or Back 4 Blood are not comparisons without merit, but being VR, the immersion is brought to a whole new level.
And the VR aspect is done extraordinarily well, and in a fashion that will suit just about every VR user!

For example, when it comes to motion, you can use teleport movement ala Half Life Alyx, or you can use regular movement via the toggles. Both have their drawbacks and positives, both suit different players.

The firearm handling is fantastic for a game like this, and again, is designed to suit all players.
You can use your off hand to steady a weapon, even one handed weapons such as pistols, or duel wield pistols, or use consumables ect.
Weapons have weight, recoil is noticeable and reloading has been handled perfectly. There are two settings, manual and easy.
Easy is where, to reload you just bring bring your firearm to the ammo on your rig and bam, magically reload your weapon - in the same vein as a lot of wave shooters.
Or you can manually reload your firearm - eject the magazine, push in a new one, rack the slide ect. As a bonus for taking the harder route and extra steps of manual, you gain a 35% damage increase to balance it out against easy reloading, which is just fantastic and opens the game to everyone.
Again, with weapon storage, you can choose to have holsters like in Saints and Sinners, or you can go for a traditional gaming weapon select wheel.

TLDR: The devs have really taken the time to make After the Fall as approachable as possible for every type of VR gamer, whether they come from Pavlov, Half-Life, Saints and Sinners or obscure wave defence games.
Firearms are fun to use, they have weight, oomph, recoil and can be operated realistically or not.

Graphics are pretty nice! If it was a PC title, not so much, but in VR they look fantastic and are very atmospheric. 

There are a large number of unlocks, a hub area, you can play solo with bots or group up with friends or strangers to tackle different difficulties or even game modes.

I don't (yet) have the playtime to declare this a must play title for VR gamers, but I'm close to doing so.

review_text:
Note on playtime: I play the game outside of Steam, so it hasn't been logging my hours.

The game can certainly be fun at times, and just simply playing from start to end I don't have a lot of huge complaints.  Being FTP, it's obviously got a lot of high end content locked behind paywalls, but it's possible to get all of it without spending a dime through in game grinding and trading of some sort or another, however this does take an extreme amount of time (which I can't really fault them for being it's their only income).

That said, the reasons I don't recommend this game are as follows (these obviously contribute to my opinion.  Not everyone would give these the same weight, or maybe even consider them as actually being negatives.  But they are to me):

1) Bugs.  There are quite a few of them.  Game breaking ones are rare to encounter, but ones that cause a level of frustration are a bit more common.  Even some new content doesn't even work correctly out of the box in their very primary function (which you would have thought had been thoroughly tested).  But that's not really the worst part of it... it's the fact that many of them are allowed to persist.  Months go by, sometimes years without a fix.  And I get that this happens with every game to some extent, but of the ones I've played, this one is worse than others (not saying it is the worst, just bad enough to be worth pointing out).  There are even entire zones of content that haven't worked right since their release 7 years ago.  No one bothers with these areas anymore because of it.  And the responses to these things?  "We'll fix it when we have the time" or "We don't have anyone left working here that knows that section of code".  They're too focused on releasing new content (cause that's their money earner).

2) End game provides no challenge and isn't very fun or engaging.  Putting aside the fact that you can hit max level with ease (by the time you're half way through the story content), once you're there and take some time to level up your gear, there's nothing left that provides much of a challenge.  The only things preventing you from soloing it all (including team focused content) are via spreading things out so you literally couldn't cover everything by yourself, or by introducing cheap gimmicks that gate your progression (boss is down to half health... activate the immunity which can only be disabled via these other means).  This didn't used to be the case.  Back in 2012-2013 when I first used to play, none of this was possible and you actually had to work with a team of people to take down bosses.  Power creep, though, has come a long way, while all the content in the game (including newly released stuff) stays at the same difficulty.  So, again, while it's fun to to play up through, that's where it ends.  After that, it holds no challenge, nothing to keep you engaged.  You just park, buff up, fire, 2 seconds later watch fireworks (and I'm not actually exaggerating... most content can die in 1-2 firing salvos and there are some builds and weapons that hit unlimited targets for full damage in a firing cone in front of you, and there are abilities to help pull them all into a single group for your ease of doing this).  It takes longer vs bosses, but the concept is still the same.

3) To go with 2, there's no real separation of content for those just reaching max level and those that have been leveling up their gear for awhile and thus are really powerful in comparison.  The more powerful player can freely enter shared content with lower powered players, and then can run around and kill everything in seconds.  Often times the lower powered players don't even have time to reach the enemies to fire at them and thus are considered as having not contributed and will get no/reduced rewards, or even "afk" penalties.  While some content does have more advanced difficulty instances for these more powerful players, they're not obligated to use them, and not all content has these.

Technically, the game was able to be brought to a normal playable state. RTX is not badly implemented. But unfortunately, The Calisto Protocol is a creative failure. There was a real chance to create a new franchise. There was both budget and time. But it turned out to be just a passable game, which was remembered only because it was first added to PS Plus and then distributed in the Epic Store. 
6/10

review_text:
I love the metroid-vania style of game, and I am a big fan of souls-like style games as well.

Unfortunately this game is not it. I understand that this game was meant to be punishing, but more then the game being punishing, it just feels bad to play. The combat is slow on clunky. Your swings are attacks are not only slow, even with a "faster" weapon, the attack animation locks you in place for a few frames before and after your swing. This makes it so you will be unable to use your dodge for longer periods of time to let the enemies just hit you. The timing of your attacks and slows take a bit of time to initiate, slightly delaying everything you try to do and messing up your timing. A huge example of when you try to do an attack while in the air. It does not trigger until you are already back on the ground. As much as I would like to call this an oversight that be patched, it is an intended feature - based on an item that locks you in place in the air for an attack. 

Don't get me wrong, you could just buy a bunch of magic rods and spam cast your way through some areas, or even just ignore a lot of the enemies all together, and that is another problem I have. There is no incentive to kill anything. You are punished, whether you mess up or not, the combat is slow and feels terrible, the hit boxes are inconsistent - at times hitting you even in your dodge, the dodge is short, slow and inconsistent, and there is no reason to really kill most of the enemies.

There are much better games to play in these genres, so I cannot recommend this one.

6/18/25 Revising again since there have been many changes in the last 8 or more months. The adrenaline system is marginally better than the boost system. I personally haven't noticed a big difference in how points or combos work. I dislike that customization is now hidden behind doing challenges. Wall-running seems less consistent after 1.0 and the ground-sliding system that was introduced was swiftly castrated by 1.0 after being combined with the slant-sliding system; the physics-based, one-system sliding is now extremely unreliable for clearing ground gaps, since the timeframe for a good slide is so small now that you'll almost always just hit your head on the top of the obstacle and ruin your combo. Also after 1.0, quite bizarrely you'll often do a sort of double roll when landing instead of one smooth roll, by jumping and then rolling midair, and rolling again on-ground. There is now a visible force field around off-map areas - I feel this would work better and not detract from the scenery so much if it were more of a proximity-based visual, rather than being constantly active. Still not enough pigeon or hanging tricks, and I feel cat-hang shimmying side to side should be faster.

Not currently recommending because of the currently unreliable mechanics and excessive catering to advanced players, as well as performance. Though I admit I have a potato, the ideal is that it can run on such as well. More specifically, 8GB RAM.

20 hours and have never completed a full lap without going off track the slightest or crashing.  I Have set no lap times on any tracks but have tried most of them several times.  After many hours thinking I'd get the feel for the horrible controls.... never happened.  You think you got it.. then the game does something unexpected and now for some reason you can no longer make a turn, and have to figure out why....  after about 4 of those relearning issues...  I give up.   Probably the worst control setup for any racing game I've ever played.  Plus even though the Unreal engine makes it look pretty.... even in first person or the camera mode, it never feels like you are there.  Something big is missing from the physics, and it makes you feel like you are racing a balloon instead of an MX bike.  Very floaty physics.  You'll also find you magically move in mid air at times  when another rider gets close. ****More Recent Update****
Can't play this game any more because I don't have the budget for controllers. It's fun, but the random falls drive me insane. The bulldozer AI are annoying as well. Nothing like getting plowed on the holeshot and then falling/getting plowed down 14 times in a race that you just won by 11+ seconds in the first moto. 



***Update***
After playing for awhile, the game isn't as bad as I originally thought. The jumps do seem to be bigger and harder to clear (at least on 250 four strokes, haven't tried 450 yet). It seems the handling could be improved because there isn't a clear area where you might crash. It feels like once you hit that value, you crash not matter what you try. The whips and scrubs are atrocious. The AI is harder as is the whole game. In MXGP 3, I could give a 30 second lead and win a 5 lap race with a decent lead. I don't see that happening in this game for awhile. I'll leave the recommendation as a no, but only because there's not enough new stuff to merit paying the current price. And Matterly Basin is missing...I thought that would be included since it was the Des Nations track last year.

**Original Review Below**


My frustration level has gone through the roof with this game. I was able to get the stuttering to end by turning off anti-aliasing and v-sync...and lowering my settings. This despite an i7 and 8GB 1070...not a huge deal though, but annoying. 

The gameplay is frustrating. I don't like to play with rewind, but I feel I have to in this game to at least have a fair advantage. The AI love to bank off of you in turns. It's also frustrating to nearly rear-end an oppenent in several turns, finally pass them, and then get pushed way wide while a line of AI riders pass you. And then that 250 that's getting pulled in the straights magically has 100hp and just does burn outs and whips you sideways in a turn for no reason. I tested the AI BS factor and found that when I went to push one off the side of a jump, it magically hit a benner, flew back into me and I ended up booted off the track while it kept on its merry way. 

The bike physics seem to be a step in the wrong direction. There's no traction on certain tracks with the bike. The throttle sensitivy seems to be like a lot of car racers; too high for a controller. The same rings true with brakes and you can only adjust by "modular" or "aggressive". Whips feel heavy and do not have a good flow. Scrubs do seem to help a little more, but the 3rd person animation is terrible. These aren't a big deal, but don't tout them if you haven't fixed them.  And while I do appreciate that you can't overjump and case the crap out of things without penalty, I do feel there are certain moments that someone would not wreck in real-life. Slowed down and maybe a sore back, sure, but not a huge wipe-out. And I'm critical because Milestone kept going on about realism in their marketing. 

I feel like I've purchased MX vs ATV All Out for a second time this year; high hopes, big disappointment.

I have played this game multiple times on different consoles, and I have to say - it has withstood the test of time.

Back when I was in 7th grade, i remember watching a schoolmate play this game during a party and was already hooked on the aesthetic and setting, but beyond that - the game is addictive for good reason.

The story is flawed, as many have pointed out, but Bioshock outshines its own shortcomings with relevant commentary, the human condition, and some of the best voice acting in gaming.
As far as gameplay goes, it is lovely to explore the city of Rapture, and managing resources while negotiating tricky, fast-paced combat with a massive amount of different methods is addicting as all hell. Different playthroughs are encouraged to try everything out, but the best way to play is to mix and match on the fly.
The art direction is fantastic, and the developers have created something truly special that pulls you into this unique world and immerses you in its mystery and grotesque appeal.

The controls are clunky and the audio has not aged well, but in spite of the rough edges, playing for a little bit will allow you to find your legs and enjoy a gaming classic.

8.5/10
Bioshock is an Outstandingly Great game.
Even when an ocean of newer titles buries it under leagues of content, it persists as an immortal relic; an accomplishment to creation and a delight for the curious and the free spirited alike.

review_text:
I know it can be hard for developers to digest negative reviews, so I'll try to make this as constructive as possible. 

There is a game-breaking softlock issue in Act 5. This isn't a 'bug'. This softlock is a symptom of the games design. It isn't a weird edge-case and you don't need to think outside of the box to make it happen. Lots and lots of people continue to complain about this gigantic issue that literally breaks your game and stops it in it's tracks. I will explain it in detail: [spoiler] Throughout the game, a parasite that is attached to you regularly drains your health at intervals. You are allowed to refill your health consumable ONCE per health station. In Act 5, you have to fight a boss which essentially consists of three rounds of combat with the same enemy that changes and adapts each time. Prior to this fight, you get to restock your health consumable. So you do the fight and unless this is your second time playing or you're somehow extremely good at this game, you've probably used up your health consumables.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]When you leave the area, the parasite decides it's going to hurt you again. Unlucky players will die here - and will be stuck with no option but to restart the act. But this isn't the 'softlock'. If you manage to survive this cinematic which hurts you (which is a TERRIBLE idea), you become unable to use your hands due to the parasite. To get through the next area, you need to use a device which temporarily destroys the parasite around your hand. This is a gameplay mechanism that is required in order to continue.[/spoiler] 


Now, the softlock: [spoiler]If you beat the boss in Act 5, survived the little cinematic where the parasite hurts you and made it to the hand cruncher AND you only have one bar of health left... you literally cannot finish Scorn. The hand cruncher - the device which is REQUIRED for gameplay progression - hurts you every time you use it. It then hurts you for a set period of seconds afterwards and then the parasite grows back. I couldn't even make it through the door. The nearest health station is beyond a puzzle you must solve - but with one bar of health, you don't have any time to complete the puzzle. You die.[/spoiler]


For those who don't want spoilers / tl;dr - Most players will become locked in Act 5 due to low health and not being able to heal.

Let me be clear: restarting the act isn't a valid fix for this problem. [b]Developers, hear me. You are charging money for this product. It is broken. You need to fix this gigantic problem.[/b] Scorn has lots of problems - and they mostly stem from the unforgiving nature of it's health system (for example: why can't we use health stations repeatedly? It's not a combat centric game. This is a walking puzzle sim.)

Other things that disappointed me:
- The sound would stop working every time the main menu was opened and would only come back when quitting and reloading.

- Zero context is given in regard to the story because there isn't one. Maybe we're supposed to figure it out ourselves, or use our imagination to fill in the blanks, but the problem is it's all blanks. There is no substance, no real plot and no narrative. The world just [i]is[/i]. You are just there doing things [i]because.[/i] The ending [spoiler]is disappointing and explains nothing.[/spoiler]


- Combat is awful and unforgiving. You can't round a corner quickly in Scorn, yet there are enemies that will literally charge at you. Other enemies can spit at you and it's almost like hitscan. There's lots of dissonance in this design. 

- Minimal world cues. I ran around for a long time, getting lost. Maybe that was the intention but it wasn't fun.

It's hard to consume negative reviews - I get it. Scorn has some great scenery, amazing sound design and is overall an intriguing and evocative experience. As a developer myself, I feel like I could make a million suggestions which would elevate it, but the softlock takes the cake. 

This game is broken. You are selling a product with a defect.

EDIT:

Wow this is exploding. I love Dark Souls. Look at my history - I played all three games this year. I can't believe how many people are getting bent out of shape over a game review. I bet you all pre-order your games, don't you? I touched a nerve because I pointed out a problem. Really? They took your money for this, you know. Stop making excuses for the developer.

SCORN was interesting and fun - but I stand by my point. SCORN has a defect. It is broken. Logical gameplay scenarios that lead to dead-ends are called softlocks; and I simply refuse to believe that "just restart the stage bro" is the solution to the softlock I mentioned. For a game about building an immersive world and experience, that's just *terrible*. It's lazy. I will die on this hill. 

People who are saying "git gud" obviously didn't read my review properly. It's not about being 'good enough' to avoid the lock. That is such a dumb, lazy, knee-jerk response. [b]Developers and designers should never put their faith in the skill of a player to avoid a softlock -- that's a really bad design philosophy. "This player sucks, so they can just get stuck in limbo forever and never complete our game." Rubbish. [/b]

They should adequately design gameplay and sequences to ensure players don't fall into these traps. The presence of this softlock suggests inadequate testing and/or response to feedback during testing.

review_text:
Now before you pull out your pitchforks and torches.  It's not a bad game by any stretch,  but it lacks in a lot of areas compared to it's roots.  The gameplay loop is solid enough and it's fun.  In fact, it has improved over some aspects of the Jet Set franchise, like the boost mechanic, the tagging system, the multiple items you can use like skateboards and bikes.  It feels smooth and responsive compared to its predecessors.  


Bomb Rush Cyberfunk has a serviceable story, but it feels like it skirts around its themes rather than fully embracing them. In contrast, the Jet Set series is unapologetically rooted in its punk identity. You could argue that Jet Set’s story isn’t particularly strong, and its gameplay feels outdated by modern standards, but its levels, music, and overall aesthetic work together to convey its message loud and clear. It doesn’t just reference rebellion—it embodies it, making its themes feel more integral to the experience. 

BRCF’s music is kind of lackluster and not as diverse as I had hoped. Some tracks are okay, while others feel flat and uninteresting—so much so that I often turn it off and listen to my own collection instead.

I have to say, the Hideki Naganuma tracks sound phoned in and overly gamified. While I'm not trying say that game music isn’t real music or that Hideki Naganuma isn’t a great artist—he absolutely is. However, these particular tracks don’t stand well on their own, and he’s certainly made better work in the past.

It’s not music I’d want to blast in my car; it’s more suited for background listening while working on a project. The Jet Set Radio series soundtracks, on the other hand, are far more diverse and hold up well on their own—featuring punk, garage rock, house, drum and bass, hip-hop, hard rock, and more

  
In conclusion, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a very solid game that successfully captures the spirit of classic skating and graffiti titles with its vibrant aesthetic, energetic soundtrack, and fluid movement. However, while it excels in style and nostalgia, it falls short in certain areas of execution, such as level design, mission variety, or depth of mechanics. Despite these flaws, it remains an enjoyable experience for fans of the genre and those looking for a stylish, fast-paced urban adventure

review_text:
It's very cryptic. There's no actual tutorial. As many have said here, villagers keep dying from starvation, and you, the player are left to wonder what's even happening. I've now sunk almost a 100 hours into the game and I still don't understand the food mechanics completely.

Here's a more in depth example of maybe the biggest downfall of the game:

There is a *complete lack of proper notifications* and the visuals are hard to understand.

There's no notification, for example, for when an enemy is within your village, attacking your villagers, or even destroying your buildings. Then you suddenly get notified that 5 villagers died almost in an instant, and your screen shakes as a few buildings collapse, due to them having been taking damage from an enemy mob for the last minute or so, which you didn't know was happening. You can't for example distinguish the screen shake effect of a meteor hit, which are very common, and a building collapsing. Ok, well now you at least know the enemy is within your village, right? Good thing you have a grab tool and banish spell that you can use to move unwanted enemies elsewhere, right? Well, that would be the case, if you could distinguish what's even happening on your screen. There's like 40 villagers and 30 animals running in every direction with exclamation points or question marks above their heads. Then there's the massive amount of clutter caused by the destroyed buildings, then there's the magic effects, with pixelated fire and purple fizzing, and finally there are the enemies in your base, who either blend in with the panicking villagers, or they hiding behind villager sprites who are attacking the enemies, or then they might hide within the buildings they are attacking. All you would have to do is cast spells at or grab these enemies and your problem would be solved. You might have already fixed what was causing the enemies getting inside your village. Too bad it's nearly impossible to get rid of the enemies inside the village, as you will be completely unable to distinguish anything from this mess. Try to grab that pesky skeleton or zombie child? Nah, here's a random animal or a piece of trash for you. Managed to grab a fire elemental that killed +5 villagers? Well, plenty more will die and buildings will collapse, as you can't distinguish which villagers or buildings the elemental set on fire.

For some reason I'm still a little drawn to this game, I really would have wanted to enjoy it. The idea is great, I think, but the execution has a lot of room for improvement. It's just far too messy, cryptic, and in general, it's not a game that's pleasant to look at. All in all, it just feels tedious to play. I do not recommend buying it, unless it's on sale and less than 5 euros. If you do buy it, get ready to be very frustrated.

review_text:
[strike] Older versions were better.
The game is now a bloom filled mess honestly, combat feels weird in general, most of the time I dont even know what Im shooting at, I just mag dump, wait to regen health then do it again, with the ocasional kick in between.
The game also seems to force you to start every level by going through this parkour section, which is honestly stupid and pointless, and on top of that for me it tends to bug and straight up not spawn the green things that allow you to dash upwards, meaning I cant play the game because I cant pass the arbitrary level put in place by the dev. [/strike]

[h1] Well, the game got updated. [/h1]
(this is gonna be long, I can feel it)
First things first, the game has undoubtebly improved in many areas, which is honestly quite commendable and straight up unexpected after the clusterfuck that were the two last updates (mainly the first one). As someone who tested this game way back in 2020, bought the game a while after, refunded it, then bought it again only to still be disappointed, I gotta say that this improvement is quite reassuring.
However, there are still a few things bugging me that make me lean more towards a not-recommended rather than a positive review, even though I would like to give it a neutral rating.

[h1] Guess I'll start off talking about what has been, in my opinion, improved: [/h1]

-Movement: Like seriously, movement was pretty good before, then it got annihilated with the Excessive update, and now its good again. It feels responsive and overall way more fun than the old movement we had.

-Gun models: They look pretty rad imo, and the inspect animations are just the icing on the cake (even if the lack of sounds when inspecting most guns is a bit of a bummer). Some of them as also still missing a secondary fire mode, which is a shame since it is one of this games most recognizable gunplay elements. But all in all, the guns feel good (At least the ones I was able to test, we'll get to that in a bit). I would also like to add that some reloads feel extremely long for a fast paced game like this, which breaks the flow of combat (this is only true for some weapons, like the heavy machinegun)
(+1 for keeping the workbench from the test branch btw, I really liked that addition.)

-Levels: They feature lootable containers, while I'm not a huge fan of the roguelite direction this game seems to be heading towards I do like having more stuff to do in the levels, the addition of vaults with workbenches and chests is also rather nice. Also that stupid parkour section at the start of every run is now gone, good riddance.

-Difficulty selector: It just looks cool man, love the little eye, such a handsome fella.

[h1] Now, for the negatives... [/h1]

-The door event: It's still there, unchanged from the last update as far as I can tell. I miss seeing the orange door, barreling towards it and simply going to the next level, because now you gotta do this discount Risk of Rain 2 event were you jump around like a madman trying to kill enough enemies to unlock the door and pass to the next level. It works for ROR2, it doesn't here. I get that some people may like it but an option to play using the legacy door system would be much appreciated.

Ingame Economy: It's really bad. You need to grind for so fucking long to unlock ONE extra gun for your character, and of course only for the duration of the run. Meaning that if you dont wanna get screwed by the game's ever increasing difficulty (another trait taken straight from ROR2) then I hope you like shooting that starter pistol because you'll be seeing it for a while, because a RANDOM GUN costs 900 crystals, and that takes a while to obtain, especially if you are planning on upgrading one of your guns or maybe getting a tactical/lethal equipment (Since you dont get ANYTHING by default, you really only have your pistol). Basically you get very little money and shit is too expensive, and getting new guns for your character is a chore and forces you to increase the threat level by farming relentlessly)

-Upgrade system / Roguelite focus: So, you wanted to hop in a game, shoot some baddies in an arena then hop off? Cool, there's like one unfinished arena and you get no reward for playing in it as far as I've seen. No money, no cards, no vines, nothing. If you want to actually get new loadouts and upgrades you are FORCED to play the roguelite mode (aka FPS ROR2 wannabe), which is not my cup of tea in this case (And I'm a huge fan of ROR2).
Instead of a casual shooter that you can quickly boot up to de-stress and quit when you feel like it, you're now stuck in this run that might take a good while to end. If you quit at any point you'll just go straight to the lobby and have to start over, so more grinding with the starter pistol.

-""Hidden mechanics"": It would be cool if the game told you about certain stuff straight away instead of making you look for it. Things like "this is where you have to go to select the arena mode", "this is how you obtain cards", "this is how you scan the area around you". As someone that has previously refunded the game, the first hour of the game is the most important thing for a new player since that's when they'll determine whether the game is worth keeping or not. If a player doesnt know how things work 1h into the game the chance of them refunding it only goes up. A few small popups would do this game wonders.

-Enemies/Combat: While most of the enemies are fine from a design perspective, the way they behave is sometimes extremely annoying, especially as the threat level goes up. They are relentless, constantly tailing your ass (that goes for EVERY enemy, even the ranged ones) when you want to regenerate health (which takes ages to start and ruins the combat flow). Seriously, some of these guys randomly hit you when you're going at 100km/h, which stops shield regen and forces you to play super passively again. Like give me some way of regenerating health while in combat, executions, combat rating DMC style, idk, just dont force me to hide or run away for what feels like 20 seconds waiting for my shields to come back. On another note, I personally felt that the enemies became really tanky really fast, so ammo goes down the drain really fast too.

-Unskippable death/revive animations: I know a lot of people have already complained about it, so I'm just adding my voice to that camp. Yeah we dont wanna see the same animation every time we die, and every time we come back to life, so please let us skip it.
An option to skip the upgrade altar would be nice too since we already have it at the base.

-Sex: No sex :(

[h1] Minor nitpicks: [/h1]

-No option to bind 2 keys to the same action, and no option to separate the interact key from the melee key (I use Mouse5 as my main melee key since my Titanfall2 days. But I can't use it here because the interact button ends up being remapped to Mouse5 too and then Im forced to interact using that key, which just feels really weird, like why have them together?)

I am a huge Hakuouki fan and have been for years.  In fact I own Kyoto Winds for both the Vita AND here on Steam, as well as previous titles.  This series is beautifully drawn, voiced and has great characters.  If you love history and the supernatural, this game is the absolute best and one of my favorites.  As someone who loves the bakumatsu/shinsengumi/vampires/demons, I HIGHLY reccomend this game if you are into the otome scene.  

One warning however that isn't explained in the description. In this half of the game your choices will determine the routes you end up on and there is a beginign to the romance story with each romancable option.  Due to how the story is written however, you only start your romance with your man of choice and there won't be a deep connection until you play the second game, Edo Blossoms which takes place in Edo and northern Japan. In this game you can choose which romance option to pick up where you left off in the story and continue on.  I know this format isn't for everyone but please bare in mind that the story is VERY LONG and there are 12 romancable options (plus a forever alone route) which is why the game was broken into parts.  Personally I find it well worth the price tag of two games.

Despite living in the shadow of the superior Dead Space, this is still a good game.  A lot of the negative reviews seem to be about issues that have since been patched.  

The main way that this game differs from Dead Space is in the combat, where Callisto Protocol has more of an emphasis on melee combat, using a dodge and counterstrike mechanic.  There's also a few firearms, but they don't really stand out as being unique in the way that Dead Space's repurposed mining equipment does.     It's fun enough though.

The story is fine, but nothing we haven't really seen before.  The voice acting is good, and the character design and facial animations stand out as being really good.  The graphics are really nice overall, with some really cool environments, but some that are rather generic.  The body horror creatures are pretty good, but not nearly as extreme as Dead Space, and the gore and death scenes are pretty good.

Basically this game's biggest flaw is that better games like it exist.  There is one thing that annoyed me though, and that's the fact that the game's actual ending is in the Final Transmission DLC.  The base game basically hits a cliff hanger in the middle of an action scene, with the DLC immediately picking up from that point for a few extra hours of gameplay.  It probably should have just been included in the base game.

review_text:
First of all, this is a intermediate review and does not represent the full game nor will it be representative for all users - it's a very specific hardware set which I can write this review for, it's not for everyone.

Second of all, Boneworks is for me - together with Half-Life:Alyx - what I would describe as AAA VR title (quality/gameplay-wise). I won't go into detail why, but it will be obvious to everyone when looking at gameplay of it. Everything is physics-based, everything can be touched, there is a "free" way of interacting with stuff, everything has weight, etc. Most other VR titles are what you would call "point and click" compared to fully fledged which is great!

Sadly, playing this on a Pimax 5K Super and Index Controllers comes with a lot of caveats for this game (which weren't a problem in Boneworks):
- Native Pimax via SteamVR won't even load the menu (it just blackscreens)
- The work around does sort of work, but I didn't remember my Pimax to be that bad in blacks (might be a Pimax XR thing, which is necessary to play at all)
- The work around (and sort of without it as well as far as I've heard) requires Index Controller to Oculus Controller emulation. Those don't have 5 fingers, not even speaking about spatial tracking of them and thus feels very digital compared to an "analog" experience with native Index Controllers.

What I have seen so far apart from my mostly hardware issues is that the physics feel a bit clunkier (mostly talking about hitting stuff and clipping into them; although there were also cases which felt A LOT better than Boneworks), can't really pin-point what it is tbh, but it's not a big deal with what this game seems to offer. Big respects to making VR more inclusive with the Quest-support but since this also requires a common base for input, this seems to hurt the PC version at least a bit.

It really hurts after those fun times in Boneworks and all the love I put forwards to Bonelab to not recommend this. But as said, this isn't the experience for everyone, but Pimax and Index and should not represent the general state of the game which is still years ahead of most other VR games, it's a league of its own. This is a mixed review:

The game's premise, mechanics, graphics, resource management, etc are all fantastic, and build the premise for a great game.

Unfortunately, as you get further into the game, is when the bugs become apparent, and you run into severe difficulty spikes.  For example, if you try to clear the corruption, you'll eventually get to the point having a building on a tile right next to corruption may not clear it (or clear it very slowly).  You'll also be able to handle almost everything the game throws at you, until suddenly the game decides to 4x the spawn rate and health of every enemy.  Maybe I'm playing the game wrong, and you're not supposed to push out?  Reading other reviews, I guess I'm supposed to migrate at some point, however it's difficult to know when, given the difficulty suddenly spiking beyond control.

Then comes the bugs.  Early game, you'll be able to build lots of things each day.  As your village grows, you get more builders, miners, etc, you begin to accomplish significantly less each day.  For example, even with plenty of resources, including resources nearby, top-tier roads, I'm still only able to build about 3 buildings per day.  Or I might have 20 waymakers (road builders), but no roads seem to be built for days on end.  Don't get me started on rations, I can't seem to get my cooks to make them ever.

Regardless, don't pass this one up.  And for goodness sake, avoid FHM2 or FHM3 like the plaugue.  This game won't do stupid trades and it will give you some real immersion beause, as I said, the AI is good and difficult to beat.

Enjoy!

(I got most of my time on Xbox) New Genesis has gotten far better since it first released. After a while you were mostly doing dailies but there is actually plenty of story content, a variety of bosses to fight, and more linear quests are now available to play too. NGS to me has always been a step above PSO2 in terms of gameplay to me with everything feeling just faster and more fluid, and the environments in the game are great like South Aelio. The music is really great because it's a Sega game, especially boss themes, they never get old no matter how much you hear them. There's plenty more stuff worth consistently playing NGS for now, but one thing that I will note is that with FUN missing you generally get less things for free (less personal shop passes), but SG rates are much more generous and how much everything costs far cheaper than it used to cost. 800 just for a chance to get story character outfits was just far too much and 500 is more fair. Mission Passes are down to 100 as well which is frankly insane.

Playing for the first time and being not overwhelmed by an MMO immediately was great. NGS' story is only now getting really impactful too, but PSO2's story is highs throughout even in Episode 4 with plenty of likeable characters and interactions between them all. Episode 1 made me cry at the end which I wasn't expecting at all. PSO2 was never free of problems though. When you got done it basically became what NGS was, just doing dailies, wasting time at the Casino, waiting for a currently available UQ, or messing up an economy, maybe dying to Phaleg, but I can't say that wasn't fun even in NGS' case because the game just felt good. PSO2 was never free of problems though like Mags sucked I hated them and they are actually so simple in PSO and don't require constant feeding to work, and gathering in PSO2 was an awful lot of time wasting just for a minor buff or XP boosts you had an abundance of regular XP boosts anyway. I wish they added more to the Casino.

Overall: Both games are really good times.

review_text:
Captain's Log, Stardate 101360.85

I have traversed the galaxies of Star Trek Online for a lot longer than the standard five year mission. I was there for the inception of the digital universe of Star Trek Online since its early days under the Perpetual banner. This was long before the cosmic shift when the Cryptic Federation took command, and before the Perfect World Empire transformed it into what can best be described as a "profit-driven space station."

During my virtual voyages, I've sporadically docked with the game to savour the infrequent narrative content. I've never fully committed to the social atmospheres of the online quadrant, nor have I obsessed over acquiring the shiniest tools in the fleet. My true satisfaction? Embodying the quintessential Starfleet captain. Navigating my own ship, participating in narrative journeys inspired by a beloved galaxy - that was the essence of it all. And yet, the game's design and recurring "financial incentives" often made me wonder if, somewhere in a corner of the Alpha Quadrant, a group of enterprising Ferengi are the ones cooking up more schemes to acquire wealth from its players.

One can't help but notice the wear and tear on the game's interfaces and systems. Each subsequent log-in introduces yet another nebulous task designed to impede my course or tempt me into depleting my stash of gold-pressed latinum. At times, it mirrors a mobile game with baffling overpriced "microtransactions."

While many in the galaxy of 2023 continue to engage with it, mainly due to the scarcity of alternatives, whispers among the fandom suggest an appetite for a more contemporary rendition of this digital adventure. But, in the unpredictable world of today's gaming nebula, can anything truly surpass our celestial expectations?

Other spacefarers have echoed my sentiments in their transmissions: the pleasure of navigating this Star Trek realm persists, but the antiquated systems, astronomical pricing for simple amenities, and incessant obstacles can make the journey feel more like a chore. The initial thrill of warp speed soon fades, and one can't help but grapple with the realisation that the cost of enjoyment may eventually exceed one's comfort zone.

End of log.

review_text:
I do not recommend this game except for die-hard fans of the series, and they shouldn't play the game without a walkthrough.  Most of the same problems with Yakuza 4 are in this game, so read that review for those things.  I played all the way through it on Normal difficulty.

However, they introduced new problems with this game, mostly linked to switching characters.  First, DO NOT get any of the locker keys with Haruka.  During the playthrough, you can't move things from her item box to other character AT ALL.  For instance, the Chunk of Ash needed to make a specific weapon - if you get it with Haruka, kiss it goodbye, because you can't get it any other way.

Second, the minigames cheat like hell this time, worse that Yakuza 4.  Sometimes your phone will tell you you have bad luck - believe it.  Sometimes it tells you you'll have good luck - DO NOT BELIEVE IT.  I like playing the Koi Koi card game, and on a "good luck" day, I got my ass handed to me and had to reload (and I play well enough to be able to score 9 platinum plates in a row, over 13000 points worth).  If you're going for 100% completion, you'll need over 20 million yen, because several of the weapons you need to craft are 800k - 1000k in price.  You'll need to gamble.  Save before gambling.

Fishing is basically impossible without a FAQ.  Getting the Maguro and Squid (not bait) for the weapons required a Google search.  Trying to do it on your own is not guaranteed, because you can get several types of fish and junk items with the same bait in the same range depending on day or night - bait costs add up, and selling fish doesn't make enough to buy more bait unless you catch a huge fish like a marlin or coelacanth.

The billiards and dart games get too hard at the advanced level, even with good dart parts.  It was better in Yakuza 0 where you got the best darts by buying them at the pawn shop, and when the game didn't mess with your aim in billiards - in short, it cheats a LOT.  And forget air hockey on the hard level - the only way to score is with heat shots, and the game loves to make you to chuck your puck in your own goal for no reason.

No pachinko or slots for the Remastered version is unfair, considering the PlayStation version still has it, and they have other gambling games like poker, blackjack, roulette, etc.

Winning at the gambling tables is more of a risk than the previous game, so keep those win items handy, and use them appropriately to win the most money.  The lack of save points make it a long run back to the casino, and you get in fights along the way, which is irritating considering the Kiwami 1 and 2 games allowed you to save anywhere.

But the worst thing about this game, by far and away, is the Coliseum.  You have to get to around 200 rank points just to break the top 10, and you only get 3 points a match (3 fights per tournament, 1 point per win).  It takes forever, but worse than that, once you get there, you get beaten to a pulp.  I'm not a young gamer - I'm good at this game, but even I have endurance limits.  When you break the top 10, the #1 guy cheats ALL THE TIME.  How?  Mohammed Ali style - when you start beating on him and gaining heat, he grabs you, and half your heat disappears before your pounding the A button will make him let go.  He does this EVERY time you gain heat.  My only match with him went around 10 - 15 minutes on him alone, not even counting the first two hard fights.  I DAMAGED my wrist and arm because I was constantly pounding the A keep to stop him from throwing me.  That's never happened to me before, ever.  My arm was so hot I couldn't keep it up.  He finally destroyed me, and that's the last time I'll ever play the Coliseum in Yakuza 5 again - probably the last time I'll ever play the game, period.  I love the story and the general mechanics, but they made it far too hard on Normal difficulty.  It was impossible for me to win, with an inventory full of Stamiman Sparks (full heal, full heat).  That should never have happened, especially with Saejima.  Oh, and you can't get any of the missable items at the Coliseum (nor levels to get Spirit Orbs), so it's not really worth it except for 100% completion.

But it did, and it happened again with the 2-on-1 fight in the Dojo with the baseball guy - they literally would not let me get a single hit in.  Without Kiryu's reversals and counterattacks, I just got beat to hell.  Saejima was the easiest to win with, and Kiryu was easy enough, but with the baseball guy it was impossible.  I gave up on Akiyama because of what happened with the baseball guy.

The Amon fight was even worst than the Coliseum.  I got through the first three all right, but with Kiryu, I got wiped.  Not only did it grab me all the time, draining all my heat, but I couldn't grab him back, EVER.  That's cheating.  Worse, when I switched to my no-break katana, I could not hit him without heat actions.  I managed to get the guy down to green, and it uncorked everything it had, blocking everything I did, unable to grab, it hit me with unblockables to the legs, and finished doing two of the main character's super moves BACK TO BACK.  I didn't stand a chance at that point.  Remember, this is supposed to be NORMAL mode.

No, you don't have to fight those battles.  I finished the game because I'd had enough of the AI cheating - the final story fight was easier by far, and I didn't even use any items to win it.  That's what made me angry.  The game shouldn't be this hard at Normal level, and it's not fun.  The inability to transfer items is not fun.  The game cheating at the minigames is not fun.  Yakuza 0, K1, K2 were fun, they didn't cheat so much.  Once you got all the skills, you were expected to maul everything in Normal mode.  Not in this game.

One last thing:  If you have no rhythm, and you hate games like Dance Dance Revolution and Guitar Hero, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.  Haruka's story is all about getting into dance battles, and the interface sucks.  Not only are button presses needed to be done in time with the music, you have to use the D-pad to chose which line you need to press the buttons on (there's 4 of them).  It's actually far worse than the usual too-fast karaoke minigame.  I don't do well with DDR-type games, but I barely made it through.  There is an Amon dance battle near the end - I tried it, it was the hard version of Haruka's initial song (twice as many buttons to mash), and after three unsuccessful tries, I gave up.  It's too hard for me, just like the karaoke stuff.  I never get 100% because of this stuff, and I hate that it's so hard, especially since you MUST succeed at these to advance the storyline.  I only managed it because the story mission difficulty remains at medium throughout.  It's quite generous considering how many presses I missed.  Too bad the Amon fight couldn't have been like that.  Poor QA in not getting things level for Normal mode.

So, don't play this unless you're a fan of the story and you're willing to skip 100% completion.  Play at your own risk.  It took two days for my arm to recover, and that was only playing games with my other hand (I'm lucky I use my mouse left-handed).  Stay away from the Coliseum, it's broken.  Save before doing the Coliseum, Amon or the Dojo fights, or you may burn all your items and still lose.  Same with the gambling.  If it's going to cheat, you might as well cheat by saving early and often.  If you have rhythm problems, take breaks between dance battles.  Save before every one.  Good luck, you'll need it if you play this game.

review_text: Really good. Glad to see the dev really branch out this time and probably reach a larger audience with options for casual and hardcore players alike. I think I own all of the games this guy has made unless there was something before WTTG. But this is the first one I'm actually playing for more than five minutes before deciding I'd rather not poop my pants and just go watch a YouTuber play instead. You are still very much in danger, but (without spoiling the mechanics I believe I have down so far) each death seems fair and explainable, which in turn makes you feel like you are learning how to combat your enemies instead of just getting frustrated. (Except for the one time I got sniped in the bedroom even though there was absolutely no angle to make such a shot, I think I know why, but I'm still going to keep this mechanic spoiler free). The main goal of the game, which others have already pointed out is like Observation Duty, is also much more interesting and fun to me then looking for hidden keys on websites in my opinion. Overall I think it's great, I'm glad to see this dev is still making games, I thought the final game from Reflect was going to be Rides with Strangers, so either I was mistaken, or he has decided to continue on developing. I sincerely hope that future games after this also continue the same trend of appealing to all horror players instead of the hardest of the hardcore. Scrutinized showed a step in that direction, and Dead Signal has brought it where it needed to be in order to be accessible to all. Great work Adam, people love your style, myself included, and the world that you have built with everything interconnecting. I think the key, which you must already be well aware of, is that this world feels grounded in reality. There's no ghosts, or wizards, or impossible experiments gone wrong. Each game feels like it could potentially happen to a person who was just in the worst place at the worst time, while being involved with the wrong things. The only thing all these characters lack is the common sense to call the police, but hey, if that was the case there would be no game.
